Almanac

Engineering Handbook

Shiv Vyas · Revision E

Almanac is a personal iOS app that gathers every signal from the devices you already wear and carry (Apple Watch, iPhone, Whoop, Fitbit, a Renpho scale, your bank, your calendar) into one local store, scores your life across nine sectors, and puts a coach called LIFO on top of all of it. This handbook is the single reference for how it is built, why it is built that way, what keeps it fast and cheap, and what it does when things go wrong. It is written to be studied: every chapter ends with a reading order through the code and questions to check yourself against.

Revision E 15 September 2026 iOS 26 · watchOS 26 · Swift 6 Architecture: MVVM Status: TestFlight build 17 Audience: the author

Part one

Foundations

The shape of the system before any screen: how the modules depend on each other, where state lives, how a screen is built, what every screen is built from, and how a person gets through the door.

  • 1. Architecture
  • 2. MVVM and project structure
  • 3. Design system
  • 4. The app shell, accounts and sign-in

Chapter one

1Architecture

Almanac is a local-first iOS app built on one bet: the value is in the join, not the collection. Seven sources of data now feed it, one table keyed by calendar day still receives all of the health signal, and every screen reads from the device before anything touches the network.

This chapter describes the system as it is on 15 September 2026, not the one the first edition planned. Since Revision D the package has grown from three targets to eight, the app has gained a watch, a bank, a second wearable, a calendar, a notes library, a nine-sector life board and a cloud tier for the coach. The architecture survived all of that because three early decisions held: one row per day, a compiler-enforced module graph, and a device that never waits for a server. Where the code and this handbook disagree, the code is right and this handbook is a bug.

1.1System context

Every source reaches the app through one of four doors: Apple Health, a vendor REST API behind a Supabase Edge Function, a system framework on the device itself, or a table in Supabase that the app reads directly over PostgREST. The Apple Watch is now both a source, through Health, and a second screen, through WatchConnectivity. Everything still converges on the local SwiftData store before a single pixel is drawn.

Each source, its door, and where its data lands:

SourceDoorLands inChapter
Apple Watch, iPhone, Renpho scaleHealthKitReader reads every HealthMetric Apple Health holdsDailyMetrics named columns and the extras bag7, 19
Whoop strapOAuth via the whoop-callback bridge, direct REST from the device, tokens in the keychainWhoopRawRecord first, then derived into DailyMetrics, SleepRecord, WorkoutRecord19
FitbitOAuth exchanged server side; fitbit-sync pulls under a refresh lease; the device never holds a Fitbit tokenDailyMetrics through the same arbiter19
Bank accountsPlaid Link in the app, four Edge Functions hold the credentialsMoneyEntry, MoneyAccount, cursor per item on the device11
CalendarsEventKitSource behind a CalendarSource protocolCalendarEvent cache with windowed queries6
Workout catalogRead-only PostgREST client, cached locallyCatalogVideo10
Live sensorsCoreBluetooth heart rate, CoreMotion on the wristWorkoutRecord on save; the readout is never persisted8, 9
YouQuick log, journal, notes, check-insWhichever model owns it, with MetricSource.manual where it competes with a sensoreverywhere

1.2Module map

LifeOSKit is a local Swift package providing compile-time boundaries. The app target contains only features and wiring, laid out per screen as described in Chapter 2. The dependency rules are enforced by the compiler, not by convention: a target that does not declare a dependency cannot import it, and the package manifest is the whole rule book. 

// LifeOSKit/Package.swift
platforms: [.iOS("26.0"), .macOS("26.0"), .watchOS("26.0")],
targets: [
    .target(name: "AppSurfaces"),
    .target(name: "DesignSystem"),
    .target(name: "Persistence"),
    .target(name: "Integrations", dependencies: ["Persistence", "AppSurfaces"]),
    .target(name: "Insights", dependencies: ["Persistence"]),
    .target(name: "Sectors", dependencies: ["Persistence"]),
    .target(name: "Assistant", dependencies: ["Insights", "Persistence"]),
    .target(name: "Motion"),
    // plus one test target per library
]
TargetOwnsDepends onWhy it is its own target
PersistenceEvery @Model class, the stores, pure logic over rows (streaks, goal evaluation, anomaly evaluation), UserScopenothingThe schema must be importable by anything without dragging a network client in with it
DesignSystemTokens, the type scale, spacing, layout metrics and every stateless primitivenothingComponents stay previewable and reusable; it also builds for macOS so tests run without a simulator
AppSurfacesThe wire types shared with the watch and the widgets: SurfaceSnapshot, LiveSessionReadout, WatchWire, WorkoutActivityAttributes, HUDPlacement, SessionRingMathnothingThree processes decode these bytes; a shared target is the only way they cannot drift
MotionRepCounter, a pure rep counter over wrist accelerationnothingRuns on the watch; must not pull SwiftData or networking onto the wrist
IntegrationsWhoop, Fitbit, Apple Health, Plaid, EventKit, Supabase auth and REST, social, profiles, push tokens, notes sync, the live effort maths, the arbiterPersistence, AppSurfacesEvery vendor is contained here; nothing above it knows a vendor exists
InsightsThe coach: tasks, engines, router, context bundle, digest, chat wire, speech endpointing, spend seriesPersistenceIt may read rows and nothing else, which is the privacy boundary as a dependency edge
SectorsThe nine sectors, their scorers, the monthly close, projections, levers, the workout planner and library filterPersistencePure scoring over stored rows; testable with fixture months
AssistantThe calendar tools the on-device model calls, and the context they run inInsights, PersistenceTools are domain logic with a strict read-only rule; they must not reach a network client mid-conversation
The rule that makes the graph worth having Persistence sits below Integrations and must not import it. That is why DailyMetrics.sourcesData stores a raw String rather than a MetricSource: the vocabulary of "who wrote this" lives one tier up, and the row only carries its name. The dependency arrow decided the type.

1.3The DailyMetrics spine

This is still the single most consequential decision in the system. One row per calendar day. Every health source writes into it; every health reader reads from it. The row has grown two bags since the first edition, and both exist to keep that sentence true as the number of sources went from two to four. 

// LifeOSKit/Sources/Persistence/DailyMetrics.swift
@Model
public final class DailyMetrics {
    #Unique<DailyMetrics>([\.date])

    /// Always `Calendar.startOfDay`. Never a timestamp.
    public var date: Date

    public var weightKg: Double?
    public var steps: Int?
    public var sleepMinutes: Int?
    // ... eleven named columns, all optional ...

    /// Everything Apple Health can supply that does not have a column of
    /// its own, as a JSON dictionary keyed by `HealthMetric.rawValue`.
    public var extrasData: Data?

    /// Who wrote each value, as a JSON dictionary keyed by `HealthMetric.rawValue`.
    public var sourcesData: Data?

    public var updatedAt: Date
    public var syncedAt: Date?
}

The named columns came first and are load-bearing: the sector scorers, the Whoop merge and the charts all read them by name. The extras bag is the long tail of Apple Health, more than thirty metrics most people have no data for, stored as [String: Double] so that adding a metric is one enum case and one mapping rather than a schema migration. The sources bag runs parallel to it and records provenance per metric per day.

Both bags decode to an empty dictionary rather than throwing when the bytes are unreadable. A day whose extras cannot be parsed still has its named columns, and losing the screen over the tail would be the worse failure. Both also treat writing nil as removing the key, never as storing a zero, for the reason the whole model is built on: absent and zero are different things, and a false zero is worse than a blank in a health app.

What the single-table choice still buys

  • Trends become a sort, not a multi-source asynchronous join. TodayViewModel.load fetches one bounded window of rows and derives the grid, the streak and today's figures in one pass.
  • The coach queries one table instead of orchestrating four network APIs mid-conversation, which is what makes an on-device model viable and what makes the cloud tier's context bundle small.
  • Offline works by default, because nothing renders from a live network call.
  • Adding a source means writing into the same row through the same arbiter. Fitbit shipped as a second wearable without a new pipeline; it is a loop around one function.
  • The widgets and the watch decode a SurfaceSnapshot that is a projection of one row, so the same steps figure appears on the lock screen, the wrist and the hub without three queries.

MetricsStore is the only way anything writes to the row. Its upsert fetches or creates the day and applies a closure, and it is a merge: fields the closure does not touch are preserved. upsertBatch exists because a save per row turned sixty days into sixty disk transactions on the main actor; a sync loop now makes one.

1.4The arbiter: merge by rank

With one wearable the merge rule was a boolean called fillGapsOnly: Health fills what Whoop left blank. With two straps that rule cannot tell a Whoop value from a typed one, which is exactly the distinction a second wearable forces. The replacement is a rank, and it is a pure function so every branch can be tested without a device, a permission prompt or a store. 

// LifeOSKit/Sources/Integrations/MetricArbiter.swift
public static func resolve(
    metric: HealthMetric,
    existing: Double?, existingSource: MetricSource?,
    incoming: Double?, incomingSource: MetricSource,
    ranking: SourceRanking
) -> (value: Double?, source: MetricSource?) {
    // A source having no reading is not evidence of zero.
    guard let incoming else { return (existing, existingSource) }
    guard existing != nil else { return (incoming, incomingSource) }

    let held = existingSource ?? MetricSource.legacy(for: metric)

    // Greater than or equal, not greater than. Equal rank means the same
    // source syncing again, which must be allowed to correct itself.
    guard ranking.rank(incomingSource, for: metric) >= ranking.rank(held, for: metric) else {
        return (existing, held)
    }
    return (incoming, incomingSource)
}

The ranks are decided per metric, because a source that is the authority on one number is a fallback on another:

RankWhoWhen
4manualAlways. A figure a person typed is never overwritten by a background sync.
3appleHealthFor metrics where healthIsAuthoritative: not claimed by a wearable and not typed, such as steps, active energy, weight from the scale. The latest reading is simply the truth, which is what lets an afternoon sync correct the morning's step count.
3the primary wearableFor metrics claimedByWearable: resting HR, HRV, SpO2, respiratory rate, every sleep stage. Whoop by default; Fitbit if the person named it primary.
2the other wearableFills a gap the primary left, never overwrites it.
1appleHealthFor wearable-claimed metrics: the fallback when no strap has spoken.
0unattributedA value written before provenance was recorded. The first sync after upgrade re-attributes it.

Rank 0 has one exception, and the exception matters. Weight and water are the two metrics a person can type. A figure typed before provenance existed is unattributed too, and reading it as unknown would let the next Health sync silently replace it. That is the one path that destroys data a person entered by hand, so MetricSource.legacy(for:) reads an unattributed value for a typed metric as typed. The test is named for the bug it prevents: anUnattributedWeightIsNotReplacedByASync.

HealthApply.write is the one place the HealthMetric vocabulary meets DailyMetrics columns. It loops the arbiter over a day's readings inside a single upsert, records the winning source in the bag as a side effect, and routes named metrics to their column and everything else to extras. The arbiter can be perfectly correct and still be wired into the wrong column; HealthApplyTests run against a real in-memory store precisely to catch that.

1.5Local first topology, and what syncs now

SwiftData on the device is the source of truth for the UI. Supabase is identity, backup for some models, the only place a secret may live, and the place to run jobs a sleeping phone cannot. The first edition had one thing syncing (nothing, in practice). This edition has a precise list, and the split is worth knowing because it decides what a second device sees.

DataWhere it livesHow it moves
Notes: folders, documents, blocksDevice and note_folders, note_documentsNoteSync pushes and pulls under a per-account cursor on every pass; the token is read per pass, never captured
Profile and avatarDevice cache and profiles, the avatars bucketProfileClient upserts the whole row; the avatar downloads only when its stamp changed
Friends, messages, groups, shared statsServer only, read liveSocialAPI, GroupAPI, SharedStatsClient over PostgREST; RLS does the guarding
Plaid itemsCredentials server side in plaid_items; cursor and item ids on the deviceFour Edge Functions; the device never sees an access token
Fitbit connectionServer side in fitbit_connectionsfitbit-sync pulls under a lease; results land in DailyMetrics
Whoop tokensKeychain, per accountThe device calls Whoop directly; only the code exchange touches the server
Coach usagelifo_usageAtomic debit per cloud turn; the ceiling in Chapter 24
Push registrations and nudgesdevice_tokens, nudge_logToken and timezone re-pushed on every foreground
Health rows, sleep, workouts, money entries, sector scores, calendar cache, chatDevice onlyThe daily_metrics tables exist in the schema from the first migration, but no client writes them today. A second device rebuilds them from the sources.

Two mechanisms make this cheap. RootView reloads every snapshot on ModelContext.didSave, so a sync that lands repaints the screen without anyone polling. And SyncStalenessPolicy decides whether an automatic pull is due at all: data older than an hour, or from before today's midnight, is worth refreshing; anything fresher is not. The day boundary is the clock that matters most, because the first open of the morning must pull the night's sleep, and a sync from 23:50 is only minutes old while knowing nothing about the night.

1.6Conflict resolution

Within the health row, the arbiter above is the conflict rule: field-level, by rank, with a same-rank writer allowed to correct itself. It replaces the field-level last-write-wins the first edition described, and it is better for the same reason: a row-level overwrite would let the 04:00 Whoop pass discard the water you logged at 23:00, and a timestamp cannot tell a strap from a person.

Across devices, for the models that sync, the rule is simpler and per model. Notes carry an origin id and an updated_at; the pull applies rows newer than the cursor and the push sends rows changed since the last push, which is last-write-wins by row on a single-writer assumption that holds because one person edits one note at a time. The profile is an upsert of the whole row with explicit nulls, because an omitted key would leave the old value standing and make deleting a birthday impossible. Social rows never conflict because they are never edited locally; only status is updatable on a friendship, and the database says so.

Known limitation The notes cursor depends on server clocks, not device clocks, so the skew problem the first edition warned about is gone for notes. It remains for anything that compares updatedAt on the device with a server timestamp, and today nothing does. If a model starts syncing health rows, the arbiter's rank must travel with the row or the merge will regress to a timestamp race.

1.7One store per account

The first edition assumed a single user and said so. That assumption is gone: several people can sign in on one device, and the way that works is the most important structural change since Revision D. Isolation is by store file, not by an owner column. 

// LifeOSKit/Sources/Persistence/UserScope.swift
public struct UserScope: Hashable, Sendable, Codable {
    /// The signed-in Supabase user id.
    public let id: String

    public func storeURL(base: URL) -> URL {
        directory(base: base).appendingPathComponent("store.sqlite")
    }

    public func directory(base: URL) -> URL {
        base.appendingPathComponent("Accounts", isDirectory: true)
            .appendingPathComponent(safeDirectoryName, isDirectory: true)
    }

    /// A defaults suite of this account's own.
    public var defaultsSuiteName: String { "account.\(safeDirectoryName)" }
}

The reasoning in the file's own comment is the whole argument: a column means a predicate on every read across twenty models, and a predicate forgotten once is a leak that looks like working software. A separate file cannot leak, because the rows are not there to be read. LifeOSContainer.make(for:) opens Application Support/Accounts/<uid>/store.sqlite, and every account also gets its own UserDefaults suite for the things that turned out to be per account rather than per device: sync cursors, connection tokens, whether the tour has been seen. Appearance, the assistant's voice and which engine answers stay in standard on purpose, because they belong to the phone.

Three pieces cooperate. AccountStore keeps the roster of accounts in defaults (ids and labels are not secrets) and one keychain item per account for the session (a refresh token is a credential). AccountSession owns which scope is open and the ModelContainer for it, and tears down every cross-account surface, the widget snapshot, the Live Activity, the watch bridge, before adopting the next one. And LIfeOSApp re-roots the whole view tree with .id(scope.id) so no screen carries the previous account's view models or scroll position into the next; a stale snapshot on screen after a switch is the same class of leak as a stale row. Chapter 4 walks through the sequence.

The upgrade path is a file move. Every install before accounts kept one unscoped default.store. adoptLegacyStore moves that file, and its -wal and -shm companions, into the first account that signs in, once, and refuses when the destination already has a store. Moving the write-ahead log matters: the database alone would leave the most recent writes behind in a log the new file cannot find, and adoptionCarriesTheWriteAheadLog pins it. Signing out leaves the store on disk; removing an account from the device is a different, louder action that does not exist yet.

1.8The privacy boundary

Three things leave the device, and each crosses a boundary that is a type or a dependency edge rather than a code review promise.

  • Derived numbers to the coach's cloud tier. RemoteChatEngine takes a ContextBundle, which is assembled on the device from digests: aggregates, deltas, sector scores, the last thirty transactions as merchant, category and amount. DailyMetrics is a SwiftData class that is not Sendable, so the compiler prevents a raw row from crossing. Chapter 14 has the shape of the bundle.
  • Content, not numbers, to the calendar assistant. Event titles cannot be aggregated without destroying their use, so this is the one deliberate exception, and it is gated behind a confirmation broker before any write. Chapter 15.
  • Three figures to friends. Streak, days tracked and workouts, plus a wellness score, and only when the person has turned sharing on in a group. publishWellnessIfShared in RootView checks the group's flag before every publish. Chapter 16.

Everything with a vendor secret runs in an Edge Function: the Whoop client secret, the Fitbit client secret, the Plaid client id and secret, the Twilio credentials, the OpenAI key, the APNs key. The app bundle holds only what is public by OAuth design, and AppConfig says so in its comments. Chapter 23 has the three-tier table.

1.9Study notes

Read in this order

  1. LifeOSKit/Package.swift, for the graph. Twenty lines, and every rule in this chapter is one of its edges.
  2. LifeOSKit/Sources/Persistence/DailyMetrics.swift, for the row and the two bags.
  3. LifeOSKit/Sources/Persistence/MetricsStore.swift, for the only write path.
  4. LifeOSKit/Sources/Integrations/MetricSource.swift then MetricArbiter.swift, for the rank and the merge.
  5. LifeOSKit/Sources/Integrations/HealthApply.swift, for where the vocabulary meets the columns.
  6. LifeOSKit/Sources/Persistence/UserScope.swift and LifeOSContainer.swift, for one store per account.
  7. LifeOSKit/Tests/IntegrationsTests/MetricArbiterTests.swift, which reads as a list of the rules in plain English.

Check yourself

  • Why does the arbiter use greater-than-or-equal rather than greater-than? So that the same source syncing again can correct its own earlier value; an afternoon Health sync must be able to raise the morning's step count.
  • Why is sourcesData a string bag rather than a typed MetricSource? Because Persistence sits below Integrations in the package graph and cannot import the enum.
  • What does an unattributed weight become on the first sync after upgrade? It is read as typed, rank 4, so Health cannot overwrite it; every other unattributed metric is rank 0 and is re-attributed.
  • Why a store file per account rather than a userID column? A column needs a predicate on every read of every model and one omission leaks; a file cannot leak rows it does not contain.
  • Which health data reaches Supabase today? None of the rows. Notes, profile, social, connection credentials and coach usage sync; DailyMetrics, sleep, workouts, money and sectors stay on the device.
  • What must move with a store when it is adopted, and why? The -wal and -shm files, or the most recent writes are stranded in a log the moved database cannot find.

Chapter two

2MVVM and project structure

Every screen in Almanac is built the same way: a Model of value types, a ViewModel that owns all state and every decision, and a View that renders and forwards intent. The folder layout mirrors that exactly, one folder per screen, so a file's path tells you its layer before you open it.

The first edition described nine view models and four tabs. There are now thirty-three observable classes, most of them view models, across sixteen feature folders and five tabs, plus a composition root that has grown to 844 lines because it is the one place every feature is wired to every other. The shape did not change. This chapter explains why it held, and adds the two things that were not in the first edition: the composition root itself, and the preview and checks harness that lets a screen be captured and verified without an account.

2.1Why MVVM here

SwiftUI will happily let a view query the database. @Query in a View is one line and works immediately, and it is the reason this app does not do it. Three specific things break:

  1. Nothing is testable without a simulator. Goal evaluation, streak arithmetic, sector scoring and the arbiter are the parts most likely to be wrong, and they would live inside a view body that only a running device can exercise.
  2. Derivation gets re-run per render. Status-per-day, the month grid, the streak, the money rollup: computed in body, they recompute on every state change, including ones that have nothing to do with them.
  3. Persistence types leak into layout code. Once a view knows what a @Model class is, changing the schema means editing views. The schema has changed many times since Revision D.

MVVM fixes all three for the price of one extra file per screen. The ViewModel does the fetching and all derivation once, hands the View a plain value type, and can be exercised in a unit test with an in-memory container in milliseconds.

The rule that makes it work A ViewModel never imports SwiftUI, and a View never imports SwiftData. Both are checkable by reading the first ten lines of a file, and between them they force everything else into place. grep -rn "import SwiftData" LIfeOS/Features/*/View returns nothing today, and it should stay that way.

Where are the view controllers?

There are none, and that is not an omission. UIViewController is UIKit's unit of screen ownership: it manages a view hierarchy's lifecycle by hand. SwiftUI replaces that whole job with declarative views that re-render from state, so the controller's two remaining responsibilities split cleanly: owning state and making decisions went to the ViewModel, and describing what is on screen went to the View struct. The one place UIKit still appears is PushDelegate, because APNs registration and the orientation query have no SwiftUI entry point, and the note editor's UITextView, because block editing needs a text view SwiftUI does not offer.

2.2What each layer owns

LayerLives inShapeMay import
Domain modelLifeOSKit/Sources/Persistence@Model classes, stores, pure logicFoundation, SwiftData
Feature modelFeatures/<Screen>/Modelstruct, Sendable, Equatable: the screen's rendered stateFoundation, Persistence value types, DesignSystem value types
ViewModelFeatures/<Screen>/ViewModel@Observable @MainActor final classFoundation, Observation, Persistence, Integrations, Sectors, Insights; never SwiftUI
ViewFeatures/<Screen>/Viewstruct: View, plus its private subviewsSwiftUI, DesignSystem, its own ViewModel; never SwiftData
Shared componentComponents/{Model,ViewModel,View}Same three shapes, reused by two or more screensAs above
Design primitiveLifeOSKit/Sources/DesignSystemStateless View structs, tokens, pure layout mathsSwiftUI only; knows nothing about the app
WiringApp/ and App/Surfaces/The scene, the shell, the root, the account session, push, the watch bridge, the harnessEverything; this is the only place that may

The distinction between the shared component and the design primitive is the one people get wrong. DesignSystem holds things that would make sense in any app: HeroNumeral, DotGrid, PillNavBar. Components holds things that are reusable but specifically about this app's data: the quick-log sheet, the Whoop connect modal, the avatar button that knows where the photo is stored.

2.3The screen first directory layout

Folders are named after screens, not after layers. Features/Money/ holds everything the Money tab is, and inside it the three MVVM folders classify each file. Finding code starts with "which screen," which is how anyone actually thinks about a bug report.

LifeOSKit/Sources/                       eight targets; see 1.2

Every feature folder has a View/; most have all three. Health/ and Life/ have no Model/ because their snapshots are assembled from other features' snapshots or from package types. Notifications/ is a single file because the inbox's state lives in PushService. A folder with fewer than three subfolders is not a violation; it is a screen that did not need the layer.

Why this works without touching the project file The app target uses a PBXFileSystemSynchronizedRootGroup. Any folder created under LIfeOS/ is picked up by Xcode automatically, because the directory structure is the project structure. Moving a screen between folders is a git mv. The corollary still holds: do not put documentation in these folders, because every file is a build input and a README.md is copied into the bundle as a resource.

2.4Anatomy of a feature folder

Every feature folder answers the same questions in the same order. Chapters 5 to 18 are each one instance of this template.

FolderContainsTest
Model/One snapshot struct per screen, plus any small enums it needs. Value types only. No methods that fetch, no dates computed from .now.Compiles without SwiftUI or SwiftData
ViewModel/One class per screen. Holds private(set) var snapshot, the context, and the funcs the view calls.Instantiable in a test with an in-memory container
View/The screen struct and its private subviews. Reads only from its view model; owns @State for presentation concerns like sheet visibility and focus.A #Preview per subview; a design-preview page for the screen

The ViewModel shape is identical everywhere, which is the point:

// LIfeOS/Features/Today/ViewModel/TodayViewModel.swift
@MainActor @Observable
final class TodayViewModel {
    private(set) var snapshot = TodaySnapshot()
    private(set) var detail: DayDetailSnapshot?

    private var context: ModelContext?
    private let calendar: Calendar

    init(calendar: Calendar = .current) { self.calendar = calendar }

    func attach(_ context: ModelContext) { self.context = context }

    /// One pass over the day rows: the day-to-status map is built once and used
    /// for both the grid and the streak.
    func load() {
        guard let context else { return }
        let store = MetricsStore(context: context, calendar: calendar)
        // Bounded: the grid needs this month and the streak needs recent
        // history, never the whole table.
        let start = calendar.date(byAdding: .day, value: -400, to: .now) ?? .distantPast
        ...
    }
}

The context arrives through attach rather than the initialiser because RootView constructs every view model as @State before the environment is available, and a snapshot with its empty default is a valid thing to render in the meantime. Two view models break the pattern for a reason each states in a comment: AssistantViewModel takes its context in init because it builds a ChatStore immediately, so RootView holds it as an optional and creates it in attachAll(); and ActivityRecorder takes a UserDefaults suite so the design preview and the checks harness can run it against disposable defaults.

A calendar is injected everywhere a date is normalised. It defaults to .current and a test passes a fixed UTC calendar, which is what makes "which day does 23:30 belong to" a deterministic question in PersistenceTests.

Injection is by context, not by protocol Every view model builds a concrete store from a ModelContext, so testing one means standing up an in-memory ModelContainer rather than passing a stub. The consequence the first edition named is still true: the package has 1,298 tests across 130 suites and the app target has none. What changed is the mitigation. Everything that can be decided by arithmetic now lives in the package where a test can reach it (SessionKeepAlive, LiveEffort, HUDPlacement, CodeDigits), and the view models that cannot be unit tested are driven by the checks harness in 2.7 instead.

2.5The composition root

RootView is where every feature is wired to every other, and it is the one file in the app that may know about all of them. Five tabs, stated rather than inferred from ordering: 

// LIfeOS/App/RootView.swift
private enum AppTab: Hashable { case today, health, money, notes, life }

@State private var tab: AppTab = .today   // deliberately not persisted: a cold launch lands on Today

private var navItems: [PillNavItem<AppTab>] {
    [
        PillNavItem(value: .today,  systemImage: "circle.grid.3x3.fill",  label: "Today"),
        PillNavItem(value: .health, systemImage: "heart.fill",             label: "Health"),
        PillNavItem(value: .money,  systemImage: "dollarsign",            label: "Money"),
        PillNavItem(value: .notes,  systemImage: "text.book.closed.fill",  label: "Notes"),
        PillNavItem(value: .life,   systemImage: "square.grid.3x3.fill",   label: "Life"),
    ]
}

Health absorbed activity, weight, recovery and wellness so the bar stays free for the other life domains. Plan lost its tab to Notes, where habits now live as a section. Settings sits behind the profile avatar on Today rather than spending a slot. The Life board maps three of its nine sectors back onto tabs, and LifeSector.ownsTab in the Sectors package is the one decision about which three; RootView reads it and asserts if the switch ever drifts.

The root does five jobs, and each is one mechanism:

  1. Owns every view model as @State, nineteen of its own plus the four connection view models the shell hands it, and attaches the context to all of them in attachAll() from a single .task. Cross-feature wiring happens here and only here: the recorder's onSaved triggers a Health sync, the coach's bundleExtras closure reads the money and life snapshots, notes get their sync client.
  2. Reloads on save, never on a timer. One .task listens for ModelContext.didSave and calls reloadAll(). A save is the only thing that can change what a screen shows while the app is running, so nothing polls. Detail pages reload only while open, because off screen they are six months of rows nobody is looking at.
  3. Draws two shells over one set of screens. A compact width gets the pill bar floating over the content; a regular width gets the same bar stood on end as a rail. The screens are identical in both; 4.9 has the rail's behaviour.
  4. Presents every sheet and cover from one place, keyed on optionals rather than parallel booleans where the sheet has content: today.detail is the only source of truth for the day sheet, openMetric is a value rather than four flags, eventSheet is an enum of create or edit.
  5. Routes what arrives from outside: a widget deep link through SurfaceCoordinator.pendingRoute, a tapped nudge through PushService.pending, a scene activation that syncs the calendar and restarts the Health watcher.

The three quick actions (calendar assistant, LIFO, begin activity) are defined once in RootView and injected through EnvironmentValues.quickActions. Notes and Life own their own NavigationStacks several levels down, and a toolbar has to be attached inside the stack it belongs to; threading an array through both would put the same three buttons in four call sites, which is how a set drifts apart.

2.6Shared components

Components/ is split into the same three folders, for the same reason: a shared piece of UI that owns state has a view model, and it belongs somewhere obvious.

ComponentStateUsed by
QuickLogSheetQuickLogViewModel: writes water and weight through MetricsStore, source manualBegin Activity, the root
AddPlanEntrySheet, AddMoneySheetStateless; a closure with the typed fieldsNotes (habits), Money
JournalEntrySheetStateless; text onlyHealth, wellness section
WhoopConnectModalReads WhoopConnectionViewModelHealth hub, Settings
CapsuleButtonStateless; quiet or prominentEvery card with a CTA
ProfileAvatarTakes photo bytes; falls back to a glyph, never initialsToday's toolbar, the profile
ProfilePhotoDownsizingPure: resizes to the bucket's capOnboarding, the edit sheet

A component earns its place in Components/ the second time it is needed, not the first. SessionHUD and ActivityControls are the recent example: they were private to Begin Activity until the video player needed them, and they were moved rather than copied.

Where the dash rule lives "A missing metric renders as a dash, never as 0" is the single most repeated rule in this app. It is enforced by type: MetricTile, IconBubbleTile, PastelFillCard, TrendStatTile and HeroNumeral all take String? and render the dash themselves. A screen cannot pass a zero it does not have, because it has nothing to pass.

2.7The preview and checks harness

Most screens need an account, a store with weeks of rows, a connected strap and a signed-in session before they show anything worth looking at. That made design review and QA slow and made the state on screen unrepeatable. The harness fixes both. LIfeOSApp checks one launch argument in DEBUG: 

// LIfeOS/App/LIfeOSApp.swift
#if DEBUG
if ProcessInfo.processInfo.arguments.contains("--design-preview") {
    HealthActivityDesignPreview()
} else {
    shell
}
#endif

HealthActivityDesignPreview builds an in-memory container, a disposable UserDefaults suite, and an ActivityRecorder that never saves to Health, then switches on --page=. Every page is a real screen fed a fixture; nothing is a mock-up. The fixture uses six real rows lifted from the catalog seed so thumbnails resolve, a WHOOP recovery of 82 and a live reading of 152 bpm, and it labels itself as sample data.

ArgumentRendersModifiers
--page=health (default)The Health hub--fitness opens the Fitness half; --dark; --large for accessibility type
--page=activityBegin Activity--live starts a backdated run and feeds twelve minutes of readings; --strength; --hud-collapsed; --live-activity requests a real Live Activity
--page=library, library-emptyThe workout library--schedule-sheet
--page=playerThe video player--video=<id> picks a seed row; --live
--page=profile, settings, connections, sharing, categoriesThe named screen
--page=checksRuns ActivityRecorderChecks and writes recorder-checks.txt to Documents

Two more harnesses sit behind build flags rather than arguments, so they cannot ship even in a debug build by accident: SurfaceDesignPreview (flag SURFACE_DESIGN_PREVIEW) renders the widget gallery, the inbox and the "Widgets & Watch" page and runs SurfaceNativeChecks; LaunchFilmPreview (flag LAUNCH_FILM_PREVIEW) renders the synthetic frames the launch film was cut from.

Native checks

The checks are the answer to "the feature layer has no tests." They are not unit tests: they run inside the app process, against real UserDefaults suites and a real in-memory container, exercising the view models the way the app does. ActivityRecorderChecks starts a session, feeds readings, counts reps, hands off to a watch that never answers, and asserts on each step; SurfaceNativeChecks proves that a notification for one account is rejected once another is signed in and that sign-out empties the widget snapshot. Each prints PASS or FAIL and a title, the QA reports paste the output verbatim, and the rule for a failing check is the same as for a failing test: fix the cause, never the check.

2.8Rules and review checklist

RuleEnforced howWhy
A View never imports SwiftDataReview: visible in the importsAll reads go through a ViewModel; the schema can change without touching layout
A ViewModel never imports SwiftUIReview: visible in the importsKeeps it testable and prevents View-shaped thinking leaking in
A View never holds a @Model instanceReview: screens take snapshotsRendering cannot fault an object or trigger a fetch mid-layout
A ViewModel publishes value types onlyReview: the snapshot struct is the surfaceNothing above the view model can mutate the database by accident
No feature folder imports another feature folderReviewSharing goes through Components, which forces the shared thing to be named
Cross-feature wiring lives in RootViewReviewOne file knows the whole graph; a feature never reaches sideways
Derivation happens in the ViewModel, never in bodyReviewbody runs far more often than data changes
Snapshot types are EquatableCompilerCheap re-render skipping, and ViewModel tests become one-liners
Every font comes from LifeOSTypescripts/check-typography.shThe app once had 376 hand-written font calls across 28 sizes
A new stored property on an existing model is optional or defaultedReview; a hang on the spinner if missedInstalled stores refuse to open otherwise. The equipment column shipped without a default and had to be fixed the same day
Anything decidable by arithmetic lives in the packageReviewA test can reach it; a view cannot be asserted on
A screen that needs an account has a design-preview pageReview; the QA report lists the capturesRepeatable state, and a capture without loading anyone's data

2.9Study notes

Read in this order

  1. LIfeOS/App/LIfeOSApp.swift: forty lines that decide whether a store is open and re-root the tree.
  2. LIfeOS/App/AppShell.swift: onboarding or app, and every URL that arrives.
  3. LIfeOS/App/RootView.swift: read attachAll() and reloadAll() first, then the content switch, then the two shells.
  4. LIfeOS/Features/Today/ViewModel/TodayViewModel.swift: the canonical view model shape.
  5. LIfeOS/Features/Today/Model/TodaySnapshot.swift: what a snapshot is and is not.
  6. LIfeOS/Features/Health/View/HealthActivityDesignPreview.swift: how a screen is rendered without an account.
  7. LIfeOS/Features/Activity/ViewModel/ActivityRecorderChecks.swift: what a native check looks like.

Check yourself

  • Why does a view model take its context through attach rather than init? Because RootView constructs them as @State before the environment context exists, and an empty snapshot is a valid first render.
  • What triggers reloadAll()? ModelContext.didSave, scene activation, and a finished recorder save. Nothing polls.
  • Where is the decision about which sectors map to a tab? LifeSector.ownsTab in the Sectors package; RootView only maps the answer onto its private enum.
  • Why are the quick actions an environment value? Notes and Life own their own navigation stacks, and a toolbar must be attached inside the stack it belongs to.
  • What is the difference between a native check and a unit test? A check runs inside the app process against real defaults and view models; a test runs in the package with no simulator. Both print a verdict; only the check can reach a view model.
  • Which two harnesses are behind build flags rather than launch arguments, and why? The surface gallery and the launch film; a flag cannot be tripped by a stray argument in a debug build.

Chapter three

3Design system

Sixteen feature folders have to read as one app. That happens because they share a small set of primitives and differ by exactly one variable, the module hue, rather than because each screen was designed carefully on its own. This chapter is the inventory of those primitives and the three scales they are built on: colour, type and space.

Everything here lives in LifeOSKit/Sources/DesignSystem, a target with no dependencies that also builds for macOS. That second fact shapes more of the code than it looks: it is why colours are explicit light and dark pairs rather than UIKit dynamic colours, why the width class is the package's own enum rather than UserInterfaceSizeClass, and why the six-box code field keeps its keyboard configuration behind an #if os(iOS). The price is a few lines per component; the return is swift test running from a terminal in seconds with no simulator.

3.1Principle

The hub is neutral; the domains are tinted. Today is a warm off-white canvas. Every domain screen is the same canvas with a whisper of its hue washed in across the top 260 points. This is a change from the first edition, where domain screens were saturated-at-top gradients: the restyle kept the hue as a tint rather than a paint job, so cards became solid white with one soft shadow instead of frosted glass fighting a gradient. The two visual languages resolved into one hierarchy, and adding a module is still a token, not a design exercise.

Three rules hold the whole thing together. The accent never varies by module and has exactly two meanings: today, and act. Numerals are the rounded face and words never are. And a missing value is a dash, drawn by the component, never by the screen.

3.2Colour tokens

// LifeOSKit/Sources/DesignSystem/Tokens.swift
public enum ModuleHue: String, CaseIterable, Sendable {
    case body, activity, recovery, nutrition, money, habits

    public var top: Color { ... }        // saturated; survives only as chart and accent ink
    public var pastel: Color { ... }     // carries the module identity on the light canvas
    public var pastelDark: Color { ... } // the muted counterpart for dark mode
}

public enum LifeOSTokens {
    /// The single accent. Means "today" and "act". Identical in both schemes.
    public static let accent = Color(red: 0.94, green: 0.34, blue: 0.18)

    /// Live session push states, on the live gradient, the same in both schemes.
    public static let pushEasy = Color(red: 0.20, green: 0.72, blue: 0.45)
    public static let pushNear = Color(red: 0.96, green: 0.65, blue: 0.14)
    public static let pushOver = Color(red: 0.90, green: 0.27, blue: 0.23)

    public static let liveGradientTop = ModuleHue.recovery.top
    public static let liveGradientBottom = Color(white: 0.97)

    public static let canvas = AdaptiveColor(light: Color(red: 0.949, green: 0.945, blue: 0.933),
                                             dark: Color(white: 0.07))
    public static let cardSurface = AdaptiveColor(light: .white, dark: Color(white: 0.13))
    ...
}
TokenValueMeaning
ModuleHue.bodyTealWeight, composition, the Health hub
ModuleHue.activityAmberMovement, the workout library
ModuleHue.recoveryBlueWhoop, HRV, sleep; also the live session gradient
ModuleHue.nutritionPurpleDeclared; no screen owns it yet
ModuleHue.moneyGreenThe Money tab and its charts
ModuleHue.habitsOrangeHabit strips, the heart-rate stat group
LifeOSTokens.accentOrange, fixedToday, the selected tab, the prominent action, the code field's focus ring
pushEasy / pushNear / pushOverGreen, amber, redHow hard the live session is pushing against the day's capacity
canvas / cardSurface / tileSurfaceOff-white and white; near-black and dark greyThe three surfaces. Tiles are solid because translucent white over a near-white canvas is invisible
dotMissed / dotFuture / dotPadding / dotOutlineGreysThe month grid's four non-day states; padding is faint rather than invisible so the month reads as one block
alertBackground / alertTextSoft red, deep redThe anomaly banner; red enough to interrupt, soft enough to live on cream
fabFill / fabGlyphInk on white, white on inkNever the same luminance; a white plus on the ink token vanishes the moment the scheme flips
cardShadow6% black, light mode onlyDark mode separates surfaces by tone; a black shadow on a black canvas is invisible cost

Colours are AdaptiveColor pairs, resolved explicitly by the consuming view with token.resolve(scheme). It is one more line per use than a dynamic colour, and it is the line that makes TokensTests possible: alertColorsDifferByScheme and fabFillAndGlyphStayOppositeInBothSchemes read both halves of a pair and compare them, which a UIKit dynamic colour would not let a terminal test do.

3.3One type scale

Before Typography.swift existed there were 376 hand-written .system(size:weight:) calls across 28 distinct sizes between 9 and 104, and three of those sizes accounted for 178 of them. Nobody chose that; it is what happens when every screen picks its own number, and the drift is invisible until two screens sit side by side. The scale has nine text steps and three numeral steps, fewer than the app had, on purpose: a scale only does its job if the steps are far enough apart that picking the wrong one is obvious. 

// LifeOSKit/Sources/DesignSystem/Typography.swift
public enum LifeOSType {
    public static let eyebrow      = Font.system(size: 11, weight: .semibold)   // tracked uppercase markers
    public static let caption      = Font.system(size: 12, weight: .regular)
    public static let label        = Font.system(size: 13, weight: .medium)     // dense rows, chips
    public static let secondary    = Font.system(size: 15, weight: .regular)
    public static let rowTitle     = Font.system(size: 15, weight: .semibold)
    public static let body         = Font.system(size: 17, weight: .regular)    // reading text
    public static let sectionTitle = Font.system(size: 20, weight: .semibold)
    public static let screenTitle  = Font.system(size: 24, weight: .bold)
    public static let display      = Font.system(size: 34, weight: .bold)       // one per screen at most

    /// The date on the hub, and nothing else. Its tracking travels with it.
    public static let masthead = Font.system(size: 104, weight: .bold)
    public static let mastheadTracking: CGFloat = -5

    public static let numeral      = Font.system(size: 28, weight: .bold, design: .rounded)
    public static let numeralLarge = Font.system(size: 44, weight: .bold, design: .rounded)
    /// The only place a size may be passed in. Hero numerals size to their space.
    public static func numeral(_ size: CGFloat, weight: Font.Weight = .bold) -> Font
}

Two families, each with exactly one job. Text is the system sans, always. Numerals are rounded, and only numerals. Rounded digits are easier to read at a glance, which is why the money screen reached for the face in the first place, and a rounded label next to a sans label is the drift the scale exists to stop. A serif was briefly the notes tab's title face and is deliberately gone: it looked right on that one screen and wrong beside every other.

The masthead is the one step outside the pattern and the reason it exists is instructive. The hub's date was flattened into display to fit the scale, which took it from 104 to 34 points and turned the masthead the whole screen is built around into an ordinary heading. A scale that cannot express the biggest thing in the app is missing a step rather than being violated by one, so the step was added, with its negative tracking attached, because a caller who took the font without the tracking would get a subtly wrong masthead.

Two companions keep the scale from being bypassed. LifeOSType.UIKitScale restates the same sizes as UIFont for the note editor's text view, so changing a step changes both. LifeOSTextRole and the .lifeOSText(_:) modifier give the same steps Dynamic Type behaviour through @ScaledMetric, so screens can adopt accessibility sizes one at a time without touching the masthead or the numerals.

3.4Space, radius and the glass panel

// LifeOSKit/Sources/DesignSystem/Space.swift
public enum Space {
    public static let half: CGFloat = 4     // the only sub-grid value, for optical nudges inside a control
    public static let x1: CGFloat = 8
    public static let x2: CGFloat = 16
    public static let x3: CGFloat = 24
    public static let x4: CGFloat = 32
    public static let x5: CGFloat = 40
    public static let x6: CGFloat = 48
    public static let x8: CGFloat = 64
    public static let x10: CGFloat = 80
}

public enum Radius {
    public static let small: CGFloat = 12
    public static let medium: CGFloat = 20
    public static let large: CGFloat = 28
    public static let pill: CGFloat = 999
}

Named by multiples rather than by role, because roles drift (someone always needs a "medium-large") while multiples cannot. Radii sit on the same grid so cards nest without optical drift. The same file holds GlassPanel, PrimaryButton and SecondaryButton. GlassPanel is where the app takes Liquid Glass from the system rather than imitating it with a material: one .glassEffect(.regular, in:), so every frosted panel in the app gets real refraction and highlights from one place, and the notes drawer, the profile's frosted panel over the photo and the coach's canvas all read as the same surface.

3.5Layout metrics: phone and iPad

Every number that varies with width lives in LayoutMetrics, for the same reason Space exists. The app distinguishes exactly two widths and maps the platform's size class onto them once, in RootView, so the package never imports UIKit's enum. 

// LifeOSKit/Sources/DesignSystem/LayoutMetrics.swift
public static func metrics(for width: LayoutWidth) -> LayoutMetrics {
    switch width {
    case .compact:
        LayoutMetrics(gutter: 20, sectionSpacing: 22,
                      maxContentWidth: .infinity, heroScale: 1.0,
                      fabBottomInset: 72, contentBottomInset: 130,
                      railInset: 0,
                      statColumns: 2, tileColumns: 3, isRegular: false)
    case .regular:
        LayoutMetrics(gutter: 32, sectionSpacing: 30,
                      maxContentWidth: 1060, heroScale: 1.3,
                      fabBottomInset: 28, contentBottomInset: 32,
                      railInset: 112,
                      statColumns: 4, tileColumns: 6, isRegular: true)
    }
}
MetricCompactRegularWhy the regular value
maxContentWidthunbounded1060Above a portrait iPad's 1024, on purpose: portrait is already one comfortable column and capping it bought only dead margin. The cap is for landscape and wide Stage Manager panes.
contentBottomInset13032Compact clears the floating pill bar, which overlaps the scroll view. Regular has a side rail instead, and the old inset left a band of dead space.
railInset0112The rail's real footprint is its 32 gutter plus its 64 width. At 80 every regular screen had its leading edge tucked under the rail; the Notes sidebar showed it plainly. The extra beyond 96 is the rail's shadow.
statColumns / tileColumns2 / 34 / 6Derived rather than measured: GridItem(.adaptive) cannot cap the count, and a 1366-point pane would take eight tiles across.

railInset is stated as a number the screens apply rather than as a safe area inset, because a safe area does not survive the trip through a NavigationStack into a ScrollView whose background ignores it; the rail ended up drawn over the first column of the month. LayoutMetricsTests pin every relationship in the table: onlyRegularWidthPaysForTheRailOnTheLeadingEdge, theContentCapOnlyBitesWiderThanAPortraitIPad, and a guard that every metric is positive.

3.6Component inventory

Thirty-four files. Each is stateless apart from animation phase, takes value types, and knows nothing about the app's models. The inventory is grouped by what the component is for.

Canvas and cards

3.7Motion pieces

Four components animate, and each earns it by being made of the app's own vocabulary rather than decoration dropped on top.

  • DotBloom is the onboarding animation: a month of dots filling in one by one with a spring per column. The first thing a new person sees is the grid they will read every morning, so the animation teaches the interface instead of entertaining. It respects reduce motion.
  • ScanlineCat is the intro's greeting, a cat drawn as horizontal scanlines or as dots on the grid's own pitch. All geometry is in ScanlineCatSilhouette (three primitives: ellipse, rect, triangle, in a unit box) and ScanlineSlicer (which cuts shapes into merged x-spans at a given y, in closed form, so slicing costs no rasterisation). Both are pure and tested; ScanlineSlicerTests is the largest suite in DesignSystemTests at 443 lines. The view only decides colour, timing and how the cat assembles on appear: rows drift in from the side they are nearest, the face goes on last and solid because a striped eye cannot read as an eye.
  • GlassGlobe is the coach's orb: a Siri-like glass slime, clear and silver, morphing on a TimelineView at 30 frames per second. Audio intensity makes it breathe. Hue is kept out of it; the colour is the light on glass.
  • SlateAurora is the coach's backdrop, a three-by-three MeshGradient from onyx through blue slate to an alabaster bloom. Fixed rather than scheme-resolved, because the coach is an immersive dark surface in both appearances.

The live gradient and push-state tints

A running session paints the recovery blue from the top to near white at the bottom, on the in-session hero, the lock screen Live Activity and the Dynamic Island alike, so the numbers read as the same data wherever they appear. On that gradient the three push colours say how hard the session is pushing against the day's capacity: green is easy going, amber is near the ceiling, red is over it. They are the same in both schemes because the gradient is. Chapter 8 has the maths that picks one.

3.8Dark mode

Every hue has a dark variant, deep top and near-black bottom, and every surface token has both halves. These were defined before any screen existed, because retrofitting a gradient system to dark mode later is significantly harder than doing it once at the start, and the restyle to a light canvas proved the point: the dark tokens changed values but no screen had to learn that dark mode exists.

No colour is defined only inside a scheme branch Every token has a light value and a dark value, always both. A colour that exists only in the dark branch renders as whatever the parent inherited in light mode, usually black on black, and usually discovered by a user rather than a preview. The two exceptions are deliberate and named: SlateAurora and the live gradient are the same in both schemes because the surfaces they paint are immersive.

3.9The typography check

The scale is only the scale if nothing else declares a font. scripts/check-typography.sh is what keeps it that way: it greps every Swift file under LIfeOS and LifeOSKit/Sources, excluding Typography.swift itself, and fails on four patterns. 

# scripts/check-typography.sh
check "Literal font sizes outside the scale (use a LifeOSType step):" \
  '\.system(size: [0-9]'

check "UIKit fonts outside the scale (use LifeOSType.UIKitScale):" \
  '\(systemFont\|monospacedSystemFont\)(ofSize:'

check "Rounded or serif faces declared outside the scale:" \
  'design: \.\(rounded\|serif\)'

check "Apple semantic text styles (use a LifeOSType step):" \
  '\.font(\.\(largeTitle\|title[0-9]*\|headline\|subheadline\|body\|callout\|footnote\|caption[0-9]*\))'

The first pattern matches a literal point size and not a computed one, because an icon drawn at a fraction of its container is not type and has no step to pick. The fourth is the subtle one: Apple's semantic styles are a second scale nobody chose, and they do not line up with ours. The script exits non-zero on any hit, so it belongs in the same pre-push habit as swift test. It is also honest about the present: the intro and signup screens still carry three .subheadline and .body calls that predate the scale, and running the script today lists exactly those three. That list is the work remaining, not a reason to loosen the check.

3.10Study notes

Read in this order

  1. Tokens.swift: the hues, the accent, the surfaces, and the comment on every one.
  2. Typography.swift: the scale and the story of the 376 calls it replaced.
  3. Space.swift: the grid, the radii, and GlassPanel.
  4. LayoutMetrics.swift: read the doc comment on railInset; it is a complete bug post-mortem.
  5. PillNavBar.swift and ActionFan.swift: one component, two orientations, and why.
  6. SignInChrome.swift: CodeField over a hidden text field, and InlineStatus.resolve.
  7. ScanlineSlicer.swift then ScanlineCatSilhouette.swift: geometry a test can assert on.
  8. scripts/check-typography.sh: run it, and read what it finds.

Check yourself

  • Why are colours AdaptiveColor pairs rather than UIKit dynamic colours? The package builds for macOS so tests run from a terminal, and a test can read both halves of a pair.
  • Which face may a word never be set in? Rounded. It is for numerals only, and a rounded label beside a sans label is the drift the scale exists to stop.
  • Why does masthead exist as its own step? Flattening the hub's date into display took it from 104 to 34 points; a scale that cannot express the biggest thing in the app is missing a step.
  • Why is railInset 112 and not 96? The rail's footprint is 32 gutter plus 64 width; the rest is breathing room for its shadow. At 80 every screen's leading edge was under the rail.
  • Why is the code field one hidden text field rather than six? So the system keyboard, .oneTimeCode autofill and paste keep working; the boxes are a rendering of that field and hold no state.
  • Which two surfaces are the same colour in both schemes, and why is that allowed? The coach's aurora and the live session gradient; both are immersive surfaces whose tokens resolve as dark by design.

Chapter four

4The app shell, accounts and sign-in

Before any tab exists, three objects decide whose data is open, whether a session still signs them in, and which shell to draw around the screens. This chapter follows a launch from @main to the first rendered tab, then the sign-in that gets a new person there, then what keeps them signed in and how several people share one phone.

4.1Intent

Signing in is required and it is the only entry point. That was already true in the first edition and the reason has only strengthened: a store belongs to an account, notes sync to one, and every connection is held per account. There is nowhere for a signed-out person's data to live that would not become somebody else's the moment they signed in. What is new is that the shell must handle more than one account on a device, must keep a session alive for someone who never closes the app, and must survive an upgrade from the single-store world without looking like it deleted a year of notes.

Working backwards

Almanac opens on the intro the first time and on Today every time after. Signing in takes an email or a phone number and a six-digit code, then a name. A returning person types the code and lands straight in the app. Two people can sign in on one phone and switch between them without either seeing the other's notes, journal or health.

Why no password?

A password is a credential to lose, store and reset. A one-time code delivered to a channel the person already controls proves the same thing with no secret at rest and no reset flow to build.

Email or phone?

Email is the default. It is free through Resend to 3,000 a month, needs no A2P registration, and carries none of the SMS failure modes. Phone goes through Twilio Verify behind an Edge Function, and when a text cannot be delivered the app offers email rather than retrying.

How does the app know I am returning?

The account tells it, not the door you came through. After the code is accepted, AuthSession.hasProfile says whether a name was ever saved; with OTP there is no other difference between signing up and signing in.

What happens if I stay in the app for two hours?

An access token lives an hour. A loop keyed on the sign-in state sleeps until 45 seconds before expiry and renews. Before that loop existed, every authenticated call after the first hour failed with a JWT expired error and nothing was watching the clock.

4.2Files and folders

LIfeOS/App/
├── LIfeOSApp.swift                    @main; owns AccountSession; re-roots per account
├── AccountSession.swift               which scope and container are open; sign in, switch, sign out
├── AppShell.swift                     onboarding or RootView; URL callbacks; session keep-alive; syncs on foreground
├── RootView.swift                     the two shells over five tabs (Chapter 2)
├── OrientationLock.swift              portrait on phone; the video player asks for more
├── PushService.swift                  APNs registration and the nudge inbox; PushDelegate
└── ChatTier.swift                     the one place the cloud engine is built

LIfeOS/Features/Onboarding/
├── Model/OnboardingModels.swift       OnboardingStep, AuthMode, IntroPage, SignupDraft, DialCountries
├── ViewModel/OnboardingViewModel.swift send, verify, profile, restore, sign out
└── View/SignupScreens.swift           SignupScaffold, IdentityScreen, CodeScreen, ProfileStepScreen

LifeOSKit/Sources/Integrations/
├── SupabaseAuth.swift                 the three auth calls over REST; AuthSession; AuthError
├── AuthSessionStore.swift             AuthSessionStoring; KeychainAuthSessionStore; InMemoryAuthSessionStore
├── AccountStore.swift                 the roster of accounts and one keychain item per account
├── SessionRefresh.swift               SessionRefresher: restore on launch and foreground
├── SessionKeepAlive.swift             when to renew a session that has not lapsed yet

LifeOSKit/Sources/DesignSystem/
