4.3Launch: from @main to the first tab

LIfeOSApp holds one piece of state, an AccountSession, and switches on whether it has a container: 

// LIfeOS/App/LIfeOSApp.swift
@ViewBuilder private var shell: some View {
    if let container = session.container {
        AppShell(onSignedIn: { session.signIn($0, session: $1) },
                 onSignedOut: { session.signOut() },
                 hasStore: true, accountID: session.scope?.id)
            .modelContainer(container)
            // Re-rooted per account, so no screen carries the previous
            // account's view models or scroll position into the next one.
            .id(session.scope?.id ?? "none")
            .environment(\.accountSession, session)
            .task(id: session.scope?.id) { purgeSeededHistoryOnce() }
    } else {
        // Nobody signed in. The onboarding flow needs no store.
        AppShell(onSignedIn: ..., onSignedOut: ..., hasStore: false, accountID: nil)
    }
}

AccountSession.init does three things before the first frame. It adopts a pre-accounts session if the roster is empty and the legacy keychain slot holds one, moving the old default.store into the new account's directory in the same breath. It removes a current account whose keychain session does not match its id, so a stale pointer can never open somebody else's store. Then it adopts the current scope, which opens the container and hands the owner id to PushService and SurfaceCoordinator. A container that cannot open is not something the person can fix, and carrying on with the previous account's container would show them somebody else's data, so the safe failure is nothing open.

AppShell is the second lock. A session alone is not enough to build the tab hierarchy: every screen below RootView reads through a ModelContext, and mounting it in a scene with no container gets as far as the first fetch before CoreData throws an NSException for an entity it cannot find, which is not catchable from Swift and takes the whole process. So the gate is three-way: 

// LIfeOS/App/AppShell.swift
if onboarding.isSignedIn && hasFinishedOnboarding && hasStore {
    RootView(whoop: whoop, fitbit: fitbit, plaid: plaid, health: health, onSignOut: { ... })
} else {
    OnboardingFlow(model: onboarding, ...)
}

hasFinishedOnboarding is an @AppStorage in the account's own defaults suite. Its job is narrower than its name: isSignedIn resolves synchronously from a keychain read, so on a relaunch that restores a session the flag is already true on the first render, instead of flashing the intro carousel for a frame before the launch task settles. The first-run tour is keyed on its own flag so it fires exactly once per account however the person arrived, and it is an overlay rather than a fullScreenCover because iOS can restore a previously presented cover at launch and two covers contending for one window silently drops one.

4.4Signing in: a code, then a name

OnboardingStep is a single enum rather than a pile of booleans, so an impossible combination cannot be represented: intro, identity, code, profile, connections, signedIn. AuthMode is which door the person came through, and it changes copy and nothing else.

SupabaseAuth is the whole auth client: no SDK, because the three calls needed here are small and a dependency would pull in far more surface than that. The anon key is sent as the API key on every call; it is public by design and Row Level Security is what protects rows. Phone is always offered because SMS goes through the otp-start Edge Function and Twilio Verify, not GoTrue's own provider; email availability still comes from auth/v1/settings, and the identity screen waits for that answer rather than offering a channel that cannot deliver. 

// LifeOSKit/Sources/Integrations/SupabaseAuth.swift
public func sendCode(to destination: String, channel: Channel) async throws {
    if channel == .phone {
        _ = try await postFunction("otp-start", body: ["phone": destination])
        return
    }
    _ = try await post("otp", body: ["email": destination, "create_user": true])
}

public func verify(code: String, destination: String, channel: Channel) async throws -> AuthSession {
    if channel == .phone {
        let data = try await postFunction("otp-check", body: ["phone": destination, "code": code])
        return try decode(data)
    }
    let data = try await post("verify", body: ["token": code, "type": "email", "email": destination])
    return try decode(data)
}

Before a phone number reaches the server, PhoneOTP.isAcceptable refuses what will never be sent to: only Indian mobiles (+91 then ten digits starting 6 to 9) and NANP numbers (+1 then ten digits) are accepted, and pumpingPrefix produces the country-plus-early-digits key the server uses to catch SMS pumping against a neighbouring range. The Edge Function enforces the same rules; this copy exists so the form can refuse without a round trip.

AuthError.fromHTTP maps every failure the classifier knows about onto a sentence a person can act on, and the Twilio cases are the interesting ones. A trial-account failure (21608) blames the account, not the number, because the number is not the problem. An opted-out number (21610) is given the remedy: text START. An unregistered campaign (30034) and a carrier block (60410) are named rather than lumped into a generic failure. And an empty-bodied 502 with no message stays channel-neutral, because email is now the default and the copy must not assume SMS. AuthErrorMappingTests has one test per case, each named for the sentence it guards.

The code screen

This is the screen people fail on, so it does the work instead of asking for it. Six boxes rather than one tracked field. Verification fires the moment the sixth digit lands. A wrong code shakes and buzzes through .sensoryFeedback(.error, trigger:) rather than quietly turning a line red, and the trigger is a counter rather than a Bool because two bad codes in a row must play twice. The Verify button stays even though the sixth digit auto-verifies, because autofill can land a full code without a keystroke and a screen with no button leaves that person nothing to press.

The resend countdown is 60 seconds, not 45: the phone Edge Function's cooldown in otp_guard.ts is 45 seconds, but email posts straight to GoTrue, governed by auth.email.max_frequency, which is 60. The countdown has to clear the stricter of the two or "Resend code" invites a 429.

4.5The returning-user door

With OTP there is no password, so signing in and signing up are the same three steps. The intro offers two doors, "Let's get started" on the last page and "Already have an account? Sign in" beneath it, and picking the wrong one is harmless by design: the branch after verify is what routes. 

// LIfeOS/Features/Onboarding/ViewModel/OnboardingViewModel.swift
let session = try await auth.verify(code: draft.code.filter(\.isNumber),
                                    destination: draft.destination, channel: draft.channel)
try AccountStore().add(Account(userID: session.userID,
                               label: session.email ?? session.phone ?? "Account"), session: session)
AccountStore().clearLegacySession()
store = KeychainAuthSessionStore(account: session.userID)
self.session = session
isSignedIn = true
// The only thing that separates a returning user from a new one, and it is
// known only now. The door they came through does not decide this; the account does.
step = session.hasProfile ? .signedIn : .profile

hasProfile is derived from user_metadata.first_name in the verify response. That is why saveProfile still writes the name to user metadata even though the profile row now lives in the profiles table: the flag that decides whether a returning person is sent through signup again is read from the session, not from a table the session has not loaded yet. AuthSession decodes the flag by hand with a default of false, because sessions already in the keychain have no such key and a synthesised decoder would throw on them and sign every existing person out on upgrade.

The profile step saves in a deliberate order: the picture goes to storage before the row, so the row is never saved pointing at an object that does not exist; a failed upload costs the picture and not the profile. A failed profile write does not strand the person at the last step either: the account exists either way, so the error is shown and the step advances to connections. onboarding.step is written to the account's defaults at that point so a relaunch mid-signup resumes at connections rather than at the profile.

4.6Keeping a session alive

Two pure pieces decide, and one loop acts. SessionRefresher.restore() is asked on launch and on every return to the foreground. Its governing rule is that signing someone out is destructive and cannot be undone without a fresh code, so it happens only when the server has definitively refused the credential: 

// LifeOSKit/Sources/Integrations/SessionRefresh.swift
public func restore() async -> Outcome {
    guard let stored = store.load() else { return .signedOut }
    guard stored.isExpired() else { return .active(stored) }
    guard let refreshToken = stored.refreshToken, !refreshToken.isEmpty else {
        store.clear(); return .rejected
    }
    do {
        let refreshed = try await auth.refresh(refreshToken: refreshToken)
        guard !Task.isCancelled,
              store.load()?.refreshToken == stored.refreshToken,
              store.load()?.userID == stored.userID else { return .signedOut }
        guard refreshed.userID.isEmpty || refreshed.userID == stored.userID else {
            store.clear(); return .rejected
        }
        let session = refreshed.carryingForward(stored)
        try? store.save(session)
        return .active(session)
    } catch let error as AuthError where Self.isRefusal(error) {   // 400, 401, 403, 422
        guard store.load()?.accessToken == stored.accessToken else { return .signedOut }
        store.clear(); return .rejected
    } catch {
        return .active(stored)   // offline, outage, rate limit: keep it and try later
    }
}

Every guard in that function is a bug that happened. Re-reading the store after the network call and comparing the refresh token is what stops a logout during a refresh from resurrecting the session. Comparing the user id is what stops a refresh from replacing the account's identity. carryingForward exists because a refresh response is allowed to be sparse and must not erase what is already known. And the authURL helper exists because appendingPathComponent percent-encoded the ? in token?grant_type=refresh_token, GoTrue answered 404, and for a while no stored session could ever be renewed: an hour after signing in every authenticated call began failing, and signing in always looked fine. AuthRefreshURLTests pins the query staying a query.

OnboardingViewModel.restoreSession coalesces concurrent callers onto one task, because Supabase rotates the refresh token on use and two concurrent refreshes would have the second present a token the first just retired, signing the person out for doing nothing but foregrounding the app during launch.

SessionKeepAlive covers the case neither event reaches: someone who keeps the app open past the hour. It is two numbers and a function, pure so the schedule can be tested without waiting an hour for it: 

// LifeOSKit/Sources/Integrations/SessionKeepAlive.swift
public static let margin: TimeInterval = 45   // inside isExpired's own minute of slack
public static let floor: TimeInterval = 5     // never a spin against the auth endpoint

public static func delay(untilExpiry expiresAt: Date, now: Date = .now) -> TimeInterval {
    max(expiresAt.timeIntervalSince(now) - margin, floor)
}

AppShell runs the loop in a .task(id: onboarding.isSignedIn), so it starts the moment somebody signs in and stops the moment they sign out rather than waking on a timer behind the signup screen. The margin is deliberately inside isExpired's sixty seconds of slack: waking earlier finds a session the refresher considers healthy, does nothing, and spends the wake for nothing. The floor is what stops a session that arrives already expired, or a clock that jumps backwards, from turning the loop into a spin.

4.7Several accounts on one device

Section 1.7 explained why isolation is a file per account. This section is the bookkeeping that makes switching safe. AccountStore keeps two things: a roster in defaults, because a list of who has used this phone is not a secret and enumerating accounts must not need a keychain read each, and a keychain item per user id, because a refresh token is a credential in its own right. 

// LifeOSKit/Sources/Integrations/AccountStore.swift
public var currentScope: UserScope? {
    // Nil rather than "the first account we can find": a current id naming an
    // account that has been signed out must never silently open somebody else's store.
    guard let id = defaults.string(forKey: Self.currentKey),
          accounts.contains(where: { $0.userID == id }) else { return nil }
    return UserScope(id: id)
}

public func add(_ account: Account, session: AuthSession) throws {
    guard !account.userID.isEmpty, account.userID == session.userID else {
        throw AccountStoreError.identityMismatch
    }
    try keychain(for: account.userID).save(session)
    ...
}

@discardableResult
public func setCurrent(_ userID: String) -> Bool {
    // Refuses an account with no stored session rather than switching to one that cannot sync.
    guard accounts.contains(where: { $0.userID == userID }),
          keychain(for: userID).load()?.userID == userID else { return false }
    defaults.set(userID, forKey: Self.currentKey)
    return true
}

KeychainAuthSessionStore() with no arguments defaults to whichever account is current, read straight from defaults rather than through AccountStore because the store is main-actor bound and this type is used from wherever a network call happens to be made. This matters more than it looks: every network client in the app builds one of these to get a token, and before accounts there was one slot, so after a switch they would all have carried on presenting the previous account's token and reading the previous account's rows.

Switching and signing out are the two places every cross-account surface is torn down, and the list is the map of what is per account:

SurfaceOn switchOn sign out
The storeContainer replaced; the view tree re-rooted by .idContainer closed; file left on disk
Widget snapshotSurfaceCoordinator.clear() then adopt the next ownerCleared; an empty snapshot is written
Live Activity and watch bridgeendAll(); bridge ended with discardSame
The recorderbeforeAccountChange deactivates itSame
PushOwner id re-attached; the inbox reloads from the new suiteRow deleted with the old token before the keychain is cleared; delivered notifications removed; APNs unregistered
Pending OAuth (Whoop, Fitbit)Left alone; keyed per accountIn-flight browser credentials cleared; saved provider links stay with their owner
Calendar and Health opt-insRead from the new suiteRemoved from the suite; the device permission stays
Plaid LinkresetForAccountChange()Same
The legacy keychain slotClearedCleared, belt and braces

The legacy slot deserves its own sentence because it is what made logging out impossible for a build. It has no user id, so it is not "one account's" session and the per-account clear never reached it; it survived every sign out and the next launch adopted it and signed the person back in, into a scene with no store open, and the first note fetch threw. A credential that can restore an account is that account's session whatever slot it sits in.

AccountDeviceAccess is the last piece: device permissions are app-wide in iOS, so Calendar access granted while one account was open must also be granted by the next one. allowsCalendar requires both the system authorisation and the account's own flag.

4.8The app delegate and push registration

PushDelegate is the whole reason the app has a delegate: the device token arrives through didRegisterForRemoteNotificationsWithDeviceToken and nowhere else, the orientation query arrives through supportedInterfaceOrientationsFor, and the watch mirroring handler must be installed at launch. PushService is one object rather than two because registration and the inbox share the state that matters: the token, which arrives long after the sign-in that asked for it and is needed again at sign out to delete the row.

  • Authorisation is never requested at launch. A permission prompt on first run, before the app has shown anyone anything worth being interrupted about, is the fastest way to a permanent no. It is asked from the notification inbox, the first time that screen is opened.
  • The registration is keyed to the active account and re-pushed on every foreground, because the row carries the timezone the send hour is read in; somebody who has flown somewhere would otherwise keep being nudged at eight in the morning where they used to live.
  • Deregistration happens before the session goes, with the token captured by value, because deleting the row needs the access token of the account whose row it is. Left behind, that row would push one person's sleep onto a phone now showing somebody else's name.
  • A nudge that arrives while the app is open is still shown. The point of the channel is that LIFO speaks first; suppressing it because someone happens to be looking at the app would drop the message entirely. A tap puts the nudge in the inbox and RootView opens the coach on it, seeding the sentence but not the numbers, which are worked out now against the store as it stands.

4.9Two shells, one set of screens

RootView reads the platform's size class once and draws one of two shells. A compact width gets the pill bar floating over the content along the bottom, and it stays put when the keyboard opens, letting the keyboard cover it: without .ignoresSafeArea(.keyboard) the whole stack is lifted and the bar rides up to sit on top of the note being written, in the strip someone is actually looking at.

A regular width gets the same bar stood on end as a left rail, as an overlay so a screen's canvas runs the full width underneath it. Overlays claim no layout room, which is why railInset exists for the screens to apply themselves. The rail withdraws while the pane is being worked with and comes back when that stops: 

// LIfeOS/App/RootView.swift
content
    // Scrolling or dragging anywhere in the pane counts as working with the
    // content. Simultaneous, not exclusive: it observes the touch rather than
    // claiming it, so scroll views, text selection and Pencil strokes all still see it.
    .simultaneousGesture(
        DragGesture(minimumDistance: 12)
            .onChanged { _ in withdrawRail() }
            .onEnded { _ in scheduleRailReturn() }   // 1400 ms later
    )
    .overlay(alignment: .leading) {
        PillNavBar(selection: $tab, items: navItems, axis: .vertical)
            .opacity(isRailVisible ? 1 : 0)
            .offset(x: isRailVisible ? 0 : -(metrics.gutter + 76))   // parked off the edge
            .allowsHitTesting(isRailVisible)
    }
    .overlay(alignment: .leading) {
        if !isRailVisible {
            Color.clear.frame(width: 28).contentShape(.rect)
                .onTapGesture { showRail() }   // a way back without scrolling something first
        }
    }

The keyboard is the other way of working with the pane, and the one where the rail is most in the way: on a landscape iPad the keyboard takes half the height and the note being written is what is left. So keyboardWillShow withdraws the rail and keyboardWillHide brings it back, and a tab change brings it back too, because a tab change is navigation, not content work. The 1400 millisecond return delay is what stops it flickering between the flicks of a fast scroll. Compact width never hides the bar: along the bottom it overlaps nothing that is being read.

Orientation

The iPhone target allows landscape in its build settings so that a workout video can be watched sideways, but almost nothing else in the app is laid out for it. OrientationLock therefore defaults to portrait on a phone and every orientation on an iPad, and the one screen that wants more asks for it while it is on screen and hands it back when it leaves. release() also requests a geometry update back to portrait, because a phone still held sideways would otherwise stay in a landscape the next screen cannot draw.

4.10Edge cases and tests

ConditionBehaviour
Session found, no store openAppShell keeps the person in onboarding; restoreSession is not allowed to promote past the gate without hasStore
Offline at launch with an expired token.active(stored): the session is kept and the next foreground tries again
Server refuses the refresh token (400, 401, 403, 422)Store cleared, .rejected, the person returns to signup with "Your session expired. Sign in again"
Rate limited or 5xx on refreshKept; a refusal must be definitive
Sign out during an in-flight refreshThe refresher re-reads the store after the network call and finds the token gone; returns .signedOut without saving
Refresh response names a different user idCleared and rejected; a refresh cannot replace the account's identity
Two restores at once (launch and foreground on a cold start)Coalesced onto one task, because the refresh token rotates on use
App kept open past the hourThe keep-alive loop wakes 45 seconds before expiry and renews
Twilio cannot deliverThe specific cause is named and "Use email instead" is offered; the flag survives the trip back to the identity screen
Wrong code, twiceShakes and buzzes both times; the counter, not a Bool, drives it
Autofill lands a code with no keystrokeNon-digits trimmed in the field, the Verify button remains
Upgrade from the single-store buildThe legacy session is adopted into the roster and default.store moved into the account's directory, once
Current account id with no matching keychain sessionRemoved in AccountSession.init; nothing opens
Store cannot be openedContainer nil, surfaces cleared, onboarding shown; never the previous account's data
Second account signs in on the same deviceOwn store file, own defaults suite, own keychain item; the roster keeps the first
Cover already presented at launchThe tour is an overlay, so nothing contends for the window

Tests

  • SessionRefreshTests: twelve cases, one per row of the refresh policy, including logoutDuringRefreshCannotResurrectTheSession and aRefreshCannotReplaceTheAccountIdentity.
  • SessionKeepAliveTests: the wake is late enough for the refresher to act, an already expired session still waits the floor, a clock jump does not spin.
  • AccountStoreTests: nobody signed in means no scope, a mismatched identity cannot open another account's store, a restored roster uses its own stored session, and the bug the type exists to fix: a second sign-in no longer overwrites the first.
  • UserScopeTests: two accounts get different files, an id cannot climb out of the accounts directory, the legacy store is adopted once and carries its write-ahead log, rows do not cross between accounts.
  • AuthErrorMappingTests, AuthRefreshURLTests, PhoneOTPTests, SignInChromeTests (status precedence and CodeDigits).
  • Native: SurfaceNativeChecks proves a delayed notification from a previous account is rejected and the next account starts with missing readings, never previous values.

4.11Study notes

Read in this order

  1. LIfeOS/App/LIfeOSApp.swift: the two-way switch on a container.
  2. LIfeOS/App/AccountSession.swift: init, then adopt(_:), then signOut().
  3. LifeOSKit/Sources/Integrations/AccountStore.swift: the roster and the keychain per account.
  4. LIfeOS/App/AppShell.swift: the three-way gate, the keep-alive loop, and handle(_ url:).
  5. LifeOSKit/Sources/Integrations/SessionRefresh.swift: read every guard as a bug report.
  6. LifeOSKit/Sources/Integrations/SupabaseAuth.swift: the three calls and AuthError.fromHTTP.
  7. LIfeOS/Features/Onboarding/ViewModel/OnboardingViewModel.swift: verifyCode and saveProfile.
  8. LIfeOS/App/RootView.swift, the wideShell and the rail functions.

Check yourself

  • Why are there two locks before RootView mounts? A session without a store reaches the first fetch and CoreData throws an exception Swift cannot catch; a store without a session is somebody's data with nobody signed in.
  • Which HTTP statuses sign a person out, and why only those? 400, 401, 403 and 422: the server refused the credential itself. 429 and 5xx are failures to answer, and a transport error is not an answer at all.
  • Why is the keep-alive margin 45 seconds rather than 90? isExpired has 60 seconds of slack; waking before that finds a healthy session and does nothing.
  • Why does KeychainAuthSessionStore() read the current account id from defaults directly? It is built from wherever a network call is made; going through the main-actor AccountStore would not be possible there, and defaulting to the current account is what stops every client presenting the old token after a switch.
  • What decides whether a person sees the profile step? AuthSession.hasProfile, derived from user metadata in the verify response. The door they tapped decides only copy.
  • Why is the resend countdown 60 seconds when the phone cooldown is 45? Email is governed by GoTrue's 60-second frequency; the countdown must clear the stricter of the two.

Chapter five

5Onboarding

Five pages of pitch with a cat that waves, then an identity, a six-digit code, a name, and the connections. Signup is mandatory and it is the only way in: a store belongs to an account, so there is nowhere for a signed-out person's data to live.

5.1Intent

Working backwards

Almanac opens on a lit 3D cat and five pages that say what the app is, one domain per page in the order the tabs appear. Signing in takes an email address or a phone number and a code, a first and last name, and then offers WHOOP, Fitbit, a bank through Plaid and Apple Health. Every connection is skippable. Nothing on the way in asks for a password. A returning user is sent straight into the app once the code is accepted; a new one gets one welcome screen and then Today.

Why is there an account at all?

Because the data outlives the phone, and because the app now supports several people on one device. The account is what lets Supabase hold notes, a profile and provider links, what Row Level Security keys every row to, and what names the SwiftData file this person's data lives in (Chapter 4). Without it a lost device is a lost year, and a second person signing in would inherit the first person's everything.

Why no password?

A password is a credential to lose, store and reset. A one-time code delivered to a channel the user already controls proves the same thing with no secret at rest and no reset flow to build.

Email or phone?

Email first. It is free through Resend to 3,000 a month, needs no A2P registration, and carries none of the SMS failure modes. An SMS costs about five cents and can fail four different ways. Phone is offered as the alternative, to the US and India only, and the app asks Supabase which channels are actually enabled before it renders the choice.

Why can every connection be skipped?

A screen that blocks on a WHOOP login is a screen people abandon. Everything Almanac shows degrades to a blank rather than a wrong number, so an unconnected app is honest, not broken. Every connection is offered again in Settings.

Flow anatomy

  • IntroScreen: five pages over one persistent SceneKit scene, with a "Skip" and a sign-in door for a returning user.
  • IdentityScreen: email and phone tabs, a dial-code picker, one field, one complaint at a time.
  • CodeScreen: six boxes, verification fired on the sixth digit, a shake on a wrong code.
  • ProfileStepScreen: photo, first and last name, birthday, height, gender, country. Only the name is required.
  • ConnectionsScreen: WHOOP, Fitbit, bank accounts, Apple Health, each with its live state.
  • FirstRunTour: one welcome screen after the account exists, shown once per account, however the person arrived.

5.2Files and folders

Features/Onboarding/
├── Model/
│   ├── OnboardingModels.swift        step enum, auth mode, intro pages, draft, dial codes, Gender
│   └── ProfilePhotoStore.swift       per-account avatar cache, LocalProfile, ProfileStore, ProfileSync

App/AppShell.swift                    chooses onboarding or RootView; owns the tour flag

OnboardingFlow lives beside ConnectionsScreen rather than in its own file because it is a twenty-line switch over OnboardingStep and nothing else. AppShell chooses between it and RootView, so the tab hierarchy is never constructed for a signed-out user. The session and account machinery it leans on is described in Chapter 4; this chapter is about the screens and the rules they enforce.

5.3Model

// LIfeOS/Features/Onboarding/Model/OnboardingModels.swift
enum OnboardingStep: Equatable {
    case intro
    case identity            // phone or email
    case code                // OTP (phone or email)
    case profile             // name, country
    case connections         // Whoop and Health, all optional
    case signedIn            // returning user; nothing left to ask
}

enum AuthMode: Equatable {
    case signUp
    case signIn
}

OnboardingStep is a single value because the alternative, a pile of booleans, can represent states that do not exist. A user cannot be on the code screen and the profile screen at once, and the type should say so. AuthMode is the door the user came through, and it changes copy and nothing else. With OTP there is no password, so sign-in and signup are the same three steps; picking the wrong door is harmless by design, because the branch after verify is what actually routes. 

// LIfeOS/Features/Onboarding/Model/OnboardingModels.swift
struct SignupDraft: Equatable {
    var channel: SupabaseAuthChannel = .email
    var phone = ""
    var dialCode = "+1"
    var email = ""
    var code = ""
    var firstName = ""
    var lastName = ""
    var country = Locale.current.region?.identifier ?? "US"

    var photo: Data?          // already downsized
    var birthDate: Date?
    var heightCM: Double?     // always centimetres, whatever the field shows
    var gender: Gender = .unspecified

    var e164: String { dialCode + phone.filter(\.isNumber) }

    var canSendCode: Bool {
        channel == .phone
            ? PhoneOTP.isAcceptable(e164)
            : email.contains("@") && email.contains(".")
    }
    var canVerify: Bool { code.filter(\.isNumber).count >= 6 }
    var canFinishProfile: Bool {
        !firstName.trimmingCharacters(in: .whitespaces).isEmpty
            && !lastName.trimmingCharacters(in: .whitespaces).isEmpty
    }
}

The draft holds what the user typed, before any of it is trusted. The three can… properties are the only validation in the feature, and they live on the model rather than in a view so a disabled button and a rejected submit can never disagree. Three details are worth noticing:

  • The photo is Data, not UIImage. That keeps the draft a value type that can be compared for equality, and it means the bytes are already the downsized JPEG that will be uploaded, so no view holds a multi-megabyte camera-roll original.
  • Height is always centimetres internally. The imperial fields on the profile step are bindings that translate for display. Storing the number in whichever unit the user happened to be typing is how a height ends up silently wrong after a locale change.
  • Only the name is required. Everything else on the profile step sharpens what the app can say, and none of it is worth blocking someone at the door for.

Gender is deliberately not a biological-sex field wearing a friendlier label. It is how someone wants to be addressed, "Prefer not to say" is the default and a real answer, and stored returns nil for it so nothing is written to the server. If health baselines ever need sex, that is a different question with different answers, and HealthConnectionViewModel already reads it from Health's own characteristic rather than from here (17.4).

DialCountries.all is built from Locale.Region.isoRegions crossed with a hand-typed table of known dial codes, so the list is complete and localised while a region with no known code is dropped rather than guessed at. Offering the wrong prefix sends an SMS into the void, and the user has no way to tell that is what happened. otpRegions is ["US", "IN"]: the country picker on the identity screen is filtered to those two, and the view model resets a draft whose locale is elsewhere to the US.

5.4ViewModel

// LIfeOS/Features/Onboarding/ViewModel/OnboardingViewModel.swift
@MainActor @Observable
final class OnboardingViewModel {
    private(set) var step: OnboardingStep = .intro
    private(set) var mode: AuthMode = .signUp
    var draft = SignupDraft()

    private(set) var isBusy = false
    private(set) var errorMessage: String?
    private(set) var phoneSendFailed = false
    private(set) var resendIn = 0
    private(set) var availableChannels: Set<SupabaseAuthChannel> = []
    private(set) var isSignedIn: Bool
    private(set) var session: AuthSession?

    private var store: any AuthSessionStoring
    private var auth: SupabaseAuth?
    private var restoreTask: Task<Bool, Never>?

    func loadChannels() async
    func restoreSession() async -> Bool
    func sendCode() async
    func verifyCode() async
    func saveProfile() async
    func signOut()
}

The rules that live here, and nowhere else:

  • Channel availability is asked, not assumed. loadChannels() reads auth/v1/settings. Email stays the default when it is configured and the draft quietly falls back to phone when it is not; phoneUnavailableNote explains a missing SMS provider rather than leaving a dead tab on screen.
  • Email sends a six-digit code, not a magic link. Including {{ .Token }} in the project's email template is what makes GoTrue send a code, and verifyCode() posts it to auth/v1/verify exactly as phone does, with no per-channel branch.
  • The account, not the door, decides what comes next. After verify the step is session.hasProfile ? .signedIn : .profile. A "Sign in" tap with no account still creates one; a "Get started" tap on an existing account skips the profile step it already has answers for.
  • Verify also records the account. The same call adds the session to AccountStore, clears the pre-accounts keychain slot, and re-points the view model's own store at the per-account slot. From here on every network client in the app reads this account's token (Chapter 4).
  • A failed profile write does not strand the user. The account already exists by then, so saveProfile() records the error and advances to .connections anyway. Blocking the last step of signup on a metadata write would trade a cosmetic failure for an unusable app.
  • The photo goes to storage before the row. saveProfile() uploads the avatar first and only then saves the profiles row, so the row never points at an object that does not exist. A failed upload costs the picture and not the profile; it is a try?.
  • Names still go to user_metadata as well. The profile row is the source of truth for display, but hasProfile is derived from user_metadata.first_name when a session is refreshed, and that is what decides whether a returning user is sent through signup again. Both writes are needed.
  • Resend is rate-limited in the UI. A sixty-second countdown starts on every send. Sixty, not forty-five: phone's Edge Function cooldown is 45 seconds, but email posts straight to GoTrue, whose auth.email.max_frequency is 60. The countdown has to clear the stricter of the two or "Resend code" invites a 429.
  • isSignedIn is stored, not computed. A computed store.load() != nil is invisible to @Observable, which once left the shell showing the app after a sign-out until something else happened to redraw it.
  • Restoring is one call, and it is shared. restoreSession() holds the in-flight Task so a launch, a foreground and the keep-alive loop arriving together await one refresh. Supabase rotates the refresh token on use, so the second of a concurrent pair would present a token the first had just retired and be refused.
// LIfeOS/Features/Onboarding/ViewModel/OnboardingViewModel.swift
func verifyCode() async {
    guard let auth, draft.canVerify else { return }
    isBusy = true
    errorMessage = nil
    defer { isBusy = false }

    do {
        let session = try await auth.verify(
            code: draft.code.filter(\.isNumber),
            destination: draft.destination,
            channel: draft.channel
        )
        try AccountStore().add(Account(userID: session.userID,
            label: session.email ?? session.phone ?? "Account"), session: session)
        AccountStore().clearLegacySession()
        store = KeychainAuthSessionStore(account: session.userID)
        self.session = session
        isSignedIn = true
        step = session.hasProfile ? .signedIn : .profile
    } catch let error as AuthError {
        errorMessage = error.readable
    } catch {
        errorMessage = "That code didn't work"
    }
}

The initialiser has one more rule worth knowing. It reads the keychain synchronously and, if a session is there, decides the opening step at once: .connections if the per-account defaults say the person got that far and quit, otherwise .signedIn or .profile by hasProfile. That is what lets a relaunch land on the app without flashing the intro for a frame.

hasProfile defaults to false on decode, by hand A session already in the keychain from before this field existed has no hasProfile key. A synthesised Decodable would throw on it and sign every existing user out on the upgrade, so AuthSession writes its own initialiser and defaults the missing key to false. That default is safe only because the flag is read once, immediately after verify(); a restored session never consults it again.

5.5View

The intro and the cat

IntroScreen renders IntroPage.all in a TabView pager under a hero that stays put while the pages slide. The pages are data rather than five hand-written views for the same reason as before: a loop cannot let page three fall out of step with page one. At accessibility text sizes the pager is replaced with a single continuous reading surface, so a nested horizontal pager does not fight vertical accessibility scrolling. The copy height is measured with onGeometryChange and the largest page wins, so the hero does not jump between pages of different length.

The hero is OnboardingCat, a UIViewRepresentable over an SCNView. It is a real lit character rather than an image sequence: an orthographic camera, an ambient light and one omni key light, a physically based coat material, and a body built from about thirty scaled spheres plus two extruded ear shapes and two extruded arcs for the smile. The horizontal ink lines that make it read as the app's dotted illustration style come from a surface shader modifier: 

// LIfeOS/Features/Onboarding/View/OnboardingCat.swift
coat.shaderModifiers = [.surface: """
    #pragma body
    float row = _surface.position.y * 16.0;
    float edge = abs(fract(row) - 0.5);
    float aa = max(fwidth(row), 0.025);
    float ink = 1.0 - smoothstep(0.14 - aa, 0.14 + aa, edge);
    _surface.diffuse.rgb *= mix(1.0, 0.035, ink);
    """]

Rows are computed from view-space y, so they stay horizontal as the cat turns, and fwidth softens each edge at the rendered resolution so the lines do not shimmer. Motion is a handful of SCNActions: a breathing rise, a head tilt, a tail curl, an eye blink on a 4.6 second keyframe loop, and a wave that plays on page change and on tap. All of it is cheap by construction: the view is capped at 30 frames per second, the scene is paused whenever the screen is not active or Reduce Motion is on, and dismantleUIView drops the scene entirely. With Reduce Motion the cat still turns to face each page, it just snaps instead of animating.

The signup scaffold

// LIfeOS/Features/Onboarding/View/SignupScreens.swift
struct SignupScaffold<Content: View, Action: View>: View {
    let title: String
    let subtitle: String
    var step = 1
    var totalSteps = 3
    var showsProgress = true
    var onBack: (() -> Void)?
    @ViewBuilder let content: Content
    @ViewBuilder let action: Action
}

Every signup step is the same shape: a back control, the wordmark, a progress rule, a title, a subtitle, one field group, and one primary action pinned to the bottom in a safeAreaInset. SignupScaffold owns that shape so the three screens differ only in their content, which is what keeps them from drifting apart visually as they are edited. Sign-in mode hides the progress rule and counts two steps rather than three; a returning user has no profile step to count.

The code screen does the work instead of asking for it

This is the screen people fail on, so it is built to remove the ways of failing. The single tracked text field is gone; CodeField from DesignSystem draws six boxes and calls back the moment the sixth digit lands, so verification fires without a tap. Autofill can land a whole code with no keystroke, so a Verify button is kept for that user. A wrong code bumps a counter, and the counter drives both a spring shake and an error haptic: 

// LIfeOS/Features/Onboarding/View/SignupScreens.swift
@State private var wrongAttempts = 0
...
CodeField(text: $model.draft.code, count: 6) { verify() }
    .shake(wrongAttempts)
    .animation(.spring(response: 0.28, dampingFraction: 0.4), value: wrongAttempts)
...
.onChange(of: model.errorMessage) { _, new in
    guard new?.isEmpty == false else { return }
    wrongAttempts += 1
}
.sensoryFeedback(.error, trigger: wrongAttempts)

A counter rather than a Bool, because two bad codes in a row must shake twice, and a Bool that is already true animates nothing.

One complaint at a time

The identity screen can have three things to say at once: a validation error, a configuration problem, and a note that SMS is off. Stacked, they read as a broken app. InlineStatus.resolve picks the single most actionable one, with precedence error, then configuration, then warning, and treats whitespace as absence so an empty string never paints a red gap. The "Use email instead" escape is kept below the status rather than folded into it: it is an action the user can take, not another thing going wrong.

The profile step

A PhotosPicker circle at the top, two name fields, then four labelled rows that read as a set: birthday, height, gender, country. The birthday picker opens on a plausible adult date thirty years back rather than today, so the wheel is not three decades of scrolling. Height shows feet and inches where the locale is imperial and centimetres elsewhere, through bindings that only translate; the stored truth is centimetres. The picked photo is downsized before it is kept, because a camera-roll original is several megabytes and this is displayed at 96 points (17.6 for the maths).

Connections, and the flow

ConnectionsScreen is the only onboarding screen that reads live state. It takes the four shared connection view models that AppShell owns, so a connection made here is already made when Settings opens later. Each row shows the provider's own statusDetail, a spinner while it connects or syncs, a "Connected" label once it has, and a disabled button with "Available when this service is enabled" when the build lacks the provider's configuration. The Apple Health row calls health.connect(), which is the permission prompt and the first sync in one; the same view model serves Today's empty-state button and the Connections page in Settings. 

// LIfeOS/Features/Onboarding/View/ConnectionsScreen.swift
struct OnboardingFlow: View {
    @Bindable var model: OnboardingViewModel
    ...
    var body: some View {
        Group {
            switch model.step {
            case .intro:       IntroScreen(onStart: { model.beginSignup() },
                                           onSignIn: { model.beginSignIn() })
            case .identity:    IdentityScreen(model: model)
            case .code:        CodeScreen(model: model)
            case .profile:     ProfileStepScreen(model: model)
            case .connections: ConnectionsScreen(model: model, whoop: whoop, fitbit: fitbit,
                                                 health: health, plaid: plaid, onFinish: onFinish)
            case .signedIn:    ProgressView().controlSize(.large)
            }
        }
        .animation(.easeInOut(duration: 0.28), value: model.step)
        .onChange(of: model.step) { _, step in
            if step == .signedIn { onFinish() }
        }
    }
}

onFinish is called from onChange rather than from the .signedIn view body, because a body can run more than once for a single state and onFinish flips persisted app state.

The welcome

FirstRunTour replaced a six-page second carousel with one scrollable screen: the cat, "Welcome home.", three rows pointing at Today, connections and the coach, and an "Open my day" button. It is presented by AppShell as an overlay rather than a fullScreenCover, because iOS can restore a previously presented cover at launch and two covers contending for one window silently drops one. Its flag, hasSeenFirstRunTour, is stored in the per-account defaults and is separate from hasFinishedOnboarding, so it fires exactly once per account however the person arrived: signup, sign-in, or skip. A 400 millisecond delay and a cancellation check keep a stale tour from presenting over a shell that is already going away.

5.6How it works

Step by step, for a new user on a fresh install:

  1. LIfeOSApp finds no account, so AccountSession.container is nil and AppShell is mounted with hasStore: false. It renders OnboardingFlow.
  2. The identity screen's .task asks auth/v1/settings which channels exist and logs, rather than shows, a missing anon key.
  3. "Send code" posts to auth/v1/otp for email or to the otp-start Edge Function for phone (Chapter 20). The step becomes .code and the sixty-second countdown starts.
  4. The sixth digit fires verifyCode(). On success the session goes into the per-account keychain slot, the account into the roster, and the step branches on hasProfile.
  5. The profile step uploads the avatar, saves the profiles row, mirrors it into the per-account local caches, writes the names into user_metadata, and records "onboarding.step" = "connections" so a quit here resumes here.
  6. Connections are offered. "Continue to LifeOS" calls onFinish.
  7. AppShell.onFinish hands the account and session to AccountSession.signIn, which opens this account's store, clears the resume marker, and animates hasFinishedOnboarding to true. The whole scene re-roots on the new account id and RootView mounts for the first time.
  8. Four hundred milliseconds later the tour fades in, once.

For a returning user the shell's launch task calls restoreSession(). If the refresh succeeds, a store is open and the step is .signedIn, it sets hasFinishedOnboarding and pulls the profile from the server with ProfileSync.pull(), because the profile belongs to the account and not to the phone that typed it. A refused refresh is the only thing that sends someone back to signup.

5.7Performance and cost

  • No store, no tab hierarchy. Onboarding never touches SwiftData. The tabs, their view models and their first fetches are constructed only after an account has a store, which is also what prevents the uncatchable Core Data exception a fetch against an empty schema would raise (Chapter 4).
  • The keychain is read synchronously at init. isSignedIn and the opening step are decided before the first render, so a relaunch that restores a session never paints the intro carousel for a frame.
  • The cat costs what a 30 fps SceneKit view costs, and only while it is on screen. It pauses when the scene phase is not active, when Reduce Motion is on, and when the view disappears. Geometry is thirty low-segment spheres; the ink lines are a few shader instructions rather than a texture.
  • One refresh, however many callers. The shared restoreTask is the difference between one token rotation and a refused second one.
  • Email is the free channel. The default channel costs nothing per send; phone is rate-limited on both sides and restricted to two regions so SMS pumping has nowhere to aim (PhoneOTP.pumpingPrefix exists for the server's benefit).
  • Avatars are 512 points, scale 1, JPEG 0.8. A profile photo is a few tens of kilobytes by the time it is held in the draft, uploaded, and cached.
  • The profile pull is two small requests. One row, and a bucket listing scoped to the account's own folder; the picture itself is only downloaded when the listing's timestamp differs from the recorded one (17.6).
  • Nothing about the intro leaves the device. The first network request is the settings probe, made when the identity screen appears, not at launch.

5.8Edge cases and tests

ConditionBehaviour
No SUPABASE_ANON_KEY in the buildisConfigured is false; the identity screen shows "Sign-in is unavailable right now" and the key name goes to the log, not the screen
SMS not enabled on the projectThe phone tab stays but a warning explains it; sending is still possible by email
Email not enabled, phone isloadChannels() flips the draft to phone silently
Locale outside the US and IndiaThe draft resets to US, +1; the country picker offers only the two OTP regions
Wrong or expired codeInline error, shake, haptic; the step stays .code so the code can be retried without resending
SMS send failsError shown and phoneSendFailed set; "Use email instead" appears and survives backing out to the identity screen, but is cleared on the way to the intro
Resend tapped earlyDisabled until the sixty-second countdown clears; no 429 is ever provoked from the client
Profile write failsError recorded, flow advances to connections; the account is already valid
Avatar upload failsRow saved without avatar_path; the local copy still shows the picture
Quit during the profile or connections stepRelaunch resumes at connections; a quit before the profile step resumes at the profile step, by hasProfile
Returning user, session in keychainRenewed at launch, then straight into the app; profile pulled from the server
Returning user, session refusedSigned out with "Your session expired. Sign in again"
Returning user, offlineStays signed in. The credential is still good; only the network is missing
Foregrounded mid-signup after an hourSession renewed, but hasFinishedOnboarding is never promoted here, so nobody is yanked out of the profile step for switching apps
Second person signs in on the same deviceGets their own store, keychain slot, defaults suite, avatar file and profile cache; the first person's remain, unopened
Reduce Motion onThe cat still faces each page, without animating; the pager selects without easing
Accessibility text sizesThe pager becomes one continuous column; the header caps its own type at xxxLarge so the wordmark and Skip stay on one line

Tests

  • SessionRefreshTests (twelve tests) drives every branch of the refresher against a stub URLProtocol: an expired session is refreshed and saved, a rejected refresh token signs out, being offline, an outage and a 429 all keep the stored session, and a logout during a refresh cannot resurrect it.
  • AuthSessionProfileTests pins the hasProfile rules: a verified user with a first name has one, a whitespace-only name does not, a stored session without the key still decodes, and a refresh does not forget it.
  • AuthErrorMappingTests maps every Edge Function failure kind, plus the generic 502 fallback on both channels, to a specific readable sentence.
  • PhoneOTPTests: Indian mobiles accepted, Indian landline lengths rejected, US and the local test number accepted, other countries and short values rejected.
  • SignInChromeTests: InlineStatus precedence and blank handling; the code field fills from the left, ignores non-digits, and drops overflow.
  • AccountStoreTests (seventeen tests) covers the roster: a second account does not evict the first, signing out clears the legacy slot too, removing an account leaves its store on disk, a mismatched identity cannot open another account's store.
  • SessionKeepAliveTests: the wake is late enough to act on, an already expired session still waits the floor, a clock jump cannot produce a spin.

The signup screens themselves have no automated test; they are exercised by hand against the project's test-number map, where +1 123-456-7890 with code 123123 returns a real session and never reaches Twilio. Email has no equivalent bypass and depends on the Resend SMTP block being pushed to the hosted project.

The guest bypass is gone Earlier editions described a "Skip for now" guest mode. It no longer exists. A store belongs to an account, notes sync to one, and connections are held per account, so there is nowhere for a signed-out person's data to live that would not become somebody else's the moment they signed in. The intro's "Skip" only skips the pitch; it lands on the identity screen.

5.9Study notes

Read in this order

  1. Features/Onboarding/Model/OnboardingModels.swift: the step enum and the draft are the whole contract.
  2. Features/Onboarding/ViewModel/OnboardingViewModel.swift: read init, verifyCode, saveProfile, restoreSession in that order.
  3. App/AppShell.swift: the gate on line 57 and the three .task blocks.
  4. LifeOSKit/Sources/Integrations/SupabaseAuth.swift: AuthSession and its hand-written decoder.
  5. Features/Onboarding/View/SignupScreens.swift: CodeScreen first, then the profile step's height bindings.
  6. LifeOSKit/Sources/DesignSystem/SignInChrome.swift: InlineStatus.resolve and CodeField.
  7. Features/Onboarding/Model/ProfilePhotoStore.swift: ProfileSync.pull and the stamp.
  8. Features/Onboarding/View/OnboardingCat.swift: the shader and the idle actions.

Check yourself

  • Why does tapping "Sign in" with no account still create one? Because OTP has no password; the only thing that distinguishes a new user is hasProfile, read after verify, and the mode only changes copy.
  • Why is the resend countdown 60 seconds and not 45? Phone's Edge Function cooldown is 45s, but email goes straight to GoTrue whose max_frequency is 60s; the client has to clear the stricter one.
  • What would break if AuthSession used a synthesised decoder? Every session stored before hasProfile existed would fail to decode and sign its user out on upgrade.
  • Why is the tour an overlay and not a fullScreenCover? iOS can restore a cover at launch, and two covers contending for one window silently drops one.
  • Why does the profile step upload the photo before saving the row? So the row can never point at an object that does not exist; a failed upload loses the picture, not the profile.
  • Why does the identity screen probe auth/v1/settings rather than assuming both channels? A phone tab whose SMS provider is off is a button that silently fails; asking first turns that into a warning with a working alternative.

Chapter six

6Today and the calendar

The hub. A month of dots, a streak, today's schedule, and four tiles that each carry their own week. Every number on it comes from one local table and one local cache, and every tap opens something rather than explaining something.

6.1Intent

Working backwards

Today opens on a grid of dots, one per day this month. Filled dots are days you hit your targets, hollow dots are misses, faint dots are days with no data, and today is orange. Under it sit your schedule for the day and the week ahead, drawn from the phone's calendar, then a streak, then four tiles: steps, sleep, weight, recovery, each with the last seven days as bars. Tap a dot and the day opens in full; tap a tile and the metric opens on a page of its own with a week, a month or a year behind it; tap the calendar icon and a month you can walk through opens.

What makes a dot fill?

Meeting 3 of 4 daily goals: steps 8,000, sleep 7h, exercise 30 min, water 2,500 ml. All five values are editable in Settings (Chapter 17). The rule is deliberately explicit; a vague definition makes the entire grid meaningless.

What happens on a day with no data at all?

It renders as no-data, not as a miss, and it is excluded from streak arithmetic entirely. Leaving your watch on the charger is not a moral failure, and a system that punishes it teaches you to distrust the streak. A day with some data is judged on what it has: if steps are logged at 500 and nothing else was recorded, that is a miss.

If I change a goal, does history change?

Yes. Status is computed on read, never stored, so past dots re-evaluate against the new target immediately. The grid answers "how am I doing against my current standard".

Where does the schedule come from?

From EventKit, through a local SwiftData cache. The permission prompt fires from the agenda card's own connect button, never at launch, and the phone's calendar app remains the source of truth: Almanac reads a window of 30 days back and 90 forward, writes go straight back to EventKit, and the cache is re-synced afterwards so it shows what the provider actually stored.

Why is there a separate month screen?

Today's month grid shows how the streak has been going and cannot leave the current month. The month screen answers the other question, what is on, across any month, with day numbers and up to three event dots per day. Two questions, two grids.
