6.3Model

The hub's snapshot

// LIfeOS/Features/Today/Model/TodaySnapshot.swift
struct TodaySnapshot: Equatable {
    var date: Date = .now
    var cells: [DotCell] = []
    var streak: Int = 0

    var steps: Int?
    var stepsProgress: Double?
    var sleepMinutes: Int?
    var sleepProgress: Double?
    var weightKg: Double?
    var recoveryPct: Double?

    var stepsWeek: TrendSeries = TrendSeries(points: [])
    var sleepWeek: TrendSeries = TrendSeries(points: [])
    var weightWeek: TrendSeries = TrendSeries(points: [])
    var recoveryWeek: TrendSeries = TrendSeries(points: [])
    var stepsTarget: Double?
    var sleepTargetMinutes: Double?

    var calendarAccess: CalendarAccessState = .notDetermined
    var agenda: [CalendarEventSnapshot] = []
    var upcoming: [UpcomingEvent] = []
    var scheduledWorkoutTitle: String?

    var hasNoHealthData: Bool {
        steps == nil && sleepMinutes == nil && weightKg == nil && recoveryPct == nil
            && stepsWeek.points.isEmpty && sleepWeek.points.isEmpty
    }
}

Every metric is an optional, and each one that has a goal carries its progress alongside it, already divided. The view receives numbers it can render and nothing it has to interpret: it never sees a DailyMetrics, so rendering cannot fault a SwiftData object or trigger a fetch mid-layout. Two things are new since the previous edition. Each figure carries its week as a TrendSeries with a slot for every day, so a gap stays a gap in the chart rather than closing up. And hasNoHealthData exists because the app used to seed sixty days of invented history at first launch, so an empty hub was unreachable; now that the numbers are real, an unconnected day is the normal first thing a person sees and the screen has to offer a connection rather than a grid of dashes.

One metric, described once

// LIfeOS/Features/Today/Model/TodayMetric.swift
enum TodayMetric: String, Identifiable, Hashable, CaseIterable {
    case steps, sleep, weight, recovery

    var icon: String { ... }          // figure.walk, moon.fill, scalemass.fill, bolt.heart.fill
    var hue: ModuleHue { ... }        // activity, nutrition, body, recovery
    var unit: String? { ... }         // nil, nil, "kg", "%"
    var baseline: RoundedBarChart.Baseline { self == .weight ? .windowMinimum : .zero }
    var higherIsBetter: Bool { self != .weight }

    func value(in row: DailyMetrics) -> Double? { ... }
    func goal(in targets: GoalTargets) -> Double? { ... }
    func format(_ value: Double) -> String { ... }
}

The tile and the detail page used to be able to disagree: the grid decided steps were figure.walk in the activity hue, and a second screen would have decided again. Icon, hue, unit, formatting, the reading a row yields and the goal a day is judged against all live here once, and both surfaces read them. It also gives the navigation destination something to be: a value the stack can carry, rather than four booleans. Weight is the one exception that runs through everything. It is read against its own window rather than against nought, because it moves about a percent over a week and bars measured from zero would be indistinguishable, and it has no goal, because it is not a target to hit.

The calendar event, in three shapes

// LifeOSKit/Sources/Persistence/CalendarEvent.swift
public struct CalendarEventSnapshot: Equatable, Identifiable, Sendable {
    public let id: UUID            // local; provisional on a provider fetch
    public let source: CalendarEventSource
    public let sourceID: String    // EKEvent.eventIdentifier, qualified for recurring rows
    public let calendarTitle: String
    public let title: String
    public let startDate: Date
    public let endDate: Date
    public let isAllDay: Bool
    public let isRecurring: Bool
    public let location: String?
    public let notes: String?
}

public struct CalendarEventDraft: Equatable, Sendable {
    public var title: String
    public var startDate: Date
    public var endDate: Date
    public var isAllDay: Bool
    public var location: String?
    public var notes: String?
}

@Model public final class CalendarEvent { ... var sourceRaw: String ... var lastSyncedAt: Date }

The @Model is the cache row. The snapshot is what views and assistant tools receive, and Sendable is the point: a tool result crosses into an inference engine (Chapter 15), and a CalendarEvent cannot make that trip. The draft is what a caller supplies to create or edit, with no id and no source, because routing decides those. The natural key of a row is (source, sourceID); the local id never leaves the device. For a recurring occurrence the source id is qualified with the occurrence's start, because EventKit reuses one identifier across a whole series. A qualified id never resolves through event(withIdentifier:), so a write against an occurrence fails with unknownEvent instead of silently editing the wrong one, and the sheet refuses such writes before that can happen.

The day sheet and the metric page

DayDetailSnapshot is Identifiable on its date because .sheet(item:) presents it. It lists every habit that currently exists, done or not, deliberately not filtered by creation date, which is why the sheet's header is a count and never a grade: an old day can list a habit that did not exist then. MetricDetailSnapshot carries a MetricRange of week, month or year and a MetricBar per bucket. The grain is not a separate choice: a week is seven days, a month thirty days, a year twelve months, because a year drawn as 365 bars is a smear three points wide and a week drawn as one bar is not a chart.

6.4ViewModel

TodayViewModel.load(): one pass over the rows

// LIfeOS/Features/Today/ViewModel/TodayViewModel.swift
func load() {
    guard let context else { return }
    let store = MetricsStore(context: context, calendar: calendar)
    do {
        let targets = try store.goals().targets
        let start = calendar.date(byAdding: .day, value: -400, to: .now) ?? .distantPast
        let rows = try store.metrics(from: start, to: .now)      // most recent first

        var statusByDay: [Date: DayStatus] = [:]
        var ordered: [DayStatus] = []
        for row in rows {
            let status = evaluate(row.reading, against: targets)
            statusByDay[calendar.startOfDay(for: row.date)] = status
            ordered.append(status)
        }

        let cells = MonthGridLayout.cells(monthContaining: .now, calendar: calendar, today: .now,
            status: { date in
                switch statusByDay[calendar.startOfDay(for: date)] {
                case .onTarget: .onTarget
                case .missed:   .missed
                case .noData, nil: .noData
                }
            })

        var rowByDay: [Date: DailyMetrics] = [:]
        for row in rows { rowByDay[calendar.startOfDay(for: row.date)] = row }
        let week = TrendSeries.days(endingOn: .now, count: 7, calendar: calendar)
        func series(_ value: (DailyMetrics) -> Double?) -> TrendSeries {
            TrendSeries(points: week.map { day in
                TrendPoint(date: day, value: rowByDay[day].flatMap(value))
            })
        }
        ...
        snapshot = TodaySnapshot(... streak: currentStreak(statuses: ordered), ...)
        if let detail { select(detail.date) }
    } catch {
        assertionFailure("Today load failed: \(error)")
    }
}

Inside load(), in order:

  1. Read GoalTargets from the store, which materialises defaults on first access.
  2. Fetch four hundred days ending now, most-recent-first. Bounded on purpose: the grid needs this month and the streak needs recent history, never the whole table.
  3. evaluate each row once into a date-keyed dictionary. Rebuilding that map inside the per-day closure would re-evaluate every row about thirty times per load.
  4. Ask MonthGridLayout for the cells, mapping DayStatus to DotState here because Persistence must not depend on DesignSystem.
  5. Compute currentStreak from the same ordered statuses.
  6. Build the four week series from the rows already in hand: a second dictionary and seven lookups per metric rather than a second query. The rows stay inside this method; only plain numbers reach the snapshot.
  7. Read today's agenda and the next seven days from CalendarStore, two windowed fetches.
  8. Read the title of any workout scheduled for today from the bookmark store and the catalog cache (Chapter 10). Two reads rather than a relationship: the catalog is a cache the next refresh can drop a row from, so a schedule pointing at a vanished video simply shows nothing.
  9. Publish one TodaySnapshot. A single assignment means a single render.
  10. If the day sheet is open, re-derive it, so an external write, a WHOOP sync or a habit tick, updates the sheet as well as the grid behind it.

A read failure trips an assertionFailure and leaves the previous snapshot in place rather than blanking the screen. Nothing about a failed local fetch is recoverable by the user, so the last good state is the most useful thing to keep showing.

select(date) builds the day sheet from three stores: the metrics row for that day, the habit ticks on it, and the events overlapping it. A day with no metrics row is not an early return; its habits are still worth showing and the metric rows render as blanks. toggleHabit writes through PlanStore and then does nothing else: the save fires ModelContext.didSave, RootView reloads every view model, and load() re-derives the open sheet. That is the one refresh path; calling select() again here would repeat the 400-day pass a second time per tap.

MetricDetailViewModel: its own object, on purpose

A view model of its own rather than more fields on TodayViewModel, because that one runs a 400-day pass on every save in the app, and hanging a year of bucketing off it would repeat that work for a screen nobody is looking at. load(metric) makes one fetch bounded by the range, then buckets in memory: 

// LIfeOS/Features/Today/ViewModel/MetricDetailViewModel.swift
let buckets = Self.buckets(range: range, endingOn: now, calendar: calendar)
guard let start = buckets.first else { return }
let rows = try store.metrics(from: start, to: now)     // one fetch, not one per bucket

var readingsByBucket: [Date: [Double]] = [:]
for row in rows {
    guard let value = metric.value(in: row),
          let bucket = Self.bucket(for: row.date, range: range, calendar: calendar)
    else { continue }
    readingsByBucket[bucket, default: []].append(value)
}
let bars = buckets.map { bucket in
    MetricBar(date: bucket,
              label: Self.label(for: bucket, range: range, calendar: calendar),
              value: readingsByBucket[bucket].map { $0.reduce(0, +) / Double($0.count) })
}

Every bucket is present whether or not it has a reading, for the same reason TrendSeries.days keeps gaps: compacting the buckets that do have readings draws a chart whose neighbouring bars are not a bucket apart, which is a quieter lie than a false zero but a lie. A day has at most one row, so the mean is that row's own value in the two short windows; it only averages anything in the year view, where a bucket is a month. The month view labels one bar in five, because thirty labelled bars on a phone is a grey smudge. The headline figure is the most recent actual reading in the window, which is usually but not always today: a night's sleep or a recovery score can be a day behind, and the year view's monthly aggregate must never replace it.

MonthViewModel: one fetch per month

The month screen fetches the visible month padded by a week either side, then groups with CalendarDayIndex.group so a cell asks a dictionary rather than the store. A month is up to 42 cells and every one wants a count; one fetch, not one per cell. The padding is what makes the leading and trailing cells answerable, since the first row of a month usually starts in the previous one. Stepping remembers the day number the person last picked separately from the selection, so walking from 31 March to February and back returns to the 31st rather than the 28th; MonthGridLayout.stepping clamps only for display.

6.5View

// LIfeOS/Features/Today/View/TodayScreen.swift
struct TodayScreen: View {
    let snapshot: TodaySnapshot
    let onSelectDay: (Date) -> Void
    let onConnectCalendar: () -> Void
    let onAddEvent: () -> Void
    let onTapEvent: (CalendarEventSnapshot) -> Void
    let onOpenToday: () -> Void
    var onConnectHealth: () -> Void = {}
    var isHealthConnected = false
    var onSelectMetric: (TodayMetric) -> Void = { _ in }
    ...
}

The screen takes a value and a set of intents and owns nothing: no view model, no store, no context. Every tap names what was tapped and stops there. What a day opens, what a metric opens, whether the permission sheet fires, are all the shell's decisions, which is what keeps this a pure function of its inputs and a preview a single literal.

One column or two

On a phone the order is month, scheduled workout, agenda, streak, health prompt, stat grid, with layout.statColumns deciding whether tiles are one or two across. On a wide pane the month, workout, agenda and streak stand in a left column capped at 520 points, and the stats stand beside them two across. The cap is the point, not merely a column count: a dot grid divides whatever width it is given by seven, so a full-width month on a 1300 point pane draws 170 point dots and shoves every stat below the fold, the opposite of what more room should buy. There is no maxContentWidth on this screen, because both arrangements are grids and the cap exists for prose.

The pieces

  • MonthCalendarView composes DateHeadline (the day numeral at masthead size), WeekdayHeader (narrow symbols rotated to the calendar's first weekday, today's column accented) and DotGrid. Cells arrive already computed; deriving them in a body would re-run the calendar maths on every render.
  • AgendaCard always renders, because it carries the three permission states. Not determined shows "Connect calendar", denied shows "Open Settings", authorised shows up to four rows grouped by DayPart (all day, morning, afternoon, evening, each with its own icon and pastel) and a "+N more" that opens the day sheet. Upcoming is a second card, shown only with access and something to show, five rows grouped by day label. Rows are capped before grouping so the card's height budget stays the same whatever shape the day has.
  • TrendStatTile is the tile with the week: label, pastel icon bubble, the numeral, and a RoundedBarChart of seven bars at 74 points on a phone and 88 on a wide pane. A week with no readings draws the plain figure and still holds the chart's height, so a dataless tile stands as tall as its siblings. Every tile is a plain button into MetricDetailScreen, built from TodayMetric.allCases rather than written out four times.
  • The health prompt appears only when there is nothing to show and nothing attached. A connected strap that has not synced yet is a different situation, and telling that person to connect something would be wrong.
  • The scheduled workout card is informational: the library is where a workout is played, and a card that opened a video would put the player two taps from a calendar grid.

The sheets

DayDetailSheet renders past days as history with static marks and gives only today controls, so the grid can never be rewritten after the fact. A not-done habit on a past day is a dash rather than a cross, because the list may include habits that did not exist that day and a cross would read as a verdict the sheet has no standing to make. A missing metric renders as a dash rather than hiding the row, so the sheet's height does not jump between days.

EventSheet is a pure function of its EventSheetPresentation, create or edit. Every write goes out through onSave and onDelete, which is what keeps it previewable without EventKit. A recurring occurrence renders read-only, fields disabled, Save and Delete hidden, with "This repeats. Edit the series in your calendar app." Editing one occurrence needs series semantics the app does not implement, and pointing at the calendar app is honest where silently mutating the occurrence would not be. The end date is clamped on save rather than blocked: a timed event floors at fifteen minutes after its start, an all-day event only at its start, since end equals start is the normal single-day shape. A new event defaults to the next full hour today, or 9am on any other day, because "next Tuesday at 16:41" is nobody's intent.

MonthScreen carries a swipe gesture on the grid to step months, chevrons for anyone who would rather aim than swipe, a date jump sheet, and a "Today" button disabled while today is selected. On a wide enough pane ViewThatFits puts the 400 point calendar panel and the agenda side by side. It never writes: create and edit leave through the caller, which owns CalendarSync, and it re-reads on ModelContext.didSave so a write from the sheet it opened lands in its dots.

The quick log and the journal

QuickLogSheet logs water and weight, the two metrics with no automatic source, and is now reached from inside Begin Activity rather than from a bar button. Water accumulates: "add 250 ml" is the intent, not "today's total is 250 ml". JournalEntrySheet is a bare text editor with no title and no fields, because asking for either is friction on the one thing that has to stay effortless.

6.6How it works

The calendar pipeline

  1. RootView.syncCalendar() runs on the launch task, on every scene activation, and after any calendar write. It does nothing unless CalendarAccessState.current is .authorized, which requires both the system permission and the per-account opt-in flag: a device permission granted for one Almanac account does not authorise another.
  2. CalendarSync.sync() asks each source whether it is authorised, fetches the window from those that are, and skips any that throw. Partial data beats an empty screen, and errors are not surfaced because sync is ambient, never a user-visible request.
  3. CalendarMerge.merge dedups across sources on lowercased title plus start date, EventKit winning because that copy is writable offline and is what the OS shows elsewhere. Google is the second source the protocol is shaped for; today only EventKit is wired.
  4. CalendarStore.apply reconciles the fetch into the cache by natural key: an existing row is updated in place and keeps its local id, a new one adopts the snapshot's, and in-window rows absent from the fetch are deleted only when their source was authoritative this pass. Rows outside the window are never touched.
  5. The save fires didSave and the hub's agenda repaints.

Writes go the other way. EventSheet hands a draft to RootView, which calls calendarSync.create, update or delete. Sync routes the write to the source that owns the event, and then runs a full sync() so the cache reflects what the provider actually stored. Providers normalise all-day handling and time zones, so trusting the local draft would drift.

Keeping today's numbers moving

A step count climbs until midnight, and a sync at breakfast is stale by lunch. Two mechanisms keep the tiles honest while the app is open. HealthSyncWindow.days(since:) decides which days a sync re-reads: always today, plus the day of the last sync and every day since, because a night's sleep is recorded against the morning it ends and the day already covered can still gain a value. A first sync backfills thirty days, the month the dot grid shows, and no further, because Health keeps the data regardless and a longer backfill can be added the day something needs it. A last-sync stamp from the future is treated as a clock change and syncs today alone.

Then HealthConnectionViewModel.startWatching() runs an HKObserverQuery per metric for as long as the app is in front. Each change re-runs the sync, then sleeps fifteen seconds; the stream buffers one event, so a day's steps arriving in dozens of batches becomes one re-read per quarter minute rather than one per batch. The observers are torn down when the app leaves the foreground, so a phone in a pocket is not running ten queries a quarter minute. The sync writes through MetricsStore, the save reloads the hub, and the numeral moves. Nothing in the watcher knows about a screen.

6.7Performance and cost

  • Bounded fetches. The hub reads 400 days; the metric page reads only its range; the month screen reads one month plus a week either side; the agenda reads one day and the next seven. Nothing reads the whole table.
  • Evaluate once, look up many times. Status and rows are keyed by day in two dictionaries with reserved capacity; the grid, the streak and the four week series are all lookups against them.
  • Bucket in memory, not in the store. The year view is one fetch and a dictionary, not twelve round trips.
  • Reload only what is on screen. reloadAll() reloads the metric page only while it is pushed, and the money detail only while it is open.
  • Event-driven, never polled. The single didSave subscription in RootView is the whole refresh mechanism; the Health observer stream is throttled to one re-read per fifteen seconds and stopped in the background.
  • One assignment, one render. The snapshot is built whole and assigned once; no intermediate state is published mid-load.
  • The chart maths is pure and static. RoundedBarChart.fraction and MonthGridLayout.cells take values and return values, so they are tested from the terminal and never recomputed inside a body.
  • The cache means the calendar works on a plane. Reads never touch EventKit directly; a sync that fails leaves the previous rows in place.
  • Nothing leaves the device. Calendar contents and the day sheet stay local. What an escalated assistant turn sends is described in Chapter 15 and Chapter 24.

6.8Edge cases and tests

ConditionBehaviour
Month boundariesLeading blanks from firstWeekday, padded to whole rows; only padding cells lack a date
Future days in the current monthRendered .future by position, never evaluated against goals
Today with partial dataRendered .today by position, so a half-logged day never shows as a miss
No data for a dayFaint dot; skipped by the streak; leading no-data days do not break it
Goal changed in SettingsNext load() re-evaluates all history; dots change
No health source connected and no dataThe tiles show dashes and a "Connect Apple Health" card appears; a connected strap that has not synced suppresses the card
Metric with no reading in the weekTile shows the figure or a dash and holds the chart's height blank
Weight week that is flatHalf-height bars: every reading is both the high and the low, and half reads as steady
Latest sleep or recovery is yesterday'sThe detail headline shows the latest actual reading and its date, never today's blank
Calendar never askedAgenda offers "Connect calendar"; the prompt fires on that tap only
Calendar deniedAgenda offers "Open Settings"
Calendar granted on the device, but for another accountNot authorised for this account until it opts in; the prompt is not shown again, the flag is
Event deleted in the Calendar appGone from the cache on the next sync, because EventKit was authoritative for its window
A source throws during syncIts previously synced rows are kept; it is not treated as having reported zero
Same event in EventKit and GoogleOne row, the EventKit copy
Recurring occurrence tappedRead-only sheet pointing at the calendar app
End dragged before startClamped on save: 15 minutes for a timed event, start itself for all-day
Multi-day or overnight eventAppears on every overlapping day in the month grid, excluding a midnight end, across daylight-saving changes
Habit tick on a past dayImpossible: past days render without controls, and toggleHabit guards on isToday as the second lock

Tests

  • GoalEvaluationTests and StreakTests: three of four is on target, two is a miss, exactly at goal counts, partial data is judged not excused, no-data days are skipped without breaking the streak.
  • MonthGridLayoutTests (eleven tests): August 2026 starts with five blanks, a Sunday-first month takes six, today overrides its status, days after today are future, stepping keeps the day number, clamps to a short month, reaches a leap 29th, and crosses a year boundary backwards.
  • TrendSeriesTests and RoundedBarChartTests: the average ignores gaps, the latest reading is not the last slot, a lone reading has no delta, points keep their gaps, the window minimum baseline spreads a metric that never nears zero, a flat week draws half bars.
  • CalendarStoreTests: applying the same fetch twice does not duplicate, an existing row keeps its local id, in-window rows absent from a fetch are deleted, out-of-window rows survive, pruning only touches authoritative sources.
  • CalendarSyncTests: a throwing source does not block the others and keeps its previously synced events, an unauthorised source is skipped, create dispatches to the first authorised source and resyncs, update routes to the owner.
  • CalendarMergeTests, CalendarFreeSlotTests, CalendarDayIndexTests: the dedup rule, gap subtraction with all-day events not blocking time, and overnight and daylight-saving spans.
  • HealthSyncWindowTests (eight tests): a first sync backfills a month, today is always included, a recent sync only re-reads today, a gap is backfilled including the day before it, a future stamp still syncs today.
The one test that matters most For every screen, an empty store must produce a snapshot whose readings are all nil. The hub, the metric page and the day sheet all obey it by construction: each optional is filled from a row that may not exist, and there is no default of zero anywhere in the path.

6.9Study notes

Read in this order

  1. Features/Today/ViewModel/TodayViewModel.swift: load() top to bottom.
  2. LifeOSKit/Sources/DesignSystem/MonthGridLayout.swift: the padding and the today/future rule.
  3. Features/Today/Model/TodayMetric.swift: why one enum describes both the tile and the page.
  4. Features/Today/ViewModel/MetricDetailViewModel.swift: the bucketing.
  5. LifeOSKit/Sources/Persistence/CalendarStore.swift: apply() and freeSlots().
  6. LifeOSKit/Sources/Integrations/CalendarSync.swift and EventKitSource.swift: the recurring-id qualification.
  7. LifeOSKit/Sources/Integrations/HealthSyncWindow.swift, then HealthConnectionViewModel.startWatching().
  8. Features/Today/View/AgendaCard.swift: DayPart and the row caps.

Check yourself

  • Why is the status map built before the grid closure and not inside it? The closure runs once per cell; building the map inside it would evaluate every row about thirty times per load.
  • Why do the week series reuse the 400-day rows? The rows are already in hand for the streak, so the week costs a dictionary and seven lookups rather than a second query.
  • What happens to a cached event whose source threw during sync? Nothing. Pruning only applies to sources that answered this pass, so the row survives.
  • Why is a recurring event's source id qualified with its start? EventKit shares one identifier across a series; qualifying it makes each occurrence a distinct cache row and makes accidental writes fail loudly.
  • Why does the metric page have its own view model? Because the hub reloads on every save in the app, and a year of bucketing must not ride along for a screen nobody is looking at.
  • Why does a Health sync re-read the day of the last sync as well as today? Sleep is attributed to the morning it ends, so a day already read can gain a value afterwards.

Chapter seven

7Health

One tab for everything the body reports: how it is doing, and what it did. Two halves behind an underline picker, one week strip that moves both to the same day, and a rule that runs through every card on the screen: a missing reading is a dash, never a zero.

7.1Intent

Revision D called this tab Body and split it four ways: Activity, Weight, Recovery, Wellness. The restructure of 25 August folded those four into two halves that answer two different questions. Health is how the body is doing: recovery, sleep, vitals against their own baselines, weight, and the journal. Fitness is what it did: calories burnt, steps, strain, the sessions themselves, and the training week. The tab bar has five slots and this one takes one of them, because Almanac is still not a fitness app; it is the place a life's signals meet, and the body is one of nine sectors (Chapter 13).

Working backwards

Open Health and the day is already chosen for you: today, with a week strip to step back. Four tracking tiles across the top show steps, sleep, weight and recovery for that day, each a door to its own history. Below them, Health or Fitness. Health opens with anything that is off, then recovery and calories, a sleep card with the night's stages, HRV and resting heart rate, blood oxygen and skin temperature read against your own fortnight, and every other reading Apple Health had for the day, grouped and listed only where a value exists. Fitness opens with the week's burn as bars, then today's movement, strain and heart rates, the day's workouts, and a card that says how the training week is adding up with a row into the workout library.

Why does the whole tab move to one selected day?

Because both halves are readings of the same day. If Health kept Tuesday and Fitness kept Thursday, a reader could compare Tuesday's recovery with Thursday's session and draw a conclusion from a comparison that was never real. RootView owns one date and fans it out to all four view models at once.

Both my iPhone and Watch count steps. Does that double?

No. Steps arrive through HKStatisticsQuery with a cumulative-sum option, which de-duplicates overlapping samples across sources. Summing raw samples client-side would roughly double every step count on a day you carried both devices.

What does "everything Apple Health holds" mean in practice?

Forty-seven metrics in a vocabulary enum, read every day the sync touches. Ten of them have named columns on the day row because scorers and charts read them by name; the other thirty-seven live in a JSON bag on the same row. The screen lists whichever groups actually have a value, so a person with a blood pressure cuff sees blood pressure and a person without never learns the row existed.

Where does weight come from?

The Renpho scale, via Apple Health. Renpho already syncs there, so Almanac never talks to Renpho directly: one less integration, one less credential to store.

What the tab deliberately does not do

  • It never diagnoses. An anomaly banner says "Resting HR is well above your 2-week baseline" and stops. "See a doctor" is a claim this data cannot support.
  • It never invents a verdict from missing data. No sleep all week means no sleep verdict, not "Low".
  • It never colours strain with the recovery bands. High recovery is good and green; high strain is hard work, and green would read as praise. Strain gets one plain accent.

Four view models, one screen

Activity, Body, Recovery and Wellness keep their own folders even though none of them owns a tab any more. A section is a view concern; what each one derives is not. Merging them into one view model would produce a class that loads a day, a week, a fortnight and sixty days for four unrelated readings, and would reload all of it whenever any part changed. Four small loaders means a date change costs exactly four fetches and nothing else.

7.3Model

Every snapshot is a value type with optional fields. That is the rule the whole app is built on, enforced by the types rather than by discipline at each call site. A day with the watch on the charger produces nils, and every nil renders as a dash. 

// LIfeOS/Features/Recovery/Model/RecoverySnapshot.swift
struct RecoverySnapshot: Equatable {
    // The day
    var recoveryPct: Double?
    var hrvMs: Double?
    var restingHR: Double?
    var dayStrain: Double?

    // Sleep quality
    var sleepMinutes: Int?
    var sleepPerformancePct: Double?
    var sleepEfficiencyPct: Double?
    var sleepConsistencyPct: Double?
    var sleepDebtMinutes: Int?

    // Vitals, each read against its own baseline
    var spo2Percentage: Double?
    var skinTempCelsius: Double?
    var respiratoryRate: Double?

    // The fortnight
    var recoveryTrend = TrendSeries(points: [])
    var hrvTrend = TrendSeries(points: [])
    var spo2Trend = TrendSeries(points: [])
    // ... five more series, the nights, naps, anomalies, weekRecovery

    var hasAnyReading: Bool {
        recoveryPct != nil || sleepMinutes != nil || dayStrain != nil || hrvMs != nil
    }
}

The fortnight rides inside the day's snapshot because half of these readings mean nothing alone. An SpO2 of 97.2 tells a reader nothing; a tenth above their own baseline does. So every vital carries a TrendSeries, and the card renders the delta from that series' average rather than the bare number.

hasAnyReading is how the screens tell "not connected" apart from "connected and quiet". Without it the Connect Whoop card would show to someone whose strap simply had a slow night.

TrendSeries keeps its gaps

// LifeOSKit/Sources/DesignSystem/TrendSeries.swift
public struct TrendPoint: Sendable, Equatable, Identifiable {
    public let date: Date
    public let value: Double?      // nil is a day with no reading
}

public struct TrendSeries: Sendable, Equatable {
    public let points: [TrendPoint]
    public var hasAnyReading: Bool { points.contains { $0.value != nil } }
    public var average: Double? {   // mean of the readings that exist
        guard !readings.isEmpty else { return nil }
        return readings.reduce(0, +) / Double(readings.count)
    }
    public var latest: Double? {    // most recent reading, not the last slot
        points.reversed().first { $0.value != nil }?.value ?? nil
    }
    public var deltaFromAverage: Double? {
        guard readings.count > 1, let latest, let average else { return nil }
        return latest - average
    }
}

Three decisions live here. The average ignores gaps rather than counting them as zero. The latest reading is the last non-nil point, because the window usually ends on a day Whoop has not scored yet. And a series with one reading has no delta: a lone value is its own average, and "0 from baseline" would imply a history that has not been collected.

The day row and its two bags

DailyMetrics keeps its ten named health columns from Revision D (steps, exercise minutes, sleep minutes, active energy, weight, water, resting HR, HRV, SpO2, respiratory rate) and the Whoop columns. What is new is a long tail of Apple Health metrics that have no column of their own, and a record of who wrote each value. 

// LifeOSKit/Sources/Persistence/DailyMetrics.swift
/// Everything Apple Health can supply that does not have a column of its
/// own, as a JSON dictionary keyed by `HealthMetric.rawValue`.
public var extrasData: Data?

/// Who wrote each value, as a JSON dictionary keyed by `HealthMetric.rawValue`.
public var sourcesData: Data?

public func extra(_ key: String) -> Double? { extras[key] }
public func setExtra(_ key: String, _ value: Double?) {
    var bag = extras
    if let value { bag[key] = value } else { bag.removeValue(forKey: key) }
    extras = bag
}

Why a bag and not thirty-seven more columns: most people have no data for most of the tail, and a column each would mean a schema change per metric for fields nothing queries. The bag keeps adding a metric to one enum case and one mapping. The one thing a bag must not lose is the distinction this model is built on: a missing key means no reading, and writing nil removes the key rather than storing a zero. Both bags are optional so a store written before they existed opens without a migration, which matters after the lesson in 10.8.

sourcesData stores raw strings rather than a typed source because Persistence sits below Integrations and must not import it. The vocabulary lives up there.

The vocabulary

HealthMetric is its own enum, deliberately not a set of HealthKit types, so the file builds and tests without the framework. It carries nine groups (movement, heart and fitness, body, sleep, vitals, intake, mind, walking, cycle), a title, a unit label, a decimal count, and three merge properties the arbiter reads: 

// LifeOSKit/Sources/Integrations/HealthMetric.swift
/// Measured by a strap worn on the body, so a wearable outranks the phone.
public var claimedByWearable: Bool {
    switch self {
    case .restingHR, .hrvMs, .spo2Percentage, .respiratoryRate,
         .sleepMinutes, .deepSleepMinutes, .remSleepMinutes,
         .coreSleepMinutes, .awakeMinutes, .timeInBedMinutes,
         .sleepEfficiencyPercentage, .readinessScore:
        true
    default:
        false
    }
}

/// A person can type this into the app, so a background sync must not
/// replace what they entered on purpose.
public var acceptsManualEntry: Bool {
    switch self {
    case .weightKg, .waterML: true
    default: false
    }
}

/// Health is the top authority among syncing sources: nothing else measures
/// this and nobody types it, so the latest reading is simply the truth.
public var healthIsAuthoritative: Bool {
    !claimedByWearable && !acceptsManualEntry
}

Cycle metrics (basal temperature, menstrual flow) are their own group and are gated by needsCycleConsent. The first authorisation request never asks for them. Not because they are more private than a heart rate, but because a permission sheet that asks every person for menstrual data is telling most of them the app has misread who they are.

7.4ViewModel

Four view models, each with the same shape: attach(context), select(date), load(). Each reads a different window and derives a different thing.

View modelWindowDerives
ActivityViewModel7 daysToday's steps, minutes, energy, resting HR; the day's workouts; seven DayValues of calories, Whoop's figure first, Health's as fallback
BodyViewModel60 daysThe latest weigh-in, the weekly delta, 14 points for the chart
RecoveryViewModel14 daysThe day's readings, eight trend series, the nights, naps, five anomaly checks, the week strip's recovery rings
WellnessViewModel7 days, plus the selected dayAverage sleep and exercise, workout days, two verdicts, the journal, the Apple Health groups

Recovery: one fetch, many readings

// LIfeOS/Features/Recovery/ViewModel/RecoveryViewModel.swift
let end = selectedDate
let start = calendar.date(byAdding: .day, value: -(Self.windowDays - 1), to: end) ?? end

// One fetch for the whole window. The selected day is picked out of
// it rather than fetched again.
let rows = try store.metrics(from: start, to: end)
let day = rows.first { calendar.isDate($0.date, inSameDayAs: end) }

let restingTrend = trend(rows, from: start, to: end) { $0.restingHR }

// History excludes the selected day: a spike must not drag the
// baseline toward itself on the very day it is being judged.
func history(_ series: TrendSeries) -> [Double?] {
    series.points.dropLast().map(\.value)
}

let anomalies = [
    AnomalyEvaluation.evaluate(metric: "Resting HR", today: day?.restingHR,
        history: history(restingTrend), threshold: .relativeAbove(0.10)),
    AnomalyEvaluation.evaluate(metric: "Skin temp", today: day?.skinTempCelsius,
        history: history(skinTrend), threshold: .absoluteAbove(1.0)),
    AnomalyEvaluation.evaluate(metric: "Blood oxygen", today: day?.spo2Percentage,
        history: history(spo2TrendSeries), threshold: .absoluteBelow(3.0)),
    AnomalyEvaluation.evaluate(metric: "HRV", today: day?.hrvMs,
        history: history(hrvTrendSeries), threshold: .relativeBelow(0.30)),
    // ... respiratory rate at .relativeAbove(0.08)
].compactMap { $0 }

The window is fourteen days because the Whoop sync window is fourteen days, so a chart never has a gap the sync could have filled. The trend helper builds a point for every calendar day in the window, not only the days with rows, which is what keeps a day Whoop never reported as a visible gap. Thresholds are relative where the metric scales with the person (heart rate, HRV) and absolute where it has a physiological unit (a degree of skin temperature means the same at any baseline). AnomalyEvaluation refuses to judge with fewer than seven readings in the history, because a noisy baseline raises false alarms.

Body: sixty days to find one number

// LIfeOS/Features/Body/ViewModel/BodyViewModel.swift
let start = calendar.date(byAdding: .day, value: -60, to: selectedDate) ?? .distantPast
let rows = try store.metrics(from: start, to: selectedDate)   // most-recent-first

let weighed = rows.compactMap { row in row.weightKg.map { (date: row.date, kg: $0) } }
var delta: Double?
if let newest = weighed.first,
   let weekAgo = weighed.first(where: { $0.date <= newest.date.addingTimeInterval(-6 * 86_400) }) {
    delta = newest.kg - weekAgo.kg
}

The hero is the most recent row that actually has a weight, which is not necessarily the most recent row. The delta is that weight minus the most recent weigh-in at least six days older; if none exists the delta is suppressed rather than computed over a shorter window, because a "weekly change" measured over two days is a wrong number wearing a right label. Sixty days rather than fourteen because people skip weeks, and a fortnight would suppress the delta for anyone who steps on the scale fortnightly.

Wellness: the journal is a note now

Revision D stored a journal entry as a PlanEntry of kind .journal. It is now a note page, one per day, in the notes store (Chapter 12). Writing twice in one evening appends to the day's page rather than filing a second entry, because two rows dated the same day would break the "did I write today" question the streak is built on. 

// LIfeOS/Features/Body/ViewModel/WellnessViewModel.swift
func addJournal(_ text: String) {
    let store = NotesStore(context: context, calendar: calendar)
    let entry = try store.journalEntry()
    var blocks = entry.blocks.filter { !($0.kind == .paragraph && $0.isEmpty) }
    blocks.append(contentsOf: NoteBlockParser.blocks(fromMarkdown: trimmed))
    try store.update(entry, blocks: blocks)
    load()
}

The same view model builds the Apple Health groups for the selected day. The week of rows above cannot answer "what did Health have for this day", so it fetches the one row separately and hands it to HealthDaySummary.groups(for:includingCycle:). The cycle switch it passes is the same UserDefaults key the sync reads, so what is on screen and what is being read can never disagree.

The connection view model

HealthConnectionViewModel is deliberately thinner than its Whoop counterpart: Health has no OAuth, no tokens and no server. What it does have is a permission model that refuses to tell the app anything, which shapes everything in it. 

// LIfeOS/Features/Settings/ViewModel/HealthConnectionViewModel.swift
enum State: Equatable {
    case unavailable          // iPad without Health, or a device that has none
    case notAsked             // never asked; the row offers to connect
    case syncing
    case synced(days: Int)    // days touched, not days with data
    case noData               // asked, and nothing came back
    case failed(String)
}

.noData deliberately does not say "denied". HealthKit never reports whether read access was granted, because admitting a refusal would leak that the user has no data of that type. Claiming a denial the app cannot see would be a guess presented as a fact, so the copy says "No data yet. Check Almanac in Health > Sharing" and points at the one place that knows.

7.5View

HealthHubScreen takes four value snapshots, two bindings, and a handful of closures. It owns no view model, which is what lets its preview be a single literal and every section be looked at in any state without a store. 

// LIfeOS/Features/Health/View/HealthHubScreen.swift
struct HealthHubScreen: View {
    let activity: ActivitySnapshot
    let weight: BodySnapshot
    let recovery: RecoverySnapshot
    let wellness: WellnessSnapshot
    var onAddJournal: () -> Void = {}
    var onConnectWhoop: () -> Void = {}
    var isWhoopConnected = false
    var onSelectMetric: (TodayMetric) -> Void = { _ in }
    var library: WorkoutLibraryViewModel?     // nil in previews
    var recorder: ActivityRecorder?           // travels with the library
    @Binding var section: HealthSection
    @Binding var selectedDate: Date
    @Environment(\.layout) private var layout

The layout, top to bottom: "Your health" as a large title with a date picker capped at today; WeekStrip; a LazyVGrid of four tracking tiles built from TodayMetric.allCases, each a button into MetricDetailScreen (Chapter 6); an UnderlinePicker over the two sections; and the section view. The content column reads layout.maxContentWidth, layout.gutter and layout.railInset from the environment, so on an iPad the same screen sits inside a bounded column beside the side rail without a second layout.

The Health half

Order matters here, and each card is a decision:

  1. AlertBanner with the anomalies. First, because "is anything off" is the question a person opens the tab to answer.
  2. A Connect Whoop card, shown only when there is no reading and Whoop is not connected.
  3. Recovery (with its RecoveryBand label in caps) and calories, two HealthReadingCards in an adaptive grid.
  4. SleepDashboardCard: the night's duration at large-title size, a SleepStageBar when stages exist, then quality rows (performance, efficiency, consistency, debt, naps), each row present only when its value is.
  5. HRV and resting HR; then blood oxygen and skin temperature, each captioned with its signed delta from the fortnight average.
  6. A Vitals StatGroup for respiratory rate.
  7. appleHealthGroups: one StatGroup per HealthDaySummary.Group that has a reading, coloured by category.
  8. WeightSection, the journal card, a "14-day trends" link, and a "Synced 3h ago" line.
// LIfeOS/Features/Health/View/HealthSegmentView.swift
/// Listed rather than designed: a panel appears for each group that has a
/// reading and the rest are simply absent, so a person with a blood
/// pressure cuff sees blood pressure and a person without never learns the
/// row existed.
@ViewBuilder
private var appleHealthGroups: some View {
    ForEach(wellness.healthGroups) { group in
        StatGroup(
            title: group.title,
            rows: group.items.map { StatGroup.Row(label: $0.title, value: $0.formatted) },
            hue: categoryStyle(group.title).0, icon: categoryStyle(group.title).1
        )
    }
}

StatGroup renders nothing at all when no row has a value; otherwise the first row with a value becomes the featured reading and the rest form an adaptive grid whose minimum cell width grows to 240 points at accessibility text sizes.

The Fitness half

Calories first, as seven RoundedBarChart bars for the week ending on the selected day with the total in the header. Then steps and active time; strain, average HR and max HR; the day's workouts as WorkoutRows (only when there are any, so most days render no empty frame); the training card; and the trends link. The training card carries the way into the workout library with today's plan already on it (Chapter 10), but only when both the library view model and the recorder were handed down, because the player the library pushes records the session.

WorkoutRow shows a "partial" label when Whoop captured less than 95 percent of a session. A workout recorded at 40 percent is not an easy workout, and letting its low strain speak for it would say exactly that. It also shows the split chip when the session followed a catalog video, so a pull day in the library reads as a pull day in the list.

The fortnight screen

WhoopDetailScreen opens with SleepCompositionChart, one column per night, because it is the only chart showing structure rather than quantity: a short night and a fragmented night look identical on the duration chart and obviously different here, which is the reason the stages are ingested at all. Below it, five TrendCharts. 

// LIfeOS/Features/Recovery/View/TrendChart.swift
/// A run of consecutive days that all have readings.
///
/// Swift Charts joins a line straight across a day it was given no mark
/// for, which would draw a reading that never happened. Splitting the
/// window into runs and giving each its own series keeps the gap a gap.
private var segments: [Segment] {
    var runs: [Segment] = []
    var current: [TrendPoint] = []
    for point in series.points {
        if point.value != nil {
            current.append(point)
        } else if !current.isEmpty {
            runs.append(Segment(id: runs.count, points: current))
            current = []
        }
    }
    if !current.isEmpty { runs.append(Segment(id: runs.count, points: current)) }
    return runs
}

The chart is a line, not bars, because the shape of a fortnight is a direction and a line draws a direction. The chrome is almost absent: no gridlines, no y axis, two date labels in the footer. The y domain is the data's own range with a quarter of headroom, never anchored at zero, because a resting heart rate plotted from zero is a flat line with no shape in it. The current figure lives in the header in text ink, because the warmer module hues fall under 3:1 contrast on this surface and a visible label is the relief.

7.6How it works

Step by step: a foreground sync

  1. RootView comes to the foreground and calls health.startWatching(). If permission has ever been asked, the view model opens reader.changes(), an AsyncStream fed by one HKObserverQuery per universal metric type.
  2. Health records a batch of steps. The observer yields once; the stream buffers at most one event, so thirty batches landing together are one reason to re-read, not thirty.
  3. The view model runs sync(). If a sync is already in flight it awaits that one rather than starting a second: a launch task and a foreground transition arriving together do one pass.
  4. HealthSyncWindow.days(since:) decides which days to re-read: always today; the day of the last sync as well (a night's sleep is recorded against the morning it ends, so a day already covered can gain a value); thirty days on a first sync or after a gap that long; only today when the stamp is in the future, because that is a clock change, not a missing sync.
  5. For each day, reader.day(_:includingCycle:) runs one query per metric. Counts use .cumulativeSum; measurements use .discreteAverage, because summing a heart rate would produce a number in the thousands. Sleep is a category, not a quantity, so one HKSampleQuery answers all six sleep metrics by hand. A metric that errors is dropped rather than failing the day: one unreadable type must not cost the other forty-six.
  6. A day Health knows nothing about is skipped rather than written. An upsert would create an empty row and put a blank day on the calendar that nothing ever fills.
  7. HealthApply.write upserts the row. For each incoming value it reads the held value and the held source, asks MetricArbiter.resolve, writes the winner into the named column or the bag, and records the winning source.
  8. MetricsStore saves. ModelContext.didSave fires. RootView.reloadAll() reloads every snapshot. The tiles repaint through the path they already used; nothing here knows about a screen.
  9. The watch sleeps fifteen seconds before listening again.

The arbiter

// LifeOSKit/Sources/Integrations/MetricArbiter.swift
public static func resolve(
    metric: HealthMetric,
    existing: Double?, existingSource: MetricSource?,
    incoming: Double?, incomingSource: MetricSource,
    ranking: SourceRanking
) -> (value: Double?, source: MetricSource?) {
    // A source having no reading is not evidence of zero.
    guard let incoming else { return (existing, existingSource) }
    guard existing != nil else { return (incoming, incomingSource) }

    let held = existingSource ?? MetricSource.legacy(for: metric)

    // Greater than or equal, not greater than. Equal rank means the same
    // source syncing again, which must be allowed to correct itself.
    guard ranking.rank(incomingSource, for: metric) >= ranking.rank(held, for: metric) else {
        return (existing, held)
    }
    return (incoming, incomingSource)
}

Revision D merged with a boolean: fill gaps only. That could not tell a Whoop value from a typed one, which is exactly the distinction a second wearable forces. SourceRanking turns a source into a rank per metric: 4 for a typed value, 3 for the authority (Apple Health for passively counted metrics, the primary strap for wearable-claimed ones), 2 for a secondary reading, 1 for a fallback, 0 for unknown. The primary wearable defaults to Whoop, so an unset preference reproduces the old behaviour exactly.

One legacy rule matters: a value written before provenance existed reads as rank 0 for almost everything, so the next sync re-attributes it. Weight and water are the exception. A figure the user typed before this shipped is unattributed too, and treating it as unknown would let the next Health sync silently replace it. That is the one path that destroys data a person entered by hand, so an unattributed value for a typed metric is read as typed.

7.7Performance and cost

  • One fetch per view model per date change. Recovery fetches fourteen rows once and picks the selected day out of them. Activity fetches seven. Nothing fetches the same window twice.
  • Observer, not timer. A step count changes dozens of times an hour and not at all overnight. A polling interval short enough to look live wastes queries; one cheap enough to run is not live. HKObserverQuery fires when Health already knows something arrived.
  • Buffer of one, sleep of fifteen. The stream uses .bufferingNewest(1) and the consumer sleeps fifteen seconds after each pass. A day's steps arrive in dozens of batches, and re-reading forty-seven metrics for each one would spend the afternoon in HealthKit to move a numeral.
  • Foreground only. enableBackgroundDelivery needs an entitlement and wakes the app to write rows nobody is looking at. The launch and foreground syncs already cover the time the app was away. stopWatching() runs on every scene deactivation so a phone in a pocket is not running ten queries a quarter minute.
  • Bounded backfill. Thirty days is the month the dot grid shows. Going further would spend forty-seven queries a day on history no screen displays, and Health keeps the data regardless.
  • Every observer completes. The handler calls completion() on the error path too. HealthKit retries a query whose handler never completed, and a silent leak of those is how an app ends up with a hundred live observers.
  • The actor. HealthKitReader is an actor because HKHealthStore is a shared resource and the sync can be entered from two places at once. The observer array is actor state rather than a local because HKObserverQuery is not Sendable.
  • Nothing leaves the device. Apple Health readings are written to the local store and never synced to Supabase. The only health figures that ever leave are the three a person chooses to share with friends (Chapter 16).
  • No chart draws from nothing. TrendChart returns no view at all when a series has no reading, so a fresh install renders no empty axes.
A unit bug worth remembering HKUnit.percent() yields 0.98 for a 98 percent blood oxygen reading. The app stores percentages as percentages everywhere else, Whoop included, so a Health-sourced SpO2 was landing two orders of magnitude below a Whoop-sourced one and rendering as "1.0". It went unnoticed because Whoop owned the field and Health only filled its gaps. HealthKitReader.scale(for:) now multiplies every percent-unit metric by 100 on the way in.

7.8Edge cases and tests

ConditionBehaviour
Watch on the charger all dayEvery Activity reading nil; dashes, never zeros
Never weighedHero reads "No weigh-in", delta suppressed, chart bars all short and grey
Fewer than 7 days between weigh-insDelta suppressed entirely rather than shortened
Gap in the middle of the fortnightPoint kept as nil; the line breaks into two runs; the axis position is preserved
Whoop not connected and nothing readConnect Whoop card shows; recovery, HRV and strain nil; sleep may still arrive from Health
Whoop connected but a quiet nighthasAnyReading is true, so no Connect card; the readings show dashes
Health permission refusedIndistinguishable from no data by Apple's design; state is .noData and the row points at Health > Sharing
Health sync while a sync is runningThe second caller awaits the first; one pass
Last-sync stamp in the futureRead as a clock change; only today is re-read
A day Health has nothing forSkipped, not upserted; no blank row on the calendar
Health and Whoop both report resting HRWhoop wins (claimed by wearable, rank 3 vs 1); Health fills the gap on days Whoop missed
Health and the user both report weightThe typed value wins (rank 4); Health may still correct a weight it wrote itself
A pre-provenance typed weightRead as typed via MetricSource.legacy; never replaced by a sync
Cycle tracking turned off after data was readHealthDaySummary hides the cycle group anyway; showing it would betray the switch
Fewer than 7 readings behind a vitalNo baseline, no anomaly, no banner
Today's reading is the spikeHistory drops the selected day so a spike cannot drag its own baseline
Whoop captured 40 percent of a sessionThe row is labelled "partial" so the low strain is not read as an easy day
Extras bag bytes are unreadableDecoded as empty; the named columns still render rather than losing the screen over the tail

Tests

  • MetricArbiterTests (10 tests): a missing reading never clears a value; Health does not overwrite Whoop; Health fills a Whoop gap; Health overwrites its own counts; a hand-entered value survives; the chosen strap overwrites the other; the secondary strap still fills a gap; an unattributed typed value is treated as typed.
  • HealthApplyTests (9 tests) against a real in-memory store: every column fills; Whoop values survive a Health sync; a later sync corrects a step count; counts are stored as integers; a write records its provenance; the long tail is attributed too. These exist because the arbiter can be perfectly correct and still be wired into the wrong column.
  • WhoopArbitrationTests (5): Whoop owns what it measures, does not overwrite the phone's exercise minutes or a typed weight, yields to the chosen strap.
  • HealthSyncWindowTests (8): a first sync backfills a month; today is always included; a recent sync re-reads only today; a gap is backfilled including the day before it; a very old sync is capped; the window never reaches the future.
  • HealthMetricVocabularyTests and CycleConsentTests: every metric has a title and group; raw values are unique; the first request never asks for cycle data; universal and cycle partition every metric.
  • AnomalyEvaluationTests (10): the baseline needs seven readings; relative and absolute thresholds flag at the boundary and stay quiet below it.
  • TrendSeriesTests (13) and SleepCompositionTests (6): averages ignore gaps; a single reading has no delta; points keep their gaps; a night with no stages is not renderable; awake counts toward the bar but not toward sleep.
Still not covered The four feature view models have no tests, for the reason recorded in the decision log: they take a context through attach rather than a protocol through init. The delta suppression in BodyViewModel and the verdict thresholds in WellnessViewModel (420 sleep minutes reads "Optimal", 20 exercise minutes counts as a workout day, 4 workout days reads "Consistent") are the ones most worth writing first.

7.9Study notes

Read in this order

  1. LifeOSKit/Sources/Integrations/HealthMetric.swift, the vocabulary and the three merge properties.
  2. LifeOSKit/Sources/Integrations/MetricSource.swift and MetricArbiter.swift, the ranking and the rule.
  3. LifeOSKit/Sources/Integrations/HealthApply.swift, where the rule meets the row.
  4. LifeOSKit/Sources/Integrations/HealthKitReader.swift, particularly changes() and read(_:on:).
  5. LIfeOS/Features/Settings/ViewModel/HealthConnectionViewModel.swift, the sync loop and the watch.
  6. LIfeOS/Features/Recovery/ViewModel/RecoveryViewModel.swift, the one-fetch pattern and the anomaly checks.
  7. LIfeOS/Features/Health/View/HealthSegmentView.swift, then TrendChart.swift.

Check yourself

  • Why does the arbiter use greater-than-or-equal rather than greater-than? Equal rank means the same source syncing again, and a source must be allowed to correct itself, which is how an afternoon sync fixes the morning's step count.
  • Why is a Health-sourced SpO2 multiplied by 100? HKUnit.percent() returns a fraction; the app stores percentages as percentages, and the mismatch rendered "1.0" for a 98 percent reading.
  • What does the observer stream's buffer size of one buy? A batch of samples is one reason to re-read the day, not thirty, and a throttled consumer never returns to a queue of stale events.
  • Why does the recovery baseline exclude the selected day? A spike on the day being judged would drag its own baseline toward itself and hide itself.
  • Why is a legacy unattributed weight treated as typed? It is the one path where a sync could destroy a value a person entered by hand.
  • Why does the app never say Health access was denied? HealthKit deliberately hides the answer, so any claim of denial would be a guess presented as fact.

Chapter eight

8Live sessions

Press Begin and a workout is recorded on the phone: a wall-clock timer that survives relaunch, a heart-rate strap over Bluetooth, an effort estimate against today's battery, and one readout struct that every surface renders, from the glass rings on the screen to the lock screen and the Dynamic Island.

8.1Intent

Until 14 September a person starting a workout saw a timer, and if they scanned and tapped for a sensor, a heart rate. They could not see how hard they were working, how much they had left, or whether they should push. Everything needed to answer those questions already reached the app: Whoop recovery and sleep performance sit in DailyMetrics, the profile carries a birth date, the workout builder collects energy, and a strap delivers beats every second. Nothing joined them. This slice is the join.

Working backwards

Tap the plus, choose Run, tap Begin. The screen turns blue. A big rounded clock counts up, and beneath it three glass rings: your heart rate against today's ceiling zone, your estimated effort against today's target band, and your battery, what you have left to spend. The last sensor you used reconnects on its own. Lock the phone and the same numbers sit on the lock screen over the same blue gradient, and in the Dynamic Island as a heart, a number, and the clock. Pause and everything freezes. Finish and the session is saved to Almanac, and to Apple Health if you asked.

Is the effort number Whoop's strain?

No, and the screen always says "estimated" next to it. It is a model on the same 0 to 21 scale, calibrated so a steady hour in zone 3 reads about 12 and a hard ninety minutes about 18. Whoop's real strain for the workout arrives later on its own record through the existing sync, and nothing here overwrites it.

What if I have not entered a birth date?

Then there are no zones, no effort and no battery, and the screen says so with one line: "Add your birth date in Profile for zones, effort and battery." A zone built on an assumed age would be a reading the person never gave, and this app refuses those. Heart rate and calories still show.

Does the timer keep going if the app is killed?

Yes. The timer is wall-clock based and written to a per-account draft at most every ten seconds, so a relaunch restores it exactly. If Health was recording, the recorder asks HealthKit to recover the active session; if it cannot, the timer is kept and the person is told the Health session is gone.

Out of scope here

Apple Watch heart rate and rep counting are Chapter 9. Following a video with the rings over it is Chapter 10. There are no server changes; this chapter is entirely on the device.

8.2Files and folders

Features/Activity/
├── Model/
