Why the maths is in two packages

LiveSessionReadout and PushState live in AppSurfaces, which depends on nothing, so the widget extension can decode them without linking HealthKit or SwiftData. The effort model lives in Integrations, which added AppSurfaces as a dependency. Nothing cycles, and swift test runs the whole model on macOS without a simulator.

8.3Model

The timer

// LifeOSKit/Sources/Integrations/ActivitySessionState.swift
/// Wall-clock based: backgrounding never stops the timer and pauses never count.
public struct ActivitySessionState: Codable, Equatable, Sendable {
    public enum Phase: String, Codable, Sendable { case running, paused, finished }
    public let id: UUID
    public let startedAt: Date
    public let activity: String
    public private(set) var phase: Phase
    public private(set) var accumulated: TimeInterval
    public private(set) var runningSince: Date?
    public private(set) var endedAt: Date?

    public func elapsed(at date: Date = .now) -> TimeInterval {
        accumulated + (runningSince.map { max(0, date.timeIntervalSince($0)) } ?? 0)
    }
    public mutating func pause(at date: Date = .now) {
        guard phase == .running else { return }
        accumulated = elapsed(at: date); runningSince = nil; phase = .paused
    }
}

A pause banks the time so far into accumulated and clears runningSince; a resume starts a new run. There is no tick. Every surface derives the elapsed time from two fields and the clock, which is what lets the lock screen use Text(timerInterval:) and count on its own without an update per second. The id is the Live Activity's key.

Zones, effort, capacity

All of this is value types and pure functions in one file. Nothing touches HealthKit, Bluetooth, SwiftData or the clock; callers pass values in.

// LifeOSKit/Sources/Integrations/LiveEffort.swift
public struct HeartRateZones: Equatable, Sendable {
    public let maxHeartRate: Int
    public init?(birthDate: Date?, on date: Date = .now, calendar: Calendar = .current) {
        guard let birthDate,
              let age = calendar.dateComponents([.year], from: birthDate, to: date).year,
              (10...120).contains(age) else { return nil }
        maxHeartRate = Int((208.0 - 0.7 * Double(age)).rounded())   // Tanaka
    }
    /// 0 below half of maximum, then one zone per ten percent up to 5.
    public func zone(for bpm: Int) -> Int { ... }
}

public struct EffortAccumulator: Equatable, Sendable {
    public static let weights: [Double] = [0, 0.15, 0.28, 0.35, 0.45, 0.63]
    public static let scale = 1500.0
    public static let maxCredit: TimeInterval = 5
    public private(set) var load: Double
    public mutating func add(zone: Int, seconds: TimeInterval) {
        guard seconds > 0, Self.weights.indices.contains(zone) else { return }
        load += Self.weights[zone] * seconds
    }
    public var effort: Double { 21 * (1 - exp(-load / Self.scale)) }
}

Max heart rate is Tanaka's estimate, and the zone bands follow Whoop's (zone 1 starts at 50 percent of max, then 60, 70, 80, 90) so the number on the HUD agrees with the number in the app the person already trusts. Each second in a zone adds that zone's weight to a running load; the load maps through a saturating curve so a very long session approaches 21 without reaching it. The six weights and the 1500 are the values that make three calibration points hold at once, and they are pinned by tests: retuning is a deliberate change with a diff, not a drift.

maxCredit matters more than it looks. A reading credits at most five seconds. A gap in the stream, a strap that dropped for forty seconds, is not effort that was measured, and crediting the whole gap at the zone of the next reading would invent it. 

// LifeOSKit/Sources/Integrations/LiveEffort.swift
public struct EffortCeiling: Codable, Equatable, Sendable {
    public let maxZone: Int
    public let targetEffort: ClosedRange<Double>
    public static let green  = EffortCeiling(maxZone: 5, targetEffort: 14...18)
    public static let yellow = EffortCeiling(maxZone: 4, targetEffort: 10...14)
    public static let red    = EffortCeiling(maxZone: 3, targetEffort: 4...10)
    public static let conservative = yellow
    public static func forCapacity(_ percent: Int) -> EffortCeiling {
        percent >= 67 ? .green : percent >= 34 ? .yellow : .red
    }
}

public struct Capacity: Codable, Equatable, Sendable {
    public enum Source: String, Codable, Sendable { case whoop, health }
    public let percent: Int
    public let source: Source
    public let measuredOn: Date
    public var ceiling: EffortCeiling { .forCapacity(percent) }
}

Capacity is today's battery: what the person has to spend and where the number came from. It is computed once at session start and kept in the draft. CapacityMath.capacity(days:now:) looks at today's row and yesterday's (yesterday stands in while today has not synced; anything older is stale) and resolves in order:

  1. Whoop. Recovery percent present and not calibrating. Blended with sleep performance when present: 0.8 * recovery + 0.2 * sleepPerformance, else plain recovery.
  2. Apple Health. HRV present, with at least three of the previous seven days carrying HRV for a baseline. The ratio to baseline maps piecewise: 0.7 to 1.0 onto 20 to 65 percent, 1.0 to 1.2 onto 65 to 90, clamped. Sleep minutes then adjust by up to plus or minus 10 against a 450-minute reference.
  3. Nothing. Nil. The UI says "Battery unknown" and the recorder uses the yellow ceiling, cautious without claiming a capacity it does not have.

The ceiling follows Whoop's recovery bands. Battery remaining drains as effort approaches the target's top: capacity * (1 - effort / target.upperBound), floored at zero. Zero is a real event, the budget spent, not a missing value. Push state is a four-way word: overLimit when the zone exceeds the ceiling's max zone or effort exceeds the target's top, nearLimit when the zone is at the max or effort is within 1.5 of the top, easy when effort is below the band and the zone is at most 2, onTrack otherwise.

The readout

// LifeOSKit/Sources/AppSurfaces/LiveSessionReadout.swift
public struct LiveSessionReadout: Codable, Hashable, Sendable {
    public var elapsed: TimeInterval
    public var runningSince: Date?
    public var heartRate: Int?
    public var zone: Int?
    public var effort: Double?          // rounded to a tenth before publishing
    public var calories: Int?
    public var distanceMeters: Int?
    public var batteryPercent: Int?
    public var capacitySource: String?  // "whoop" or "health"
    public var ceilingMaxZone: Int?
    public var ceilingTarget: ClosedRange<Double>?
    public var reps: Int?
    public var setIndex: Int?
    public var push: PushState

    /// Anchor for `Text(timerInterval:)`, so the system ticks the timer
    /// without an update per second.
    public var timerAnchor: Date? { runningSince?.addingTimeInterval(-elapsed) }
    public var isPaused: Bool { runningSince == nil }
}

This is the one value every live surface renders. Every reading is optional because a missing sensor is not a zero. WorkoutActivityAttributes.ContentState is a typealias to it, so the widget and the app can never disagree about what a session looks like. LiveSessionReadout+Text is the one place a reading becomes a string, so the HUD, the tiles and the lock screen agree on rounding and on the dash that means no reading.

8.4ViewModel

ActivityRecorder is the largest view model in the app, and it is an NSObject because it is the HKWorkoutSessionDelegate and HKLiveWorkoutBuilderDelegate. It owns the timer, the sensor, the zones, the effort accumulator, the capacity, the draft, the Live Activity controller and the readout. 

// LIfeOS/Features/Activity/ViewModel/ActivityRecorder.swift
@MainActor @Observable
final class ActivityRecorder: NSObject, HKWorkoutSessionDelegate, HKLiveWorkoutBuilderDelegate {
    var selection: RecordedActivity = .walk
    var saveToHealth = HKHealthStore.isHealthDataAvailable()
    var timer: ActivitySessionState?
    private(set) var busy = false
    var saved = false
    var healthSaved = false
    var energy: Double?
    var distance: Double?
    var heartRate: Double?
    var capacity: Capacity?
    private(set) var readout: LiveSessionReadout?
    var source: SessionSource = .phone
    var zones: HeartRateZones?
    var effort = EffortAccumulator()
    var lastReadingAt: Date?
    let sensor: LiveHeartRateSensor
    /// Injected so previews and checks can fix an age without a profile.
    var birthDate: () -> Date? = { ProfileStore.load().birthDate }
    var whoopConnected: () -> Bool = { false }
    private let liveActivity = WorkoutLiveActivityController()
    private static let draftKey = "activeWorkoutDraft"

Three things about its shape. Its dependencies on the world (the birth date, whether Whoop is connected, whether a watch is nearby, Health authorisation) are closures, so the checks harness can fix them without a profile, a strap or a permission sheet. Its defaults are the UserDefaults.currentAccount suite, so a draft belongs to one account and an account switch clears it. And it has active, flipped off by deactivate(), which every async continuation checks before touching state, so a session that finishes after sign-out writes nothing.

Start

// LIfeOS/Features/Activity/ViewModel/ActivityRecorder.swift
func start(backdatedTo backdatedStart: Date? = nil,
           following video: (id: String, split: String, title: String, channel: String)? = nil) async {
    guard active, !busy, !hasSession else { return }
    busy = true; error = nil; saved = false; healthSaved = false; timer = nil
    zones = HeartRateZones(birthDate: birthDate())
    capacity = loadCapacity()
    effort = EffortAccumulator(); lastReadingAt = nil
    source = .phone
    recordingHealth = saveToHealth
    defer { busy = false }
    if await handOffToWatch() { return }                 // Chapter 9
    sensor.prepareForSession(whoopConnected: whoopConnected())
    do {
        if saveToHealth && source == .phone {
            try await healthStore.requestAuthorization(toShare: Self.workoutTypes, read: Self.workoutTypes)
            guard healthStore.authorizationStatus(for: HKObjectType.workoutType()) == .sharingAuthorized else {
                error = "Allow workout saving in Health, or turn off Save to Apple Health to use the timer."
                return
            }
            let session = try HKWorkoutSession(healthStore: healthStore, configuration: configuration)
            let builder = session.associatedWorkoutBuilder()
            builder.dataSource = HKLiveWorkoutDataSource(healthStore: healthStore, workoutConfiguration: configuration)
            let started = backdatedStart ?? .now
            if timer == nil { timer = ActivitySessionState(activity: selection.rawValue, at: started) }
            session.startActivity(with: started)
            try await builder.beginCollection(at: started)
        } else if timer == nil {
            timer = ActivitySessionState(activity: selection.rawValue, at: backdatedStart ?? .now)
        }
        persist()
    } catch { ... }
}

The clock is read after Health answers, not before. A permission sheet can sit open for a minute, and a timer started before it would count that minute as exercise. Zones and capacity are computed once here; the capacity is nine days of rows read through CapacityInputs, the same helper the workout planner uses, so the battery on the HUD and the battery on the library's Today card are plainly the same number.

A reading arrives

// LIfeOS/Features/Activity/ViewModel/ActivityRecorder.swift
func receiveHeartRate(_ bpm: Int, at date: Date) {
    guard active, isRunning else { return }
    heartRate = Double(bpm); heartRateDate = date
    if let zones {
        effort.add(zone: zones.zone(for: bpm),
                   seconds: EffortAccumulator.credit(previous: lastReadingAt, at: date))
    }
    lastReadingAt = date
    persistReading(at: date)
    guard let builder, healthStore.authorizationStatus(for: .quantityType(forIdentifier: .heartRate)!) == .sharingAuthorized else { return }
    let sample = HKQuantitySample(type: .quantityType(forIdentifier: .heartRate)!,
        quantity: HKQuantity(unit: HKUnit.count().unitDivided(by: .minute()), doubleValue: Double(bpm)), start: date, end: date)
    builder.add([sample]) { _, _ in }
}

Paused readings accrue nothing because the guard on isRunning drops them. The first reading after a resume credits nothing because togglePause cleared lastReadingAt, so the credit function has no previous date and returns zero. Both are pinned by checks. The strap's beats are also written into the Health builder, so a workout saved to Health carries the heart-rate series the strap measured.

Two persist paths

// LIfeOS/Features/Activity/ViewModel/ActivityRecorder.swift
/// State changes: always write the draft and sync.
func persist() {
    refreshReadout()
    writeDraft()
    syncLiveActivity()
}
/// Readings arrive every second: always refresh and sync (the controller
/// throttles the publish), but write the draft at most every ten seconds.
func persistReading(at date: Date) {
    refreshReadout()
    if lastDraftWriteAt.map({ date.timeIntervalSince($0) >= 10 }) ?? true { writeDraft(at: date) }
    syncLiveActivity()
}

refreshReadout() calls LiveReadoutBuilder.readout(...), the pure join of timer, heart rate, zones, effort, capacity, energy, distance, reps and set into one struct. The draft is a Codable private struct with every field optional after the first slice, so a draft written before reps or videos existed still decodes.

Finish and save

finish() marks the timer finished and, for a Health-backed session, calls session.stopActivity and returns; the delegate's .stopped callback is what calls saveFinished(), because collection completes only after HealthKit reaches that state. saveFinished() ends collection, finishes the workout, then writes the local WorkoutRecord with a stable id: 

// LIfeOS/Features/Activity/ViewModel/ActivityRecorder.swift
let id = "almanac:\(timer.id.uuidString)"
var fetch = FetchDescriptor<WorkoutRecord>(predicate: #Predicate { $0.externalID == id })
fetch.fetchLimit = 1
if try context.fetch(fetch).isEmpty {
    let row = WorkoutRecord(externalID: id, start: timer.startedAt,
        durationMinutes: Int(timer.elapsed() / 60), activityName: timer.activity, energyKcal: energy)
    row.distanceMeters = distance
    row.videoID = pendingVideoID; row.split = pendingSplit
    if selection == .strength { row.sets = completedSets + [reps ?? 0] }
    context.insert(row)
}
try context.save()
liveActivity.end()
saved = true; defaults.removeObject(forKey: Self.draftKey)
sensor.stopStreaming()
onSaved?()

The stable id is why "Repeated save creates one workout" passes: tapping Finish twice, or a restore after a save that half-completed, finds the row and does not insert a second. A Health failure mid-save keeps the timer and says "Your activity is kept here. Saving failed. Try Save again."

The sensor

LiveHeartRateSensor speaks the Bluetooth SIG heart-rate service (0x180D, measurement 0x2A37). It handles 8-bit and 16-bit frames, treats a no-contact flag as no reading, and rejects values outside 20 to 250. Scans stop after 30 seconds. What the live-session slice added is memory: the last connected peripheral's identifier is written to the per-account defaults under lastHeartRateSensorID on every successful connection and cleared on an explicit disconnect. 

// LIfeOS/Features/Activity/ViewModel/LiveHeartRateSensor.swift
/// Called by the recorder at session start. Reconnects the last sensor,
/// or looks for a lone WHOOP when the account is connected to WHOOP and
/// nothing was ever paired here.
func prepareForSession(whoopConnected: Bool) {
    if rememberedPeripheralID != nil { reconnectIfRemembered() }
    else if whoopConnected { autoPairWhoop() }
}

reconnectIfRemembered uses retrievePeripherals(withIdentifiers:) and connects directly; if nothing connects in 20 seconds it falls back to a scan and connects the discovered peripheral whose identifier matches. autoPairWhoop scans and connects only when WhoopAutoPair.choice(among:) finds exactly one name containing "WHOOP". Several stop the scan with "More than one WHOOP nearby. Choose one under Manage." Nothing auto-pairs a device that is not a WHOOP, because another person's chest strap in a gym is not a reading this person owns.

8.5View

BeginActivityScreen is a sheet with two states. Before a session: a heading ("Make time to move."), the timer card on an activity pastel, a "Follow a video" link into the library, the six-activity picker (Walk, Run, Cycle, Strength, Yoga, Other), the controls, the connections panel, and a quick-log shortcut. During a session: the whole background becomes a blue-to-canvas gradient 380 points tall, the navigation bar goes dark, and the hero replaces the card. 

// LIfeOS/Features/Activity/View/BeginActivityScreen.swift
private func liveHero(_ readout: LiveSessionReadout) -> some View {
    VStack(alignment: .leading, spacing: 8) {
        HStack {
            Label(model.selection.rawValue, systemImage: model.selection.icon).font(LifeOSType.rowTitle)
            Spacer()
            Text(readout.isPaused ? "Paused" : readout.push.headline).font(LifeOSType.label)
                .padding(.horizontal, 10).padding(.vertical, 5)
                .background(.white.opacity(0.22), in: Capsule())
        }
        if let following = model.following {
            Text("Following: \(following.title) · \(following.channel)")
        }
        TimelineView(.periodic(from: .now, by: 1)) { timeline in
            Text(duration(model.timer?.elapsed(at: timeline.date) ?? 0))
                .font(.system(size: 72, weight: .medium, design: .rounded)).monospacedDigit()
        }
        Text("Elapsed time").font(LifeOSType.caption).opacity(0.85)
        SessionRings(readout: readout, activity: model.selection, zonesAvailable: model.zonesAvailable,
                     countsAutomatically: model.source == .watch,
                     onAddRep: { model.addRep() }, onRemoveRep: { model.removeRep() },
                     onNextSet: { model.nextSet() }, isExpanded: $hudExpanded)
    }
    .foregroundStyle(.white)
}

The clock lives on its own line at 72 points rather than inside the rings, because a timer plus five readings does not fit in one capsule, and the reading that truncated when it was tried was the battery percentage, the one number that must never be half a number.

The rings

SessionRings is a GlassEffectContainer with two shapes. Expanded, a rounded rectangle holding three rings (heart, effort, battery) and, for strength, a rep count, with the rep buttons on a second row inside the same glass. Collapsed, a capsule with the clock, a pulsing heart, the bpm and, for strength, the reps. Tapping the top row toggles between them. It always draws white on glass over a dark wash (.black.opacity(0.30)) so the text reads over a bright frame of video or the pale foot of the gradient alike, and the glass is tinted by the push state. 

// LIfeOS/Features/Activity/View/SessionRings.swift
/// One beat per beat: a scale wave at the live tempo, still when there
/// is no reading to keep time to.
private var pulsingHeart: some View {
    TimelineView(.animation(paused: SessionRingMath.beatPeriod(bpm: readout.heartRate) == nil || readout.isPaused)) { timeline in
        let period = SessionRingMath.beatPeriod(bpm: readout.heartRate) ?? 1
        let phase = timeline.date.timeIntervalSinceReferenceDate.truncatingRemainder(dividingBy: period) / period
        let beat = max(0, sin(phase * .pi * 2))
        Image(systemName: "heart.fill").scaleEffect(1 + 0.35 * beat)
    }
}

The ring fills come from SessionRingMath, pure and tested: the heart ring is the zone over today's ceiling zone, the effort ring is effort over the top of the target band, the battery ring is the percent. A missing reading is an empty ring, never a full one; nothing has been earned yet. The effort ring turns red only past the band, not at its top. The animation timeline is paused when there is no reading or the session is paused, so a still heart costs no frames.

The tiles

Under the hero, glass tiles in an adaptive grid: heart rate with the zone in its label and a freshness rule (a reading older than 15 seconds shows a dash and the sensor's status as its caption); effort with "of 14" as its unit and the battery and its source as caption; reps for strength; calories; distance for walk, run and cycle only. Yoga hides the effort tile: a zone ceiling has no meaning on a mat.

Controls

ActivityControls was extracted from the screen so the video player offers exactly the same buttons in the same order. Two screens that both stop a workout should not disagree about what stopping looks like, and the confirm-discard dialog travels with the button that raises it.

8.6How it works

Step by step: a run with a strap

  1. Begin. start() builds zones from the birth date and capacity from nine days of rows, asks Health, creates the session and builder, starts the timer at the moment Health answered, and persists. sensor.prepareForSession reconnects the remembered strap.
  2. A frame arrives on characteristic 0x2A37. HeartRateMeasurement.beatsPerMinute decodes it; the sensor calls onReading.
  3. receiveHeartRate credits at most five seconds of the reading's zone to the accumulator, records the time, and calls persistReading.
  4. refreshReadout rebuilds the readout: zone from the bpm, effort rounded to a tenth, battery from capacity and effort, push state from zone and effort against the ceiling.
  5. The rings and tiles observe readout and redraw. The draft is written if ten seconds have passed. The Live Activity controller is asked to sync.
  6. LiveActivityThrottle.shouldPublish decides. First state always; a pause, a push-state change or a reps change always; a heart-rate move of 3 bpm or more only if 3 seconds have passed since the last publish; anything else only after a 10-second floor; an identical readout never.
  7. The builder's own statistics callback delivers energy and distance sums, and the watch's heart rate when there is no strap. It updates the same fields and calls persist().
  8. Pause: the timer banks, the Health session pauses, lastReadingAt clears. Readings still arrive and are dropped.
  9. Finish: stop the Health activity, wait for .stopped, end collection, finish the workout, write the record, end the Live Activity, clear the draft, stop the strap.

The Live Activity

Widget extensions cannot render materials, so the lock screen's "glass" tiles are white at 18 percent over a linear gradient from LifeOSTokens.liveGradientTop (the recovery hue) to liveGradientBottom, with a radial white highlight and a half-point white stroke. Row one: the activity icon in a circle, the name, the push headline (or "Paused"), and the timer as Text(timerInterval:). Row two: four tiles, heart with the zone as eyebrow, effort with "EST" and "of 14", calories (or reps and set for strength), and battery with a small ring. A tile with no value shows the dash in the same weight, never a zero.

The Dynamic Island's compact leading is a heart and the bpm tinted by push state; compact trailing is the timer, or reps for strength; minimal is the zone number in a tinted circle. The keyline tint follows push state. Every surface deep-links to SurfaceRoute.activity.url.

8.7Performance and cost

  • No tick. The timer is two fields and the clock. The lock screen counts on its own through Text(timerInterval:); the in-app clock is a one-second TimelineView, which SwiftUI runs only while the view is on screen.
  • Draft writes are rate-limited. A reading a second would be a UserDefaults write a second. persistReading writes at most every ten seconds; state changes (pause, resume, finish) always write.
  • ActivityKit updates are throttled by a pure function. The sensor streams every second; the lock screen does not need to. The 3-second minimum on heart-rate-driven updates and the 10-second floor on everything else keep the activity inside ActivityKit's budget, and the rule is tested rather than tuned by eye. Updates are chained through a Task so they land in order.
  • Effort is O(1) per reading. One multiply-add into a load; the curve is evaluated on read. Nothing keeps a series.
  • Capacity is computed once. Nine rows at session start, then kept in the draft. A restored session does not re-read the store.
  • The pulse is free when still. The heart's TimelineView(.animation) is paused whenever there is no bpm or the session is paused.
  • Scans end. Thirty seconds, then stop, so a sheet left open is not draining the radio. The reconnect fallback times out at twenty.
  • Nothing leaves the device. A workout is a local WorkoutRecord and, optionally, an HKWorkout. The Live Activity uses pushType: nil. There is no server in this chapter.
  • Every continuation checks active. A delegate callback, a recovered session, a finish that lands after sign-out: all guard on it, so a stale session cannot write into the next account's store.
Open on hardware The spec flags one background-execution question: whether iOS 26 keeps the app running during a phone-side HKWorkoutSession or whether workout-processing must join UIBackgroundModes. The plist today carries remote-notification and bluetooth-central. The wall-clock timer means the elapsed time is right either way; what a suspended app would lose is effort accrual for the suspended minutes.

8.8Edge cases and tests

ConditionBehaviour
No birth dateNo zones, effort or battery; heart rate and calories only; one hint line under the tiles

Tests

  • LiveEffortTests (18 tests): a 30-year-old has max 187; 94 bpm is zone 1, 131 is zone 3, 169 is zone 5; no birth date yields nil; the calibration points (an hour in zone 3 is about 12, thirty minutes in zone 2 about 6, ninety hard minutes about 18) within 1.0; effort is bounded below 21 and never decreases; credit caps gaps at 5 and starts at 0; Whoop 80 with sleep 90 gives 82 and green; yesterday stands in; calibrating falls through; Health capacity needs a baseline and moves with sleep; battery drains against the target top; push state follows zone and effort; the builder keeps absence and uses the conservative ceiling without capacity; auto-pair picks exactly one WHOOP; todayCapacity reads the store.
  • LiveSessionReadoutTests (9): round trip keeps absence; a paused readout has no anchor; headlines are words; the throttle publishes first and on meaningful change, spaces heart-rate updates, floors small changes at ten seconds, publishes on a reps change; text formatters keep absence and rounding.
  • SessionRingMathTests (5) and ActivitySessionStateTests (4): fills, over-band, beat period; background time and pauses; identity survives a draft round trip; BLE frames decode.
  • ActivityRecorderChecks, 34 checks run in the simulator against an in-memory store and disposable defaults suites, launched with --design-preview --page=checks. They cover what Swift Testing cannot reach: the timer starting without Health, capacity at start, readings yielding zone and effort, pause and resume accrual, draft restore with and without Health, cross-account isolation, idempotent save, the remembered sensor, and the video stamping cases of Chapter 10.

The design QA report records 1231 package tests passing after this slice, the in-session screen captured on iPhone and iPad in both schemes, and the lock screen and Dynamic Island captured from the simulator with a fixture that requests a real Live Activity behind the --live-activity argument.

8.9Study notes

Read in this order

  1. LifeOSKit/Sources/Integrations/ActivitySessionState.swift, the timer with no tick.
  2. LifeOSKit/Sources/Integrations/LiveEffort.swift, top to bottom: zones, accumulator, ceiling, capacity, the maths, the builder.
  3. LifeOSKit/Sources/AppSurfaces/LiveSessionReadout.swift, the struct and the throttle.
  4. LIfeOS/Features/Activity/ViewModel/ActivityRecorder.swift: start, receiveHeartRate, the two persist paths, saveFinished.
  5. LIfeOS/Features/Activity/ViewModel/LiveHeartRateSensor.swift, the remember-and-reconnect path.
  6. LIfeOS/App/Surfaces/WorkoutLiveActivityController.swift and AlmanacWidgets/WorkoutLiveActivity.swift.
  7. LIfeOS/Features/Activity/View/SessionRings.swift, then ActivityRecorderChecks.swift as the executable spec.

Check yourself

  • Why is the timer started after Health answers rather than before? A permission sheet can sit open for a minute, and a timer started first would count it as exercise.
  • Why does one reading credit at most five seconds? A gap in the stream is not effort that was measured; crediting the gap would invent it.
  • What makes "Repeated save creates one workout" true? The record's external id is derived from the timer's UUID and looked up before insert.
  • Why does the lock screen not need an update every second? It renders Text(timerInterval:) from an anchor date; only readings, not time, need an update, and the throttle spaces those.
  • Why do zones live in Integrations but the readout in AppSurfaces? The widget must decode the readout without linking HealthKit or SwiftData; AppSurfaces depends on nothing.
  • When does the effort ring turn red? Only past the top of the target band, not at it.

Chapter nine

9The Watch companion

When an Apple Watch is paired, the watch owns the workout and the phone shows it. Heart rate, energy, reps and sets cross the mirrored HealthKit session once a second; pause, resume, end and the rep buttons cross back. A pure rep counter on wrist acceleration fills the slot the HUD reserved, labelled "auto" because its accuracy on real movement is still unmeasured.

9.1Intent

Before this slice the watch app was a read-only dashboard: steps, sleep and movement mirrored from the phone, with no way to start, see or end a workout. A person wearing a watch and no strap saw a timer on the phone and no beats, because the phone only ever received heart rate from a Bluetooth strap. And strength sessions showed a "reps" slot that never filled.

Working backwards

Tap Begin on the phone with a watch on your wrist and the phone says "Asking your Apple Watch…". Within a few seconds Almanac opens on the watch with the workout running, and the phone's rings show the watch's heart rate. Or start from the watch: choose Strength, and the phone's lock screen shows the session before you have touched the phone. Curl, and the rep count on your wrist climbs on its own; tap +1 if it missed one, tap −1 if it counted an extra. Pause on either device and both pause. End on either and exactly one workout lands in Health, saved by the watch.

Who owns the session?

Whichever device created the HKWorkoutSession. When a watch is paired, installed and Health saving is on, the watch does, and it alone writes the workout to Health. The phone never creates a session of its own for a watch-owned workout, so nothing is saved twice. When no watch answers within ten seconds, the phone path from Chapter 8 runs unchanged.

Why is the rep count labelled "auto" on the watch and not on the phone?

Only a watch session counts reps by itself. On a phone-only strength session every rep is a tap, and calling that "auto" would invert the honesty label.

What has actually been verified on a real watch?

Nothing yet. The rep counter is pinned by tests on synthetic signals, the wire format and the recorder's watch path are pinned by tests and simulator checks, and both targets build. The watch simulator cannot run a real workout session, so the watch screen is verified by compilation only. Five hardware checks and two recovery-behaviour checks are recorded as pending in the QA report, to be run by the author on his own phone and watch.

9.2Files and folders

AlmanacWatch/                                the watchOS target, added to the pbxproj by hand
├── AlmanacWatchApp.swift                    the scene: dashboard or workout; WatchBridge for the snapshot
├── WatchAppDelegate.swift                   handle(configuration) and handleActiveWorkoutRecovery()
├── WatchWorkoutController.swift             the session, the builder, the counter, the packets
└── WatchWorkoutScreen.swift                 timer, heart rate with zone chip, reps, pause, end

LIfeOS/App/Surfaces/
└── WatchSessionBridge.swift                 one per app: the mirrored session and its delegate

LIfeOS/Features/Activity/ViewModel/
└── ActivityRecorder+Watch.swift             hand-off, adopt, packets, commands

LifeOSKit/Sources/Motion/                    Foundation only; links on watchOS
└── RepCounter.swift                         samples in, a count out

LifeOSKit/Sources/AppSurfaces/
└── WatchWire.swift                          WatchPacket, PhoneCommand, the version gate

LifeOSKit/Tests/
├── MotionTests/RepCounterTests.swift        six calibration cases on synthetic sine waves
└── AppSurfacesTests/WatchWireTests.swift    round trips, unknown version, kind gate

Why Motion is its own package target

The watch target links two package products, AppSurfaces and Motion, and neither depends on anything. CoreMotion stays in the watch target: the controller feeds CMDeviceMotion.userAcceleration samples at 50 Hz into the pure counter. That is what lets the algorithm be tuned against synthetic signals on macOS, and later against a recording from hardware, without a watch in the loop.

9.3Model

The wire format

// LifeOSKit/Sources/AppSurfaces/WatchWire.swift
/// What the watch sends the phone over the mirrored session's data channel.
/// Every reading is optional: a packet without heart rate says "no reading",
/// never zero. `completedSets` holds reps per finished set, oldest first.
public struct WatchPacket: Codable, Equatable, Sendable {
    public var kind: String = WatchWire.packetKind
    public var v: Int = WatchWire.version
    public var sentAt: Date
    public var heartRate: Int?
    public var heartRateAt: Date?
    public var energyKcal: Double?
    public var reps: Int?
    public var setIndex: Int?
    public var completedSets: [Int]?
}

public enum PhoneCommand: String, Codable, Sendable {
    case configure, pause, resume, end, nextSet, addRep, removeRep, discard
}

public struct PhoneCommandEnvelope: Codable, Equatable, Sendable {
    public var kind: String = WatchWire.commandKind
    public var v: Int = WatchWire.version
    public var command: PhoneCommand
    public var sentAt: Date
    public var maxHeartRate: Int?      // sent once with .configure
}

Both shapes carry a version, currently 2, and a kind. The version gate is strict: a packet with an unknown v is ignored, never guessed at. The kind field exists because the two shapes otherwise share every required key (v and sentAt), and a command would decode as an empty packet. A test pins that a command is never read as a packet. 

// LifeOSKit/Sources/AppSurfaces/WatchWire.swift
public static func packet(from data: Data) -> WatchPacket? {
    guard let packet = try? decoder.decode(WatchPacket.self, from: data),
          packet.kind == packetKind, packet.v == version else { return nil }
    return packet
}

Dates are encoded as seconds since 1970. heartRateAt is when the reading was measured, not when the packet was sent, so effort accrual on the phone credits the right seconds.

The two commands that end a session

end finishes the workout and saves it to Health on the wrist. discard throws it away. The distinction is the fix for a critical finding in the final review: the phone originally sent end when it refused a mirrored session or the person discarded, which would have written a stub workout into Health for a session the person had thrown away.

The rep counter

// LifeOSKit/Sources/Motion/RepCounter.swift
public struct RepCounter: Sendable {
    public struct Sample: Sendable { public var t: TimeInterval; public var x, y, z: Double }
    public let settleSeconds: Double      // 1.0
    public let minPeriod: Double          // 0.6
    public let maxPeriod: Double          // 4.0
    public let threshold: Double          // 0.15
    public private(set) var reps: Int = 0
    private let fastTau = 0.15
    private let slowTau = 2.0
    private var axis: Vec?
    private var riseT: TimeInterval?
    private var refractoryUntil: TimeInterval = -.infinity

    /// Feed one sample; returns true when this sample completed a rep.
    public mutating func add(_ sample: Sample) -> Bool
    public mutating func reset()
}

The algorithm, as it stands after two corrections during implementation:

  1. Each axis is smoothed twice with exponential moving averages: a fast one (0.15 s) follows the movement, a slow one (2 s) follows posture and gravity drift. Their difference is a vector d.
  2. The first lift whose magnitude passes the threshold, and is still growing, fixes the axis for the set. The rising condition is the second fix: settling can end mid-fall, and locking the axis onto a fading swing spent the first cycle on a half swing and undercounted by exactly one in two of six tests.
  3. The signal s is d projected onto that axis. It is signed: a rep is a swing, not a rectified bump. The first version rectified the signal with sqrt(x²+y²+z²), and a fall crossing could then structurally never follow a rise.
  4. A rep is a rise of s above +threshold followed by a fall below −threshold, with the half cycle between them lasting between 0.3 and 2.0 seconds.
  5. Nothing counts during the first second after reset(), the person picking up the weight, and each counted rep starts a 0.3-second refractory window.
Calibration is synthetic Every constant is pinned by tests on 50 Hz sine waves with white noise. Ten cycles at 1 Hz and 0.4 g count ten; 0.08 g counts nothing; 3 Hz jitter counts nothing; one ten-second push counts nothing; nine cycles whose first second is swallowed by settling count eight. Real-world accuracy is unknown until hardware. The "auto" label and the +1 and −1 buttons are the honesty.

9.4ViewModel

On the wrist

// AlmanacWatch/WatchWorkoutController.swift
@MainActor @Observable
final class WatchWorkoutController: NSObject, HKWorkoutSessionDelegate, HKLiveWorkoutBuilderDelegate {
    enum State { case idle, starting, running, paused, ending }
    private(set) var state: State = .idle
    private(set) var accumulated: TimeInterval = 0
    private(set) var runningSince: Date?
    private(set) var heartRate: Int?
    private(set) var energyKcal: Double?
    private(set) var reps: Int?
    private(set) var setIndex: Int?
    private(set) var completedSets: [Int] = []
    private(set) var maxHeartRate: Int?
    private(set) var mirroringFailed = false
    private var counter = RepCounter()
    /// Taps on "+1", kept apart from the counter so the next automatic rep
    /// adds to them instead of overwriting them.
    private var manualReps = 0
    private var lastPacketAt: Date = .distantPast

start(_:) flips state to .starting synchronously before its first await, so a second Start tap during the authorisation prompt cannot open a second session. It requests Health sharing for workouts, heart rate and energy, creates the session and builder, begins collection, then calls startMirroringToCompanionDevice(). A mirroring failure is recorded, not fatal: the watch still records and saves; the phone simply does not see it. For strength it starts device motion at 50 Hz. 

// AlmanacWatch/WatchWorkoutController.swift
motion.startDeviceMotionUpdates(to: .main) { [weak self] data, _ in
    guard let self, let data else { return }
    MainActor.assumeIsolated {
        guard self.state == .running else { return }
        let acceleration = data.userAcceleration
        if self.counter.add(RepCounter.Sample(t: data.timestamp, x: acceleration.x, y: acceleration.y, z: acceleration.z)) {
            self.reps = self.counter.reps + self.manualReps
            self.sendPacket(force: true)
        }
    }
}

.main is the main-thread queue, so the handler is already on the main actor; assumeIsolated keeps every sample in order rather than scattering fifty hops a second through Task. The manual tally is separate from the counter's so that an automatic rep adds to the taps instead of overwriting them, which was the critical bug the review found. removeRep() spends the manual tally first and then offsets the automatic one, never below zero, and does nothing while the count is unknown, because a dash must not become a zero.

The clock is kept the way ActivitySessionState keeps it on the phone: a pause banks accumulated, a resume starts runningSince. The screen's timer is anchored at runningSince - accumulated, so it reads the workout's elapsed time rather than the time since this run began.

Ending has two paths, and they must never be confused. end() stops the activity; the .stopped delegate callback then ends collection, calls finishWorkout(), and the .ended callback resets. discard() detaches the delegates first, so no late .ended re-enters the teardown, then discards the builder and ends the session without finishing it. recover(), wired from handleActiveWorkoutRecovery(), adopts a session still active in HealthKit after watchOS relaunched the app; a session already stopped is settled at once, and a recovered strength session restarts motion with an unknown rep count rather than a zero.

On the phone: the bridge

// LIfeOS/App/Surfaces/WatchSessionBridge.swift
/// Owns the workout session mirrored from the watch. One per app: HealthKit
/// hands the session to whichever handler is installed at launch, so the
/// bridge is installed by the app delegate and the recorder subscribes.
@MainActor
final class WatchSessionBridge: NSObject, HKWorkoutSessionDelegate {
    static let shared = WatchSessionBridge()
    private(set) var session: HKWorkoutSession?
    private(set) var placeholderSessionID: UUID?
    private var dropping = false
    var onSession: ((HKWorkoutSession) -> Void)?
    var onPacket: ((Data) -> Void)?
    var onStateChange: ((HKWorkoutSessionState, Date) -> Void)?
    var hasSession: Bool { session != nil && !dropping }

    static func installMirroringHandler() {
        healthStore.workoutSessionMirroringStartHandler = { session in
            Task { @MainActor in
                let bridge = WatchSessionBridge.shared
                let unattended = bridge.onSession == nil
                bridge.adopt(session)
                if unattended { bridge.requestPlaceholderActivity(for: session) }
            }
        }
    }

The handler is installed from PushService's app delegate at launch, before any session can arrive. The placeholder matters for a workout started on the wrist: HealthKit launches the phone app in the background with no scene and so no recorder. The Live Activity has to be requested inside that launch, so the bridge asks for it itself, keeps the id, and the recorder's timer adopts that id when a screen finally attaches, so the card already on screen is updated rather than duplicated. 

// LIfeOS/App/Surfaces/WatchSessionBridge.swift
/// Whether a watch could take the session right now.
static var watchAvailable: Bool {
    guard WCSession.isSupported() else { return false }
    let wc = WCSession.default
    // Not `isReachable`: on iOS that is true only while the watch app is
    // already in the foreground, which is never the case for a person
    // tapping Begin on the phone.
    return wc.activationState == .activated && wc.isPaired && wc.isWatchAppInstalled
}

/// Sends a last command and drops the session only once it has left, in
/// the send's completion handler: releasing the session in the same
/// run-loop turn can cancel the send before the watch ever hears it.
func end(after command: PhoneCommand) {
    guard let session, let data = try? WatchWire.encode(PhoneCommandEnvelope(command: command, sentAt: .now)) else {
        end(); return
    }
    dropping = true
    session.sendToRemoteWorkoutSession(data: data) { _, _ in
        Task { @MainActor in self.end() }
    }
}

dropping exists because hasSession stays true through that window, and without it the next Start would refuse the hand-off against a session already on its way out.

On the phone: the recorder's watch half

// LIfeOS/Features/Activity/ViewModel/ActivityRecorder+Watch.swift
func handOffToWatch() async -> Bool {
    guard saveToHealth, watchAvailable(), let watch, !watch.hasSession else { return false }
    // Ask on the phone first. Authorization is shared with the paired
    // watch, so without this the first prompt a person ever sees is on the
    // wrist, while the phone is already counting down its ten seconds.
    guard await healthAuthorizationForHandoff() else { return false }
    let configuration = HKWorkoutConfiguration()
    configuration.activityType = selection.healthType
    source = .watch
    notice = Self.waitingForWatch
    try? await WatchSessionBridge.startWatchApp(configuration)
    let deadline = Date.now.addingTimeInterval(watchHandoffTimeout)
    while Date.now < deadline, watch.session == nil, active {
        try? await Task.sleep(for: .milliseconds(100))
    }
    guard active else { return true }
    if let mirrored = watch.session {
        if timer == nil { adoptMirroredSession(mirrored) }
        if notice == Self.waitingForWatch { notice = nil }
        return true
    }
    source = .phone
    notice = "Apple Watch did not answer. Recording on iPhone."
    return false
}

The hand-off is offered only when the workout is meant for Health, since the watch writes it there; a person who turned Health saving off keeps the phone. No timer starts until the watch answers, so nothing counts a session the watch may never take, and busy keeps the button reading "Starting…".

adoptMirroredSession handles both arrivals: the answer to a hand-off, and a session the person started on the wrist. If the phone is already recording its own session it refuses with a notice and sends discard. Otherwise it builds a fresh timer starting where the watch started, adopting the bridge's placeholder id if there is one, ends any stray Live Activity, stops the strap (the watch streams its own heart rate; two feeds would double every reading into the effort accrual), sets recordingHealth false so the draft never claims a Health session of the phone's own, and sends configure with the person's max heart rate so the watch can show a zone chip. 

// LIfeOS/Features/Activity/ViewModel/ActivityRecorder+Watch.swift
func receiveWatchPacket(_ data: Data) {
    guard active, hasSession, source == .watch, let packet = WatchWire.packet(from: data) else { return }
    // The counts are applied before that reading, so the one refresh carries
    // this packet's reps rather than the previous packet's.
    let refreshes = packet.heartRate != nil && packet.heartRateAt != nil && isRunning
    if let energy = packet.energyKcal { self.energy = energy }
    if selection == .strength {
        if let value = packet.reps { reps = value }
        if let value = packet.setIndex { setIndex = value }
        if let value = packet.completedSets { completedSets = value }
    }
    if let bpm = packet.heartRate, let at = packet.heartRateAt { receiveHeartRate(bpm, at: at) }
    if !refreshes { persistReading(at: packet.sentAt) }
}

Heart rate goes through the same receiveHeartRate as a strap reading, so effort accrual, throttling and the Live Activity stay one path. The ordering comment records a bug the checks found: a packet carrying both a heart rate and a rep change once published the previous rep count, because the single readout refresh ran inside receiveHeartRate before the counts were applied.

addRep, removeRep and nextSet each have two paths: on a watch session they send the command and wait for the echo packet; on a phone session they count locally. Pause, resume and finish likewise send commands for .watch and let the mirrored session's state change drive the timer, exactly as the phone's own session delegate does.

9.5View

AlmanacWatchApp shows WatchWorkoutScreen whenever the controller is not idle and the dashboard otherwise. The dashboard gained a Start workout button that presents a List of six activities in a sheet, because watchOS has no Menu. The scene's .task wires both delegate handlers and then drains any configuration or recovery that arrived before the task ran, so either order reaches the controller. 

// AlmanacWatch/WatchWorkoutScreen.swift
if let runningSince = workout.runningSince, workout.state == .running {
    Text(timerInterval: runningSince.addingTimeInterval(-workout.accumulated)...Date.distantFuture, countsDown: false)
        .font(.system(size: 34, weight: .semibold, design: .rounded)).monospacedDigit()
} else if workout.state == .paused {
    Text(Duration.seconds(workout.accumulated).formatted(.time(pattern: .minuteSecond)))
}
HStack(spacing: 6) {
    Image(systemName: "heart.fill").foregroundStyle(.red)
    Text(workout.heartRate.map(String.init) ?? "\u{2014}").font(.title2.monospacedDigit())
    if let max = workout.maxHeartRate, let bpm = workout.heartRate {
        Text("Z\(zone(bpm: bpm, max: max))").font(.caption2).foregroundStyle(.secondary)
    }
}

The screen is minimal on purpose: the activity name, the timer, heart rate with a zone chip once the phone has sent configure, and for strength the rep count over "reps · auto", the set number, and three buttons on two rows (−1 and +1, then Next set full width) because three bordered buttons split a 41 mm screen three ways and "Next set" wraps at about 48 points. Pause or Resume and End sit at the bottom. It uses the system font and the app's orange; the watch target does not link the design system. The zone bands are duplicated here in five lines because the watch cannot see HeartRateZones in Integrations.

On the phone, the surfaces from Chapter 8 grew a rep slot: the rings show the count and "auto" or "reps"; the tiles gain a Reps tile captioned "Counted from your wrist · auto" or "Tap +1 for each rep" and, after a set, "Earlier sets: 2 reps"; the Dynamic Island's compact trailing shows reps instead of the timer for strength; the lock screen's third tile shows the set and reps instead of calories. The connections panel says "Apple Watch is recording this session", "Apple Watch ready", or "Apple Watch not nearby".

9.6How it works

Step by step: started on the phone

  1. Begin, with Health saving on and a paired watch. The phone asks for its own Health authorisation first, because authorisation is shared with the paired watch and the first prompt should be on the phone.
  2. HKHealthStore.startWatchApp(toHandle:) launches Almanac on the watch with the configuration. The phone says "Asking your Apple Watch…" and polls the bridge every 100 ms for up to ten seconds.
  3. The watch delegate's handle(_:) passes the configuration to the controller (or parks it in pendingConfiguration if the scene's task has not run yet). The controller starts the session and begins mirroring.
  4. HealthKit calls the phone's workoutSessionMirroringStartHandler. The bridge adopts the session and calls onSession; the recorder's adoptMirroredSession builds the timer from the watch's start date and sends configure.
  5. Packets arrive once a second and on every rep. Heart rate accrues effort; reps and sets update the readout; the rings, tiles and Live Activity refresh through the Chapter 8 paths.
  6. Pause on the phone sends pause; the watch pauses its session; the mirrored state change comes back through the bridge and pauses the phone's timer. Pause on the watch takes the same last two steps.
  7. Finish on the phone sends end through end(after:) and calls saveFinished(), which writes the local record with the sets and never touches a builder. The watch ends collection, finishes the workout into Health, and resets.

Started on the wrist

Steps 4 to 7 are the same. The difference is step 3: there is no phone scene yet. HealthKit launches the phone app in the background, the bridge adopts the session unattended and requests the placeholder Live Activity, and when the person opens the phone the recorder attaches, finds watch.session already held, adopts it, and takes over the card by its id.

Ownership rules, stated once

  • The watch is offered the session only when saveToHealth is on.
  • The phone never creates a Health session for a .watch workout, and never writes an HKWorkout for one.
  • If the phone is already recording when a mirrored session arrives, it keeps its own and discards the mirrored one. It never merges, and it never ends it, since ending means saving.
  • A finished, saved timer is the resting Done screen; a workout started on the wrist then is a new one, not a continuation.
  • A .watch draft restores with Health saving on, asks recoverActiveWorkoutSession, hands anything returned to the bridge, and otherwise keeps the timer and waits for the next packet.

9.7Performance and cost

  • Packets are rate-limited on the watch. sendPacket(force: false) sends at most once a second from the builder's statistics callback; a rep forces one immediately because a rep is what the person is watching.
  • No strap and watch at once. Adopting a mirrored session stops the Bluetooth stream, so two feeds cannot double the effort accrual, and the radio is not held open for nothing.
  • Motion samples never leave the main actor. assumeIsolated on the .main queue keeps 50 samples a second in order without 50 task hops.
  • The counter is O(1) per sample. Two EMAs, one projection, a few comparisons. It keeps no history.
  • Motion stops on every end. end, discard, a failed start and the delegate's failure path all call stopMotion(), so the accelerometer is not left running after a session.
  • One placeholder at a time. A second session arriving before the recorder adopts the first cannot leave two cards on screen.
  • The hand-off costs nothing when there is no watch. watchAvailable is three synchronous reads of WCSession; a person with no watch never waits.
  • Nothing leaves either device. The mirrored session's data channel is HealthKit's own, device to device. No server, no push.

9.8Edge cases and tests

ConditionBehaviour
Watch paired but does not answer in 10 s"Apple Watch did not answer. Recording on iPhone." and the phone path runs
Health saving offNo hand-off; the phone records; no notice
Phone refuses Health authorisation before the hand-offHand-off skipped; the phone path runs and shows its own error
Phone already recording when a watch session arrivesWatch session discarded with a notice; the phone session continues
Packet with an unknown versionIgnored; nothing changes
Packet without a heart rateEnergy and counts apply; heart rate stays as it was; one refresh
Packet with heart rate and a rep changeCounts applied first, then the reading, so the one publish carries the new count

Automatic rep after a manual +1Summed, not overwritten
−1 with an unknown countNo change; a dash must not become a zero
−1 at zeroStays at zero

A throw after startActivity on the watchDelegates detached, session ended, builder discarded, state back to idle; no late callback can revive it

Tests

  • RepCounterTests (6): the five calibration cases plus reset.
  • WatchWireTests (5): packet round trip keeps absence; unknown version ignored; command round trip; removeRep round trip; a command is never read as a packet.
  • LiveSessionReadoutTests: reps round trip and format; the throttle publishes on a reps change. LiveEffortTests.builderCarriesRepsAndSet. WorkoutSetsTests: sets round trip through setsData. ActivitySessionStateTests.aTimerCanAdoptAnExistingIdentity.
  • ActivityRecorderChecks, the watch cases: a phone strength session starts at set 1 with zero reps; remove rep never goes below zero; manual reps and sets count; a watch packet never reaches a phone session; finishing writes the sets; the wait says so; a watch that does not answer falls back; a seeded .watch draft restores as a watch session with Health saving on; an unknown-version packet changes nothing; a current-version packet carries reps and heart rate through; finishing a watch session writes the local record and never claims a Health save.
Pending on hardware Recorded in docs/design/watch-companion/report.md as unverified: (1) start from the phone and see the watch launch and the HUD show watch heart rate within 10 seconds; (2) start from the watch and see the phone's Live Activity appear; (3) ten slow bicep curls against the auto count; (4) pause on the watch and see the phone pause; (5) finish and find exactly one workout in Health. Plus two from the draft port: the −1 correction landing on the number the other device shows, and whether watchOS actually calls handleActiveWorkoutRecovery() and the adopted session mirrors and saves. The package test count after this slice was 1247 in 163 suites; the checks page passed 29 of 29.

9.9Study notes

Read in this order

  1. LifeOSKit/Sources/AppSurfaces/WatchWire.swift, the two shapes and the gate.
  2. LifeOSKit/Sources/Motion/RepCounter.swift with its tests open beside it.
  3. AlmanacWatch/WatchWorkoutController.swift: start, startMotion, addRep, removeRep, end, discard, recover.
  4. LIfeOS/App/Surfaces/WatchSessionBridge.swift, particularly watchAvailable, end(after:) and the placeholder.
  5. LIfeOS/Features/Activity/ViewModel/ActivityRecorder+Watch.swift, top to bottom.
  6. The source == .watch branch of ActivityRecorder.attach.
  7. AlmanacWatch/AlmanacWatchApp.swift and WatchAppDelegate.swift for the before-or-after wiring.

Check yourself

  • Why does watchAvailable not read isReachable? On iOS it is true only while the watch app is in the foreground, which is never so when the person taps Begin on the phone; startWatchApp exists to launch it.
  • Why is the session dropped inside the send's completion handler? Releasing it in the same run-loop turn can cancel the send before the watch hears it.
  • Why does the phone ask for Health authorisation before offering the watch? Authorisation is shared; without it the first prompt lands on the wrist while the phone is counting down.
  • What does kind prevent? A command decoding as an empty packet, since the two shapes share every required key.
  • Why are manual and automatic reps tracked separately? So an automatic rep adds to the taps instead of overwriting them.
  • Why is discard a separate command from end? On the wrist end means finish and save; sending it for a refused session would write a stub into Health.

Chapter ten

10The workout library

A curated table of 122 verified YouTube workouts, a pure planner that turns preferences, today's battery and the week's splits into one session, a library that filters the catalog to it and says every time it had to widen, and a player that puts the glass rings over the video wherever the person drags them.

10.1Intent

Almanac could show what the body did and how recovered it was, but never suggested a session and had no way to follow one. The request was plain: pull up workouts from YouTube matching what the person wants to do (strength, then push, pull, legs, arms, chest), coordinated with how much they can push today, with the live HUD on the video. Three constraints shaped everything that follows.

  • The app ships free. No runtime AI calls, no per-user YouTube API quota. The catalog is a table the service role writes; the app reads it with the person's own token and caches it.
  • YouTube's terms. Videos play in YouTube's own player and nothing may obscure its controls or branding. The rings default to the top leading corner, the region farthest from the control bar, and a drop onto that bar is moved off it.
  • A video the catalog cannot verify never ships. Every id is checked against YouTube's keyless oEmbed endpoint at seed time, and the seed migration is generated, never hand-edited.

Working backwards

Open Health, Fitness, "Plan today's workout". The Today card already knows: "Pull day. You did push on Saturday, so today is pull. Battery 83% · up to zone 5. 30 min." Below it a rail of chips (Saved, then the splits with Pull already lit, then three lengths, then the equipment you said you own) and a list of videos with real thumbnails, the channel, the minutes, three intensity dots and the split. Search by title, channel or muscle. Tap the heart to keep one; hold a row to schedule it for a day, and a "Tue 15" chip appears on it. Tap a row and the video opens in YouTube's player; tap Start and the rings float over the picture. Drag them wherever you like, tap the corner button or turn the phone for full screen, and the same video keeps playing.

Why not let the AI plan the workout?

Cost and honesty. A pure function from four inputs is free, deterministic, and every rule in it is a test. The reason it gives ("You did push on Saturday, so today is pull.") is the rule itself, in words.

What happens offline?

The cache is the source the screen renders; the network only ever adds to it. A refresh that fails leaves the last catalog on screen and says "Showing the last catalog we downloaded." An empty cache with no network says "The library needs a connection the first time." and never a fake list. Thumbnails come from YouTube's image host and fall back to a deliberate tile.

Why does the Saved list ignore today's plan?

A heart is a decision the person already made. Intersecting saves with the plan hid a push video saved today from tomorrow's pull-day Saved list, while its heart was still filled in the full list. The Saved chip is a different list, not a narrower one: the saved rows, newest mark first, narrowed only by the search.
