10.3Model

The catalog

-- supabase/migrations/20260915090000_workout_videos.sql
create table public.workout_videos (
  youtube_id   text primary key,
  title        text not null,
  channel      text not null,
  duration_s   integer not null check (duration_s > 0),
  goal         text[] not null,        -- strength | hypertrophy | endurance | mobility
  split        text not null,          -- push | pull | legs | upper | lower | full | core | arms | chest | back | shoulders | mobility | cardio
  muscles      text[] not null default '{}',
  equipment    text[] not null default '{}', -- none | dumbbells | barbell | bands | machine | kettlebell
  intensity    smallint not null check (intensity between 1 and 3),
  verified_at  timestamptz not null,
  updated_at   timestamptz not null default now()
);
alter table public.workout_videos enable row level security;
revoke all on public.workout_videos from anon, authenticated;
grant select on public.workout_videos to authenticated;
create policy "catalog is readable when signed in" on public.workout_videos
  for select to authenticated using (true);

Enums are text, as the notes table does, so a new split lands as data. The revoke all is not decoration: Supabase grants all on a new public table to anon and authenticated by default, so without it the sentence "signed-in users get read-only access" would be untrue at the grant layer. It also takes away TRUNCATE, which bypasses row-level security. The final review added it, matching the social groups table.

The seed today holds 122 rows: 22 cardio, 16 upper, 16 mobility, 15 legs, 8 each of push, pull and full, 7 lower, 5 core, 5 arms, 4 each of chest, back and shoulders. Seventy-five come from FitnessBlender, thirteen each from Sydney Cummings and Heather Robertson, five from Caroline Girvan, and the rest from a handful of others. Intensity skews moderate: 71 at 2, 40 at 1, 11 at 3. Thumbnails are not stored; the app derives https://i.ytimg.com/vi/<id>/hqdefault.jpg.

The cache

// LifeOSKit/Sources/Persistence/CatalogVideo.swift
/// A cached catalog row. The server is the source of truth; a refresh
/// replaces the set, so a video pulled from the catalog disappears here.
@Model
public final class CatalogVideo {
    #Unique<CatalogVideo>([\.youtubeID])
    public var youtubeID: String
    public var title: String
    public var channel: String
    public var durationS: Int
    public var goal: [String]
    public var split: String
    public var muscles: [String]
    public var equipment: [String]
    public var intensity: Int
    public var verifiedAt: Date
    public var cachedAt: Date
    public var durationMinutes: Int { Int((Double(durationS) / 60).rounded()) }
}

CatalogStore.upsert updates matches, inserts new rows and deletes absent ones, so the cache mirrors the server after every successful refresh. It builds its lookup with uniquingKeysWith rather than uniqueKeysWithValues: the primary key makes a duplicate id impossible from the real table, and a trap on a malformed response is a crash where keeping the last row is not.

The bookmark

// LifeOSKit/Sources/Persistence/WorkoutBookmark.swift
/// A person's mark on a catalog video: saved for later, scheduled for a day,
/// or both. One row per video id; absent means neither.
@Model
public final class WorkoutBookmark {
    #Unique<WorkoutBookmark>([\.youtubeID])
    public var youtubeID: String
    public var saved: Bool
    /// A calendar day start, never a timestamp.
    public var scheduledFor: Date?
    public var updatedAt: Date
}

BookmarkStore.toggleSaved and schedule delete the row when it ends up neither saved nor scheduled, so the table never accumulates empty marks. Both read the row's fields before a possible delete, because a deleted model is not a thing to ask questions of. schedule normalises to startOfDay with the caller's calendar so a picker's time of day never decides which day a workout lands on.

Preferences and the record

UserGoals gained three columns: trainingGoal: String?, equipmentRaw: [String] = [], sessionMinutes: Int?. WorkoutRecord gained split: String? and videoID: String?, written when a session started from a video and nil for freeform sessions, and setsData from Chapter 9. Every one is optional or defaulted, for the reason in 10.8.

10.4ViewModel

The planner

// LifeOSKit/Sources/Sectors/WorkoutPlanner.swift
public static func plan(goal: String?, sessionMinutes: Int?, batteryPercent: Int?,
                        recentSplits: [(date: Date, split: String)], now: Date,
                        calendar: Calendar = .current) -> TrainingPlan {
    let minutes = sessionMinutes ?? 30
    let recent = recentSplits.filter { $0.date >= weekAgo && $0.date <= now }.sorted { $0.date > $1.date }
    let cap: Int = { switch batteryPercent {
        case .some(let b) where b >= 67: return 3
        case .some(let b) where b >= 34: return 2
        case .some: return 1
        case .none: return 2 } }()

    if (batteryPercent ?? 100) <= 33 || (batteryPercent == nil && hardYesterday) {
        return TrainingPlan(split: "mobility", minutes: minutes, maxIntensity: 1,
                            reason: "Recovery is low today, so this is a mobility day.")
    }
    switch goal {
    case "mobility": ...
    case "endurance": return TrainingPlan(split: "cardio", ..., reason: "Endurance today, paced by your battery.")
    case "strength", "hypertrophy":
        if let last = recent.first(where: { rotation.contains($0.split) }) {
            let next = rotation[(rotation.firstIndex(of: last.split)! + 1) % rotation.count]
            return TrainingPlan(split: next, ..., reason: "You did \(last.split) on \(weekday), so today is \(next).")
        }
        return TrainingPlan(split: "push", ..., reason: "First session this week: push.")
    default:
        return TrainingPlan(split: "full", ..., reason: "Set a goal for a plan built around you.")
    }
}

Four rules in order: a red or unknown-after-a-hard-day battery forces mobility at intensity 1; a mobility or endurance goal picks its own split, capped by battery; strength and hypertrophy rotate push, pull, legs off the most recent of those three within seven days; no goal means full body. The weekday in the reason is looked up on an en_US_POSIX copy of the calendar, because some process environments resolve the locale to abbreviated names and the reason string should be deterministic. The battery cap on intensity is the same band table as the effort ceiling in Chapter 8, so "up to zone 4" on the Today card and the yellow ring on the HUD are the same fact.

The filter

// LifeOSKit/Sources/Sectors/WorkoutLibraryFilter.swift
public static func apply(videos: [LibraryVideo], plan: TrainingPlan, goal: String?, split: String?,
                         band: DurationBand?, equipment: Set<String>, query: String = "") -> (rows: [LibraryVideo], note: String?) {
    let chosenSplit = split ?? plan.split
    // The intensity cap and the equipment the person owns are never
    // widened away: a battery ceiling and a kit list are facts, not
    // preferences to relax when the list comes back short.
    let base = videos.filter { video in
        video.intensity <= plan.maxIntensity
            && (equipment.isEmpty || !Set(video.equipment).isDisjoint(with: equipment))
            && (normalizedQuery.isEmpty || matches(video, query: normalizedQuery))
    }
    var note: String?
    var result = base.filter { $0.split == chosenSplit && inBand($0) }
    if result.isEmpty {
        result = base.filter { $0.split == chosenSplit }
        if !result.isEmpty { note = "Widened to any length." }
    }
    // Only when the split is the plan's own. A chip the person tapped is
    // an instruction, and answering it with another split while the chip
    // still reads selected would be the screen contradicting itself.
    if result.isEmpty, split == nil {
        result = base.filter { video in goal.map { video.goal.contains($0) } ?? true }
        if !result.isEmpty { note = "Widened to any split for your goal." }
    }
    let rows = result.sorted { closeness to plan.minutes, then title }
    return (rows, note)
}

The plan first: its split, its intensity cap, its length give or take fifteen minutes. An empty result widens one step at a time and says which step it took, so a short list is never a mystery. Three things never widen: the intensity cap, the equipment, and the search query. The rows are ordered by closeness to the requested length, then title, so a 30-minute plan lists the 28-minute video before the 45.

The view model

// LIfeOS/Features/Workouts/ViewModel/WorkoutLibraryViewModel.swift
func load() {
    guard let context else { return }
    let store = MetricsStore(context: context, calendar: calendar)
    let today = now()
    goals = try? store.goals()
    videos = (try? CatalogStore.all(context: context)) ?? []
    loadBookmarks()
    capacity = CapacityInputs.todayCapacity(store: store, now: today, calendar: calendar)

    let weekAgo = calendar.date(byAdding: .day, value: -7, to: today) ?? today
    let recent: [(date: Date, split: String)] = ((try? store.workouts(from: weekAgo, to: today)) ?? [])
        .compactMap { record in record.split.map { (date: record.start, split: $0) } }

    plan = WorkoutPlanner.plan(goal: goals?.trainingGoal, sessionMinutes: goals?.sessionMinutes,
                               batteryPercent: capacity?.percent, recentSplits: recent,
                               now: today, calendar: calendar)
    applyFilters()
}

Everything the screen needs is read in one pass: preferences, the cache, today's battery, and the week of splits the rotation turns on. The clock and the calendar are injected so tests can fix a day. Every filter property (splitFilter, durationBand, equipmentFilter, query, savedOnly) re-runs applyFilters() on set, which maps the cached models into LibraryVideo values, calls the pure filter, and maps the chosen ids back. 

// LIfeOS/Features/Workouts/ViewModel/WorkoutLibraryViewModel.swift
func refreshIfDue(force: Bool = false) async {
    guard let context, !isRefreshing else { return }
    let newest = videos.map(\.cachedAt).max()
    let due = force || newest.map { now().timeIntervalSince($0) > Self.refreshInterval } ?? true
    guard due else { return }
    guard let baseURL = AppConfig.supabaseURL, let anonKey = AppConfig.supabaseAnonKey else { noteOffline(); return }
    guard let token = sessions.load()?.accessToken else { noteSignedOut(); return }
    isRefreshing = true
    defer { isRefreshing = false }
    do {
        let rows = try await WorkoutCatalogClient(baseURL: baseURL, anonKey: anonKey).videos(accessToken: token)
        guard CatalogRefresh.shouldReplace(cacheCount: videos.count, incoming: rows.count) else {
            refreshNotice = "The catalog came back empty. Showing the last one we downloaded."
            applyFilters()
            return
        }
        try CatalogStore.upsert(rows, context: context, now: now())
        refreshNotice = nil
        load()
    } catch {
        noteOffline()
    }
}

The refresh runs when the newest cached row is more than a day old, or on pull to refresh. A signed-out person is told to sign in rather than to find signal, because the catalog is read with their own token. And a 200 with no rows is refused by CatalogRefresh.shouldReplace: an unseeded table, a policy that stopped matching, or a range quirk all look like an empty array at the client, and replacing a full cache with that would leave a person who had the whole library a second ago with nothing.

Bookmarks are refetched after every change rather than mutated in place, because toggleSaved and schedule can delete a row, and a deleted model left in the dictionary would be read by the next row that asks. pruneStaleSchedules runs on every load and clears any day that has passed, keeping the save, so a row never carries a stale chip and the schedule sheet never opens on a day its own picker will not accept.

10.5View

The library

WorkoutLibraryScreen is pushed on whichever stack the person is already on (the Fitness segment's training card, or Begin Activity's "Follow a video"), so the way back is the way they came. It sits on a GradientCanvas in the activity hue with the Today card, a status line when the list is non-empty, the chip rail, then the rows or an empty state. The search field is in the navigation bar drawer, always visible, covering no row. The preferences sheet is raised once, decided in attach rather than in every load, because deciding it in load put the sheet back up the moment a Health sync ran.

Rows are cards in a LazyVStack, so scheduling is a context menu rather than a swipe: only a List row can be swiped. The heart is a sibling of the opening button, never inside it, because SwiftUI gives a button nested in a button no defined semantics and saving a video would also open it. The channel and the minutes are two Texts, not one: a long channel name used to push the minutes off the end of the line, and the minutes are the number a person scans for. The channel truncates; the minutes never do. A scheduled row shows its day chip in place of the equipment chips, because four chips beside a thumbnail truncate to "T…" and "Dum…".

The player

// LIfeOS/Features/Workouts/View/YouTubePlayerView.swift
/// The web view behind the player, owned by the screen rather than the view.
///
/// Portrait, full screen and landscape are different layouts of the same
/// player, and SwiftUI gives a view in a different branch a different
/// identity, which would mean a new web view and a video starting over every
/// time the phone turned or the full screen button was tapped.
@MainActor
final class YouTubePlayerHost {
    let webView: WKWebView
    fileprivate var loaded: String?
    init() {
        let configuration = WKWebViewConfiguration()
        configuration.allowsInlineMediaPlayback = true
        configuration.mediaTypesRequiringUserActionForPlayback = []
        webView = WKWebView(frame: .zero, configuration: configuration)
    }
}

VideoWorkoutScreen holds one YouTubePlayerHost in its state and shows the same web view in three layouts. Portrait: the player at 16:9 with the rings floating over it and a full-screen button in the corner; "Open in YouTube" (always present, not only after a failure, because a video the owner barred from embedding says so inside the player where nothing this screen can see reaches); the title, channel, minutes and chips; then either "Start this workout" or the elapsed clock, the rep buttons and ActivityControls. Full screen, entered by the button or by turning the phone: black, the player letterboxed or filling, and one overlay holding the rings, a Start pill before the session, and two glass buttons (session controls in a sheet, and exit). 

// LIfeOS/Features/Workouts/Model/VideoWorkoutLayout.swift
static let embedOrigin = "https://www.youtube-nocookie.com"
static let idPattern = /^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{11}$/

static func embedURL(youtubeID: String) -> URL? {
    guard youtubeID.wholeMatch(of: idPattern) != nil else { return nil }
    // `fs=0` removes YouTube's own full screen button. That button hands
    // the video to a system layer above the whole app, where no HUD can
    // be drawn; the screen offers its own full screen instead.
    return URL(string: "https://www.youtube-nocookie.com/embed/\(youtubeID)"
        + "?origin=\(embedOrigin)&enablejsapi=1&playsinline=1&rel=0&modestbranding=1&fs=0")
}

The id pattern is checked before anything is interpolated into a URL or the wrapper page, and a row that fails shows "This video will not play here." There is no JavaScript bridge: the person taps YouTube's play button, the one gesture the embed needs, and the recorder times the session rather than trying to follow the video's clock.

The draggable HUD

// LifeOSKit/Sources/AppSurfaces/HUDPlacement.swift
/// (0, 0) is the top leading corner inside the inset; (1, 1) the bottom
/// trailing one.
public struct Anchor: Equatable, Sendable {
    public var x: Double
    public var y: Double
    public static let topLeading = Anchor(x: 0, y: 0)
    public var stored: String { "\(x),\(y)" }
}

/// Where a dropped HUD settles: inside the container, and off the strip
/// it is not allowed to cover, on whichever side of it is nearer and fits.
public static func settle(origin: CGPoint, hud: CGSize, container: CGSize, inset: CGFloat,
                          avoiding strip: CGRect?) -> CGPoint

A position is kept as an anchor, a fraction of the free travel in each axis, rather than a point. The same anchor puts the rings in the same relative place over a small player in portrait, a letterboxed one in full screen and the whole screen in landscape, and it stays meaningful when the HUD collapses to the bar. DraggableHUD stores one anchor per placement ("compact", "fullscreen", "landscape") in AppStorage. The rings follow the finger freely while dragging; the settle rule is applied once, on release, so it reads as a snap rather than a wall. The strip it avoids is the bottom 56 points of the player, where YouTube draws its control bar and logo. Four accessibility actions move it to each corner. It renders at zero opacity until measured, because a HUD drawn at the inset for one frame and then jumping to its saved spot reads as a glitch on every appearance.

Orientation

// LIfeOS/App/OrientationLock.swift
@MainActor
enum OrientationLock {
    static let standard: UIInterfaceOrientationMask =
        UIDevice.current.userInterfaceIdiom == .pad ? .all : .portrait
    private(set) static var mask = standard

    static func allow(_ allowed: UIInterfaceOrientationMask) { ... }

    /// Back to the default, and back upright: a phone still held sideways
    /// would otherwise stay in a landscape the next screen cannot draw.
    static func release() {
        allow(standard)
        guard standard == .portrait else { return }
        for scene in UIApplication.shared.connectedScenes.compactMap({ $0 as? UIWindowScene }) {
            scene.requestGeometryUpdate(.iOS(interfaceOrientations: .portrait))
        }
    }
}

The iPhone target now lists landscape in its build settings so the player can turn, but almost nothing else in the app is laid out for it. So the app delegate answers every orientation query from OrientationLock.mask, which defaults to portrait on a phone; the player screen asks for .allButUpsideDown in onAppear and hands it back in onDisappear, forcing the scene upright so the next screen is not asked to draw a landscape it has no layout for. iPad keeps every orientation, as it always has.

10.6How it works

Step by step: from curation to a saved session

  1. A human edits scripts/catalog/catalog.json. verify.ts parses it (ids match the eleven-character pattern, goals and splits and equipment are from the fixed vocabularies, intensity is 1 to 3, no duplicate ids), then calls YouTube's oEmbed endpoint for every id and fails the run if any returns an error, a title that does not start with the row's title, a channel that differs beyond case and spacing, or a duration more than 10 percent off a length stated in the title.
  2. It writes the seed: one upsert per row and one trailing delete ... where youtube_id not in (...) naming every verified id, so a seed run is a full sync and a row dropped from the JSON leaves the server on the next push. An empty catalog is refused before a single network call, because the trailing delete would make it a migration that wipes the table. After the first push the file name is frozen, so later passes use --out to write a new timestamped migration.
  3. The library opens. attach loads the cache, the preferences, today's capacity and the week's splits, plans, filters, and raises the preferences sheet once if no goal is set. .task calls refreshIfDue().
  4. If the newest cached row is older than a day, one PostgREST select runs with the person's token. Rows replace the cache unless the answer is empty and the cache is not.
  5. Tapping a row pushes VideoWorkoutScreen. The web view loads a wrapper page, based at the privacy-enhanced host, containing an iframe of the embed URL.
  6. Start maps the split to an activity (cardio to .other, mobility to .yoga, everything else to .strength) and calls recorder.start(following:) with the video's id, split, title and channel. The video belongs to this start: a start that bails leaves nothing behind for the next freeform walk.
  7. The rings appear over the player through DraggableHUD. The session runs exactly as in Chapters 8 and 9.
  8. Finish writes the record with videoID, split and sets. The Fitness segment's row shows the split chip; tomorrow's planner reads it for the rotation.
The embed that would not play On the first spot-check zero of six seed videos rendered; every one gave YouTube's "Error 152" card. Loading the embed URL straight into the web view gave the harder error 153; wrapping it in an iframe on a page of our own moved every id to 152; the fix was matching the query's origin parameter to the page's own baseURL and pointing both at youtube-nocookie.com. Six of six then rendered. The report records the elimination.

10.7Performance and cost

  • Zero per-user API cost. The catalog is one table read with the anon key and the person's JWT. No YouTube Data API, no quota, no key. Thumbnails are static images from YouTube's CDN.
  • One fetch a day. refreshInterval is 86,400 seconds; a refresh is otherwise only on pull. The library works entirely from the cache after the first download.
  • Curation is free at runtime. Verification runs on a laptop before a migration; the app never verifies anything.
  • The planner and filter are pure and cheap. One pass over at most 122 rows per filter change, with the cached models mapped to value types once per pass. No index is needed at this size.
  • One web view. The player host lives in the screen's state, so rotation and full screen never reload the video or lose the person's place.
  • Bookmarks are one dictionary. A row asks a dictionary, not the store; the dictionary is rebuilt after a write, when the store is the truth.
  • Capacity is shared, not recomputed differently. CapacityInputs.todayCapacity serves the recorder and the planner, so the battery is read once the same way.
  • The HUD's settle is pure. Corner cases (a HUD wider than its player, a drop onto the control strip) are tests rather than thumbs on a device.
  • What leaves the device. One authenticated read of the catalog; image requests to i.ytimg.com; the embed to youtube-nocookie.com, the privacy-enhanced host. Bookmarks, schedules and preferences never leave.

10.8Edge cases and tests

A field added to an existing @Model must be optional or defaulted Commit 2d01bd8 on 15 September: the goals row gained equipmentRaw: [String], a mandatory array with no default. SwiftData refused to migrate any store written before it ("Validation error missing attribute values on mandatory destination attribute"). The container never opened, the shell had no account to show, and the app sat on the signed-in spinner. The fix is = []; the guard is SchemaMigrationTests.fieldsAddedToTheGoalsRowHaveDefaults, which walks the entity's attributes and asserts each added one is optional or has a default. Every column added since (bookmarks, split, videoID, setsData, the extras and sources bags) follows the rule.
ConditionBehaviour
First open, no network"The library needs a connection the first time." with a wifi.slash glyph; never a fake list
Later open, no networkLast catalog shown; "Showing the last catalog we downloaded."
Signed out"Sign in to download the library." rather than a connection message
Server answers 200 with zero rowsCache kept; "The catalog came back empty. Showing the last one we downloaded."
Server answers zero rows to an empty cacheReplaced, because there is nothing to lose
No goal setPreferences sheet once; plan is "full" with "Set a goal for a plan built around you."
Battery 0 to 33Mobility at intensity 1 regardless of goal
Battery unknown after a hard dayMobility; unknown otherwise caps intensity at 2
No video at the plan's lengthWidened to any length, and the list says so
No video at the plan's splitWidened to any split for the goal, only when no split chip is tapped
A split chip tapped and nothing matchesEmpty state; the chip is an instruction and is not widened away
Widened list while offlineBoth lines shown, one under the other
Saved chip with nothing saved"Nothing saved yet. Tap the heart on a workout to keep it here."
A schedule for a day that has passedCleared on load; the save is kept
Schedule sheet seeded with a past dayClamped to today, the picker's floor
Unsave a scheduled rowRow kept for its schedule; unschedule an unsaved row deletes it

Leaving the player sidewaysrelease() forces the scene upright

Tests

  • WorkoutPlannerTests (6): red battery is mobility; strength rotates after the most recent split; the first session of the week is push; endurance and mobility goals; unknown goal is full body; unknown battery after a hard day is mobility.
  • WorkoutLibraryFilterTests (9): widens to any length then any split; keeps the intensity cap while widening; orders by closeness then title; an explicit split chip is not widened away; equipment and band narrow without widening; search matches title, channel or muscle and survives widening; the saved list ignores the plan but not the query; an empty query changes nothing.
  • CatalogRefreshTests (3), CatalogVideoTests (2: upsert is idempotent and removes missing rows; goals and workout columns default to absent), WorkoutBookmarkTests (4), WorkoutCatalogClientTests (2: the request carries both keys and selects everything; arrays decode and an unknown split is kept as text), HUDPlacementTests (9), SchemaMigrationTests (1).
  • scripts/catalog/verify_lib_test.ts: 7 Deno tests for parsing, title and channel matching, duration plausibility, the SQL, and the empty-catalog refusal.
  • ActivityRecorderChecks: finishing stamps the video and split; a failed start does not stamp the next session; a wrist-started session carries no stale video; a restored draft keeps its video.

The QA report records 1266 package tests in 168 suites after this slice, 34 of 34 recorder checks, the library captured on iPhone in both schemes and on iPad, the empty state, the schedule sheet, and the player before and during a session. The landscape capture is recorded as pending: at the time of the report the iPhone was still portrait-only, and the rotation the player now asks for arrived with the full-screen commit the following day.

10.9Study notes

Read in this order

  1. scripts/catalog/verify_lib.ts, then verify.ts: what a row must be before it can ship.
  2. supabase/migrations/20260915090000_workout_videos.sql: the table and why the revoke comes before the grant.
  3. LifeOSKit/Sources/Sectors/WorkoutPlanner.swift with its tests open.
  4. LifeOSKit/Sources/Sectors/WorkoutLibraryFilter.swift, the widening and the saved list.
  5. LIfeOS/Features/Workouts/ViewModel/WorkoutLibraryViewModel.swift: load, refreshIfDue, applyFilters, loadBookmarks.
  6. LIfeOS/Features/Workouts/View/YouTubePlayerView.swift and VideoWorkoutLayout.swift, the origin fix.
  7. LifeOSKit/Sources/AppSurfaces/HUDPlacement.swift, then DraggableHUD.swift, then OrientationLock.swift.

Check yourself

  • Why does the seed end with a delete? So a seed run is a full sync; a row removed from the JSON leaves the server on the next push instead of living forever.
  • Why is an empty 200 not believed? An unseeded table or a policy that stopped matching looks the same as an empty catalog, and replacing a full cache with it strands the person.
  • Which three filters are never widened, and why? Intensity cap, equipment, search: a battery ceiling and a kit list are facts, and a query is what the person is typing.
  • Why is the web view held in the screen's state? Each layout branch would otherwise get a fresh view identity and restart the video on every rotation.
  • Why is the HUD position an anchor and not a point? A fraction of free travel survives a size change: the small player, full screen, landscape, and the collapse to a bar.
  • What did commit 2d01bd8 teach? A mandatory field added to a shipped model with no default stops the store from opening at all, and now a test guards it.

Chapter eleven

11Money

Real transactions from a real bank, exact to the cent, on six pastel bands. The device holds the ledger, the server holds only the credential, and every figure on the tab is derived from rows that actually happened.

11.1Intent

The Money tab answers six questions, one per side tab: what came in and went out, where it went, what repeats every month, what is being saved towards, what hurts, and the ledger itself. It reads from a bank connected through Plaid, or from transactions typed in by hand, and it never invents a row. The sample month that used to stand in before a bank was linked is gone. An empty month shows the empty state.

Working backwards

Connect a bank once and Almanac keeps the last two years of transactions on the phone. The net for the month is the first thing on the screen with a one-word verdict under it. Budgets are buckets that claim categories, so a renamed category never silently stops counting. Tap any category, any merchant, or any row to see six months of it on a page of its own.

Why is the savings rate sometimes blank rather than 0%?

A savings rate against no income is undefined, not zero. Rendering 0% says you saved nothing when what happened is that nothing was earned. The whole app draws that distinction and this is its sharpest case.

Where do my transactions live?

On the device, in SwiftData. The Edge Functions hand each sync delta straight back to the phone and store nothing but the bank credential. A compromise of the database exposes a token, not a ledger of where you shop.

Why can Plaid never be called from the app?

Every Plaid endpoint needs a client id and a secret on the request, and an .ipa is a zip file. Any secret compiled into the binary is public the moment it ships, so the four Plaid calls run in Edge Functions and the app talks only to those, authenticated with its own Supabase session.

What happens to a pending charge?

Stored and shown, greyed, but excluded from every rollup. Plaid re-issues a pending transaction under a new id when it settles and sends the old id in removed, so counting it twice is the default failure and the rollup refusing to see pending rows is what prevents it.

The arithmetic is in the package, not in the feature. summarise, BudgetPeriod.assess, SpendSeries, RecurringSpend and MoneyParts are all free functions or value types with no store and no context, which is why the money rules are among the best-tested code in the app. The app target still has no test target of its own, so anything that decides something is pushed down to where it can be tested.

11.3Model

MoneyEntry, shaped for Plaid from the first line

// LifeOSKit/Sources/Persistence/MoneyEntry.swift
@Model
public final class MoneyEntry {
    public var id: UUID
    public var externalID: String?      // Plaid transaction_id, nil for manual
    public var sourceRaw: String
    public var date: Date               // always startOfDay
    public var amount: Double           // positive = in, negative = out
    public var currencyCode: String
    public var merchant: String
    public var category: String?        // display text, never keys arithmetic
    public var categoryCode: String?    // Plaid personal_finance_category.detailed
    public var merchantID: String?      // Plaid merchant_entity_id
    public var logoURL: String?
    public var accountID: String?
    public var accountName: String?
    public var pending: Bool
    ...
    public var isSpending: Bool {
        amount < 0 && !pending && !MoneyCategoryRule.isTransferLike(categoryCode)
    }
}

Three pairs of fields look redundant and are not. category is what the row shows; categoryCode is what the rollup and the buckets key on, so renaming a label can never change a savings rate. merchant is the descriptor the bank sent; merchantID is Plaid's stable entity, so NETFLIX.COM and Netflix are one merchant where the id exists and two strings where it does not. And MoneyAccount keeps both type and subtype, because "is this money owed" reads the first and "is this a credit card" reads the second, and a mortgage is a loan with a balance and no meaningful utilisation.

Every field added since the first edition (merchantID, logoURL, subtype, mask, availableBalance, creditLimit) is optional. That is what makes each one a lightweight SwiftData migration: a row written before the field existed reads back nil, and the app never hangs on the launch spinner the way it does when a new field lacks a default.

Sign convention: positive is money in Plaid's amount is positive when money leaves the account. This app's is the opposite. PlaidMapping negates on the way in, and the rule is written on the type, on the mapping, and on the scorer, because a silent flip turns a salary into the month's largest expense and nothing crashes.

The rollup

// LifeOSKit/Sources/Persistence/MoneyEntry.swift
public func summarise(entries: [MoneyEntry], accounts: [MoneyAccount] = []) -> MoneySummary {
    var income = 0.0
    var expenses = 0.0
    for entry in entries where !entry.pending
        && !MoneyCategoryRule.isTransferLike(entry.categoryCode) {
        if entry.amount > 0 { income += entry.amount } else if entry.isSpending { expenses += -entry.amount }
    }
    return MoneySummary(
        income: income,
        expenses: expenses,
        netWorth: accounts.isEmpty ? nil : accounts.reduce(0) { $0 + $1.netWorthContribution }
    )
}

Transfers between your own accounts and credit card payments appear as a real debit and a real credit. Counting them leaves net correct but overstates both income and expenses, and the savings rate is computed from those two. MoneyCategoryRule.isTransferLike matches TRANSFER_IN_ and TRANSFER_OUT_ as underscore-delimited prefixes plus the card-payment code, and nothing else. The underscore matters: without it a code that merely starts with the same letters would be excluded as if it were a transfer, which is a test (aCategoryThatMerelyStartsLikeATransferIsStillSpending) rather than a hope.

MoneyParts, or why cents are split in the kit

// LifeOSKit/Sources/Persistence/MoneyParts.swift
public init(_ amount: Double) {
    // Round in the unit that has to carry: cents, as an integer.
    let totalCents = Int((abs(amount) * 100).rounded())
    self.isNegative = amount < 0 && totalCents > 0
    self.whole = totalCents / 100
    self.cents = totalCents % 100
}

The one rule is that rounding happens to the cent before anything is split. Splitting a Double first and rounding each half lets 19.995 render as "$19.100", and lets the float noise in 0.1 + 0.2 leak into the cents. Money that displays as the wrong number is the worst bug a finance screen can have, so the split lives where it is tested against 19.995, 999.999, thirty 19.99s, negatives and zero, and MoneyFigure in the view only draws what it is handed.

SpendBucket and the claim key

// LifeOSKit/Sources/Persistence/SpendBucket.swift
@Model
public final class SpendBucket {
    public var name: String
    public var monthlyLimit: Double     // always positive; the store rejects anything else
    public var claimedRaw: [String]     // MoneyEntry.claimKey values
    public var sortOrder: Int
    ...
}

extension MoneyEntry {
    public var claimKey: String? { categoryCode ?? category }
}

A budget is a bucket that claims one or more raw categories. This survives Plaid renaming a category, works for manual entries (which have no code and fall back to their free-form category), and lets one budget cover what Plaid calls three different things. The rejected alternatives, raw strings and merchant rules, both fail silently: a renamed category simply stops counting and the budget quietly reads as under. A budget that silently stops counting is worse than no budget.

The snapshot

MoneySnapshot carries everything the six sections render: the summary figures, the budget and unclaimed bands, categories with a precomputed share, recurring charges, the seven-day week, the donut slices, a goal, and four connection flags. Two of those flags exist because a bank linked seconds ago has no transactions yet: hasConnectedBank keeps the screen out of the empty state, and isFetchingHistory keeps it out of "you spent nothing this month" while Plaid is still assembling the history.

11.4ViewModel

MoneyViewModel.load(connection:) fetches the calendar month to date plus the accounts, calls summarise, assesses the buckets through BudgetPeriod, and then derives every list and series from the same entries. It is called from RootView.reloadAll() on every store save in the app, and again after the Plaid sync that reloadAll kicks off. 

// LIfeOS/Features/Money/ViewModel/MoneyViewModel.swift
let logos = Self.logoMap(from: entries)
let rows = Self.rows(from: entries, logos: logos)
let categories = Self.categories(from: entries, expenses: summary.expenses)

snapshot = MoneySnapshot(
    income: summary.income, expenses: summary.expenses, net: summary.net,
    savingsRate: summary.savingsRate, netWorth: summary.netWorth,
    recent: rows, budgets: budgetRows, unclaimed: unclaimedRows,
    categories: categories,
    recurring: Self.recurring(from: entries, calendar: calendar, logos: logos),
    week: Self.week(from: entries, now: .now, calendar: calendar),
    slices: Self.slices(from: categories),
    spendCount: entries.filter(\.isSpending).count,
    goal: Self.goal(saved: summary.net),
    monthLabel: Date.now.formatted(.dateTime.month(.wide).year()),
    isConnected: !entries.isEmpty || !accounts.isEmpty || !bankNames.isEmpty,
    hasConnectedBank: !bankNames.isEmpty,
    isFetchingHistory: connection?.isFetchingHistory ?? false,
    reconnectPrompt: reconnect,
    lastSyncedAt: connection?.lastSyncedAt
)

Four derivations are worth reading closely.

  • Categories are grouped from isSpending rows only, the same predicate summarise uses, so the list sums to the "Spent" figure above it. Uncategorised spend is kept rather than dropped, because the gap is exactly the spend nobody labelled.
  • Logos are mapped twice, by merchantID where Plaid gave one and by lowercased merchant name always. A row Plaid sent without a logo borrows from any sibling that has one, and a manual "Netflix" picks up the mark from the Plaid rows. A borrowed logo never changes grouping. It is a picture beside a name, not an identity.
  • Slices fold the categories to the five largest plus "Other" through SpendSeries.fold, then assign each an opacity step. Shares are of the full month, so the slices still sum to one.
  • The goal reads a target and a name from the account's UserDefaults suite and reports this month's net as progress, clamped at zero. There is no account history to total, so a lifetime figure would be invented. As of this revision nothing in the app writes those two keys: the "Set a goal" button opens the bucket editor, so the goal band always shows "No goal set" until a setter is built.

Bucket editing goes through the store. saveBucket creates or updates, then reconciles claims by unclaiming what was dropped and claiming what was added. The store owns the single-holder rule: claim removes the key from whichever bucket held it and returns that bucket's name so the sheet can say "Held by Groceries, saving moves it here". Nothing resolves collisions at read time, because by then the same transaction has already counted twice.

MoneyDetailViewModel is a second view model rather than more fields on the first. Six months of rows for a page nobody is looking at, re-run on every save in the app, is the kind of work that makes a tab feel slow. RootView reloads it only while its page is up.

11.5View

The Money tab is the one screen in the app that is not cards on the warm canvas. It is full-bleed pastel bands on pure white, because money is mostly figures and a figure wants a block of colour behind it. MoneyPalette is therefore its own palette, not LifeOSTokens: paper, one near-black ink, and six pastels (sage, butter, clay, mint, mist, stone) stepped a little darker and more saturated than the reference screens because the paler versions washed out to grey on a real phone at real brightness.

The rail, two ways

On a phone the app's own nav bar is a floating pill along the bottom, so the side is free and MoneySectionRail is a 62-point vertical rail with a glyph and a short word per section. On iPad the nav bar stands on end against the left edge, and a second vertical rail beside it would be two parallel bars of chrome doing unrelated jobs. So on a regular width the rail lies down into a row of chips above the content, carrying the full titles ("Where it went" rather than "Spend") because a horizontal chip has the room. One matchedGeometryEffect id makes the selection block slide between sections instead of cross-fading.

Bands, cards and the grid

// LIfeOS/Features/Money/View/MoneySections.swift
struct MoneyBandStack<Content: View>: View {
    @ViewBuilder let content: Content
    @Environment(\.layout) private var layout

    var body: some View {
        if layout.isRegular {
            LazyVGrid(
                columns: [GridItem(.adaptive(minimum: 340, maximum: 620), spacing: Space.x1)],
                alignment: .leading, spacing: Space.x1
            ) { content }
        } else {
            VStack(spacing: 0) { content }
        }
    }
}

Every section is a MoneyBandStack of MoneyBands. Stacked on a phone, the section is clipped as one rounded block and the bands have square corners; in the iPad grid each band is its own card with its own corners, because a single 340-point column down the middle of an iPad is most of the screen saying nothing.

A band that holds a chart or a list is a MoneyCard. Its header keeps the eyebrow and the figure, so a collapsed card still says its number; what folds is the chart or the list under it. Nothing is dropped by collapsing, and every card starts open. The handful of chart cards with a stable identity remember their state in UserDefaults under money.card.collapsed.<id>; a day of transactions uses transient state, since a key per calendar day forever is not a preference anyone set.

The six sections

SectionBandsWhat it decides
In and outNet with verdict, Earned, Spent with pinstripes of income consumed, This week (card), Kept %, Net worthKept and Net worth are omitted, not zeroed, when undefined
Where it wentSpent by category (donut card), one band per category with swatch, count, share barA category folded into "Other" keeps its band but gets no swatch
Every monthRecurring total (card with rows), "A year of these" at twelve times the monthly sumThe annual figure is the argument for cancelling anything
Saving forGoal progress, Still to find with months at this month's pace, or "No goal set"A month that kept nothing gets no arrival date
What hurtsTotal, one band per pressure point, Edit budgetsPressure points are assembled on the snapshot, not in the view
RecentCount with Add, a collapsible card per dayThe day header shows settled net and counts pending beside it

pressurePoints is an extension on the snapshot, because deciding what belongs on the "what hurts" list is a judgement about money, not about layout. Three rules feed it: a bucket over its limit, unclaimed spend (money leaving with no bucket watching it), and recurring charges when they are more than a fifth of the month's spending. Below that threshold a subscription pile is a fact, and it already has its own tab.

Rows that never wrap

Every row is one line. The amount is fixedSize and drawn first; the name takes what is left, scales to 0.8, then trails off. This replaced layoutPriority(1) on the name column, which starved the amount into "+…00" and stacked "PENDING" letter by letter. A word cut in half reads as a different category, so names scale before they truncate.

Charts

Three charts, all Swift Charts, all one ink at stepped opacity with no y-axis and no grid. The figure above each chart is the number; the marks are the shape. The week chart draws an empty track for every day so a day still to come is visibly a slot and not a gap, and labels only today. The donut uses SectorMark with a 1.5-point angular inset so two adjacent steps of the same ink read as two slices rather than a gradient, and chartAngleSelection turns a tap into a category page. The six-month chart adds a dashed RuleMark at the average of the completed months. The money pastels were run through the dataviz validator as a categorical palette and failed every check, which is the long way of saying what the one-ink rule already said.

The merchant tile

Plaid's logos come as 100 by 100 PNGs on whatever background the merchant chose. Bare, a row of them is a row of mixed squares that breaks the band. MerchantTile puts the mark in a paper-white circle with a hairline, and gives the category-glyph fallback the same footprint, so a list with and without logos lines up. AsyncImage loads it; a failed load shows the glyph.

11.6How it works

Connect

  1. PlaidConnectionViewModel.connect() asks plaid-link-token for a token. The function calls /link/token/create with the Supabase user id as client_user_id and returns only the link token.
  2. PlaidLinkPresenter.present opens Plaid's LinkKit sheet. The presenter is the only file in the app that imports LinkKit, and it holds the live Handler statically because a bank using OAuth sends the user out to Safari; a handler released while they are away has nothing to hand the redirect back to, and the connection dies silently at the last step.
  3. LinkKit returns a public_token. The app posts it to plaid-exchange, which refuses a second connection to the same institution (two Items with overlapping transactions under different ids cannot be deduplicated on the device), calls /item/public_token/exchange, and writes the access token into plaid_items. The response carries the item id and the institution name, never the token.
  4. The view model records the item with a nil cursor, sets isFetchingHistory, and runs a sync straight away.

The OAuth banks are the reason web/ exists. Plaid sends the browser to almanac.shivvyas.com/plaid-oauth when the bank is done. The apple-app-site-association file claims exactly that path, so iOS hands the URL to the app and the HTML page is never rendered. It renders only when the handoff fails, and its whole job is to tell a stranded person to open the app without claiming the connection failed, because by then Plaid has usually already succeeded. The link token that session was built with is kept in UserDefaults rather than memory, so a process killed during the round trip can resume the same Link session on relaunch, and the view model re-registers the completion closure on attach because the original one died with the old process.

Sync

// LifeOSKit/Sources/Integrations/PlaidSync.swift
let rows = try PlaidMapping.ingestRows(from: delta.added + delta.modified,
                                       accounts: delta.accounts)
try money.ingest(rows)
try money.remove(externalIDs: delta.removed.map(\.transaction_id))
try money.upsertAccounts(PlaidMapping.accountRows(from: delta.accounts))

// Only now. Every throw above leaves the cursor where it was, and
// the next run replays this page into an idempotent upsert.
if let cursor = delta.next_cursor {
    items.setCursor(cursor, for: delta.item_id)
}

This ordering is the whole design in three lines. A cursor advanced before a successful ingest is a page of transactions Plaid will never send again. That is also why the cursor lives on the device, per Item, in UserDefaults rather than on the server or in the Keychain: a server-advanced cursor would permanently lose a page to an app that crashed mid-ingest, and a Keychain cursor would survive a reinstall that the SwiftData database does not, leaving Plaid replaying nothing into an empty app. The cursor must die with the data it describes.

The function fetches at most three pages per invocation to stay inside its wall clock and reports has_more; the view model loops up to twenty times, so an initial pull of years of history finishes across several runs rather than stopping part-way and looking complete. Balances are fetched opportunistically after the transactions, and a failure there travels separately as balance_error: /transactions/sync serves cached data and succeeds even with an expired bank login, while /accounts/balance/get does a live fetch and is the call that actually throws ITEM_LOGIN_REQUIRED. That is what raises the reconnect banner without discarding the transaction pages already fetched.

Sync is triggered by reloadAll through syncIfDue, which applies the shared SyncStalenessPolicy: stale after an hour, or across a day boundary, or when the recorded time is in the future because the clock moved backwards. Before it checks staleness it runs replayHistoryOnce, which clears every cursor exactly once under a versioned flag so rows synced before the logo field existed gain their logo on the next pass. A replay on every launch would pull years of rows daily; a replay once is free, because Plaid bills per connected Item, not per call.

Disconnect

plaid-disconnect calls /item/remove and deletes the row. A connected Item bills monthly, so this is not optional polish. The client discards the response body and succeeds on the status alone, because reading a field that carries no further information only creates a way for a disconnect that worked to be reported as a failure. Local history is kept by default; deleting that Item's entries is a separate, explicit choice.

11.7Performance and cost

  • Batched ingest. externalID has no index and ingest runs on the main actor. A per-row fetch inside the loop would be an unindexed table scan per row, thousands of times on an initial pull. MoneyStore.ingest fetches every id the page touches once, builds a dictionary, keeps it current as rows are inserted so a duplicate id within the page still upserts, and saves once for the whole page. remove and upsertAccounts do the same.
  • Three pages per function call, twenty calls per sync. Bounded work on both sides, with has_more carrying the continuation.
  • Sync only when stale. One rule, shared with Whoop and Fitbit, keeps the sync off every save and every foreground.
  • One month loaded per save; six months only while the detail page is up. The tab view model is cheap because it reads the calendar month to date. The detail view model is separate so its six-month fetch runs only when its page is open.
  • No per-row lookups in the view. Category shares, logo URLs, slice opacities and day groupings are computed once on the snapshot. Views divide nothing and look nothing up.
  • Reads and writes serialised. UserDefaultsPlaidItemStore is Sendable and wraps every read-modify-write in an NSLock, so a cursor set from one task cannot lose an update from another. The test concurrentCursorSetsDoNotLoseUpdates pins it.
  • Private by construction. The server holds one row per bank containing the access token and an institution name. Transactions, merchants, categories and logos never touch Postgres. Nothing about spending is sent to a logo service either: the logo URL is Plaid's own, in a response already being paid for.
  • Cost. No new Plaid products since the first connection: Transactions and Accounts only, no /transactions/recurring (a separately billed product that RecurringSpend replaces for free from history). Plaid bills per connected Item per month, which scales with the number of banks a person links. The app targets one user on the free tier today; the pricing question is deferred, not answered, and must be answered before a second person connects a bank. See Chapter 24.
  • Offline. Every band renders from SwiftData. A sync failure leaves the previous snapshot on screen with its own timestamp, which is honest, rather than replacing it with zeros. A network outage never disconnects a saved bank.

11.8Edge cases and tests

ConditionBehaviour
No entries, no accounts, no bankEmpty state with Connect and Add, not a screen of zeros
Bank linked, first sync returns nothing"Fetching your transactions" with a Check again button. Never rendered as an empty month
Expenses but no incomeSavings rate omitted; verdict reads "No income logged"
Pending transactionShown at 45% opacity with a Pending label; excluded from income, expenses, net, categories, the donut and the day's settled net
Pending charge settles under a new idThe new id upserts, the old id arrives in removed and is deleted; no duplicate
Transfer between own accounts, card paymentKept in the ledger, excluded from income and spending by category code
Credit card with a balanceSubtracts from net worth by type, never by subtype
Bank reports no credit limit or no available balanceStored as nil, never zero. Utilisation against a zero limit is 100% by arithmetic and unknowable in fact
Plaid sends an unreadable datePlaidMapping throws, the sync fails, the last known-good snapshot stays. A silently dropped row is a wrong total with no error anywhere
Device west of GreenwichDates parse in the store's own calendar, so a transaction Plaid dates the 1st is not stored as the 31st and moved into last month
Ingest throws mid-pageCursor stays where it was; next sync replays the page into the idempotent upsert
One bank's login expiresThat item is reported in needsReconnect; every other bank still syncs; the reconnect banner shows and the figures below it are labelled as from the last sync
One bank fails for another reasonReported in failedItems; the "last synced" timestamp is not stamped on a sync that partly failed
Bank removed on another deviceThe sync response omits it, so the local item cache drops it too
Same bank connected twiceRefused by plaid-exchange before the exchange is spent, backstopped by a unique constraint on (user, institution)
Item store fails to decodeItem list resets to empty and self-heals from the next sync, with every cursor reset; logged so a mystery full resync has a cause
Bucket limit of zero or lessRejected by the store with limitNotPositive; the form's Save is disabled
Key claimed by two bucketsImpossible: claim moves it and the sheet says where from
Refund in a budgeted categoryNets within its bucket instead of inflating income
Two coffees in one weekNot a subscription. Recurrence needs two distinct months at an amount within 25% of its own median; income is never a subscription
Account switchThe view model deactivates, the presenter resets, and the next account reads its own UserDefaults suite and store

Tests

All in LifeOSKit, all passing, all without a network or a Plaid account:

  • PersistenceTests/MoneyTests: the sign convention, the undefined savings rate, pending exclusion, transfer and card-payment exclusion, the underscore-prefix rule, upsert on the provider id, removal of a settled pending charge, merchant entity and logo round trips, and that isSpending matches what the summary counts.
  • PersistenceTests/MoneyPartsTests: the carry at 19.995 and 999.999, float noise, zero-padded cents, a zero that is never negative, grouping of large balances.
  • PersistenceTests/SpendBucketTests: a key moves rather than being held twice, deleting a bucket frees its keys, the claim key prefers the code over the label.
  • SectorsTests/BudgetPeriodTests: refunds net within a bucket, income never appears as unclaimed, adherence is 1.0 at the limit and decays linearly to 0 at double it.
  • InsightsTests/SpendSeriesTests and RecurringSpendTests: week boundaries, an empty month at zero in the middle of a run, fold leaving a list at or under keep plus one alone, the median resisting a single price rise.
  • IntegrationsTests/Plaid*: the client's error mapping through a stub URLProtocol, a missing session never reaching the network, disconnect succeeding on status alone, the mapping's negation and time-zone behaviour, the wire format's optional fields, and PlaidSyncTests pinning that a failed ingest leaves the cursor where it was and a balance login failure raises reconnect without losing the transactions.

11.9Study notes

Read in this order

  1. LifeOSKit/Sources/Persistence/MoneyEntry.swift, for the sign rule and summarise.
  2. LifeOSKit/Sources/Integrations/PlaidMapping.swift, the negation and the date parsing.
  3. LifeOSKit/Sources/Integrations/PlaidSync.swift, the ingest-then-cursor ordering.
  4. LifeOSKit/Sources/Persistence/MoneyStore.swift, the batched upsert and the claim rule.
  5. LifeOSKit/Sources/Sectors/BudgetPeriod.swift, the pure budget assessment.
  6. LIfeOS/Features/Money/ViewModel/MoneyViewModel.swift, how the snapshot is derived.
  7. LIfeOS/Features/Money/View/MoneySections.swift, bands, cards and the grid.
  8. supabase/functions/plaid-sync/index.ts, the server half of a sync.

Check yourself

  • Why does the cursor live in UserDefaults and not the Keychain? The Keychain survives a reinstall and the database does not; a cursor that outlived its data would make Plaid replay nothing into an empty app.
  • What would go wrong if the cursor advanced before ingest? A page that failed to save would never be sent again, and the total would be silently short.
  • Why is a card payment excluded from spending? The purchases on the card were already spending; the payment is the same money moving, and counting it inflates expenses and lowers the savings rate.
  • Why does a budget claim a category code rather than a merchant or a label? A label can be renamed and a merchant can be spelled three ways; a silently non-counting budget is worse than none.
  • Why is a missing credit limit stored as nil rather than zero? Zero renders as 100% utilised and looks like a fact; nil renders as nothing, which is the truth.
  • Why is the donut one ink at stepped opacity? The six pastels fail as a categorical palette; a sequential encoding of one hue passes, and identity is carried by the legend and the matching swatches on the bands, never by colour alone.

Chapter twelve

12Notes and the plan

A block editor over a PARA library, synced to Supabase, with a derived index underneath that turns a pile of pages into something you can ask questions of. Habits are the one thing from the old Plan tab that did not become a page, and this chapter explains why.

Revision D described a Plan tab with four lists behind a segmented pill. That tab is gone. Goals, content items, loose notes and journal entries all became pages on 26 August 2026, migrated once and never rewritten, and the tab slot they occupied now belongs to Notes. What survived is the one plan kind that is not a document: a habit, which is a daily tick with a streak behind it. 12.9 covers what is left of the plan; everything before it is the notes tab as it is on disk today.

12.1Intent

Working backwards

Notes is a library with four shelves and a page you can write on. Every page is a list of blocks: paragraphs, headings, to-dos, quotes, code, a sketch you draw in line with the text. Type a slash to change what a line is, type two brackets to link to another page, and the page you linked to lists you at the bottom. Pick up a Pencil and it writes, draws or annotates depending on where it is. Everything saves on the device first and reaches the server afterwards.

Why PARA rather than folders you name yourself?

Because PARA sorts by actionability, not by subject. A note about running belongs under a marathon project while the race is ahead and under the area that outlives it once the race is run. Encoding that as the top of the hierarchy is the method's whole point, so NoteBucket is an enum with four cases rather than four folders a person could rename into meaninglessness. The app calls the third shelf Research, because PARA's own word, Resources, is vaguer than what the shelf holds.

Why blocks instead of one text field with formatting?

A block editor's trick is that the document is a list of small typed pieces rather than one string with ranges hung off it. Splitting, merging, reordering and turning a paragraph into a to-do become list operations, and none of them can corrupt the others. The operations themselves are pure functions in NoteBlockEditor, tested against literal arrays rather than a screen.

If blocks are JSON inside the page, how does the app find every open to-do?

It does not search the JSON. On every save, NoteIndexer mirrors the page's to-do blocks and wiki links into two derived SwiftData models, NoteTask and NoteLink. They are never pushed to the server, and every row can be rebuilt from the documents, so the worst an indexer bug can do is show a stale list. The repair is one function.

Does a note leave the device?

Only when someone is signed in, and only after the write has landed locally. NoteSync pushes dirty rows to two Postgres tables guarded by row level security, then pulls what other devices wrote. Sync can fail without anyone noticing and without losing an edit: push runs before pull, the newer updatedAt wins, and a row is marked synced only after the server confirms it.

What Notes deliberately does not do, yet: collections that cut across the shelves, goals as their own model, a mindmap of the link graph, voice capture, a share extension. Those are phases three to six of the notes redesign spec and none of them has code. Phase one, the index layer, shipped. Phase two, the phone's Inbox stream and its pinned composer, was built on 28 August and then set aside in the 13 September restyle: the store still knows what an Inbox is and the screen still compiles, but nothing routes to it. 12.5 says exactly what the phone shows instead.
