Where the boundaries fall Persistence owns the shape of a note and every rule about it. Integrations owns how it travels. The app target owns how it looks and what a keystroke means for the caret. NoteAccentPalette is the one deliberate join: accent names are a persistence concern, colours are a design concern, and DesignSystem depends on nothing, so the two meet in a 66-line file in the app rather than in either package.

12.3Model

The page

A page is a NoteDocument. Every field carries a default, because SwiftData adds a property to an existing store without a migration plan only when it can fill it in, and this model has grown four times since it was created. 

// LifeOSKit/Sources/Persistence/NoteDocument.swift
@Model
public final class NoteDocument {
    public var id: UUID = UUID()
    public var title: String = ""
    public var icon: String = ""
    public var kindRaw: String = NoteKind.note.rawValue     // note | journal | task
    public var bucketRaw: String = NoteBucket.projects.rawValue
    public var accentRaw: String = NoteAccent.sage.rawValue
    public var folderID: UUID?                              // nil: loose on the shelf
    public var blocksData: Data = Data()                    // the blocks, JSON encoded
    public var drawingData: Data?                           // a PKDrawing, when inked
    public var entryDate: Date?                             // the day a journal entry is about
    public var dueDate: Date?
    public var statusRaw: String = PlanStatus.todo.rawValue
    public var isFavorite: Bool = false
    public var openedAt: Date?                              // drives Recent; written on open
    public var archivedAt: Date?                            // Archive is this flag, not a bucket
    public var filedAt: Date?                               // nil means still in the Inbox
    public var syncedAt: Date?
    public var deletedAt: Date?                             // a tombstone, reaped after push
    public var originPlanEntryID: UUID?                     // the plan row this came from
}

Four of those fields carry the whole design, and each earns a sentence.

  • blocksData is JSON, not a relationship. Blocks are only ever read and written as a document, no query asks for one block, and a relationship would buy one migration hazard per block field in exchange for nothing. When the JSON cannot be decoded the getter hands back a blank page rather than throwing: the bytes stay on disk untouched until someone saves over them, and the person at least has somewhere to type.
  • archivedAt is a flag, not a fifth shelf. An archived page keeps the bucket it was filed on, so restoring it needs no decision.
  • filedAt is the whole Inbox concept. A bucket cannot answer "has anyone decided where this goes", because every page has a bucket from the moment it is created. The stamp is written by filing and never by editing, so a page you keep writing in stays unfiled until you choose a home for it.
  • syncedAt and deletedAt are the sync contract. updatedAt > syncedAt is the entire dirty test. A delete writes a tombstone the server can pull as a fact, rather than an absence it cannot observe.

Three enums sit behind the raw strings. NoteKind decides how a page is listed, not how it is edited: a note, a journal entry titled by its day, or a task page that exists to hold to-dos. NoteBucket is the four shelves. PlanStatus is reused from the old plan rather than declared again, which is what lets the monthly close in Chapter 13 read goal progress off notes without learning a second vocabulary. Raw strings with typed accessors, for the reason Revision D gave: a new case is a code change, not a migration, and an unrecognised value reads as the default instead of failing the fetch.

A NoteFolder is the same shape with fewer fields: a name, an emoji or an accent dot, a shelf, an optional parentID, and the same syncedAt and deletedAt pair. Folders nest arbitrarily in the model and one level in practice.

The block

// LifeOSKit/Sources/Persistence/NoteBlock.swift
public struct NoteBlock: Codable, Sendable, Identifiable, Equatable {
    public var id: UUID
    public var kind: NoteBlockKind      // paragraph, three headings, three lists, quote,
                                        // callout, code, divider, sketch
    public var text: String
    public var isChecked: Bool          // kept on every block so a tick survives a transform
    public var indent: Int              // 0 through 4, purely visual
    public var drawing: Data?           // sketch blocks only
    public var sketchHeight: Double?    // dragged height, so ink crops the same on every device
    public var dueDate: Date?           // to-do blocks only; authored, so it lives here
    public var goalID: UUID?            // to-do blocks only; authored, for the same reason
}

Two details matter. Indent is a number on a flat array, not a tree: a nested list item is still a sibling, which is what keeps every editing operation a list operation. And dueDate and goalID live on the authored block rather than on the derived NoteTask row, because the row is rebuilt on every save and would lose them.

NoteBlockParser owns the Notion-style typed prefixes. candidates is every prefix sorted longest first, and that order is the whole correctness argument: - [ ] starts with - , so checking kinds in declaration order would turn every to-do typed by hand into a bullet reading "[ ] whatever". --- and the code fence are whole-line markers rather than prefixes, so a line reading "--- and then some" stays a paragraph. The same type renders blocks as Markdown for the share sheet and for the coach's context window, and parses Markdown back into blocks for paste and for the plan migration. Round-tripping is not a goal; a sketch becomes _[sketch]_ on the way out, because saying a drawing was here beats dropping it silently.

NoteLinkScanner finds [[wiki links]]. Case is preserved in what was typed and folded at lookup, so [[Marathon]] and [[marathon]] reach the same page without rewriting either.

The derived rows

// LifeOSKit/Sources/Persistence/NoteIndex.swift
@Model
public final class NoteTask {
    public var id: UUID = UUID()          // the block's own id: stable across reindexes
    public var documentID: UUID = UUID()  // scoped by page, so a pasted block cannot collide
    public var text: String = ""
    public var isChecked: Bool = false
    public var indent: Int = 0
    public var dueDate: Date?
    public var goalID: UUID?
    public var sortOrder: Int = 0         // position in its page
    public var documentUpdatedAt: Date = Date.distantPast   // copied down, so a cross-page
}                                                           // list can order pages

@Model
public final class NoteLink {
    public var sourceID: UUID = UUID()
    public var targetTitleFolded: String = ""   // lowercased: one edge per title
    public var targetID: UUID?                  // nil: the page does not exist yet
}

Two rules make these safe. They are never pushed, so two devices cannot disagree about them. And every row is reconstructible from the documents, so any inconsistency is repaired by NoteIndexer.rebuildAll. A NoteTask keeps the block's own id so the row is stable across reindexes rather than churning a new identity on every keystroke; it is scoped by documentID because a block copied and pasted into a second page keeps its id.

A resolved edge can dangle NoteLink.targetID being non-nil is not proof the page is still there. reindex only rewrites the edges out of the document being saved, so renaming or deleting a page leaves every edge that pointed at it holding an id that now names something else or nothing at all. The next launch's rebuildAll repairs them. Until then a consumer must treat the lookup as a miss it can survive, not as a page it is owed. This is written on the model so it is not rediscovered as a mystery bug.

What views see

Views never hold a NoteDocument. NoteCardSnapshot is a page flattened for display: title, icon, excerpt, accent, folder name, task progress, whether it has ink, how many links it carries. NoteFolderSnapshot is a folder row with its children already attached and a count that rolls up through them. NotesSnapshot is everything the sidebar needs in one read. NoteBacklink is a page that links here, with the line the link appears on, so the backlinks pane shows context rather than a bare list of titles.

12.4ViewModel

Three view models, one per concern, and the store does the deciding for all of them. NotesStore lives in the package because the app target has no test target, so any rule worth pinning (what "All" includes, when a page is filed, what order a shelf sorts in) is put where swift test can reach it.

The library

// LIfeOS/Features/Notes/ViewModel/NotesViewModel.swift
@Observable @MainActor
final class NotesViewModel {
    private(set) var snapshot: NotesSnapshot = .empty
    private(set) var cards: [NoteCardSnapshot] = []
    private(set) var isSearching = false

    var selection: NoteSelection = .recent { didSet { if selection != oldValue { load() } } }
    var filter: NoteShelfFilter = .all   { didSet { if filter != oldValue { load() } } }
    var sort: NoteSort = .recentlyEdited { didSet { if sort != oldValue { load() } } }
    var query: String = ""               { didSet { if query != oldValue { load() } } }

    func attach(_ context: ModelContext, sync: NoteSyncing? = nil)
    func load()
    func createNote(kind: NoteKind = .note, title: String = "") -> UUID?
    func openTodaysJournal() -> UUID?
    func createFolder(named:in:icon:)  func renameFolder(_:to:)  func deleteFolder(_:)
    func toggleFavorite(_:)  func toggleArchive(_:)  func delete(_:)  func move(_:to:folderID:)
}

NoteSelection is one enum rather than a pair of optionals, because "a folder is selected" and "a shelf is selected" are mutually exclusive and two nullable properties make a fourth, meaningless state representable. load() reads the snapshot once, then either a search or the cards for the selection. Every mutating method funnels through mutate(id:), which fetches the live object, applies the change through the store, reloads, and fires a sync. Nothing in the UI waits on the server; the write has already landed locally by the time requestSync() runs, and a failure there only means the next pass carries the row.

NoteSyncing is a one-method protocol the view model asks for, so a preview and a design capture can hand it nothing. The real NoteSync conforms in one line at the top of RootView, which is the only place that knows both types.

The page

NoteEditorViewModel holds the blocks in memory and writes them back on a delay. Saving on every keystroke would mean a SwiftData write and a didSave notification per character, and every screen in the app reloads on that notification. 

// LIfeOS/Features/Notes/ViewModel/NoteEditorViewModel.swift
private func scheduleSave() {
    guard !isLoading else { return }
    saveMessage = "Saving…"
    saveTask?.cancel()
    saveTask = Task { [weak self] in
        try? await Task.sleep(for: .milliseconds(600))
        guard !Task.isCancelled else { return }
        self?.saveNow()
    }
}

/// Called on the way out, so a page closed inside the debounce window still lands.
func flush() {
    saveTask?.cancel()
    saveTask = nil
    saveNow()
}

Ticking a checkbox is the exception: it is a decision, not a keystroke, and toggleCheck saves at once so it survives the app being closed a second later. The screen calls flush() on disappear and whenever the scene leaves the active phase.

The keystroke rules are not here. splitBlock, backspaceAtStart, indent, transform and completeLink each call the matching pure function on NoteBlockEditor, apply the returned blocks, move the caret to the returned focus, and schedule a save. The view model also tracks the two queries the accessory bar renders: slashQuery, the text after a leading slash, and linkQuery, the partial title inside an unclosed [[. linkSuggestions filters a title index the model refreshes after every save, and resolveLink creates the page when nothing carries that title, the way Obsidian does.

setDrawing compares bytes before writing, because PencilKit reports a change on every stroke and on every tool switch, and rewriting identical bytes would mark the page dirty for a sync that carries nothing new.

The Inbox

NoteInboxViewModel is 78 lines: a chip, a draft, a sticky to-do toggle, and a capture() that hands the draft to NotesStore.capture, clears it on success and leaves it alone on failure so a thought is never silently dropped. It is thin by the same rule as LifeBoardViewModel: what a chip means lives in the store. It compiles, its store methods are tested, and no screen constructs it today.

12.5View

Two shells over one library

NotesHubScreen reads layout.isRegular from the environment and builds one of two arrangements. Both drive the same NotesViewModel and the same NoteShelfScreen; only the chrome around the shelf differs.

The phone is a NavigationStack with the shelf at its root. The leading toolbar button presents the library as a full-height sheet titled "Your library", and choosing anything in it sets the selection, clears the path and closes the sheet in one binding, so the rail and the sheet cannot drift apart about what a tap does. A page is pushed onto the path. Two small pieces of state, pendingNewFolder and pendingRename, exist because a sheet cannot present a second sheet: the library records what was asked for, dismisses, and the hub presents the folder sheet in onDismiss.

The iPad is an HStack of up to three columns: the rail, the shelf, and the open page. Whether the third column exists is measured, not derived from the size class. 

// LIfeOS/Features/Notes/View/NotesHubScreen.swift
private static let libraryWidth: CGFloat = 268
private static let minShelfWidth: CGFloat = 340
private static let minPageWidth: CGFloat = 520   // below this the page stops being somewhere you would write

private var isThreeColumn: Bool {
    guard layout.isRegular else { return false }
    let spokenFor = layout.railInset + (isLibraryVisible ? Self.libraryWidth : 0)
    return paneWidth - spokenFor >= Self.minShelfWidth + Self.minPageWidth
}

A single overall threshold was wrong: at 1024 points a pane read as wide enough, but the library and the tab rail take 380 of that before the shelf and the page have divided anything, leaving a 310-point column to write in. Subtracting what is already spoken for is what lets collapsing the library buy a third column on a screen that could not otherwise hold one. Rotating an iPad or resizing a Stage Manager window flips isThreeColumn, and the open page moves between the detail column and the navigation path with it, or it would vanish. Exactly one of openPage and a .page route on the path is ever non-empty, which is what stops them disagreeing.

The detail column rebuilds its editor per page with .id(openPage), so the editor never shows the previous page's blocks for a frame while the new ones load. NoteEditorHost exists because @State cannot be initialised from a navigation destination's argument; it creates the editor view model in a .task keyed on the document id and keeps it alive while the page is on screen.

The rail and the library

The iPad rail, NotesSidebar, is text rows on the canvas rather than a List, which brings its own background, separators and insets, all of which would have to be undone. Recent and Favourites lead, Habits pushes its own screen, then the four shelves, each expanded on first launch because four collapsed rows tell a new user nothing about what PARA is. Every shelf and folder row is a drop destination for NoteDragPayload; a drop on a shelf files the page loose on it, and a drop on Archive archives rather than refiles, because Archive is a state, not a place. The drop highlight is a different colour from the selection highlight: "this is where it will land" and "this is what you are looking at" are different statements.

The phone library, NotesLibraryList, is the same inputs and callbacks in the app's own card vocabulary: Recent, Favourites and Habits as a row of tiles, then each shelf as one soft card with its folders under a hairline and a quiet row to add one. The whole list sits inside one GlassEffectContainer, so neighbouring glass tiles merge and separate as they move rather than each rendering its own lens. Colour is Apple's: system grays for every icon square and fill, and the accent orange for exactly one thing, whatever is selected.

The shelf

NoteShelfScreen is a header, a search field, a count, a kind filter (shown only when a shelf or folder is selected, since Recent and Favourites already cut across kinds), a sort menu with the four orders NoteSort allows, and a LazyVStack of NoteCard. Each card carries its move targets as a menu as well as being draggable, because drag and drop is a pointer gesture and the same move has to exist for a finger.

The page

NoteEditorScreen caps its measure at 760 points even on an iPad, because prose at 1000 points across is unreadable and this is the one screen in the app that is genuinely prose. Above 1040 points of editor width, and only when there are backlinks to show, the backlinks list moves out from under the text into a 280-point inspector column beside it.

The body is a ZStack: a column of NoteBlockRow underneath, and an InkCanvasView sized to the measured height of that column on top. A canvas sized to the screen instead would clip strokes the moment the page scrolled. Under the last block sits 160 points of clear, tappable space that focuses the last block, because without it the bottom half of a short page is dead.

Each block row draws its gutter mark in SwiftUI and its text in UIKit. Putting the bullet inside the text view as a literal character was the alternative, and it makes the bullet deletable, which means a list item can silently stop being one. BlockTextView wraps a UITextView for three things SwiftUI's text field cannot do here: intercept Return so it splits the block instead of inserting a newline, intercept Backspace at offset zero so it merges with the block above, and paint [[links]] as the person types. Apple Pencil Scribble arrives free with UITextView, which is the fourth. Every font comes from LifeOSType.UIKitScale, so a heading in a note is the same size as the same heading anywhere else in the app.

NoteAccessoryBar is one strip above the keyboard with three states that take turns: a slash menu while slashQuery is set, a link picker while linkQuery is set, otherwise a formatting bar with indent, ink and dismiss. Three floating panels competing for the same corner of a phone screen was the alternative. Escape backs out one layer at a time: the block menu, then the link picker, then the keyboard. Closing the page on the first press would lose someone mid-sentence.

The Pencil rule

There are two kinds of drawing on a page and they are deliberately different. SketchBlockView is a block in the flow: it pushes the text below it down and moves with the paragraph it belongs to, which is what a diagram between two paragraphs wants. It is Pencil-only by default on iPad so a finger still scrolls past it, and finger-drawable by default on a phone. InkCanvasView floats over the whole page for annotation.

The ink layer used to claim every Pencil touch, on the theory that picking up the Pencil should mean drawing. The cost was hidden and larger than the benefit: a layer that swallowed the touch first meant Scribble could never fire anywhere, and sketch blocks were unreachable for the same reason. So the rule is stated by where the Pencil is, not by what it is. Over a text block it writes. Over a sketch block it draws in that block. With ink mode on, it annotates the page, and a double-tap or squeeze of the Pencil turns ink mode on without a trip to the toolbar.

NoteToolPicker is one PKToolPicker shared by the ink layer and every sketch block. Two of them fight: whichever became visible last wins, and the loser leaves a stale observer behind that keeps receiving tool changes for a canvas nobody is drawing in. It also tracks which canvases already observe, because PencilKit keeps duplicate observers rather than ignoring them and a view that updates twenty times would otherwise register twenty.

The hardware keyboard

NotesCommands is a CommandMenu installed in the scene, so its shortcuts work wherever focus is and appear in the overlay an iPad shows when Command is held. It reads a NotesCommandTarget from focusedSceneValue: a struct of closures, one per action, because opening a page means pushing on a phone and filling the detail column on an iPad and the scene must not have to know which. closePage is optional and nil when nothing is open, which is what greys out Command-W rather than letting it fire into an empty column. Command-Option-0 is Recent and Command-Option-1 to 4 are the shelves, matching how editors number their tabs.

12.6How it works

Step by step, from a keystroke

  1. The UITextView reports text, or a Return, or a Backspace at offset zero. NoteBlockRow forwards it as a closure call.
  2. The editor view model applies the matching NoteBlockEditor function to its block array, moves the caret, and schedules a save 600 milliseconds out. A second keystroke inside that window cancels the first task.
  3. saveNow() fetches the live document and calls NotesStore.update, which returns early if the blocks are equal and otherwise assigns them and calls touch.
  4. touch stamps updatedAt, calls NoteIndexer.reindex, and saves once. Every document mutation in the store funnels through this one function, which is why the index is rewritten here and nowhere else.
  5. reindex fetches and deletes the page's existing rows, inserts one NoteTask per to-do block, and, only if the page carries any links, builds the folded title index and inserts one NoteLink per link.
  6. The view model refreshes its backlinks and title index, updates the "Saved on this device" label, and asks NoteSync to run.

The indexer's two deletes

reindex and rebuildAll delete rows differently, on purpose, and the code says not to "fix" either to match the other. 

// LifeOSKit/Sources/Persistence/NoteIndexer.swift
// Inside reindex: fetch and delete each, NOT `context.delete(model:where:)`.
// The batch form runs against the persistent store and cannot see rows
// inserted earlier in this same unsaved transaction, so a second reindex
// would duplicate rows instead of replacing them.
let existing = try context.fetch(
    FetchDescriptor<NoteTask>(predicate: #Predicate { $0.documentID == documentID })
)
for row in existing { context.delete(row) }

// Inside rebuildAll: the batch form is correct HERE. This deletes everything
// before anything is inserted, and the rows it clears are already saved.
try context.delete(model: NoteTask.self)
try context.delete(model: NoteLink.self)

rebuildAll also starts from empty rather than reindexing page by page, because a per-document pass never visits a page that is no longer there, and so could never clear the rows a deleted page left behind.

Filing

Where a page lands, and when it counts as filed, is decided in the store and pinned by tests.

  • createDocument stamps filedAt only when a folder was given. Choosing a folder is choosing a home. A page created loose on a shelf is not filed, because the shelf was the default, not a decision.
  • capture writes one block into Areas with no title and no filedAt. The title is left empty on purpose: displayTitle already falls back to the first textual block, so storing the sentence twice would show it twice on the card.
  • move stamps filedAt if it is nil. Editing never does.
  • Deleting a folder empties it onto its parent rather than taking the pages with it. Losing a folder is an organising decision; losing what was in it is a different decision that must never be made by implication. Those pages change outside touch, so the store reindexes them by hand in the same loop.

Sync

NoteSync coalesces overlapping calls into one in-flight task, reads the access token fresh from the keychain on every pass rather than capturing it (the app shell refreshes the session hourly, so a captured token would be stale within the hour), and returns quietly for a guest. Then:

  1. Push folders first. A page whose folder has never been pushed would arrive pointing at a row the server does not have, and a pull on another device would file it at the root until the folder caught up.
  2. Push documents in batches of 25. A page carrying ink is large, and a person offline for a week can have many. One oversized body is a 413 that fails every page in it, including the small ones. Each batch is marked synced as soon as the server confirms it, and the mark does not touch updatedAt, so an edit made mid-flight stays dirty.
  3. Pull rows newer than the cursor, rewound one second so a row written in the same instant as the cursor is not stranded on the far side of it. For each row: a local copy newer than the server's wins and stays dirty; a tombstone deletes the local row after clearing its index; an update reindexes; an insert stamps filedAt from createdAt, because a page from another device was filed on the device that made it and is not new capture here. Ink that was too large to push comes back null, and null means "not carried", not "erased", so the local drawing is kept.
  4. Advance the cursor to the newest updatedAt seen, in the per-account defaults suite rather than the shared one, so two people on one device cannot read each other's position.

The one trigger in the app today is a write: every mutating path in the two view models ends in requestSync(). There is no launch or foreground pull, so on a second device the first pull happens as the tail of the first push.

The one-time migrations

RootView.attachAll runs three idempotent steps on every launch. PlanNoteMigration.seedIfEmpty creates one Journal folder, and only when the tree is completely empty, because pre-filling shelves with folders nobody asked for is how a fresh install feels like someone else's mess. PlanNoteMigration.run turns goals, content, notes and journal entries into pages (12.9). NoteIndexMigration.run stamps every page that predates the Inbox as filed, then rebuilds the index. That stamp is keyed by a marker in the per-account defaults, and the marker is spent only when there was history to interpret: on a fresh install the first launch runs before the first pull, and consuming the one-shot on an empty store would leave every page that arrives afterwards stranded in the Inbox.

12.7Performance and cost

  • One write per pause, not per character. The 600 millisecond debounce in the editor is the single most consequential number in this chapter: without it every keystroke would fire a SwiftData save and a didSave notification that reloads every view model in the app.
  • The title index is built once per rebuild, not once per page. Letting each reindex build its own made rebuildAll quadratic in the size of the library: one fetch of every document per document, decoding the blocks of each untitled page every time, on the main actor before the UI was live. rebuildAll now builds the index once and passes it down.
  • A page with no links never fetches the library. reindex scans for links first and returns before building a title index when there are none, which is most pages. Otherwise the editor would pay a fetch of every document on every debounced keystroke.
  • Delete and reinsert beats a diff. A page holds tens of blocks, the rewrite is cheap, and a diff would need its own correctness argument for every field.
  • The sidebar is one read. NotesStore.snapshot walks the folders and documents once to build the tree, the per-shelf counts, the recent list and the favourites. Four separate reads would each walk the same rows.
  • Search has no index and does not need one. It is a substring match over titles and block text, case and diacritic insensitive, capped at 40 results. That is fine until a person has thousands of notes, and the derived rows are where an index would go when it is needed.
  • Ink stays on the device past 1.5 megabytes. A dense PencilKit page is a few hundred kilobytes, a pathological one is megabytes, and base64 adds a third. One runaway page must not stall every other page's sync behind it, so NoteDocumentRow leaves oversized ink out of the payload and the page syncs its text.
  • Opening a page does not dirty it. markOpened advances openedAt without touching updatedAt, so reading on one device cannot fabricate an edit that wins a sync conflict against a real one on another.
  • Blocks travel as real JSON. The blocks column is jsonb, so a malformed document is refused by Postgres at write time rather than surfacing on another device later, and a future server-side reader can query into it.
  • Cost is zero beyond Postgres rows. No AI, no third-party service, no per-user fee. Two tables, five indexes, one policy each, all scoped to auth.uid(). user_id defaults to auth.uid() on the server and the client never sends it, so ownership is decided from the token rather than asserted by the device.

12.8Edge cases and tests

ConditionBehaviour
Return on an empty list itemOutdents one level if it can, otherwise the item becomes a paragraph. That is how every editor gets out of a list.
Backspace at the start of a list itemStrips the indent first, then the kind, then merges into the block above. A plain paragraph merges its whole tail, not just the first word.
Backspace in the first blockNot the editor's to consume; UIKit does what it would normally do.
Backspace onto a drawn sketchRefused. An untouched sketch is removed; one with ink is not swallowed.
Typing --- then more textStays a paragraph. Dividers and code fences fire only on their own line.
A to-do turned into a paragraph and backKeeps its tick, because isChecked is kept on every block.
Two pages share a titleThe older one wins the link, every launch, because the title index is built in createdAt order.
A link to a page that does not existThe edge is kept unresolved; following it creates the page in the current shelf.
Same block id on two pages (copy and paste)Two task rows, scoped by document. Neither collides.
Page archivedLeaves every stream; its task rows stay in the index but the To-dos chip filters them by live page.
Page deleted locallyTombstoned, index cleared, row reaped only after the server confirms the push.
Tombstone pulled for a page this device never hadAlready satisfied; nothing is inserted.
Local edit newer than the server's copyLocal wins and stays dirty; the next push carries it up.
Ink larger than 1.5 MBText syncs, drawing stays local, and a pulled null never erases it.
Blocks JSON cannot be decodedThe editor gets a blank page; the original bytes stay on disk until saved over.
A row from the server with an unknown block kindThat block is dropped, not guessed at. A row with no id or timestamp is refused.
Fresh install, empty storeThe index migration does not spend its one-shot, so pulled pages are not swept into the Inbox.
Signed outEverything works locally; sync returns without an error. The first pass after sign-in carries it all up.
Page closed inside the debounce windowflush() on disappear and on leaving the active scene phase saves it anyway.

Tests

The notes layer is the most heavily tested feature in the package: 151 tests across eleven suites, all runnable from the terminal with no simulator.

  • NoteBlockEditorTests (35): every Return and Backspace rule above, indent bounds, numbered runs restarting, slash and link query detection, sketch insertion and protection.
  • NoteBlockTests (15): prefix resolution and longest-match ordering, Markdown round trips, link scanning, and that a block written before dueDate existed still decodes.
  • NotesStoreTests (34): filing rules, folder deletion rehoming, tombstones, dirty tracking, journal-once-per-day, backlinks, search reaching archived pages, capture, and that the index is updated by every write path including emptying a folder.
  • NoteIndexerTests (16): rows in and out, block identity kept, deleted pages keep no rows, edges resolve or stay unresolved, rebuild is idempotent and clears orphans.
  • NoteIndexMigrationTests (4): existing pages are stamped and indexed, a later capture is not swept up by a second run, an empty store does not spend the one-shot.
  • NoteStreamTests (8): what each chip shows, newest first, archived pages leave every stream, only a page given a folder is born filed.
  • NoteWireFormatTests (16): the round trip, blocks as JSON not a string, journal dates on the same calendar day, oversized ink left behind, the client never claiming ownership, unknown kinds dropped.
  • NoteSyncIndexTests (4): a pulled page is indexed, an updated one reindexed, a tombstoned one loses its rows, a pulled page is not in the Inbox. apply is internal rather than private so these run without a network.
  • PlanNoteMigrationTests (8) and PlanStoreTests (10): see 12.9.

12.9The plan that remains

PlanEntry still exists with all five kinds, and PlanScreen still renders four sections. Only one of them is reachable. The notes tab's library offers a Habits row that pushes PlanScreen with section: .constant(.habits) and showsSections: false, and the add sheet in RootView sets plan.section = .habits before it opens. Goals, notes and content are pages now.

Why habits stayed behind

A habit is a daily tick with a streak behind it. Today toggles those ticks live from its own screen, and turning a habit into a document would either break Today or leave two rows claiming to be the same habit. So HabitTick stays a flat table keyed by entryID and day, PlanStore.tickedHabitIDs(on:) answers a whole day in one fetch for Today, and the streak rule from Revision D is unchanged: 

// LifeOSKit/Sources/Persistence/PlanStore.swift
public func streak(for entry: PlanEntry, endingOn end: Date = .now) throws -> Int {
    let ticks = try recentTicks(for: entry, days: 365, endingOn: end)
    var count = 0
    for (index, done) in ticks.reversed().enumerated() {
        if done { count += 1 }
        else if index == 0 { continue }   // today still open
        else { break }
    }
    return count
}

Walk backwards from today, counting until a gap. An unticked today is skipped rather than treated as a break, because the day is not over; yesterday unticked still ends the streak.

How the rest moved

PlanNoteMigration.run is idempotent through originPlanEntryID on each page rather than through a flag in UserDefaults, because a flag says "this device has migrated", which is the wrong question once a second device syncs the same pages down. PARA's own rule decides where each kind lands:

Plan kindShelfFolderPage kindNote
goalProjectsGoalstaskDetail becomes blocks; status survives. Milestone targets were dropped, which the spec's Goals phase is meant to restore.
contentProjectsContenttaskDue date carried over.
noteResearchNotesnote
journalAreasJournaljournalThe old title field was the whole text, so the day becomes the title and the text becomes the first block.
habitstaysNot migrated.

Folders are made only when there is something to put in them, and the original plan rows are left in place. They are what the months already closed were scored against, and rewriting history to match a new filing system is the kind of thing an app should never do behind someone's back. NoteEvidence is the bridge the monthly close uses: journal dates come off journal pages by entryDate, and a project page's status is what its to-do blocks say when it has any, because ticking the last box is a clearer statement that a thing is done than remembering to flip a menu afterwards.

12.10Study notes

Read in this order

  1. LifeOSKit/Sources/Persistence/NoteBlock.swift: the block, the parser, the link scanner. Everything else is built on this shape.
  2. LifeOSKit/Sources/Persistence/NoteBlockEditor.swift: what Return and Backspace mean, as pure functions. Read the tests beside it.
  3. LifeOSKit/Sources/Persistence/NoteDocument.swift: the page and its four load-bearing nullable dates.
  4. LifeOSKit/Sources/Persistence/NotesStore.swift: every read and write. Notice that touch is the only place the index is rewritten.
  5. LifeOSKit/Sources/Persistence/NoteIndexer.swift: the two different deletes and the once-per-rebuild title index.
  6. LifeOSKit/Sources/Integrations/NoteSync.swift: push before pull, and the four rules in its header comment.
  7. LIfeOS/Features/Notes/View/NotesHubScreen.swift: the measured three-column rule and the page that moves between column and stack.
  8. LIfeOS/Features/Notes/View/InkCanvasView.swift: the Pencil rule, and why it used to be wrong.

Check yourself

  • Why are blocks JSON inside the page rather than SwiftData rows? Blocks are only ever read and written as a document; a relationship would add a migration hazard per field for no query that needs it. The derived rows exist for the one query that does.
  • What single field is the Inbox? filedAt. Nil means nobody has chosen where the page belongs. Filing stamps it; editing never does.
  • Why does reindex fetch-and-delete while rebuildAll uses the batch delete? The batch form cannot see rows inserted earlier in the same unsaved transaction, so inside reindex it would duplicate rows. rebuildAll clears already-saved rows before inserting anything, so the batch form is correct there.
  • What made a rebuild quadratic, and what fixed it? Each page's reindex built its own title index by fetching every document. rebuildAll now builds it once and passes it down; a single save still builds it on demand, and only when the page has links.
  • Why push folders before documents, and why batches of 25? A page arriving before its folder would be filed at the root on another device until the folder caught up. One oversized body is a 413 that fails every page in it, including the small ones.
  • Why did habits not become pages? Today ticks them live from HabitTick; a document version would either break Today or duplicate the habit.

Chapter thirteen

13The Life board and the nine sectors

Nine sectors of a life, scored once a month by a rule that shows its evidence and a person who has the last word. The same arithmetic that closes a month also projects the month still being lived, so the board can say where a sector will land and which lever moves it most.

13.1Intent

Shiv had been scoring himself by hand every month across nine sectors: Family, Romance, Soul, Friends, Growth, Money, Mission, Body, Mind. The practice worked. What it lacked was evidence and memory: a feeling recorded on a page, nothing underneath it, and no way to see a year at a glance. The app already held much of the evidence and had no concept of a sector at all. The Life tab is that concept.

Five decisions settled the shape, and the reasoning is what a future reader needs.

  • The app proposes, the user decides. Every month a rule proposes a score per sector with the rows behind it; the person confirms or overrides, and the person's number is what gets stored. Full automation was rejected because Romance and Soul have no honest data source, and one invented number costs trust in all nine.
  • Monthly close, as a ritual. Scores change once a month. Between closes the board holds steady, and Today remains the daily surface. A continuously drifting score duplicates Today's job and invites gaming the number.
  • Rules score, the model explains. A deterministic rule computes the number; the on-device model turns the evidence rows into one sentence. A model-judged score could differ on two runs with no way to see why, and a score you cannot explain is a score you stop trusting.
  • The close-time check-in fills the cold start. A sector with no tracked data asks two or three short questions during the close. The answers become its evidence, stored and comparable next month, so every sector is scorable in month one.
  • No overall life score. An average of nine sectors sits near the middle forever and moves by fractions, which reads as nothing happening in a month where one sector collapsed and another soared. The header carries the two facts that prompt action instead: the lowest sector and the biggest mover.

Two later projects extended the spine. The sector screens project gave every sector the same history screen and amended the original "board as hub" decision: Body, Money and Mission now open a history like the other six, with an extra row through to their full tab. The dry run project added the in-flight mode, where a sector shows a range it can still close in rather than a number, and a ranking of what still moves it.

The view models are deliberately thin. There is no test target for the app, so nothing put in a view model can be unit tested; every decision about a score, a band, a schedule or a history lives in the Sectors package, where 222 tests in SectorsTests and another 34 in PersistenceTests cover it.

13.3Model

The nine sectors

// LifeOSKit/Sources/Persistence/LifeSector.swift
public enum LifeSector: String, Codable, Sendable, CaseIterable {
    case family, romance, soul, friends, growth, money, mission, body, mind

    /// Reading order on the board. Kept separate from `allCases` so that
    /// adding a sector later cannot silently reshuffle the grid.
    public static let boardOrder: [LifeSector] = [
        .family, .romance, .soul,
        .friends, .growth, .money,
        .mission, .body, .mind,
    ]
}

Raw values are written to the store, so a case may be added but never renamed: a rename orphans every score already recorded against it. The same append-only rule applies to check-in question ids.

A scored month

// LifeOSKit/Sources/Persistence/SectorScore.swift
@Model
public final class SectorScore {
    public var sectorRaw: String
    public private(set) var month: Date       // always the first day of the month
    public var proposedScore: Int?            // what the rule said, nil with no evidence
    public var userScore: Int?                // what the person said, nil until decided
    public var closedAt: Date?
    public var evidenceData: Data?            // the rows, frozen at close time
    ...
    public var isScored: Bool { userScore != nil }
}

proposedScore and userScore are both kept, permanently. The distance between what the rule computed and what the person felt is the most interesting number in the system, and averaging them would erase it. The evidence is archived rather than recomputed: change a goal in March and February's reasoning must still read the way it did in February. Every row is keyed by Date.startOfMonth, so closing August on 3 September files the score under 1 August.

The one scoring rule

// LifeOSKit/Sources/Persistence/Evidence.swift
public struct EvidenceRow: Codable, Sendable, Equatable {
    public let label: String
    public let value: String          // already formatted, rendered verbatim
    public let normalised: Double     // clamped into 0...1 on the way in
    public let weight: Double         // never negative; zero means shown, not counted
}

public struct Evidence: Codable, Sendable, Equatable {
    public let rows: [EvidenceRow]

    public var proposedValue: Double? {
        guard !rows.isEmpty else { return nil }
        let totalWeight = rows.reduce(0) { $0 + $1.weight }
        guard totalWeight > 0 else { return nil }
        let weighted = rows.reduce(0) { $0 + $1.normalised * $1.weight }
        return (weighted / totalWeight) * 10
    }

    public var proposedScore: Int? { proposedValue.map { Int($0.rounded()) } }
}

Identical for all nine sectors: each row normalises to 0...1, rows are weighted, the weighted mean scales to 0...10 and rounds. One arithmetic path means one thing to test and one thing to explain. A sector with no evidence proposes nothing, not zero: zero out of ten for Romance in month one is both wrong and demoralising. Weights live in code, not in settings, because user-editable weights turn every score into a dial to twist until the number is agreeable. A zero-weight row is how a scorer shows a figure (earned, spent, unclaimed) without letting it argue.

The scorers

SectorScorerRows (weight)Proposes nothing when
BodyBodyScorerdays on target (2), sleep vs goal (1), exercise vs goal (1)no day carries any data
MoneyMoneyScorerearned (0), spent (0), budgets kept (3, when buckets exist), kept of what came in (2 with buckets, 3 without), spend vs last month (1), unclaimed (0)no transactions
MissionMissionScorergoals moved (2), habits kept (1)no plan entries moved, or only blocked ones
GrowthGrowthScorertargets met (2), goals completed (1)no targets tracked and no goals
MindJournalScorer + CheckInScorerdays written (2), vs last month (1), how clear was your head (2)nothing written and nothing answered
SoulJournalScorer + CheckInScorerdays written (2), vs last month (1), how settled (2), a note (0)nothing written and nothing answered
Family, Romance, FriendsCheckInScorertwo scored questions (2 each) and one free-text note (0)no answers

Every scorer is built from values already fetched, never from a store, which is why evidence() neither throws nor awaits and why every scoring test runs without a container. Two details recur. Days with no data are excluded rather than scored as misses, so a charging night does not argue against the person. And "blocked" plan work returns nil from progressFraction rather than zero: waiting on someone else is not a failure of the person being scored.

Money's rule changed when budgets arrived. With buckets, adherence takes the top weight and the saving rate steps down, because a budget is a plan the person set and beating it measures what they decided mattered, where a saving rate measures what happened to be left over. Without buckets the evidence is exactly what it was before budgets existed, which withNoBucketsTheEvidenceIsUnchangedFromToday pins.

Check-in questions

// LifeOSKit/Sources/Sectors/CheckInQuestion.swift
case .friends:
    [
        CheckInQuestion(id: "friends.seen", prompt: "How often did you see friends?", options: scale, weight: 2),
        CheckInQuestion(id: "friends.depth", prompt: "Did any of it go beyond small talk?", options: [
            CheckInOption("no", 0.0), CheckInOption("once", 0.5), CheckInOption("more than once", 1.0),
        ], weight: 2),
        CheckInQuestion(id: "friends.note", prompt: "Who is worth calling next month?", options: []),
    ]

Each option carries its own place on the shared scale. A question with no options is free text: recorded as context, shown on the close, never scored. An answer that matches no option is stale data from a question that has since changed, and it is dropped rather than guessed at.

13.4ViewModel

The board

LifeBoardViewModel.load() builds nine Cards in board order, each with a six-month history for the sparkline. In closed mode a card carries last month's userScore; in flight it carries a SectorBand instead. The header is BoardSummary (lowest and biggest mover, comparing the last two closed months) or, in flight, the days left and the mean share of the month that is decided. The close banner is decided by CloseSchedule. 

// LifeOSKit/Sources/Sectors/CloseSchedule.swift
let oldestGap = scoredCounts
    .filter { month, scored in
        scored < totalSectors && month >= earliestAllowed && month <= previousMonth
    }
    .keys
    .min()

if let oldestGap { return oldestGap }
return scoredSectorsInPreviousMonth < totalSectors ? previousMonth : nil

The oldest month with a gap inside a twelve-month look-back is offered first, so a gap two months back surfaces before a more recent one and is never buried. The fallback to the previous month exists to break a deadlock in the naive version: a query over SectorScore rows only sees months that already have a row, rows are created only by record(), and record() runs only during a close. On a fresh install there are no rows, so the query returns nothing, no banner shows, and no close can ever start.

The close

MonthlyCloseViewModel drives one pass. advance() asks CloseProgress for the first sector in board order that is neither committed in the store nor skipped this session, loads that sector's stored answers, loads the month's inputs once through MonthInputsLoader, and recomputes. recompute() is the single call into the factory, and it runs on every answer, including one keystroke at a time into a free-text field. 

// LIfeOS/Features/Life/ViewModel/MonthlyCloseViewModel.swift
func recompute() {
    guard let sector else { return }
    evidence = SectorEvidenceFactory.evidence(
        for: sector, inputs: monthInputs, answers: answers, calendar: calendar
    )
    proposed = evidence.proposedScore
    chosenScore = ChosenScore.seeded(
        current: chosenScore, hasChosen: hasChosenScore,
        proposed: proposed, previousUserScore: previousUserScore
    )

    let isEmptyNow = evidence.isEmpty
    if NoteRequest.shouldRequest(wasEmpty: evidenceWasEmpty, isEmptyNow: isEmptyNow) {
        scheduleNoteRequest(for: sector)
    }
    evidenceWasEmpty = isEmptyNow
}

Three pure policies sit behind that method, each a few lines and each tested.

  • ChosenScore.seeded. Before the person touches the stepper, the number shown tracks the proposal, falling back to last month's score, then to 5. The moment they touch it, their pick is authoritative and no later recompute may replace it, however small the change that triggered the recompute.
  • AnswerPersistence.isImmediate. A choice button is one discrete event and saves at once. Free text is a stream of keystrokes, and every context.save() makes RootView reload nine view models, so text is debounced 600 milliseconds and flushed synchronously before Skip or Next clears the answers.
  • NoteRequest. The sentence is requested only on the transition from no evidence to some, after a 400 millisecond debounce, and applied only if the sector on screen is still the one it was asked about. Asking on appearance would ask about nothing for a check-in sector, and a request in flight when the close advances must not write its sentence over the next sector's.

commit() records the proposal and its evidence, then commits the chosen score. SectorStore.record returns an existing decided row untouched and SectorStore.commit refuses to overwrite a decided score, so the store does not depend on the view model getting the "never re-offer a committed sector" rule right. skip() moves on without writing anything; a skipped sector stays genuinely unscored and is offered again next time, because a score nobody looked at is noise in the history.

In flight

InFlightSectorViewModel.load() reads the current month's inputs and answers, builds the SectorBand and the Leverage ranking, and notes whether the ceiling came from GoalTargets.default so the screen can say whose numbers they are. Answers given here are written against the current month through the same saveAnswer upsert the close uses, so an answer given on the 12th is visible, scored, and revisable at close with no new model.

13.5View

The deck

SectorStack lays the nine cards out at their full height (190 points) and pulls each one up over the one before it, so all that shows is a 78-point band carrying the sector and its score. Tapping a card lifts it clear of the deck: its z-index jumps, the cards below slide down by the open height less the peek, and the space that appears carries the trend line, a six-month RoundedBarChart, and an Open button. Only one card is ever open, because a deck with several cards open is a list with gaps in it. An open card is sized to what it has to show: 320 points with a chart, 226 without, so a sector with one month does not spend space on a void.

Nothing renders below the band while a card is closed. A covered card has only the peek of room and anything taller gets sliced by the card in front; the trend line used to show as a clipped strip of letter-tops under every title. VoiceOver reads every card whole, because the visual truncation must never truncate what is spoken.

Nine cards that physically overlap need nine distinct colours, and the app's shared ModuleHue has six. SectorPalette.tone is therefore a second, feature-local palette: one muted earth family in light and dark, with a single shared cardInk chosen so it clears contrast on all nine. The six-case hue mapping still exists for the close and the detail screen, which use shared components that take a ModuleHue.

The banner

CloseBanner is deliberately not AlertBanner. That component is red on pink with an ECG glyph and it is the app's anomaly surface: it means something is wrong with your body. An unclosed month is a piece of admin, and borrowing the alarm styling for it spends the alarm. The banner is a dashed outline, collapsed by default, because the deck is the reason anyone opens this screen.

The close screen

One sector per screen, titled "4 of 9". Questions first where the sector has them, then a PastelFillCard with the proposal (its own dash when there is no evidence: not scored badly, not scored at all), the evidence rows label left and value right, the model's sentence if one arrived, "Last month you said 7", and a HeroNumeral with a 0...10 stepper. Skip and Next in the toolbar. The sheet owns its view model, and the board reloads on dismissal rather than on completion, because scoring three sectors and swiping the sheet away used to leave the deck showing dashes for scores that were already saved.

The history screen

Four bands, each omitted rather than rendered empty: the trend as bars from the window minimum (a score is a rating, not a count building from nought, so a flat year of 4s and a flat year of 9s must not both draw as full bars), the reasoning frozen at the latest close, every question's answers laid across the last six months with a dash for a month not answered, and the free-text notes newest first. Observations sit above them when there are any. Body, Money and Mission get one extra row, "Open Body", and LifeSector.ownsTab is the one place that decides which three.

The in-flight screen

The range at display size, the days left, then "What moves it most" as a ranked list of levers with their worth in points, the check-in questions for a sector that has them, and the floor and ceiling evidence under "If nothing changes" and "If you finish at your targets". Money with no buckets says so in a line instead of inventing a ceiling. A ceiling built from default targets is disclosed in one line and points at Health.

13.6How it works

Loading a month

MonthInputsLoader.load is the only place store reads happen for scoring. It builds a MonthWindow (the exact instants a month spans, with a half-open [start, end) for filtering and an inclusive lastDay for the stores whose to: bound is by day), reads metrics, goals, transactions, buckets, plan entries, project pages and journal dates, filters the undated stores by updatedAt or createdAt, and assembles one MonthInputs. It moved out of the close view model when the in-flight board needed the same thing for the current month, and the move fixed a bug the in-flight case exposed: PlanStore.recentTicks reads a day with no tick as a miss, so running the window to the end of a month still being lived scored every day still to come as a habit already broken. Habits are now judged only across the days already lived.

Notes changed what the loader reads without changing what old months mean. Journalling and goals moved to note pages, so NoteEvidence bridges them in, and the legacy plan entries are still read and summed alongside, because a month already closed must keep scoring the way it did.

Projecting the rest of it

// LifeOSKit/Sources/Sectors/ProjectedInputs.swift
public static func coasting(
    _ inputs: MonthInputs, progress: MonthProgress, calendar: Calendar = .current
) -> MonthInputs {
    guard progress.remainingDays > 0, progress.elapsedDays > 0 else { return inputs }
    let remaining = Double(progress.remainingDays)
    let elapsed = Double(progress.elapsedDays)
    var projected = inputs

    if let average = averageReading(inputs.readings) {
        projected.readings += Array(repeating: average, count: progress.remainingDays)
    }
    let earned = inputs.amounts.filter { $0 > 0 }.reduce(0, +)
    let spent = -inputs.amounts.filter { $0 < 0 }.reduce(0, +)
    if earned > 0 { projected.amounts.append(earned / elapsed * remaining) }
    if spent > 0 { projected.amounts.append(-(spent / elapsed * remaining)) }
    projected.budget = inputs.budget.map { scaled($0, by: (elapsed + remaining) / elapsed) }
    ...
    return projected
}

Coast means continuing at the current pace, not stopping. This is the subtle one. For Body the two are nearly the same, since BodyScorer counts only days with data. For Money they are opposites: spending nothing for the rest of the month is the best case, so an empty tail would put the floor above the ceiling and invert the card. One definition serves every sector, and it is the one that reads correctly for spend.

Perfect fills the remaining days at the person's own targets. Not a theoretical maximum, which produces ceilings nobody reaches, and not a personal best, which is undefined in month one. A ceiling built from GoalTargets is reachable by definition, and it makes setting a target consequential for the first time. Only a tracked metric is raised, and always with max against the running average: a person already averaging 20,000 steps against an 8,000 target must not be "perfected" down to 8,000. Perfecting spend spends up to each bucket's remaining allowance and no further, and cannot repair a bucket already blown. Income is not a lever and keeps coasting. Goal statuses are never touched, because a ceiling must never assume a goal closes.

One lever perfected is built on the coast and then overwrites only the dimension named, so a lever's delta is never contaminated by a second lever quietly improving beside it. Leverage.ranked runs the factory once per tracked lever, subtracts the coasting value, clamps at zero (perfecting a lever cannot make a month worse, and a negative row would read as advice to stop), and sorts. A sector scored only from answers has no levers.

The band

// LifeOSKit/Sources/Sectors/SectorBand.swift
public var decided: Double? {
    guard let floor, let ceiling else { return nil }
    return min(max(1 - Double(ceiling - floor) / 10, 0), 1)
}

Decided is literally the share of the score that can no longer move. The board header shows the mean across only the sectors that have a band, not all nine, because a sector nobody has evidence for has not been judged settled or unsettled; folding it in would let silence read as certainty. Money with no buckets has no ceiling: nothing in the data says what a good remaining spend would be, zero is a fantasy and any other figure is invented, so the card shows a floor and points at bucket setup. A ceiling below its floor is always a projection bug, never a fact, and is clamped up.

History and observations

SectorDetailViewModel fetches twelve months of scores and their answers, maps them to plain records, and makes one pure call: SectorHistory.build. Only decided months appear. Question tracks follow the order the questions are asked in and align by index to the months, so a missing answer leaves a gap rather than shifting later answers left. Free text becomes a note, not a track.

Observations are two deterministic rules, both needing three calendar-adjacent months so a single unusual month never fires one: the same answer three months running, and the person scoring below the proposal three months running. The second is the signal the spine kept proposedScore and userScore in separate columns to preserve: the rule is measuring something the person does not feel. "Consecutive" is checked on the calendar, not on array position, because a partial close can leave a sector unscored in the middle month and three entries spread across a longer stretch are not three months running. No model is called from this screen at all, which also keeps it free and instant.

The sentence

SectorNoteTask is an on-device CoachTask with no remote name. Its prompt is only the rows the rule used, so the sentence cannot cite a figure that played no part in the number, and it deliberately never carries last month's score, because the instructions forbid mentioning a score and feeding the model a number on the same scale works against that. The close runs it through the ordinary CoachRouter so availability caching and refusal handling behave as they do everywhere else; an unavailable model leaves the close fully usable with rows and no sentence.

13.7Performance and cost

  • Inputs loaded once per sector, not per keystroke. The close rebuilds MonthInputs in advance(); recompute() only re-runs the factory against values already in memory. Scoring is a handful of reductions over small arrays and runs on every keystroke without cost.
  • Free text debounced, choices immediate. One context.save() per pause rather than per character, because every save reloads nine view models. The pending value is flushed synchronously on Skip, Next and screen dismissal so no keystrokes are lost.
  • One model call per sector, at most. The sentence is requested on the transition into having evidence, debounced 400 milliseconds, on device, and discarded if the sector has moved on. Nothing about a sector leaves the phone.
  • No model on the board or the history. Observations are rules. The board is nine store reads and a summary.
  • In-flight is eight factory runs per sector at most. Two for the band and one per tracked lever (up to four for Body and Growth, one elsewhere). It is recomputed when the board mode switches and when a screen loads, not continuously.
  • The archive is a JSON blob per row. Evidence is encoded once at close and decoded on read; nothing is recomputed against changed goals, and the history screen renders the stored strings verbatim.
  • Everything is local. Sector scores, answers and evidence are SwiftData rows in the account's own store. There is no sync for them and no server table. Cost is zero.

13.8Edge cases and tests

ConditionBehaviour
Fresh install, no rows at allThe banner offers the previous month; without the fallback no close could ever start
August never closed, September endsAugust is offered first; the oldest gap within twelve months wins
A month older than the look-back is partialNever offered; one ancient partial month must not pin the banner forever
Sector has no evidenceProposes nothing; the card shows a dash and the stepper seeds from last month or 5
Person adjusts the stepper, then edits a noteThe recompute runs but ChosenScore keeps their number
Leaving the close midwayCommitted sectors stay committed; reopening resumes at the first unscored one
SkipNothing is written; the sector is offered again next time
Re-recording a decided sectorThe store returns the row untouched; the archive never lies
Committing twiceThe first decision stands
Note arrives after the close advancedRejected by NoteRequest.shouldApply
Model unavailable or refusesRows shown, no sentence, close fully usable
Closing August on 3 SeptemberFiled under 1 August by startOfMonth, in the store's injected calendar
Twelve journal entries on one afternoonOne day written; distinct days are counted, not entries
Blocked plan itemExcluded from judgement rather than scored zero
Metric never logged this monthAbsent from the Body rows and from Growth's target count, and not offered as a lever
Money in flight without bucketsFloor only, no ceiling, no decided share; the card explains why
Last day of the monthThe band collapses to a single number; a finished month has nothing left to move
Already exceeding a targetThe ceiling keeps the running average; it never asks for less
Bucket already blownA perfect finish cannot unspend money; that row stays where it is
Skipped a sector in the middle monthThree entries are not three months running; both observation rules stay silent
December to JanuaryCounts as consecutive across the year boundary
Answer matches no current optionDropped; a changed question does not score stale text
Question last answered seven months agoIts track is hidden rather than rendered as a prompt over dashes

Tests

  • PersistenceTests/EvidenceTests: the weighted mean scales to ten, no rows and zero total weight propose nothing, normalised values clamp, proposedScore is always the rounded proposedValue.
  • PersistenceTests/SectorStoreTests and SectorScoreTests: idempotent record, commit closes once, re-recording leaves a closed score alone, scoredCounts reflects a genuine partial close, month normalisation under an injected calendar.
  • SectorsTests, one suite per file: every scorer, the factory's routing and Soul and Mind's merge without double counting, CloseSchedule, CloseProgress, ChosenScore, AnswerPersistence, NoteRequest, MonthWindow (leap February), MonthProgress (today counts as elapsed), MonthInputsLoader against an in-memory container (habits judged only on days lived, a closed month still judging every day), ProjectedInputs (perfect scores at least as well as coasting, spend up to the allowance and no more, goals untouched), Leverage (a lever at target is worth nothing, never less than nothing), SectorBand (ceiling never below floor, collapses on the last day, Money without buckets), SectorHistory, SectorObservations, BoardSummary (ties go to the drop), and LifeSectorTab.
  • InsightsTests/SectorNoteTests: the prompt carries every row, the previous score never reaches it, the task runs on device.

13.9Study notes

Read in this order

  1. LifeOSKit/Sources/Persistence/Evidence.swift, the one rule.
  2. LifeOSKit/Sources/Sectors/BodyScorer.swift, then MoneyScorer.swift, to see two scorers shape rows.
  3. LifeOSKit/Sources/Sectors/SectorEvidenceFactory.swift, the routing and the merges.
  4. LifeOSKit/Sources/Sectors/MonthInputsLoader.swift, where the stores are read.
  5. LIfeOS/Features/Life/ViewModel/MonthlyCloseViewModel.swift, the close pass and its three policies.
  6. LifeOSKit/Sources/Sectors/ProjectedInputs.swift, coasting and perfect.
  7. LifeOSKit/Sources/Sectors/SectorBand.swift and Leverage.swift.
  8. LIfeOS/Features/Life/View/SectorStack.swift, the deck.

Check yourself

  • Why does a sector with no evidence propose nil rather than zero? It has not been judged badly; it has not been judged. Zero for Romance in month one is wrong and demoralising.
  • Why are proposedScore and userScore both stored? The gap between them is the signal; the standing-gap observation is the first place it is read.
  • Why is the evidence archived rather than recomputed? A goal changed in March must not rewrite what February's reasoning said.
  • What does coasting mean, and why not an empty tail? The rest of the month looks like the part already lived; an empty tail would put Money's floor above its ceiling.
  • Why does the in-flight board never compute a score of its own? The moment a projection scores by another path, the band and the close can disagree, and a band that contradicts the close is worse than none.
  • Why does CloseSchedule fall back to the previous month? Rows exist only after a close, so a query over rows can never start the first close.

Chapter fourteen

14LIFO, the coach

LIFO is the one screen in Almanac that talks back. It reads a fortnight of your own numbers, your month's money and your nine sector scores, answers in cards rather than paragraphs, can listen and speak, remembers the conversation it is in, and, once a day at most, speaks first. This chapter is how all of that is built, where the words go, and what it costs.

14.1Intent

Working backwards

Ask LIFO how you slept this week and it answers with a table of your actual nights, on the cloud when the cloud can answer and on the phone when it cannot. Say it out loud and it stops listening when you stop talking, reads one warm sentence back while the cards are still arriving, and never reads a table aloud. Ask a follow-up and it knows what it said. Some mornings it sends a line first: three short nights against your own baseline, a streak that today would break, a strong week worth naming. Tap it and the conversation opens on that sentence.

Which model answers?

The cloud first, the device second. The cloud tier is OpenAI's gpt-5-mini behind the lifo-agent Edge Function; the device tier is Apple's Foundation Models. It used to be the other way round on the grounds that the free engine should be tried first, and the result was a worse common answer with the better one appearing only when the weaker model failed outright. Quality picks the tier; a metered daily cap on the server is what keeps that affordable.

What leaves the phone?

On a cloud turn, one rendered text block: a fortnight of derived daily numbers, the month's money summary with up to thirty recent transactions, the sector scores, and the last twenty turns of the conversation. Never the raw Whoop series (HRV, SpO2, skin temperature, respiratory rate), which exist only in the on-device render. Every answer carries a disclosure you can open that shows the verbatim text that was sent and which tier answered.

How does it avoid inventing numbers?

Two ways. The prompt is the data: the model is told to cite only figures that appear in the text it was given, and the render omits a missing field rather than writing zero. The reply is then parsed by CoachResponse into paragraphs, tables and lists, and a table cell displays exactly the string the answer supplied; nothing is recalculated on the way to the screen.

Why cards instead of a paragraph?

A paragraph about six metrics is six numbers hidden in prose. The coach is instructed with a small presentation grammar (a marker string, then rules: short paragraph for a simple question, a two-column table for metrics, up to three bullets for actions, at most three sections) and the screen renders those shapes natively. A short answer stays short; nothing is forced into a dashboard.

What the coach deliberately does not do: it has no tools. The calendar assistant in Chapter 15 carries six and runs a tool loop; LIFO carries none, which is exactly what lets its whole reply be streamed. It does not diagnose, it does not pick investments, and it declines requests that are not about coaching this person over their own data, because the guardrail that says so lives on the server where a client cannot strip it.
