16.3Model

Every type the screens render is a Codable value decoded straight from PostgREST. There is no SwiftData model in this feature: nothing social is cached on the device, and a screen that loses the network shows what it last fetched plus one quiet sentence. 

// LifeOSKit/Sources/Integrations/SocialAPI.swift
public struct SocialProfile: Codable, Sendable, Equatable, Identifiable {
    public let userID: UUID
    public let displayName: String
    public let firstName: String?      // every field past the name is optional:
    public let country: String?        // a question someone may decline to answer
    public let birthDate: Date?
    public let heightCM: Double?
    public let avatarPath: String?     // the object's path inside the avatars bucket
}

public enum FriendshipStatus: String, Codable, Sendable { case pending, accepted }

public struct Friendship: Codable, Sendable, Equatable, Identifiable {
    public let id: Int
    public let requester: UUID
    public let addressee: UUID
    public let status: FriendshipStatus
}

public struct SocialMessage: Codable, Sendable, Equatable, Identifiable {
    public let id: Int                 // negative while provisional, see ChatViewModel
    public let sender: UUID
    public let recipient: UUID
    public let body: String
    public let createdAt: Date
}

A friendship is one row whoever asked first, pending until the addressee accepts. The unique constraint is on the ordered pair, and the API guards the reverse direction before inserting. A profile that pads itself with placeholders for the fields somebody skipped looks broken rather than private, which is why the optionals stay optional all the way to the screen.

The decoder is the one piece of the model worth a paragraph. PostgREST emits timestamps with fractional seconds, which the default date strategy does not parse, and a bare date column such as birth_date arrives with no clock at all, which neither ISO 8601 formatter accepts. Before the third branch was added, a profile carrying a birthday failed to decode entirely, taking the person's name down with it. SocialAPI.decoder tries fractional, then plain, then the day format, and is internal rather than private so a test can exercise each branch.

Groups

// LifeOSKit/Sources/Integrations/GroupAPI.swift
public struct SocialGroup: Codable, Sendable, Equatable, Identifiable {
    public let id: UUID
    public let name: String
    public let description: String
    public let ownerID: UUID
    public let members: [GroupMember]              // decoded from the embedded group_members
    public var isInvitation: Bool { members.first?.status == "invited" }
}

public struct GroupMember: Codable, Sendable, Equatable, Identifiable {
    public let groupID: UUID
    public let userID: UUID
    public let status: String                      // invited | accepted
    public let sharesActivity: Bool
    public let sharesWellness: Bool?               // optional: added by a later migration
}

public struct GroupMessage: Codable, Sendable, Equatable, Identifiable {
    public let id: Int
    public let groupID: UUID
    public let sender: UUID
    public let body: String
    public let clientID: UUID                      // the idempotency key a retry reuses
    public let createdAt: Date
}

public struct LeaderboardEntry: Codable, Sendable, Equatable, Identifiable {
    public let userID: UUID
    public let displayName: String
    public let avatarPath: String?
    public let score: Int                          // 0 to 100
    public let position: Int                       // the server's rank, ties included
    public let updatedAt: Date
    public let source: String?                     // appleHealth | whoop | fitbit
    public let day: String?
}

groups(token:) asks for social_groups with the caller's own group_members row embedded and filtered, so one request returns the groups and, for each, whether this person is a member or merely invited. sharesWellness is optional because the column arrived in a second migration and an older row shape must still decode.

Shared figures and wellness days

// LifeOSKit/Sources/Integrations/SharedStatsClient.swift
public struct SharedStats: Codable, Sendable, Equatable, Identifiable {
    public let userID: UUID
    public let shares: Bool          // the owner's standing answer
    public let streak: Int?          // nil is "not sent", not zero
    public let daysTracked: Int?
    public let workouts: Int?
    public var hasFigures: Bool { shares && (streak != nil || daysTracked != nil || workouts != nil) }
}

shares is separate from the figures because they say different things. A person who turned sharing on this morning and has not opened the app since is sharing, with nothing to show, which is not the same as having declined. The profile screen draws the panel only when hasFigures is true: a row of dashes is not a fact.

SocialWellnessDay is one day's three scores with a source per score and an observedAt. Its shape is enforced twice, once in Swift and once by the table's check constraints: a score and its source are both null or both present, and every score is between 0 and 100.

16.4ViewModel

Five plain @Observable classes, none with retry logic of its own. Each reads the session from the keychain on every call rather than capturing the token once, because AppShell refreshes the session hourly and on foregrounding, and a screen left open across that refresh would otherwise strand itself on a rotated token with endless 401s. Identity does not rotate, so myUserID is the one thing still safe to capture.

A newer search never loses to a slower older one

Search re-runs on every keystroke, so an older request can still be waiting on the network when a newer one is issued. Without tracking which query is in flight, a slow response for "al" could land after the fast response for "alex" and silently replace the right results with the wrong ones. 

// LIfeOS/Features/Social/ViewModel/FriendsViewModel.swift
private var searchTask: Task<Void, Never>?
private var searchGeneration = 0

func search() {
    searchTask?.cancel()
    searchGeneration += 1
    let generation = searchGeneration
    // ... guards that name why nothing would happen: no config, signed out, no id yet
    let issuedQuery = query
    searching = true
    searchResults = []
    searchTask = Task {
        defer { if generation == searchGeneration { searching = false } }
        do {
            try await Task.sleep(for: .milliseconds(250))
            let results = try await api.search(trimmed, accessToken: accessToken)
            guard !Task.isCancelled, issuedQuery == self.query else { return }
            searchResults = results.filter { $0.userID != myUserID }
        } catch {
            guard !Task.isCancelled, issuedQuery == self.query else { return }
            errorMessage = Self.reason("Search failed", error)
        }
    }
}

Three guards together: the previous task is cancelled, a 250 millisecond sleep debounces the keystrokes, and the response is applied only if the query it was issued for is still the query on screen. The generation counter is what lets the defer clear the spinner for the latest search alone. The signed-in person is filtered out of results, because finding yourself in your own friends search is noise.

The three early guards each set a sentence instead of returning silently, because saying nothing is what "it just spins" looks like from the outside. reason(_:_:) carries the server's own message through: an expired token, a missing grant and a dropped connection all arrive as "it did not work" otherwise, and PostgREST always says which.

A send can never lose its row

// LIfeOS/Features/Social/ViewModel/ChatViewModel.swift
private(set) var messages: [SocialMessage] = []   // refresh() only ever assigns this
private(set) var pending: [SocialMessage] = []    // provisional rows, kept apart
private var nextProvisionalID = -1                // server ids are always positive

func send() async {
    guard !sending else { return }
    let text = draft.trimmingCharacters(in: .whitespacesAndNewlines)
    guard !text.isEmpty, text.unicodeScalars.count <= 2000, let api, let accessToken, let myUserID else { return }

    let provisionalID = nextProvisionalID
    nextProvisionalID -= 1
    pending.append(SocialMessage(id: provisionalID, sender: myUserID, recipient: friend.userID,
                                 body: text, createdAt: .now))
    sending = true
    do {
        try await api.send(text, to: friend.userID, accessToken: accessToken)
        pending.removeAll { $0.id == provisionalID }
        if draft.trimmingCharacters(in: .whitespacesAndNewlines) == text { draft = "" }
        await refresh()
    } catch {
        pending.removeAll { $0.id == provisionalID }
        errorMessage = "Message wasn’t confirmed. Your draft is still here; check the conversation before trying again."
    }
    sending = false
}

The optimistic row goes into pending, not messages, so a poll landing mid-send can never wholesale-replace it. The screen renders messages + pending. A failed post removes the row it added rather than leaving a message on screen that never sent, and keeps the draft. Reentry is guarded so a fast double-tap before the disabled state applies cannot post twice. The draft is cleared only if it still equals what was sent, so a sentence typed during the round trip is not thrown away.

Group chat goes one step further. GroupViewModel.send generates a clientID per attempt and reuses it on retry; the server's send_group_message inserts with on conflict (sender, client_id) do nothing and returns the existing id, so a retry after a timeout that actually landed cannot post a duplicate. A failed send is held in failedSend with a Retry button, the composer is disabled until it is resolved, and a later refresh that finds the client id in the timeline clears it.

The rest

  • InboxViewModel loads three things, not one per friend: the friendships, the profiles behind them, and the whole mailbox in one 200-row request. The grouping into one thread per counterpart is InboxDigest.threads, in the package, because it is the only real logic the inbox has and it should be testable without a network. The badge counts requests only: a conversation is not a task.
  • GroupsViewModel loads the groups, then publishes the day's wellness scores if any group has sharing on, then reads and, if sharing is on, pushes the three profile figures. A refresh is skipped while a change is busy, and its results are dropped if the signed-in user changed while it was in flight.
  • GroupViewModel refreshes under a generation counter too, and checks the roster before anything else: if the caller is no longer an accepted member, it sets accessLost, clears the messages and board, and the screen says so instead of rendering a stale chat. Messages merge by id rather than replace, so a page loaded through older() survives a poll. The leaderboard has its own generation so a metric or day switch cannot be overwritten by the previous request landing late.

16.5View

Social is reached from the profile, not from a tab. ProfileOverview offers a Together shortcut, and ProfileScreen pushes SocialHubScreen for it. This is a place you go, not a home you live in, and the bar is the scarcest surface in the app.

Together

SocialHubScreen is an UnderlinePicker with three sections. People embeds FriendsScreen. Groups lists invitations first, each as a panel with Decline and Join, then the joined groups as an adaptive grid of coloured cards. Rankings is the same grid with a trophy and "View leaderboard", and opening a group from it lands on the leaderboard section instead of the chat. The toolbar carries the inbox tray and a Create button; CreateGroupScreen takes a name up to 60 characters, a description up to 240, and invitees chosen from the friends list, capped at 49 so the group never exceeds 50. It generates its group id up front, which is what makes a retried create idempotent on the server.

People

FriendsScreen is one list with three shapes. A search field that, once typed in, replaces the screen's own sections with results. Otherwise requests above friends, in that order, because a decision waiting on you outranks a list you already know. A search result's trailing control is always exactly one of Add, Requested or Friends, never a fourth "request me back" state; accepting still happens from the requests section, which already owns that decision. Tapping a friend opens UserProfileScreen, which shows the photo, the relationship's actions (message and remove, accept and decline, cancel a sent request, or add), and the shared figures panel when there are figures to draw.

Conversations

FriendChatScreen and the group chat share SocialMessageBubble and SocialComposer. Mine is ink on the right with a small bottom-trailing radius; theirs is paper on the left. Day separators appear where the calendar day changes. The composer shows a counter past 1800 characters and disables send past 2000, the same limit the table's check constraint enforces. followLatest is read from scroll geometry: the list follows a new message only if the reader was already within 140 points of the bottom or the message is their own, so someone reading history is not yanked down by a reply. Polling runs in a .task(id: scenePhase) loop and stops the moment the scene leaves the active phase.

The chat's first version on 27 August rode a night aurora. The 14 September restyle replaced that with SocialCanvas, the cream gradient every social screen now shares, with a dark counterpart, so a conversation and the friends list read as one place.

The leaderboard

SocialLeaderboard keeps the server's ranks intact, ties included. A podium of three is drawn only when it would not arbitrarily feature some people from a tie that crosses the podium boundary, and the winner's avatar is larger only when all three ranks are distinct. Accessibility sizes skip the podium for a single readable list. Each row prints the score, the source device and how long ago it synced, and the footer says the one thing a reader needs: equal scores share a rank; compare the same day; devices and goals differ. A DisclosureGroup explains the selected metric's formula in plain words, and a date picker allows today or yesterday and nothing else, matching the server's window.

Style

SocialTheme is four pastels (coral, mint, lilac, yellow) chosen by a stable hash of a uuid, so a person or a group is the same colour on every screen and every launch. SocialAvatar shows the profile photo when there is one and initials on that pastel when there is not. InitialBubble in the inbox hashes the name by hand for the same reason: String.hashValue is randomised per launch, and a friend who changed colour every time the app opened would be a small, constant lie.

16.6How it works

Friendship, end to end

  1. On appear, FriendsViewModel upserts the caller's own profiles row from the local profile name. This is what makes the person findable; a failure here is the difference between having friends and not, and it used to be discarded. It is now a publishWarning that outlives a successful list fetch.
  2. Search is an ilike filter on display_name, limited to 20, with %, * and backslash escaped first so a search for a literal "50%" does not match everything.
  3. Add fetches the caller's own friendships and, if the pair is already linked in either direction, returns without inserting. Idempotent, not an error: asking someone who already asked you is not a mistake worth surfacing. The button flips to Requested before the round trip so it does not flicker.
  4. Accept sends a PATCH carrying exactly one column, status. The database grants update on friendships to that column alone, and Postgres enforces column grants before policies even run, so the same statement that accepts a request can never smuggle in a new requester or a new timestamp.
  5. Remove is a DELETE scoped by id, the same call for declining a pending request and ending an accepted friendship, since either way the row stops existing.
  6. Sending a message requires the sender column in the body, and RLS insists it equal auth.uid(). The only place that identity exists on the device is the access token's sub claim, so SocialAPI.subject(ofAccessToken:) reads it without verifying the signature. Verification is the server's job; this only reads a claim already trusted to authenticate every other call.

Groups, end to end

Reads are plain PostgREST selects gated by is_group_member, a security definer helper that exists to avoid recursive membership policies and that takes the caller only from auth.uid(). Every write is an RPC, because each has an invariant a bare insert cannot hold: create_social_group checks every invitee is an accepted friend and rolls the whole thing back if one is not; invite_group_member locks the group row before counting to 50; leave_social_group hands ownership to the longest-standing member or deletes the group when the owner was the last one; send_group_message locks the group so a concurrent removal cannot race a send in. The anon role is revoked from all of them, and truncate, which bypasses row level security, is revoked from everyone.

Wellness scores, end to end

RootView.socialActivity assembles a SocialActivitySnapshot from the local store: the streak, a count of tracked days, a count of workouts, and the last 30 days of DailyMetrics run through SocialWellness.scores against the person's exercise and sleep goals. The scoring rules are strict on purpose.

  • Effort is exercise minutes over the goal, capped at 100. Apple Health uses exercise time, WHOOP tracked workout time, Fitbit fairly plus very active minutes. A duplicate reading is never summed across providers; MetricArbiter already chose one source per metric and the score uses that one.
  • Rest is sleep minutes over the goal, capped at 100. Extra sleep earns no extra points.
  • Recharge is 50 + 100 × (0.6 × (HRV ÷ usual HRV − 1) + 0.4 × (1 − RHR ÷ usual RHR)), clamped to 0 to 100, where "usual" is the median of at least seven distinct earlier days within 28, all from the same provider, never including today. A WHOOP reading still calibrating, a non-finite number, an HRV outside 0 to 500 or a resting rate outside 20 to 150 yields nil, not zero. Fifty means near your own baseline, and the screen says this is an estimate, not a recovery percentage.
  • Only today and yesterday are published. The server refuses a day outside current_date − 2 to current_date + 1, an observation more than five minutes in the future or four days in the past, and an older observation can never overwrite a fresher row.
  • The day key is a Gregorian local date even when the device uses another calendar, so two people in different locales rank on the same day.

Publishing happens from RootView after provider state changes, from the hub on refresh, and when sharing is switched on, and only if some group has shares_wellness set. The server-side ranking function joins members with sharing on to their daily row and rank()s by the chosen metric, so ties share a position and a null score is simply absent from the list rather than ranked last.

16.7Performance and cost

  • Three requests to build the inbox, not one per friend. Friendships, profiles by an in.() list, and the whole mailbox in one 200-row request ordered newest first. The limit is on messages, not conversations, so a very busy thread can crowd a quiet one off the end. That is the right failure: what falls off is what was least recent.
  • Polling is bounded to an open screen. Five seconds in a direct chat, eight in a group, both inside .task(id: scenePhase) so backgrounding ends the loop. No screen polls while not on screen, and nothing polls the friends list at all.
  • Search is debounced and cancelled. 250 milliseconds, one in-flight request, late responses dropped. A person typing a six-letter name costs at most one or two round trips rather than six.
  • Optimistic writes, no waiting. Add flips to Requested and a message appears in pending before the round trip; both are reverted on failure rather than left lying.
  • Group messages page by id. Fifty newest on open, id.lt for older, merged into the existing dictionary so a poll cannot discard a loaded page.
  • Avatars are downloaded per row with a token and cached only by the task. SocialAvatar keys its .task on avatarPath, so a list that re-renders does not refetch faces unless the path changed.
  • Nothing raw leaves the phone. The leaderboard endpoint receives three integers, three source names, a day and a timestamp. HRV, heart rate and sleep minutes stay in DailyMetrics. The profile figures are three counts. There is no AI in this feature and no token budget to protect.
  • Cost is Postgres rows and PostgREST calls. No realtime channel, no storage beyond the avatars bucket Chapter 17 owns, no third-party chat. The gin index on display_name, the two friendships indexes, the (least, greatest, created_at) conversation index and the (group_id, id desc) timeline index are the whole query plan.

16.8Edge cases and tests

ConditionBehaviour
Signed outEvery screen shows a one-sentence guest state, never a request that 401s into a blank screen.
No display name yetThe friends screen says to add a name in Edit profile; no row is published and nobody can find you.
Publishing the profile failsA warning that survives a later successful friends fetch, because "nobody can find you" outlives "the list loaded".
Slow search response arrives after a newer oneDropped. Only the query still on screen may write results.
Search for "50%"Wildcards escaped; it matches the literal text.
Both people request each otherThe second request is a no-op; one row links the pair.
Accept sends more than statusRejected by the column grant before RLS runs.
Message to someone who is not an accepted friendRefused by the insert policy on messages.
Send times out but landedDirect: the pending row is removed and the draft kept, with a sentence asking to check the conversation first. Group: retry reuses the client id and the server returns the existing row.
Double-tap sendReentry guard; one post.
Message from a person no longer in profilesDropped from the inbox rather than shown nameless.
Removed from a group while it is openThe next refresh sets accessLost; chat, board and members are cleared and the screen says so.
Owner leavesOwnership passes to the longest-standing member; if none, the group and its chat are deleted.
Invite a non-friendThe RPC raises and, on create, the whole group creation rolls back.
Group at 50 membersInvite refused under a row lock, so two concurrent invites cannot both succeed.
Sharing switched offSharedStatsClient.push sends explicit nulls rather than omitting the figures, because an upsert leaves omitted columns standing.
Sharing on, nothing pushed yethasFigures is false; the panel is omitted.
Pending friend reads shared figuresRefused by the profile_stats policy, which requires accepted.
Fewer than 7 baseline days, or mixed providersRecharge is nil and the person is unranked for that metric.
Score day out of the server's windowThe publish raises; an older observation never overwrites a fresher row.
Two equal scoresSame rank from rank(); the podium is skipped if the tie crosses its boundary.
Accessibility text sizesNo podium; one readable list. Friend request rows stack vertically.

Tests

Sixty Swift tests in five suites, all pure: request builders are static and free of self, so a test asserts on the URLRequest a call would produce without a network or a stub URLProtocol.

  • SocialAPITests (22): every decode branch including the bare birthday, wildcard escaping, the accept sending only status, the friendship request being a no-op in both directions, the sender derived from the token's subject, and a refusal carrying the server's reason.
  • GroupAPITests (9): groups scoped to the caller, no request without a valid session, message pages read newest first and shown chronologically, retry preserving the idempotency key, the wellness upload carrying day and source and no raw signals, and a membership denial arriving as an error rather than an empty success.
  • SharedStatsClientTests (8): sharing off nulls the figures rather than omitting them, an empty id list never leaves the device, the two hasFigures cases.
  • SocialWellnessTests (15): missing and recorded zero remain different, goal progress capped, manual and unattributed data excluded, the baseline cannot mix providers or use today, duplicate days cannot complete calibration, non-finite signals yield no score, the Gregorian day key in other calendar locales, naps cannot replace the main night.
  • InboxDigestTests (6): one row per person carrying their newest message, the newest conversation leads, a message from someone with no profile is dropped.

The database has its own suite: 43 pgTAP assertions for groups and chat and 23 for the wellness leaderboard, each file inserting disposable identities inside a transaction that is rolled back, switching to the authenticated role and setting the JWT claim by hand. They pin the things Swift cannot: that creation is idempotent, that a blank name is a constraint error, that an invalid invitee rejects creation atomically, that authenticated cannot truncate, that nonmembers and invitees cannot read rankings, and that a stale device write does not overwrite a fresher row. The wellness suite ran with the CLI's pgTAP runner unavailable, through the management API instead; the validation notes record that live two-account verification and three-provider accounts were not exercised.

16.9Study notes

Read in this order

  1. supabase/migrations/20260827130000_friends_and_messages.sql: three tables and seven policies. Everything in Swift is shaped by these.
  2. LifeOSKit/Sources/Integrations/SocialAPI.swift: the request builders, the decoder, and subject(ofAccessToken:).
  3. LIfeOS/Features/Social/ViewModel/FriendsViewModel.swift: the search generation counter and the three named guards.
  4. LIfeOS/Features/Social/ViewModel/ChatViewModel.swift: pending kept apart from messages.
  5. supabase/migrations/20260914090000_social_groups.sql: why every write is an RPC, and the row locks inside them.
  6. LifeOSKit/Sources/Integrations/SocialWellness.swift: the three formulas and every reason a score is nil.
  7. supabase/migrations/20260829120000_shared_stats.sql: why the figures are a separate table from profiles.
  8. LIfeOS/Features/Social/View/SocialLeaderboard.swift: the podium rule for ties.

Check yourself

  • Why are the shared figures not columns on profiles? The select policy on profiles is using (true) for every signed-in user, because search needs it, and row level security is row level. A column there would be world-readable. A table of its own gets a policy that can name friendship.
  • How does a slow search response lose to a faster newer one? The task is cancelled, and the response is applied only if the query it was issued for still equals the query on screen. A generation counter clears the spinner for the latest search alone.
  • Why can a poll never erase a message being sent? Provisional rows live in pending; refresh() only ever assigns messages; the screen renders the sum.
  • Why does accept send only one column? The database grants update on friendships to status alone. Any other key fails the whole request before RLS runs.
  • Where does the sender id in a message come from? The access token's sub claim, read without verification, because the server already verified it when it issued the token and verifies it again on the request.
  • What makes a group retry safe? A client-generated clientID reused on retry, and a unique (sender, client_id) on the server with on conflict do nothing returning the existing id.
  • Why is Recharge nil for a new WHOOP user? It needs seven earlier distinct days from the same provider within 28, none still calibrating, and today never counts toward its own baseline.

Chapter seventeen

17Profile and settings

A face in the corner of Today opens everything that used to be behind a gear: who you are, what your tracking adds up to, your friends, every connection with its own live state, the goals that decide a good day, and the account switcher. Settings is a page inside the profile, not a tab.

17.1Intent

Working backwards

Tap your photo on Today and the screen fills with it, fading into a gradient sampled from the picture itself. Under your name sit three figures that describe who you have been: day streak, days tracked, workouts. Then today's living numbers, then all-time totals, then three doors: Together, Connections, Settings. Edit the profile from a glass sheet that saves locally first and publishes after. Settings holds appearance, the five daily goals, the accounts signed in on this device, which engine the coach uses, whether it speaks, and a summary of every connection with a green dot for on and a hollow one for off.

Why a face instead of a gear?

A gear says "settings"; a face says "you", and everything that was behind the gear is about you. The button falls back to a person glyph rather than initials, because a single letter in a circle reads as an avatar that failed to load.

Why is the profile on the server now?

Because signing in on a second phone, or as a second account on this one, used to produce a profile with no name and no picture: both lived only on the device that typed them. The profiles row and the avatars bucket are the source of truth; the device keeps a per-account cache so the screen draws instantly and draws offline.

What does Settings do when Health access was denied?

It cannot know. HealthKit read authorisation is opaque by design, so the row says "No data yet. Check Almanac in Health > Sharing" rather than asserting a state it cannot verify.

Why can I edit the goals?

Because the dot grid is the app's central claim, and a claim you cannot calibrate is one you stop believing. Defaults are 8,000 steps, 7h sleep, 30 min exercise, 2,500 ml water, 3 of 4 required.

17.3Model

Three shapes of a profile

// LifeOSKit/Sources/Integrations/ProfileClient.swift
public struct RemoteProfile: Codable, Sendable, Equatable {
    public var firstName: String
    public var lastName: String
    public var country: String
    public var birthDate: Date?
    public var heightCM: Double?
    public var gender: String?        // nil is "prefer not to say"
    public var avatarPath: String?    // a path in the bucket, never a URL

    public var displayName: String { fullName.isEmpty ? "Someone" : fullName }

    public func payload(userID: String) -> [String: Any] {
        var row: [String: Any] = [ "user_id": userID, "display_name": displayName, ... ]
        row["birth_date"] = birthDate.map { SupabaseREST.day($0) } ?? NSNull()
        row["height_cm"] = heightCM ?? NSNull()
        row["gender"] = gender ?? NSNull()
        row["avatar_path"] = avatarPath ?? NSNull()
        return row
    }
}

RemoteProfile is the row as the server holds it. Two decisions are written into it. The avatar is stored as a path, {user_id}/avatar.jpg, never a URL, because a URL bakes in the project host and the signing scheme, both of which outlive their correctness. And cleared fields are sent as explicit nulls rather than omitted, because the save is an upsert of the whole row: an omitted key would leave the old value standing and make deleting a birthday impossible. displayName is never empty because the column is not nullable and a profile with no name is still a profile that friend search has to match.

LocalProfile, in ProfilePhotoStore.swift, is the per-account display cache, and ProfileStore.save(_ remote:) only ever writes it from what the server confirmed, so the two cannot drift. The profile used to live in auth.users.user_metadata with a copy in a single UserDefaults key. That payload rides inside the JWT on every authenticated request, which is the wrong place for anything that grows, and the copy was not keyed by account, so with two accounts on one device the second saw the first's name. 

// LifeOSKit/Sources/Integrations/ProfileClient.swift
public enum AvatarStamp: Sendable, Equatable {
    case missing           // no such object in the bucket
    case unknown           // the object exists, but the listing did not say when it changed
    case at(String)        // the object exists and last changed at this stamp
}

Three cases rather than an optional string, because "there is no object" and "the object is there but undated" want opposite answers. Collapsed into a single nil, the safe reading of nil is "do not download", and then a device with nothing cached downloads nothing, ever, and shows an empty circle for a profile that has a picture.

The goals draft and the stats

// LIfeOS/Features/Settings/Model/GoalsDraft.swift
struct GoalsDraft: Equatable {
    var steps: Int = 8000
    var sleepMinutes: Int = 420
    var exerciseMinutes: Int = 30
    var waterML: Double = 2500
    var requiredCount: Int = 3
}

// LIfeOS/Features/Settings/View/ProfileScreen.swift
struct ProfileStat: Identifiable, Equatable {
    let id: String
    let value: String
    let label: String
}

The draft is a separate type from UserGoals on purpose. Editing writes to the draft; committing validates it into the row. Binding steppers straight to the persisted model would write to the database on every increment and re-evaluate a month of history mid-drag. ProfileStat is a label and a pre-formatted string: the profile shows facts and never computes one.

AppConfig: what is public and why

AppConfig reads the bundle's Info.plist for the Supabase URL and anon key, the WHOOP, Fitbit and Plaid redirect URIs, the ElevenLabs key, and the function endpoints derived from the project URL. Everything here is public by design except the ElevenLabs key, which is gitignored but still extractable from a shipped .ipa and therefore never logged. Client secrets for WHOOP, Fitbit and Plaid are deliberately absent: they live only in Edge Function environments (Chapter 23). An unresolved build setting comes through as a literal $(…), so string(_:) treats that prefix as absent. The app answers to two URL schemes, almanac and the older lifeos, so the WHOOP redirect bridge can point at either without the app and the server having to ship together.

17.4ViewModel

SettingsViewModel

draft is the one mutable published property on this view model, and it is mutable because SwiftUI's @Bindable needs it to be. load() copies the goals row into it; save() writes the row back in one context.save(), which is what makes the dot grid re-evaluate. The rule is the user's, not hard-coded. SettingsScreen calls save() from onChange(of: model.draft), so each stepper commits once per change rather than once per dismissal.

Four connections, four shapes

Each provider has its own view model because each has a different relationship with credentials, and the differences are the point.

ProviderWhere the token livesSign-in surfaceWhat the view model owns
Apple HealthNowhere; it is a permissionThe system sheet, onceWhether it was asked, the sync cursor, the cycle switch, the foreground watch
WHOOPKeychain on the device, plus a server copy for restoreSafari, by UIApplication.openPKCE attempts, the manual desktop code, stalled sign-ins, sync with a staleness policy
FitbitA row on the server onlyASWebAuthenticationSession in-appPKCE attempts and a "connected" flag per account; the server is the authority
Bank accounts (Plaid)Access tokens on the server behind service-role RLS; item ids and cursors on the devicePlaid Link, sometimes via a bank's OAuth in SafariLink presentation, exchange, paged sync, reconnect state, disconnect with or without history

Health is deliberately the thinnest, because it has no OAuth, no tokens and no server, and the one thing it does have is a permission model that refuses to tell us anything. connect() asks once, records that it asked, decides the cycle-tracking default, syncs, and starts the watch. After that "Connect" becomes "Sync", because iOS shows the sheet exactly once and offering to connect again would be a button that visibly does nothing. The cycle-tracking switch is offered to everyone and defaulted from Health's own sex characteristic, not from the gender asked at signup: that field says how someone wants to be addressed, and using it here would get the answer wrong in both directions and strand everyone who chose "Prefer not to say". Turning the switch on asks for the extra permission there and then, so the prompt arrives with the tap that caused it.

WHOOP opens sign-in in Safari rather than an in-app web session because WHOOP's login sits behind a Cloudflare bot challenge that never clears inside ASWebAuthenticationSession. That decision creates two problems the view model then has to solve. Leaving for Safari looks identical whether or not the person comes back, so resolveStalledConnect() waits two seconds after the app becomes active and, if the card is still connecting with no token, returns it to disconnected. Two seconds is the whole subtlety: the redirect usually lands a moment after activation, so resolving immediately would cancel sign-ins about to succeed. And a challenge behind a VPN or Private Relay can hang forever, so beginManual() offers a desktop URL and a code field; the PKCE verifier never left this phone, so a transcribed code alone is not enough to impersonate it. Pending attempts are persisted, not held in memory, because iOS may terminate the app while Safari is up, and the callback is matched to the attempt whose state it carries because tapping Connect twice starts two valid authorisations.

Fitbit is thinner than WHOOP, and the missing half is the point. Fitbit rotates its refresh token on every use, so exactly one writer may hold it, and that writer is a row in the database. The view model hands a code to the fitbit-token function and asks fitbit-sync what the state is. A "connected" flag per account is remembered only so the card does not flash "Not connected" on every launch while the server is asked.

Plaid keeps LinkKit behind one seam. PlaidLinkPresenter is the only file that imports it, which is what lets the connection view model be tested against the PlaidClient alone. The presenter holds the live handler itself, because a bank using OAuth sends the person out to Safari and a handler released while they are away has nothing to hand the redirect back to. It also keeps the link token in the account's defaults, because the case that matters is the process not surviving: resume(from:) rebuilds a handler on the original token and calls resumeAfterTermination. The completion closure died with the old process, so PlaidConnectionViewModel.attach re-registers onResumedConnect every time. Sync runs the cursor loop up to twenty pages per pass and sets isFetchingHistory between connecting and the first transaction arriving, because Plaid fetches history asynchronously and an empty first sync must not render as "you spent nothing this month" (Chapter 11).

All four share three habits. A launch and a foreground arriving together coalesce into one sync through a held Task or an isSyncing flag. isConnected is false while connecting, so the summary dot never claims success while Safari is still open. And every failure is a sentence: "Whoop needs new permissions. Disconnect, then connect again" is a different problem from "Whoop sign-in expired", and collapsing them once sent people around the reconnect loop with no idea why it kept failing.

17.5View

The profile page

ProfileScreen is presented as a fullScreenCover from the avatar on Today. It owns a NavigationStack, the local profile and photo as state, the edit sheet, and a single destination enum for its four pushes: notifications, friends, connections, settings. Every push is a value, so the destination is a function of it. ProfileOverview is the presentation, shared with the DEBUG fixture, and is forced into the dark colour scheme with a hidden navigation bar because it is drawn over the photo. 

// LIfeOS/Features/Settings/View/ProfilePhotoBackdrop.swift
static func extract(from data: Data?) -> Self {
    guard let data, let image = UIImage(data: data) else { return fallback }
    let thumbnail = UIGraphicsImageRenderer(size: CGSize(width: 48, height: 48), format: format)
        .image { _ in image.draw(in: CGRect(x: 0, y: 0, width: 48, height: 48)) }
    guard let source = CIImage(image: thumbnail) else { return fallback }
    func average(_ y: CGFloat) -> Color {
        let bounds = CGRect(x: 0, y: y, width: 48, height: 16)
        let result = source.applyingFilter("CIAreaAverage",
            parameters: [kCIInputExtentKey: CIVector(cgRect: bounds)])
        ...
    }
    return Self(top: average(32), middle: average(16), bottom: average(0))
}

The gradient behind the profile is sampled from the photo: a 48 pixel thumbnail, three CIAreaAverage passes over its top, middle and bottom thirds, and the three colours become a diagonal gradient. It is recomputed only when the photo changes, through .task(id: photo). Over that sit a blurred copy of the whole photo at 35 percent, the portrait cropped 1.3 to 1 from the top and masked to fade out, and a dark wash that keeps white text readable. With no photo the backdrop is the fallback palette and a soft orange ellipse.

On a phone the portrait sits at the top and the page scrolls. At 760 points or wider the layout becomes a 340 point identity column beside a 540 point details column, the portrait becomes a rounded card, and the backdrop drops the portrait layer. Under the name are up to three parts of a subtitle: country, height, age. Then, in order, "Your rhythm" (three cumulative figures), "Today" (only the readings that exist), "Over time" (only totals above zero), and the three doors, all on clear Liquid Glass panels. An empty profile at accessibility sizes collapses every grid to one column.

The edit sheet

ProfileEditSheet is the same fields as signup, reachable at any time, because signup asks once and never again, which is fine for a name and wrong for a photo. It saves locally first and publishes after: the local copy is what the app displays, so writing it first means the change is visible immediately and survives a failed request. Dismissal, though, waits for the publish. The row is what friend search reads, so a save that only ever reached the device would leave someone invisible to everyone looking for them while their own screen said it worked. On failure the sheet stays open with the reason, Save becomes "Try again", and Cancel becomes "Close anyway", because the local copy is already written and trapping someone in a sheet they cannot satisfy is worse than letting them out informed. Removing a photo is a delete on the bucket rather than a null in the row; leaving the object behind would keep serving a face the person took down.

Settings and Connections

SettingsScreen is a page pushed from the profile with no inner stack and no Done: the back chevron is the way out, which is what makes it feel like a place rather than an overlay. Its cards, top to bottom: appearance (system, light, dark), the five goal steppers, the accounts signed in on this device with a radio to switch, the coach tier (automatic, cloud, on-device), the voice toggle and its three voices, "At a glance" with Notifications and Widgets & Watch, the connections summary, and Log out. Switching accounts does not sign anybody out: each account keeps its own store, cursors and connections, so moving between them is opening a different file rather than tearing one down (Chapter 4).

The connections summary used to be one row with a chain-link icon reading "Whoop, Health, banks" over WHOOP's status line, which said nothing about the other two. It now shows every source, one line each, with a green dot for on and a hollow one for off. Never red: not being connected is a choice someone is allowed to make, and an alarm dot next to WHOOP would nag every user who does not own one. While a sync runs the dot is replaced by a spinner, because the honest answer to "is it on" is "ask me in a second". ConnectionsSettingsScreen is the page it opens, one card per source with a chip whose colour is its meaning: orange asks for a tap, green reports one that already happened. The Fitbit card's "Sync" calls the forced refresh rather than reopening OAuth, and the Health card's "Sync" replaces "Connect" once the sheet has been shown.

Where the actions live

The calendar assistant, LIFO and Begin Activity are the app's three free-floating actions. They used to be laid flat on home and collapsed into a bottom-corner fan on every other tab, which put the control people reach for most in a different place depending on where they were and hid it behind a trigger on four of the five. They are now a [QuickAction] defined once in RootView, injected through the quickActions environment value, and drawn by .quickActionsToolbar() across the top of every tab as an ActionFan in its row arrangement: 34 point bare glyphs sized for a 44 point bar. The environment value is the mechanism because Notes and Life own their own NavigationStacks several levels below the root, and a toolbar has to be attached inside the stack it belongs to. The fan arrangement still exists in ActionFan, with its arc from 90 to 170 degrees and its 106 point radius chosen so three 52 point circles never overlap, but nothing in the app uses it today. The plus becomes a timer glyph labelled "Current activity" while a session is running.

17.6How it works

The avatar stamp, step by step

  1. AppShell's launch task restores the session and, if the person is signed in with a store open, calls ProfileSync.pull().
  2. The profiles row is loaded and mirrored into the per-account defaults. If the row says there is no picture, the local file is deleted, so a photo removed on one phone does not survive on another forever.
  3. The account's folder in the bucket is listed (one object, never the whole bucket) and the object's updated_at becomes an AvatarStamp.
  4. shouldDownloadAvatar decides: missing never downloads, unknown downloads only when there is no local copy, a dated stamp downloads when there is no copy or the stamp differs from the recorded one.
  5. After a download the stamp is recorded, and only when the listing gave one. Saving a photo clears the stamp first, because the stamp describes the bytes on disk; a photo taken on this device has no server stamp yet, and keeping the old one would make the next sync believe the copy it holds is the one already up there.

Every step re-checks that the signed-in account is still the one the pull started for, so an account switch mid-pull cannot write one person's face into another person's folder.

The photo maths

// LIfeOS/Components/Model/ProfilePhotoDownsizing.swift
static let side: CGFloat = 512
static let sizeLimit = 5_242_880          // the bucket's file_size_limit, kept in step by hand

static func jpeg(from image: UIImage) -> Data? {
    let ratio = min(side / image.size.width, side / image.size.height, 1)
    let size = CGSize(width: image.size.width * ratio, height: image.size.height * ratio)
    let format = UIGraphicsImageRendererFormat.default()
    format.scale = 1
    let resized = UIGraphicsImageRenderer(size: size, format: format).image { _ in
        image.draw(in: CGRect(origin: .zero, size: size))
    }
    var quality: CGFloat = 0.8
    var data = resized.jpegData(compressionQuality: quality)
    while let current = data, current.count > sizeLimit, quality > 0.3 {
        quality -= 0.1
        data = resized.jpegData(compressionQuality: quality)
    }
    return data
}

Scale 1 is the line that matters. The renderer otherwise draws at the device's scale, so a 512 point box becomes a 1536 pixel bitmap on a 3x phone: nine times the pixels asked for, which undoes most of the downsizing. The quality loop is a backstop against a pathological image, not the primary way the output is kept small. The limit is deliberately the bucket's real ceiling rather than something tighter, because a client-side constant below the server's would start rejecting uploads from installs running older code with nothing on screen to explain it.

The stats under the name

RootView computes the three panels from the store at the moment the profile opens. "Your rhythm" is the streak from Today's snapshot plus two fetchCount calls, which never materialise a row. "Today" lists only the readings that exist: a missing one is left out rather than dashed, so the panel always reads as facts, and money is deliberately absent because a sample-data default would put invented dollars on a person's face. "Over time" sums steps and sleep from one fetch of the daily rows, a few hundred small objects at most, and counts habit ticks, calendar events and scored sectors with fetchCount; zero-valued figures are left out.

17.7Performance and cost

  • Two small requests per launch, and the third only when needed. The profile pull is a row and a one-object listing; the picture downloads only on a changed stamp.
  • Reads are signed-in-only, not signed-URL-per-face. The bucket is private, but any signed-in user may read any avatar, which is what keeps a friend list from needing a signed URL per face on every refresh (Chapter 16).
  • Uploads replace in place. x-upsert: true rather than a delete and an insert, so a person changing their picture is never briefly without one.
  • The gradient is three 48-pixel averages, recomputed only when the photo changes. The CIContext is shared and built with intermediate caching off.
  • Goals commit once per change, not once per frame. The draft absorbs the stepper; the row is written on onChange.
  • Syncs coalesce. Every connection view model folds a launch and a foreground into one pass, and WHOOP, Fitbit and Plaid consult SyncStalenessPolicy before spending a request.
  • Provider secrets never reach the device. Fitbit tokens never even pass through it; Plaid access tokens sit behind service-role-only RLS.
  • Per-account defaults, per-account files. Cursors, "was Health asked", the cycle switch, the avatar and the profile cache all live in the account's own suite or directory, so an account switch is a lookup change, not a purge.

17.8Edge cases and tests

ConditionBehaviour
Goal set out of rangeUnreachable: the steppers bound each value (sleep 240 to 660 in 15s, steps 1,000 to 30,000 in 500s, exercise 5 to 180, water 500 to 6,000 in 250s, required 1 to 4)
Health deniedUndetectable. The row reads "No data yet" and points at Health > Sharing; "Connect" becomes "Sync"
Health on an iPad.unavailable; the row says so and its button is disabled
WHOOP sign-in abandoned in SafariCard returns to disconnected two seconds after the app becomes active, unless a manual code is pending
WHOOP code expired or reused"Code expired or already used. Get a fresh one" (a 400), distinct from "Server not configured" (a 500)
WHOOP token lacks a scope"Whoop needs new permissions. Disconnect, then connect again"; not "expired"
WHOOP linked on another deviceRestored from the server copy on the first syncIfStale; a 404 means never linked
Fitbit refresh token refused.needsReauth; the chip reads "Reconnect", an action rather than an error
Fitbit sign-in cancelledNot a failure: the card reads as it did before
Bank OAuth outlives the processLink resumed on relaunch from the stored token; the completion is re-registered on attach
Bank already connected"That bank is already connected"
Bank login invalidated.needsReconnect(name); the summary dot is hollow because a stale login is not working
Disconnect a bankHistory kept unless asked; revoking a credential is not a request to erase the past
Profile publish failsLocal copy saved; sheet stays open with the reason and offers Try again or Close anyway
Offline when editing the profileSame, with a sentence that says the profile is saved on this device but not published yet
Photo removed on another deviceThe next launch's pull deletes the local copy
Bucket listing failsRead as .unknown: a device with a copy keeps it, a device without one downloads
Account switched mid-pullEvery write step re-checks the signed-in id and bails

Tests

  • RemoteProfileTests: a profile survives the round trip, a birthday comes back on the same calendar day, cleared fields are sent as nulls, the display name is never empty, the avatar path is the account's own folder.
  • AvatarTransferTests (nine tests): the authenticated download route with a bearer token, a listing with and without the object, unknown versus missing, and every branch of shouldDownloadAvatar including the one that gets forgotten: an unknown stamp with nothing cached still downloads.
  • AccountStoreTests and UserScopeTests: two accounts get different store files, an id cannot climb out of the accounts directory, rows do not cross between accounts, removing an account leaves its store on disk.
  • PlaidClientTests, PlaidItemStoreTests, PlaidSyncTests: the four functions, the per-item cursor, and the paged sync (Chapter 11).
  • FitbitOAuthTests, FitbitSyncTests, WhoopTokenTests, WhoopArbitrationTests: the PKCE URLs, the state check, the sync outcomes.
  • SyncStalenessPolicyTests: the rule every automatic sync consults.

The screens are verified by build and by capture: the profile QA of 14 September 2026 checked the phone and iPad layouts, the glass editor, and the empty profile at accessibility text size, using a generated teal illustration to exercise the photo-colour path. Remote saving and photo library selection were not run against a live account in that pass.

17.9Study notes

Read in this order

  1. LifeOSKit/Sources/Integrations/ProfileClient.swift: AvatarStamp and shouldDownloadAvatar.
  2. Features/Onboarding/Model/ProfilePhotoStore.swift: ProfileSync.pull(), then the stamp accessors.
  3. Features/Settings/View/ProfileEditSheet.swift: save().
  4. Features/Settings/ViewModel/HealthConnectionViewModel.swift: connect, decideCycleDefault, startWatching.
  5. Features/Settings/ViewModel/WhoopConnectionViewModel.swift: resolveStalledConnect and finish(callbackURL:).
  6. Features/Settings/View/PlaidLinkPresenter.swift: resume(from:).
  7. App/RootView.swift: quickActions, profileStats, profileAllTime.
  8. LifeOSKit/Sources/DesignSystem/ActionFan.swift: why the row and the fan are one component.

Check yourself

  • Why does AvatarStamp have three cases and not two? "Missing" must never download and "unknown" must download when nothing is cached; one nil cannot say both.
  • Why is the avatar stored as a path and not a URL? A URL bakes in the host and the signing scheme; both can change while the object stays where it is.
  • Why does ProfileEditSheet save locally first but wait for the publish before dismissing? Local first makes the change visible and durable; waiting makes a publish failure visible, because an unpublished profile is one nobody can find.
  • Why does the WHOOP stall check wait two seconds? The redirect usually lands just after the app activates; resolving at once would cancel sign-ins about to succeed.
  • Why is the cycle-tracking default read from Health rather than from the gender field? The gender field is a form of address, its own comment says so, and using it would be wrong both ways and strand the default answer.
  • Why is sizeLimit exactly the bucket's ceiling? A tighter client constant would reject uploads from older installs one release early, silently.

Chapter eighteen

18Widgets, Live Activities and notifications

Three surfaces outside the app: a Home and Lock Screen widget with a Watch complication behind it, a Live Activity and Dynamic Island for a running session, and a push channel that lets LIFO speak first. All three share one rule: the surface is handed a small, credential-free value and never a store, and every value is owned by exactly one account.

18.1Intent

Working backwards

Put "Your day" on the Home Screen and it shows steps against the goal, sleep and movement, refreshed after Almanac syncs and blanked after six hours or at midnight, whichever comes first. Add the circular complication to a watch face and the step gauge is there. Begin an activity and the Lock Screen carries a blue card with the timer, heart rate zone, estimated effort, calories and battery; the Dynamic Island shows the heart rate and the timer, and the zone number when minimal. Once a day, at eight in the morning your time, LIFO may send one sentence about your sleep, your steps or a streak; tap it and the conversation opens on that sentence. A notification inbox in the profile keeps the last hundred.

What does a widget actually get?

A SurfaceSnapshot: an owner id, when it was generated, when it expires, and four numbers. No token, no store, no rows. It is written as one encoded value into the App Group, so a reader can never join fields from two accounts.

Why does it expire?

Because a widget that shows yesterday's steps as today's is worse than one that says "Open Almanac to sync". Six hours is long enough to be useful between launches and short enough that a stale number does not survive a night. The timeline carries an explicit expiry entry so the blanking happens even when WidgetKit delays a refresh.

Why is the Live Activity throttled?

The heart-rate sensor streams every second and ActivityKit has an update budget. The lock screen does not need a new frame per beat; it needs one when something meaningful changed. A pure LiveActivityThrottle decides, and the timer ticks itself through Text(timerInterval:) without any update at all.

Who decides whether to send a nudge?

The server, as a pure function with tests. The device's whole job is to be reachable, to say which time zone eight in the morning is in, and to open on what arrived. The numbers are not in the payload: a phone that has been offline for days re-evaluates locally rather than opening on figures two days stale.

AppSurfaces is its own package target with no dependencies because three processes import it: the app, the widget extension and the watch app. It holds value types and pure functions only, so nothing about a store, a keychain or a network client can leak into an extension that must stay small and must launch cold in a few milliseconds.

18.3Model

The snapshot the widget reads

// LifeOSKit/Sources/AppSurfaces/SurfaceSnapshot.swift
public struct SurfaceSnapshot: Codable, Equatable, Sendable {
    public static let appGroup = "group.com.shivvyas.lifeos"
    public static let storageKey = "surface.snapshot.v1"
    public var ownerID: String?
    public var generatedAt: Date
    public var expiresAt: Date
    public var measuredAt: Date?
    public var steps: Int?
    public var stepGoal: Int
    public var sleepMinutes: Int?
    public var exerciseMinutes: Int?

    public init(ownerID: String? = nil, generatedAt: Date = .now, measuredAt: Date? = nil,
                steps: Int? = nil, stepGoal: Int = 8000, sleepMinutes: Int? = nil,
                exerciseMinutes: Int? = nil, calendar: Calendar = .current) {
        ...
        let midnight = calendar.date(byAdding: .day, value: 1, to: calendar.startOfDay(for: generatedAt))!
        expiresAt = min(midnight, generatedAt.addingTimeInterval(6 * 3600))
        self.steps = steps.flatMap { $0 >= 0 ? $0 : nil }
        self.stepGoal = max(1, stepGoal)
        ...
    }

    public func isAvailable(at date: Date = .now) -> Bool {
        ownerID != nil && date >= generatedAt.addingTimeInterval(-60) && date < expiresAt
    }
    public func supersedes(_ previous: Self?) -> Bool {
        previous.map { generatedAt > $0.generatedAt } ?? true
    }
}

The initialiser is where the rules live. A negative reading becomes nil rather than a lie, a goal of zero becomes one so progress can never divide by nothing, and the expiry is the earlier of midnight and six hours. A snapshot with no owner is a tombstone: it is what sign-out writes, and it is never available. supersedes exists because WatchConnectivity can deliver a queued older application context after a newer reply, and the watch must not replace a fresh value with a stale one. 

// LifeOSKit/Sources/AppSurfaces/SurfaceSnapshot.swift
public enum SurfaceRoute: String, CaseIterable, Sendable {
    case today, health, activity, notifications
    public var url: URL { URL(string: "almanac://\(rawValue)")! }
    public init?(url: URL) {
        guard url.scheme == "almanac", url.user == nil, url.password == nil,
              url.port == nil, url.path.isEmpty, url.query == nil, url.fragment == nil,
              let host = url.host, let route = Self(rawValue: host) else { return nil }
        self = route
    }
}

Routes are the four places a widget tap can land. The parser accepts exactly almanac://host and nothing else: no path, no query, no credentials, no port. That is deliberate, because the same scheme carries OAuth callbacks, and a widget URL must never be mistaken for one.

The readout the Live Activity renders

// LifeOSKit/Sources/AppSurfaces/LiveSessionReadout.swift
public struct LiveSessionReadout: Codable, Hashable, Sendable {
    public var elapsed: TimeInterval
    public var runningSince: Date?       // nil while paused
    public var heartRate: Int?
    public var zone: Int?
    public var effort: Double?           // WHOOP's 0 to 21 scale, rounded to a tenth
    public var calories: Int?
    public var distanceMeters: Int?
    public var batteryPercent: Int?
    public var capacitySource: String?   // "whoop" or "health"
    public var ceilingMaxZone: Int?
    public var ceilingTarget: ClosedRange<Double>?
    public var reps: Int?
    public var setIndex: Int?
    public var push: PushState

    public var timerAnchor: Date? { runningSince?.addingTimeInterval(-elapsed) }
    public var isPaused: Bool { runningSince == nil }
}

This is the one value every live surface renders: the in-app HUD, the lock screen and the Dynamic Island. Every reading is optional because a missing sensor is not a zero. WorkoutActivityAttributes.ContentState is this very type, so the app and the extension cannot disagree about its shape. timerAnchor is the trick that makes the timer free: Text(timerInterval: anchor...distantFuture) lets the system tick the clock itself, so an activity update is needed only when a reading changes, never per second. PushState carries its own headline, "Easy going", "On track", "Near your limit", "Over your target", so the words never drift between surfaces. 

// LifeOSKit/Sources/AppSurfaces/LiveSessionReadout.swift
public enum LiveActivityThrottle {
    public static let heartRateStep = 3
    public static let floor: TimeInterval = 10
    public static let readingInterval: TimeInterval = 3

    public static func shouldPublish(previous: LiveSessionReadout?, next: LiveSessionReadout,
                                     lastPublishedAt: Date?, now: Date) -> Bool {
        guard let previous, let lastPublishedAt else { return true }
        if previous == next { return false }
        if previous.isPaused != next.isPaused { return true }
        if previous.push != next.push { return true }
        if previous.reps != next.reps { return true }
        switch (previous.heartRate, next.heartRate) {
        case let (old?, new?) where abs(old - new) >= heartRateStep:
            return now.timeIntervalSince(lastPublishedAt) >= readingInterval
        case (nil, .some), (.some, nil):
            return now.timeIntervalSince(lastPublishedAt) >= readingInterval
        default: break
        }
        return now.timeIntervalSince(lastPublishedAt) >= floor
    }
}

Read it as a ranking of what deserves a frame. A pause, a push-state change or a rep always publishes at once. A heart rate that moved three beats or more, or appeared or vanished, publishes if three seconds have passed. Anything smaller waits ten. An identical readout never publishes. Because it is a pure function it is pinned by tests instead of thumbs on a device.

The inbox entry and the nudge

// LifeOSKit/Sources/AppSurfaces/InboxEntry.swift
public struct InboxEntry: Codable, Equatable, Identifiable, Sendable {
    public let id: String                 // "\(day)|\(trigger)"
    public let ownerID: String
    public let text: String
    public let trigger: String
    public let day: String
    public let receivedAt: Date
    public var isRead: Bool

    public static func inserting(_ entry: Self, into entries: [Self], ownerID: String) -> [Self] {
        guard entry.ownerID == ownerID else { return entries.filter { $0.ownerID == ownerID } }
        var result = entries.filter { $0.ownerID == ownerID }
        if !result.contains(where: { $0.id == entry.id }) { result.append(entry) }
        return Array(result.sorted { $0.receivedAt > $1.receivedAt }.prefix(100))
    }
}

The id is the day plus the trigger, which is exactly the uniqueness the server enforces in nudge_log, so a notification delivered twice, once as a banner and once as a tap-through, is one row. inserting filters to the owner, deduplicates, keeps existing read state, and caps at a hundred. NudgePayload, in Integrations, is the same three fields parsed out of a notification's userInfo, and it returns nil rather than throwing for a notification that is not ours: something to ignore, not something to report.

18.4ViewModel

SurfaceCoordinator: one writer for the App Group

// LIfeOS/App/Surfaces/SurfaceCoordinator.swift
func publish() {
    guard let ownerID, let context, sharingEnabled else { return }
    let store = MetricsStore(context: context)
    let now = Date.now
    let row = try? store.metrics(from: now, to: now).first
    let goals = try? context.fetch(FetchDescriptor<UserGoals>()).first
    let next = SurfaceSnapshot(ownerID: ownerID, measuredAt: row?.updatedAt,
        steps: row?.steps, stepGoal: goals?.stepsGoal ?? 8000,
        sleepMinutes: row?.sleepMinutes, exerciseMinutes: row?.exerciseMinutes)
    // Coalesce saves unrelated to health. Still renew the Watch lease hourly.
    if let previous = snapshot, previous.ownerID == next.ownerID,
       previous.steps == next.steps, previous.sleepMinutes == next.sleepMinutes,
       previous.exerciseMinutes == next.exerciseMinutes, previous.stepGoal == next.stepGoal,
       previous.measuredAt == next.measuredAt,
       next.generatedAt.timeIntervalSince(previous.generatedAt) < 3600 { return }
    write(next)
}

publish() is called from RootView.reloadAll(), which means on every save in the app. Most saves are notes, money or a habit tick, and none of those change the four numbers, so the coalescing guard is what stops a widget reload and a watch transfer per keystroke. The hour limit is the exception: even with nothing changed, the snapshot is rewritten hourly so its expiry keeps moving and the watch's copy stays fresh. write stores the value, asks WidgetKit to reload every timeline, and sends the same bytes to the watch as an application context (queued, survives the watch being asleep) and, if it is reachable, as a message.

adopt(ownerID:context:) is called by AccountSession whenever a store is opened. If the snapshot on disk belongs to a different owner, or there is no owner, or sharing is off, a tombstone is written before anything else, so the next account starts with missing readings and never with the previous account's values. sharingEnabled is the toggle on the Widgets & Watch page; turning it off writes the tombstone at once.

WorkoutLiveActivityController

// LIfeOS/App/Surfaces/WorkoutLiveActivityController.swift
func sync(_ readout: LiveSessionReadout, timer: ActivitySessionState, icon: String) {
    guard timer.phase != .finished else { end(); return }
    if current == nil {
        current = Activity<WorkoutActivityAttributes>.activities.first { $0.attributes.sessionID == timer.id }
    }
    let now = Date.now
    guard current == nil || LiveActivityThrottle.shouldPublish(previous: lastState, next: readout,
                                                               lastPublishedAt: lastPublishedAt, now: now) else { return }
    lastState = readout; lastPublishedAt = now
    let content = ActivityContent(state: readout, staleDate: now.addingTimeInterval(8 * 3600))
    if let current {
        let preceding = updates
        updates = Task { await preceding?.value; await current.update(content) }
    } else if ActivityAuthorizationInfo().areActivitiesEnabled {
        current = try? Activity.request(attributes: WorkoutActivityAttributes(sessionID: timer.id,
            name: timer.activity, icon: icon), content: content, pushType: nil)
    }
}

The recorder calls sync on every state change and every reading; the controller decides whether that becomes an ActivityKit call. Three details carry weight. The activity is keyed on the session id, so a relaunch, or a session the watch started whose card was requested before the phone's timer existed, adopts the activity already on screen rather than orphaning it. Updates are chained through a single Task so they land in order. And the stale date is eight hours out, which means a phone that dies mid-run leaves a card that the system will eventually grey rather than one that claims a heart rate forever. endAll() is called on every account change and sign-out so no session card outlives its owner.

PushService: registration and the inbox in one object

One object rather than two because the two halves share the state that matters: the device token. It arrives asynchronously from the system long after the sign-in that asked for it, and it is needed again at sign-out to delete the row. The service keeps the token in UserDefaults.standard (it belongs to the phone), and everything else per account.

  • Asks late, on purpose. requestAuthorization() is called from the inbox screen's button, never at launch. A permission prompt on first run, before the app has shown anyone anything worth being interrupted about, is the fastest way to a permanent no. A denied status short-circuits: registering anyway would silently succeed and produce a token that can never deliver anything.
  • Registers on every foreground. syncRegistration() upserts the token, the account id and the current time zone. The zone is what the send hour is read in, so somebody who has flown somewhere would otherwise keep being nudged at eight in the morning where they used to live. The row is keyed on the token, so a second account on the same device replaces the first account's row in one upsert.
  • Deregisters before the session goes. AppShell's sign-out captures the outgoing access token by value and deletes the row with it, because the delete needs the token of the account whose row it is, and the keychain is cleared a line later. Left behind, that row would push one person's sleep onto a phone showing somebody else's name.
  • Attaches per account. attach(ownerID:) re-reads the inbox from that account's defaults suite and clears any pending route if the owner changed. receive refuses an entry whose owner is not the attached account, and refuses an id the person has already cleared, so a delayed duplicate cannot resurrect a dismissed check-in.
  • Reads back what the system already delivered. refreshInbox() walks deliveredNotifications(), so a notification that arrived while the app was dead, and was never tapped, still lands in the inbox on the next open.

18.5View

The widget, in every family

HealthTimeline produces two entries: the snapshot now, and, if it has not already expired, a nil entry at its expiry. The policy asks for a refresh after thirty minutes. The view switches on the family. The inline accessory is a label of steps and sleep. The circular accessory is a Gauge of step progress. The rectangular accessory is the wordmark, the two figures and "Updated 7:41". The small home widget is the step numeral at 34 points against the goal with a progress bar; medium adds sleep and a movement line; large and extra large add a movement tile and a "Begin activity" link that deep-links to almanac://activity. Every figure is privacySensitive(), so a locked phone redacts it. The empty state is one sentence per family and never a zero. BeginActivityWidget is a second, accessory-only widget whose whole job is the deep link. The watch bundle ships the same HealthWidget with only the accessory families, and the watch canvas is plain black.

The Live Activity

Widget extensions cannot render materials, so the "glass" tiles on the lock screen card are translucent white at 18 percent over the live gradient with a half-point hairline. The card is the activity's icon and name, the push headline in the push tint, the timer at title size, then four tiles: heart rate with the zone as eyebrow, effort with "of 18" as unit once there is a reading, calories or, in a strength session, the set and reps, and battery with a tiny ring. The Dynamic Island's expanded view puts the name leading, the timer trailing, and four readings across the bottom with an "Open activity" link. Compact shows a heart and the beats per minute leading and either the timer or the reps trailing. Minimal is the zone number in a circle of the push tint, or a pause glyph. keylineTint follows the push state, so the island's outline goes green, amber or red with the person's effort. Every text field is privacySensitive().

The inbox and the settings page

NotificationInboxScreen is reached from the bell on the profile and from Settings. It shows the permission card first ("Enable notifications" when never asked, "Notification settings" otherwise), then either "You're all caught up" or the unread count, a "Read all" button, one panel per entry, and "Clear read notifications". Tapping an entry marks it read and opens a full-screen LifoCoachScreen seeded with the sentence, so the notification is an opening line rather than a reminder (Chapter 14). The screen refreshes from delivered notifications on appear and on every return to the foreground. SurfaceSettingsScreen is the Widgets & Watch page: the sharing toggle and four short guides for adding the widgets, the complication and the activity timer.

18.6How it works

The widget path

  1. A save anywhere fires ModelContext.didSave; RootView.reloadAll() calls SurfaceCoordinator.shared.publish() first.
  2. publish() reads today's row and the goals, builds a snapshot, and returns early unless one of the four numbers, the goal, or the measured time changed, or an hour has passed.
  3. write() encodes the snapshot into the App Group defaults under one key, reloads every WidgetKit timeline, and sends the bytes to the watch.
  4. The widget's timeline provider decodes it on the next reload, renders it if isAvailable, and schedules its own blank entry at expiresAt.
  5. The watch app decodes the context or message, keeps it only if it supersedes the copy it holds, writes it to its own App Group and reloads its complication. Its dashboard redraws on a sixty-second TimelineView, so the expiry takes effect without a message.

The Live Activity path

  1. The recorder rebuilds its readout on every state change (persist()) and every sensor reading (persistReading(at:)), then calls syncLiveActivity(). The draft is written at most every ten seconds; the readout is refreshed every time.
  2. The controller either finds the activity for this session id, or asks LiveActivityThrottle whether the change deserves an update, or requests a new activity if the person has them enabled.
  3. On finish, discard, account change or sign-out the activity is ended immediately. endStrayLiveActivities() removes any card that belongs to a different session id, because only one activity belongs on screen.

The nudge path

  1. Once an hour, pg_cron calls lifo-nudge. The job selects the rows in device_tokens whose local hour is eight, evaluates the triggers over the account's rows, claims the day in nudge_log, phrases one sentence, and sends it through APNs with a collapse id so a phone that was off for three days gets today's nudge rather than three, and a twelve-hour expiry so a morning observation never turns up stale (Chapter 20).
  2. PushDelegate.willPresent hands the notification to PushService.receive. A nudge that arrives while the app is open is still shown as a banner, because suppressing it would drop the message entirely; nothing else surfaces it.
  3. PushDelegate.didReceive is the tap. The entry is marked read and pending is set to the payload.
  4. RootView watches pending and, on the launch task and every foreground, checks it directly too, because a notification tapped from a cold launch lands before the view exists and onChange never fires for it. openNudge clears it, seeds the coach with the sentence, and presents LIFO, deferring behind any open profile or inbox cover.

18.7Performance and cost

  • A widget launch reads one defaults key. No store is opened in the extension; AppSurfaces has no dependencies, so the extension links almost nothing.
  • Publishes are coalesced. Saves unrelated to health cost no widget reload and no watch transfer; only a changed number or the hourly lease renewal does.
  • Timelines refresh themselves. Two entries and a thirty-minute policy; the blanking at expiry costs no process wake at all.
  • The timer is free. Text(timerInterval:) ticks in the widget process; an ActivityKit update is spent only on a meaningful change, and the throttle's floor of ten seconds keeps a jittery sensor from burning the budget.
  • The watch gets bytes, not rows. An application context is a few hundred bytes and is delivered whenever the watch next wakes.
  • APNs costs nothing per send, and the job sends at most once a day per person. The unique key on nudge_log is claimed before any model call, so an overlapping cron run cannot double-spend the phrasing.
  • Silence is the common path. Most hourly runs evaluate triggers and send nothing, which costs a query and no inference.
  • Dead tokens are pruned. An "unregistered" answer from Apple deletes the row, so the job does not push at a wiped phone forever.
  • The inbox is capped at a hundred, and cleared ids at two hundred.
