Only then does it ask the model to phrase, with a prompt of roughly 300 tokens carrying the trigger's figures and an instruction to use only those. Every fired trigger carries a fallback sentence, so an OpenAI outage delivers the observation plainly rather than swallowing it. A refusal is the one failure that sends nothing, the same distinction EscalationPolicy draws on the device between a transient fault and a safety decision. The phrasing spend debits the nudge kind against its own cap of 4,000 tokens, a runaway guard more than a budget.

A forced send exists for proving delivery: {"test_user_id": ...} bypasses the triggers, the cooldown and the send hour, writes no log row and spends no tokens, and reports how many tokens were found and how many sends succeeded. Silence being the design, there was otherwise no way to know the APNs half was wired without waiting days for a real trigger. 

-- supabase/functions/lifo-nudge/schedule.sql (NOT a migration, run once per project)
select cron.schedule('lifo-nudge-hourly', '0 * * * *', $$
  select net.http_post(
    url := (select decrypted_secret from vault.decrypted_secrets where name = 'lifo_project_url')
           || '/functions/v1/lifo-nudge',
    headers := jsonb_build_object('Content-Type', 'application/json',
      'Authorization', 'Bearer ' ||
        (select decrypted_secret from vault.decrypted_secrets where name = 'lifo_nudge_key')),
    body := '{}'::jsonb, timeout_milliseconds := 55000);
$$);

The schedule is deliberately not a migration. It needs the project's own function URL, which differs per environment, and the service-role key, which must never be committed; both are read from Vault. Hourly rather than daily because the send hour is local and a single daily run would serve one time zone.

20.5Tests

Two kinds. The Deno tests run with deno test in supabase/functions/_shared/ and touch no network: 100 tests across seven files.

FileTestsPins
lifo_test.ts44Task config, the guardrail's presence on every task, schema validation, refusal handling, the chat body's message order, role filtering, the three bounds, tool-call normalisation, tuning and its removal, streaming gating, SSE reassembly across split reads
nudge_test.ts25Day arithmetic across month and year ends, local hour and day in the user's zone, the quiet window, cooldown, each trigger's firing and non-firing cases, trigger order, fallback sentences
fitbit_test.ts10Failure kinds, quota header, token form, the scope list holds nothing unread, each collection's path
apns_test.ts9JWT header and claims, base64url, PEM tolerance, payload carries no numbers, collapse and expiry headers, dead-token detection from both answers, provider token reuse
otp_twilio_test.ts7Twilio code classification and that every kind has a status
plaid_test.ts4The three failure kinds and a non-JSON body
otp_session_test.ts1A returning user's phone is found in GoTrue's stored format

The pgTAP files in supabase/tests/ run inside a transaction that is rolled back, so the disposable users and groups they insert never persist. social_groups.test.sql switches request.jwt.claim.sub between an owner, a friend and an outsider and checks the rules from each seat: an invitee sees the group but not the roster, cannot send chat or read the leaderboard, cannot forge membership with a direct update (error 42501), a retried send does not duplicate, an outsider sees nothing. group_wellness.test.sql checks that activity sharing does not grant health-score consent and that no score is stored before the second opt-in. These are the tests that catch an RLS mistake, which otherwise looks like an empty screen.

20.6Email templates

magic_link.html and confirmation.html are the same design: a card on the app's canvas colour with an accent band across the head, the dot grid drawn with table cells so it survives image blocking, and the six-digit {{ .Token }} in a 42-point monospaced span with 12 pixels of letter spacing. Tables and inline styles throughout, because email clients strip style blocks, ignore flexbox, and Outlook renders through Word. No images anywhere: nothing to host or have go missing in a year. The subject lines are set in config.toml, and supabase config push is what sends the templates to the hosted project.

20.7The static site

web/ is a two-file site deployed on Vercel at almanac.shivvyas.com. Its only job is to make Plaid's OAuth redirect land back inside the app. 

// web/.well-known/apple-app-site-association
{ "applinks": { "details": [ {
    "appIDs": ["Z42YU5W6WY.com.shivvyas.lifeos"],
    "components": [ { "/": "/plaid-oauth*" } ]
} ] } }

Banks that use OAuth hand the browser to the bank, and the bank redirects to a URI Plaid was told about in advance. On iOS that must be a universal link, because a custom scheme cannot be registered with Plaid and would not survive the hop through Safari. The association file claims the one path, vercel.json forces its content type to application/json (without which iOS ignores the file and every OAuth connection silently falls back to Safari), and plaid-oauth.html is the fallback page a person sees only when the link does not resolve. That page must not look like an error and must never claim the connection failed, because by then Plaid has usually already succeeded; it offers an almanac://plaid-oauth button back into the app. The README lists the four steps the repository cannot do: DNS, the Plaid dashboard's allowed redirect URIs, the PLAID_REDIRECT_URI secret, and the Associated Domains capability on the App ID.

20.8Study notes

Read in this order

  1. supabase/functions/_shared/supabase.ts, the door every function uses.
  2. supabase/migrations/20260811164841_initial_schema.sql for the policy shape, then 20260914090000_social_groups.sql for the definer-function shape.
  3. _shared/lifo.ts top to bottom, then lifo-agent/index.ts.
  4. _shared/nudge.ts, then lifo-nudge/index.ts, then schedule.sql.
  5. _shared/otp_guard.ts and otp_twilio.ts together.
  6. plaid-exchange/index.ts for the cleanup pattern.
  7. supabase/tests/social_groups.test.sql, to see RLS tested from three seats.

Check yourself

  • Why must resolveUser run before serviceClient in every function? The service role bypasses RLS. A user id taken from the request body would let any signed-in person read anyone's bank credential.
  • Which tables have RLS enabled with zero policies, and what does that mean? otp_events, plaid_items, lifo_usage, fitbit_connections, nudge_log, whoop_connections. Nobody but the service role can read or write them, including the row's own owner.
  • Why does the social groups migration grant only select to clients? Every write has a rule (friends only, 50 max, owner succession, idempotent sends) that a row policy cannot express, so writes go through definer functions that raise.
  • Why is the guardrail prompt on the server and not in the app? A client cannot strip what it never carries, and a client system message is refused so it cannot displace it.
  • What does the streamed path do that makes it not a free path through the cap? It asks for include_usage and debits in flush, which runs even when the client abandons the stream.
  • Why is schedule.sql not a migration? It needs the per-environment function URL and the service-role key, both read from Vault at run time.
  • What breaks if lifo-agent is deployed before the proactive_nudges migration? Its three-argument lifo_debit call fails until the migration creates that signature; deploy order is migration first, then both functions.

Chapter twenty-one

21Data reference

Every type a screen reads through, as it exists in LifeOSKit/Sources/Persistence today: twenty SwiftData models, the value types beside them, and the stores that are the only way anything writes. The package depends on nothing, builds for macOS, and is where the app's most important rule lives.

21.1Four rules every model obeys

The models below look different but they were written to the same four rules. Learn the rules and most of the reference reads itself.

  1. Every metric is optional. A missing value and a zero must never be the same thing. Zero steps means you did not move; nil steps means the watch was on the charger. In a health app a false zero is worse than a blank, because it is a wrong number presented with confidence. The optional travels unchanged from the column through the snapshot to the tile, which renders the dash itself.
  2. A field added to an existing model is optional or defaulted. SwiftData will not migrate a store in place when a mandatory attribute has no default, and it does not fail loudly: the container never opens, the shell has no account to show, and the app sits on its spinner. Section 21.13 tells the story of the day this happened.
  3. Enums are stored as raw strings with typed accessors. kindRaw, statusRaw, bucketRaw, sectorRaw. A new case is a code change rather than a migration, and an unknown value read back from an older store falls to a sensible default instead of failing the row.
  4. Views never hold a @Model. Every store hands out a detached value type: PlanItemSnapshot, CalendarEventSnapshot, NoteCardSnapshot, ChatMessageSnapshot. A managed object handed to a card is a live handle on the database and a reason every view needs a container to preview. The snapshot costs one map per fetch and buys back both testability and the compile-time guarantee that nothing above the store mutates rows.
Why raw JSON bags appear so oftenFive models keep an array or dictionary as encoded Data rather than as a relationship: DailyMetrics.extrasData, WorkoutRecord.setsData, NoteDocument.blocksData, ChatMessage.eventIDsData and SectorScore.evidenceData. The reasoning is the same each time: the value is only ever read and written as a whole, no query asks for one element of it, and a relationship would cost one migration hazard per field in exchange for nothing. Where a query is needed, the JSON is mirrored out into derived rows instead, which is exactly what NoteTask and NoteLink are.

21.2DailyMetrics

One row per calendar day, the join key for the entire application. #Unique([\.date]) makes a second row for the same day impossible, and date is always Calendar.startOfDay, never a timestamp.

PropertyTypeWritten byNotes
dateDateMetricsStoreUnique. Start of day.
weightKgDouble?Health, Quick logRenpho writes Health; Health writes here
stepsInt?Health, FitbitDe-duplicated by HealthKit across watch and phone
activeEnergyKcalDouble?Health, Fitbit
exerciseMinutesInt?Health, Fitbit
sleepMinutesInt?Health, Whoop, FitbitAttributed to the morning you woke
waterMLDouble?Quick logNo automatic source exists
restingHRDouble?Health, Whoop, Fitbit
hrvMsDouble?Health, Whoop, FitbitSDNN from Health, RMSSD from Whoop; the arbiter decides
whoopRecoveryPct, whoopDayStrain, whoopSleepPerformancePctDouble?WhoopExist nowhere else
spo2Percentage, skinTempCelsius, respiratoryRateDouble?Whoop, HealthThe scored daily surface Whoop reports
whoopCalories, whoopAverageHR, whoopMaxHRDouble?WhoopFrom the cycle record
whoopSleepConsistencyPct, whoopSleepEfficiencyPct, whoopSleepDebtMinutesDouble?, Double?, Int?WhoopSleep need components live on SleepRecord
whoopRecoveryIsCalibratingBool?WhoopOptional so an existing store migrates; a calibrating score is rendered with a marker, never compared
extrasDataData?HealthJSON [String: Double] keyed by HealthMetric.rawValue: the long tail of Health metrics with no column of their own
sourcesDataData?Health, Whoop, Fitbit, Quick logJSON [String: String]: who wrote each value, read by the arbiter
updatedAtDateMetricsStoreDrives field-level last-write-wins
syncedAtDate?reservednil means never pushed. Health rows are not pushed today; see Chapter 20

Two design points deserve a closer look. The first is why the named columns stopped growing. Height and max heart rate are absent on purpose because they are constants, and a column restating the same value on every row is noise. Everything else Apple Health can supply lands in the extras bag, added by one enum case and one mapping, because most people have no data for most of it and a schema change per metric for fields nothing queries is the wrong trade.

// LifeOSKit/Sources/Persistence/DailyMetrics.swift
public func setExtra(_ key: String, _ value: Double?) {
    var bag = extras
    if let value { bag[key] = value } else { bag.removeValue(forKey: key) }
    extras = bag
}

Writing nil removes the key rather than storing a zero. The bag keeps the distinction the whole model is built on: a key that is missing means no reading, and nothing ever writes a zero to stand in for one. The getter returns an empty dictionary rather than throwing when the bytes cannot be read, because a day whose extras are unreadable still has its named columns, and losing the screen over the tail would be the worse failure.

The second is provenance. sourcesData is a parallel bag rather than a field folded into extras, because that bag is numbers and a source is a name. It stores a raw string rather than a typed MetricSource because Persistence sits below Integrations and must not import it; the vocabulary lives up there. A store written before provenance existed reads back no attribution, which MetricArbiter treats as rank zero for everything except the two typed metrics, weight and water, where an unattributed value is read as typed so that the next Health sync cannot silently replace a figure a person entered by hand.

21.3UserGoals, goal evaluation and anomalies

UserGoals is a singleton by convention: exactly one row, created with defaults on first access by MetricsStore.goals().

PropertyTypeDefaultUsed by
stepsGoalInt8,000Dot grid, Dry Run ceiling
sleepMinutesGoalInt420Dot grid, Dry Run ceiling
exerciseMinutesGoalInt30Dot grid, Dry Run ceiling
waterMLGoalDouble2,500Dot grid, Dry Run ceiling
requiredCountInt3How many of the four make a good day
trainingGoalString?nilWorkout library planner
equipmentRaw[String][]Workout library filter
sessionMinutesInt?nilWorkout library planner

The last three were added on 14 September 2026 for the workout library, and the middle one is the field that briefly shipped without a default. The row converts to GoalTargets, a plain Sendable struct, before it reaches any scorer or view model.

Evaluation

// LifeOSKit/Sources/Persistence/GoalEvaluation.swift
public func evaluate(_ reading: DayReading, against targets: GoalTargets) -> DayStatus {
    guard reading.hasAnyData else { return .noData }
    var met = 0
    if let steps = reading.steps, steps >= targets.steps { met += 1 }
    if let sleep = reading.sleepMinutes, sleep >= targets.sleepMinutes { met += 1 }
    if let exercise = reading.exerciseMinutes, exercise >= targets.exerciseMinutes { met += 1 }
    if let water = reading.waterML, water >= targets.waterML { met += 1 }
    return met >= targets.requiredCount ? .onTarget : .missed
}

A day with no metrics at all is .noData, excluded from judgement, because leaving the watch on the charger is not a failure. A day with some data is judged on what it has, so an unlogged metric cannot launder a bad day into a blank one. Exactly meeting a goal counts, since the comparison is greater-or-equal. currentStreak expects statuses most-recent-first, treats .noData as transparent, counts .onTarget, and stops at the first .missed.

Anomalies

AnomalyEvaluation flags one vital sitting outside its own recent range. The baseline needs at least seven actual readings (minimumBaselineDays) or there is no verdict, which is the app-wide rule that absence of data is never a judgement. Thresholds are relative for metrics that scale with the person (heart rate) and absolute for metrics with a physiological unit (a degree of skin temperature means the same at any baseline). The wording rule for anything rendered from an AnomalyFinding is descriptive, never diagnostic: "well above your baseline" is a fact, "see a doctor" is a claim the data cannot support.

21.4Source records and the raw archive

WorkoutRecord and SleepRecord hold data that is genuinely not daily. They roll up into DailyMetrics, which is derived state and always safe to recompute from them.

ModelKeyFields worth knowing
WorkoutRecordexternalID (provider id or the recorder's UUID)start, durationMinutes, activityName, energyKcal, strain, averageHR, maxHR, distanceMeters, altitude gain and change, percentRecorded, sportID, six optional zone-minute columns, setsData (reps per set as JSON), split and videoID for sessions that followed a catalog video
SleepRecordexternalIDstart, end, attributedDate (the morning you woke), performance, consistency and efficiency percentages, light, REM, SWS, awake and no-data minutes, cycle count, respiratory rate, sleep need, debt, need from strain, need from nap (negative or zero), disturbance count, isNap: Bool?
WhoopRawRecord#Unique([\.kind, \.externalID])kind is a String, not an enum, so a collection never seen lands as data; payload, receivedAt

Three small decisions on WorkoutRecord show the rules at work. Six zone columns rather than one array, because SwiftData stores scalars cleanly and an array attribute would be a migration this does not need. percentRecorded kept, because a workout at 40 percent recorded is not a workout with a low strain, and collapsing the two would be the false zero the app refuses. setsData as JSON with empty sets stored as nil, so an existing store migrates without a plan and a session with no sets is not a session with an empty list.

WhoopArchive is the reader and writer of the raw archive. It upserts on (kind, externalID) because a re-sync returns records already seen, and it has a batched store(_:) that saves once per page, because a save per record turns a fourteen-day sync into hundreds of disk transactions on the main actor. FitbitSync reuses the same archive under fitbit- kinds, since it was already a generic raw-record store and only its name is Whoop-specific. The archive is why a derivation bug six months out is fixable without asking a rate-limited API for the data again.

21.5Money

Four models and three value types. The one sentence to remember is written into the type: positive is money in, negative is money out. Plaid is the opposite, its amount is positive for outflows, and the ingestion layer negates on the way in. A silent sign flip turns income into expenses and every rollup lies, which is why the convention is a doc comment on the class rather than a note in a spec.

ModelFieldsInvariant
MoneyEntryid, externalID (Plaid transaction_id), sourceRaw, date, amount, currencyCode, merchant, category, categoryCode, merchantID, logoURL, accountID, accountName, pending, timestampsdate is start of day; externalID is the upsert key; categoryCode keys arithmetic and category is display text only
MoneyAccountexternalID, name, type, subtype, mask, availableBalance, creditLimit, currentBalance, currencyCodecredit and loan types contribute -abs(balance) to net worth; creditLimit is never defaulted to zero because utilisation against zero computes to 100 percent and means nothing
SpendBucketname, monthlyLimit, claimedRaw, sortOrderlimit is positive; a claim key is held by at most one bucket, enforced on write

The spending predicate is one property so that the category list always sums to the figure above it:

// LifeOSKit/Sources/Persistence/MoneyEntry.swift
public var isSpending: Bool {
    amount < 0 && !pending && !MoneyCategoryRule.isTransferLike(categoryCode)
}

MoneyCategoryRule.isTransferLike keeps transfers between your own accounts and credit card payments out of both income and expenses: they appear as a real debit and a real credit, so counting them leaves net correct while overstating both sides, and the savings rate is computed from those two. It matches the underscore-delimited prefix (TRANSFER_IN_, TRANSFER_OUT_) rather than a bare prefix, because without the underscore a code that merely starts with the same letters would be excluded as if it were a transfer.

MoneySummary.savingsRate is nil when income is zero. Undefined is not zero, and this is the sharpest case of the app's central rule. MoneyParts splits an amount for display and rounds to the cent before splitting, because splitting a Double first lets a fraction of .995 round up to 100 cents and render as $19.100. It lives in the kit, where it is tested, rather than in a view where it is eyeballed. MoneyEntry.claimKey is categoryCode ?? category: Plaid's raw detailed code when there is one, else a manual entry's free-form category.

21.6Plan entries and habit ticks

PlanEntry is one model carrying five kinds: goal, habit, note, content and journal. A block renderer can lay out any entry without knowing which feature produced it, and a new kind is an enum case rather than a table. PlanStatus is todo, inProgress, done, blocked or scheduled, and both enums are stored raw so an unknown value reads as .note and .todo.

HabitTick is one completion of a habit on one day, separate from the entry because a habit's history is a set of days rather than a field, and because it lets the existing dot grid render a habit exactly like the Today grid. PlanItemSnapshot is the detached form, with fraction derived from progressValue and progressTarget and clamped to 0...1.

The plan tab's goals and journal entries were migrated onto note pages on 27 and 28 August 2026. PlanNoteMigration runs once, idempotent through NoteDocument.originPlanEntryID rather than a flag, so a second device does not produce a second copy of everything the first one migrated. The rows it deliberately leaves behind still score months that were already closed, which is why NoteEvidence returns both.

21.7Calendar events and chat messages

CalendarEvent is a cache of provider events, never the source of truth for them. The natural key is (source, sourceID), and sourceID is EventKit's identifier qualified with the occurrence start for recurring rows, because EventKit reuses one identifier across a series. CalendarEventSnapshot is the value form, and being Sendable is the point: a tool result crosses into an engine, and a @Model cannot make that trip. CalendarEventDraft is what a caller supplies to create or edit, with no id and no source, because routing decides those. CalendarDayIndex.group indexes overlapping events onto every visible day with an exclusive end date.

ChatMessage persists a conversation locally only. It carries toolSummaries, rendered as activity chips, and eventIDsData, the ids of the events a reply was about. Ids rather than the events, on purpose: an event can be moved or deleted after the sentence about it was written, and a card showing what was true last Tuesday is worse than no card. They are re-resolved against the calendar when the conversation reopens through CalendarStore.events(withIDs:), so a deleted event simply stops appearing. ChatStore.append takes an at date for tests, because appends in a tight loop share a wall-clock timestamp and the recency ordering must not be flaky over ties.

21.8Notes

Notes are the largest model family and the only one synced to Supabase. Four persisted models, two derived, and a set of value types.

ModelRoleFields worth knowing
NoteFolderA folder on one of the PARA shelvesname, icon, bucketRaw, accentRaw, parentID (nests arbitrarily), sortOrder, syncedAt, deletedAt (a tombstone, so a folder removed on one device disappears on the other)
NoteDocumentOne page: note, journal entry or task listtitle, icon, kindRaw, bucketRaw, accentRaw, folderID, blocksData, drawingData (a PKDrawing), entryDate, dueDate, statusRaw (reuses PlanStatus), isFavorite, openedAt, archivedAt, filedAt, syncedAt, deletedAt, originPlanEntryID
NoteTaskDerived: one to-do block hoisted out of its pageid is the block's own id; scoped by documentID; text, isChecked, indent, dueDate, goalID, sortOrder, documentUpdatedAt (denormalised so a cross-page list can order pages)
NoteLinkDerived: one [[wiki link]] edgesourceID, targetTitleFolded (lowercased), targetID (nil when the page does not exist yet; non-nil is not proof it still does)

Two fields on NoteDocument carry whole features. The Inbox is filedAt and nothing else: every page has a bucket from the moment it is created, so a bucket cannot answer "has anyone decided where this goes", and the stamp is written by filing, never by editing, so a page you keep writing in stays in the Inbox until you decide otherwise. The Archive shelf is archivedAt, a flag rather than a bucket, so a restored page returns to the shelf it came from instead of needing to be refiled. Every field carries a default because this model will keep growing and rule two applies.

NoteBlock is a value type with a kind (paragraph, three headings, bulleted, numbered, todo, quote, callout, code, divider, sketch), text, isChecked, indent 0 through 4, optional drawing and sketchHeight for sketch blocks, and optional dueDate and goalID for to-dos. The whole array is stored as JSON. A block editor's trick is that the document is a list of small typed pieces rather than one string with formatting hung off ranges, so splitting, merging and turning a paragraph into a to-do all become list operations, and none of them can corrupt the others. Nesting is purely visual: a nested item is still a sibling in the array.

NoteBlockParser.shortcut resolves Notion-style typed prefixes, and the order of its candidates is the whole correctness argument: - [ ] starts with - , so checking kinds in declaration order would turn every to-do typed by hand into a bullet reading [ ] whatever. Longest match first is the only rule that cannot be broken by adding a kind later. NoteLinkScanner finds [[targets]], preserving case in the text and folding it at lookup. NoteBucket is the four PARA shelves as an enum rather than four folders a person could rename into meaninglessness, with research standing in for PARA's vaguer "resources". NoteAccent is eight named pastels, colour living in the design system so that Persistence never imports SwiftUI and swift test keeps running on macOS.

The value types: NoteCardSnapshot (a page flattened for a card, with doneCount, taskCount, hasInk, linkCount), NoteFolderSnapshot (a sidebar row with its children already attached, built once in the store rather than by the view walking a flat list on every render), NotesSnapshot (everything the sidebar needs in one read), NoteBacklink, NoteStreamChip and NoteStream (a chip resolves to either cards or tasks, because flattening to-dos into cards would lose which page each came from). NoteEvidence is the bridge the monthly close reads: journal dates for the journalling streak, and project statuses where a page with to-do blocks reports what those blocks say rather than its own menu property.

21.9Sectors

LifeSector names the nine sectors: family, romance, soul, friends, growth, money, mission, body, mind. Raw values are written to the store, so a case may be added but never renamed, since a rename orphans every score recorded against it. boardOrder is kept separate from allCases so adding a sector cannot silently reshuffle the grid.

// LifeOSKit/Sources/Persistence/SectorScore.swift
@Model
public final class SectorScore {
    public var sectorRaw: String
    /// Always the first day of the month being scored.
    public private(set) var month: Date
    /// What the rule said, or nil when there was no evidence at all.
    public var proposedScore: Int?
    /// What the person said. Nil until they pass through this sector.
    public var userScore: Int?
    public var closedAt: Date?
    /// The rows behind the proposal, frozen at close time.
    public var evidenceData: Data?
}

Both scores are kept permanently, because the distance between what the rule computed and what the person felt is the most interesting number here, and averaging them would erase it. The evidence is archived rather than recomputed: change a goal in March and February's reasoning must still read the way it did in February. month is private(set) and normalised through Date.startOfMonth on the way in, so closing August on 3 September files the score under 1 August.

CheckInAnswer stores one answer to one question for one sector-month, as text whatever the question's shape, because its value is comparison against last month rather than arithmetic. Evidence is the one shared scoring rule: a weighted mean of EvidenceRows on a 0...10 scale, clamped on the way in rather than trusted, with proposedValue nil when there is nothing to go on. Deliberately not zero: a sector with no evidence has not been judged badly, it has not been judged. proposedScore is expressed in terms of proposedValue so a projection sorting on the unrounded value can never rank against a different number than the one shown.

21.10The workout catalog and bookmarks

CatalogVideoRow is the wire row, snake_case on the server and decoded by the client; CatalogVideo is the cached copy with #Unique([\.youtubeID]), the same ten fields plus cachedAt, a computed thumbnailURL on i.ytimg.com and durationMinutes. The server is the source of truth: CatalogStore.upsert replaces the whole set, updating matches, inserting new rows and deleting absent ones, so a video pulled from the catalog disappears here. It builds its lookup with uniquingKeysWith rather than uniqueKeysWithValues, because a trap on a malformed response is a crash where keeping the last row is not.

WorkoutBookmark is a person's mark on a video: saved, scheduledFor (a calendar day, never a timestamp), or both. One row per video and absent means neither, so BookmarkStore.toggleSaved and schedule both delete a row that ends up neither saved nor scheduled. The store reads row.saved into a local before the delete, because a deleted model is not a thing to ask questions of, even one it answered correctly a line earlier. Bookmarks are local only.

21.11Accounts, scopes and the container

Until 27 August 2026 the app had one store file, no owning column on any model, and one keychain slot. A second person signing in on the same device inherited the first person's notes, journal, chat, money and health data. The server was never the problem, since Row Level Security scopes every row to auth.uid(); the device was.

UserScope is the answer: a struct holding the Supabase user id, with storeURL(base:) under Application Support in a directory named for the account, and defaultsSuiteName for a UserDefaults suite of the account's own. Isolation is by file rather than by an owner column on forty models, because a column means a predicate on every read, and a predicate forgotten once is a leak that looks like working software. A separate file cannot leak: the rows are not there to be read. The defaults suite matters as much as the store: sync cursors, connection tokens and "have they seen the tour" were all in the shared suite, and a second account would have resumed a notes pull from the first account's cursor and silently missed every row written in between. Device preferences (appearance, the assistant's voice, which engine answers) stay in standard on purpose, because they belong to the phone rather than to whoever is signed in on it.

// LifeOSKit/Sources/Persistence/LifeOSContainer.swift
public static let schema = Schema([
    DailyMetrics.self, UserGoals.self, WorkoutRecord.self, SleepRecord.self,
    WhoopRawRecord.self, PlanEntry.self, HabitTick.self,
    MoneyEntry.self, MoneyAccount.self, SpendBucket.self,
    SectorScore.self, CheckInAnswer.self, CalendarEvent.self, ChatMessage.self,
    NoteDocument.self, NoteFolder.self, NoteTask.self, NoteLink.self,
    CatalogVideo.self, WorkoutBookmark.self,
])

Twenty models. LifeOSContainer.make(for:) opens one account's store; make(inMemory:) serves tests and previews. Two adoption paths move a store rather than copy it, which is atomic and costs the same for one note or a thousand: adoptLegacyStore(into:) moves SwiftData's default.store into the first account that signs in after the upgrade, so scoping the store never looks like the app deleting a year of notes, and adopt(_:into:) hands one scope's store to another. Both refuse when the destination already has a store, because choosing which of two rows wins for every model in the schema has no obviously right answer, and both move the -wal and -shm files alongside the database, since moving the database alone leaves the most recent writes behind in a log the new file cannot find.

AccountDeviceAccess records that device permissions are app-wide in iOS but permission to import that device's calendar into an account must also be granted by that account. SampleMetricsPurge deletes every DailyMetrics row once, removing the sixty days of invented history a fresh install used to seed. The seeded values did more than look wrong: most Health fields were fill-gaps-only, so every seeded day refused the real reading for as long as it existed. Only the derived table is removed; workouts, sleep and Whoop records are left and a resync rebuilds the days.

21.12The stores

Every store is a @MainActor value type over a ModelContext, with the calendar injected so tests are not at the mercy of the machine's locale. The pattern is MetricsStore's, and every later store copied it.

StoreReadsWritesThe rule it enforces
MetricsStoremetrics(from:to:) most-recent-first, workouts(on:), workouts(from:to:), sleepRecords(from:to:includingNaps:), goals()upsert(date:apply:), upsertBatch(dates:apply:), upsertSleepRecord, upsertWorkoutRecordOne row per day; a merge, never a replace, so Health and Whoop can write the same row safely. One save per batch.
MoneyStoreentries(from:to:) always bounded, monthEntries(containing:), accounts(), buckets()add, delete, ingest, remove(externalIDs:), upsertAccounts, bucket CRUD, claim, unclaimUpsert on the provider id; one fetch per page instead of one per row, because externalID is unindexed and an initial multi-year pull is thousands of rows on the main actor; a claim key held by one bucket.
PlanStoreentries(kind:), recentTicks, tickedHabitIDs(on:), streak(for:)add, delete, setStatus, toggleTickAt most one tick per entry per day; ticks deleted with their entry.
NotesStoredocuments, folders, cards, recent, favorites, snapshot, search, backlinks, indexedTasks, indexedLinks, inbox, stream(for:), pendingDocuments, pendingFolderscreateFolder, createDocument, capture, journalEntry, update(_:blocks:), rename, icon, accent, status, due date, drawing, move, favourite, markOpened, archive, delete, markSyncedEvery write reindexes in the same transaction; deletes are tombstones; markSynced never touches updatedAt, so an edit made mid-flight stays dirty.
CalendarStoreevents(from:to:) half-open, events(withIDs:), snapshot(id:), freeSlotsapply(_:window:authoritative:)Reconciles one provider fetch: match on (source, sourceID), keep the local id, delete rows absent from the fetch only for sources actually fetched this pass.
SectorStorescores(forMonth:), score(_:month:), history, scoredCounts(before:), answersrecord, commit(userScore:to:), saveAnswerA decided sector is never rewritten: record returns it untouched and commit refuses a second decision.
ChatStorerecent(conversationID:limit:) oldest first, latestConversationIDappendLocal only. Chat history never leaves the device.
CatalogStore, BookmarkStoreall, bookmark(for:), scheduled(on:)upsert, toggleSaved, scheduleThe catalog is replaced whole; an empty bookmark row is deleted.

MoneyIngesting is the write side of MoneyStore as a protocol, so PlaidSync can be tested against a store that fails on demand. Failure is the interesting case: the cursor must not move when the ingest did not happen. CalendarStore.freeSlots has a nonisolated static pure core that merges busy intervals, subtracts them from the window and drops gaps shorter than the requested duration; all-day events do not block time, because "Anniversary" is context, not a meeting.

Three one-time migrations sit beside the stores. PlanNoteMigration is described above. NoteIndexMigration stamps every page that predates the Inbox as filed, then builds the index, idempotent through a marker in the account's own defaults suite; the marker is only spent when there was history to interpret, because on a fresh install the first launch runs before the first pull and consuming the one-shot then would strand every page that arrives afterwards in the Inbox. NoteIndexer is the only writer of NoteTask and NoteLink. It deletes and reinserts rather than diffing, never saves on its own because it runs inside the transaction already changing the document, and fetches rows to delete rather than using the batch delete(model:where:), because the batch form runs against the persistent store and cannot see rows inserted earlier in the same unsaved transaction. rebuildAll is the opposite: the batch form is correct there because everything is cleared before anything is inserted. It builds the folded title index once for the whole pass, since building it per document made a rebuild quadratic in the size of the library.

21.13Adding a field without breaking installed stores

On 15 September 2026 the goals row gained equipmentRaw: [String], mandatory and with no default. SwiftData refused to migrate any store written before it. The container never opened, the shell had no account to show, and the app sat on the signed-in spinner. The error, when it surfaces at all, reads "Validation error missing attribute values on mandatory destination attribute". The fix was one character group, = [], and a test that holds the added columns to the rule:

// LifeOSKit/Tests/PersistenceTests/SchemaMigrationTests.swift
@Test func fieldsAddedToTheGoalsRowHaveDefaults() throws {
    let goals = try #require(LifeOSContainer.schema.entities.first { $0.name == "UserGoals" })
    let added = ["trainingGoal", "equipmentRaw", "sessionMinutes"]
    for name in added {
        let attribute = try #require(goals.attributesByName[name], "missing \(name)")
        #expect(attribute.isOptional || attribute.defaultValue != nil,
                "\(name) has no default and is not optional")
    }
}

The rule, and how the models already follow it: whoopRecoveryIsCalibrating: Bool? and SleepRecord.isNap: Bool? are optional rather than defaulted Bools; ChatMessage.eventIDsData: Data? and WorkoutRecord.setsData: Data? are optional JSON; every field on NoteDocument and NoteFolder carries an initial value. When you add a field to a model that has rows on somebody's phone, make it optional or give it a default, and add its name to the list in that test.

Why the app hangs instead of crashingAccountSession opens the container for the current account after the session is restored. A container that throws leaves the session without a store, and the shell renders its waiting state until one arrives. Nothing is wrong with the shell; the failure is a step earlier, which is why the symptom looks like a network problem and is not.

21.14Study notes

Read in this order

  1. LifeOSKit/Sources/Persistence/DailyMetrics.swift, for the rule and the two bags.
  2. MetricsStore.swift, for the upsert-as-merge pattern every store copies.
  3. GoalEvaluation.swift and Streak.swift, the shortest pure logic in the app.
  4. MoneyEntry.swift, for a type that carries its own sign convention.
  5. NoteDocument.swift then NoteBlock.swift, for JSON-in-a-column and the parser order argument.
  6. NoteIndexer.swift, for the fetch-versus-batch-delete distinction.
  7. UserScope.swift and LifeOSContainer.swift, for per-account stores and the two adoption moves.
  8. Tests/PersistenceTests/SchemaMigrationTests.swift, then add a field to a model in a scratch branch and watch it fail.

Check yourself

  • Why is savingsRate nil rather than zero when there is no income? Because undefined is not zero; rendering 0 percent would be a confident wrong number.
  • What breaks if NoteIndexer.reindex used context.delete(model:where:)? A second reindex in the same unsaved transaction would duplicate rows, because the batch delete cannot see rows inserted earlier in that transaction.
  • Why is LifeSector a case you may add but never rename? Raw values are stored; a rename orphans every score already recorded against it.
  • Why does the store move -wal and -shm with the database? SQLite keeps the most recent writes in the write-ahead log; moving the database alone leaves them in a file the new location cannot find.
  • How does the Inbox know a page is unfiled? filedAt is nil. Buckets cannot answer, because every page has one from creation.
  • Why does MoneyStore.ingest fetch all ids up front? externalID is unindexed and this runs on the main actor; one scan per page instead of one per row.

Chapter twenty-two

22Production edge cases

The register below is the difference between a demo and something you can rely on. Each row is a condition that will occur in normal use, not a theoretical one, and each names where in the code or the test suite the behaviour is pinned. The feature chapters cross-reference the rows that apply to them.

22.1How to read this register

Three columns. Condition is what happens in the world. Behaviour is what the app does about it, in the present tense, because every row here describes code on disk today. Pinned by names the test, native check or pure function that holds the behaviour in place, so that a future edit which changes it fails somewhere visible. A row marked by design has no test because the behaviour is structural: a type that cannot cross a boundary, a table with no policies. A row marked hardware is unverified in the simulator and waits on a physical device; those are listed again in Appendix A.

Two themes recur. The first is the rule from 21.1: absence is never zero, and a screen with no data shows its designed empty state rather than a number nobody earned. The second is that destructive outcomes, signing someone out, moving a sync cursor, replacing a cache, happen only on a definitive answer from the server and never on a transport failure, a rate limit or an empty response that is more likely a bug than a fact.

22.2Time and calendars

ConditionBehaviourPinned by
Sleep spans midnightAttributed to the morning you woke, through SleepRecord.attributedDate. A nap is stored with isNap and excluded from night-by-night viewsWhoopTests, WhoopSleepMath
A Whoop cycle boundary is not a calendar dayCycles are attributed to the day the cycle starts, sleep to the day it ends. Documented so the mismatch is not read as a bugWhoopDerivation
Travel across time zones"Today" follows the device's current zone; a day can be shortened or lengthened. The nudge job counts windows back from the user's local day, not UTC midnight, and a device token without a usable zone never sendsnudge_test.ts; device_tokens.timezone not null
DST transitionCalendar.startOfDay handles the 23 or 25 hour day; nothing computes days by adding 86,400 secondsby design
Month boundaries on the gridLeading blanks computed from firstWeekday; padded to whole rowsMonthGridLayoutTests
A month is scored on the third of the next monthFiled under the first of the month scored, through Date.startOfMonth, which is enforced on SectorScore.month as private(set)SectorScoreTests, SectorStoreTests
The planner names a weekday in its reasonWeekday symbols are read through an en_US_POSIX copy of the calendar, because a host calendar with an empty locale returns abbreviationsWorkoutPlannerTests
The clock moves backwardsA future last-sync is treated as stale and the sync runs; a session keep-alive delay never drops below five seconds, so a jumped clock cannot spin against the auth endpointSyncStalenessPolicyTests, SessionKeepAliveTests
First open of the morning, last sync at 23:50The day boundary triggers a sync regardless of staleness, because the night's sleep is new information a minutes-old sync knows nothing aboutSyncStalenessPolicyTests
Device clock skew against the serverCan let a stale local write win a field-level merge. Accepted and documented; the server's touch trigger stops a client advancing updated_at past the server's clock on synced tablesknown limitation; touch_updated_at()

22.3Apple Health

ConditionBehaviourPinned by
Read access deniedUndetectable by design: HealthKit reports only whether it asked, since revealing a refusal would leak that the user has no data of that type. The reader queries anyway, an empty result renders the empty state, and the settings row links out to Health rather than claiming a connection stateHealthKitReader doc; HealthKitError.authorisationRefused is only for the write request
iPhone and Watch both count stepsDe-duplicated by HKStatisticsCollectionQuery. Raw samples are never summedby design
Health corrects a sample after it was readObserver queries fire on change rather than a timer polling; the sync window always re-reads today and the day of the last sync, because a night's sleep lands on the morning it endsHealthSyncWindowTests
Thirty-one days of history missingThe window never goes further back than thirty days, the month the dot grid shows. Health keeps the data, so a longer backfill can be added when something needs itHealthSyncWindow.maximumDays
Health and Whoop write the same dayMetricsStore.upsert merges; each source touches its own columns and MetricArbiter decides contested ones by rankMetricArbiterTests, HealthApplyTests
Health sends a value for a metric a person typedManual rank 4 beats every automatic source; a value with no recorded source for weight or water is read as typed, so the upgrade to provenance cannot let a sync replace a hand-entered figureMetricArbiterTests, MetricSource.legacy(for:)
Same source syncs again with a corrected valueEqual rank wins, because greater-or-equal is the comparison; a source may correct itselfMetricArbiterTests
Weight recorded in poundsRead through HKUnit conversion, stored in kilogramsby design
Cycle trackingAsked as a second, separate prompt, defaulted from Health's own sex characteristic, offered either wayHealthKitReader.requestCycleAuthorization
Simulator has no health dataExpected. The design preview fixtures and the checks harness drive every screen without HealthHealthActivityDesignPreview
Seeded sample history on an old installSampleMetricsPurge deletes every daily row once; workouts, sleep and Whoop records rebuild them on resync. Typed water and weight from before the purge are lost, and this is stated in the type's doc comment rather than hiddenSampleMetricsPurge

22.4Whoop

22.17Study notes

Read in this order

  1. LifeOSKit/Sources/Integrations/SessionRefresh.swift, the clearest statement of "destroy only on a definitive refusal".
  2. SyncStalenessPolicy.swift and SessionKeepAlive.swift, two pure clocks.
  3. MetricArbiter.swift and MetricSource.swift, then the tests beside them.
  4. PlaidSync.swift, for store-then-move-cursor.
  5. supabase/functions/lifo-agent/index.ts, for every failure path a cloud call has.
  6. supabase/functions/_shared/nudge.ts and apns.ts, for the fallback and collapse rules.
  7. LIfeOS/Features/Activity/ViewModel/ActivityRecorderChecks.swift, the native checks that stand in for tests.
  8. docs/design/watch-companion/report.md, for what is still unverified.

Check yourself

  • Which HTTP statuses sign a person out, and why not 429? 400, 401, 403 and 422 are the server refusing the credential; 429 and 5xx are the server failing to answer.
  • Why does the Plaid cursor live in UserDefaults and not the Keychain? The Keychain survives a reinstall and the database does not; a surviving cursor would replay nothing into an empty app.
  • What happens to an empty catalog response? The cache is kept; an empty answer is believed only when there was nothing to lose.
  • Why is a refused model reply still debited? It consumed real tokens; an unmetered path would let off-topic questions burn budget for free.
  • How can two cron runs not double-send? The log insert precedes the send and the primary key makes the second insert conflict.
  • What does a watch hand-off do when Health saving is off? It is never offered; the watch writes to Health, so the phone keeps the session.

Chapter twenty-three

23Operations

How to build the app from a clean machine, what has to exist on the server side before it signs anyone in, how a build reaches TestFlight, and how the code is kept honest: 1,298 package tests, 100 Deno tests, 7 catalog tests, a native checks harness, a typography guard and a way of working that survives six sessions editing one checkout.

23.1Setup runbook

1 · Local build

git clone https://github.com/shivvyas2/LifeOS.git
cd LifeOS
cp Config/Secrets.example.xcconfig Config/Secrets.xcconfig
swift test --package-path LifeOSKit      # no simulator needed
open LIfeOS.xcodeproj

The package declares an iOS 26 platform and also builds for macOS purely so that swift test runs from the terminal. The Xcode project holds four targets: LIfeOS (the phone and iPad app, still spelled with the capital I because renaming a target churns the project file for no user-visible gain), AlmanacWatch, AlmanacWatchWidgets and AlmanacWidgets. The display name under the icon is Almanac; the bundle id is com.shivvyas.lifeos; the team is Z42YU5W6WY. The app's folders under LIfeOS/ are picked up automatically, as described in Chapter 2.

A missing Secrets.xcconfig does not fail the buildxcconfig substitution of a missing variable yields an empty string. A clean checkout builds, archives and launches, then shows a sign-in screen that can never sign anyone in. Confirm the file exists and is populated before archiving on any machine that is not the usual one.

2 · Supabase

supabase link --project-ref <ref>
supabase db push                          # 18 migrations: schema, RLS, functions, seed
supabase config push                      # auth: email OTP via Resend, SMS, Apple, templates
supabase secrets set \
  OPENAI_API_KEY=... \
  WHOOP_CLIENT_ID=... WHOOP_CLIENT_SECRET=... \
  FITBIT_CLIENT_ID=... FITBIT_CLIENT_SECRET=... \
  PLAID_CLIENT_ID=... PLAID_SECRET=... PLAID_ENV=sandbox \
  PLAID_REDIRECT_URI=https://almanac.shivvyas.com/plaid-oauth \
  TWILIO_ACCOUNT_SID=... TWILIO_AUTH_TOKEN=... TWILIO_VERIFY_SERVICE_SID=... \
  OTP_PEPPER=... \
  APNS_KEY_ID=... APNS_TEAM_ID=Z42YU5W6WY APNS_BUNDLE_ID=com.shivvyas.lifeos \
  APNS_KEY="$(cat AuthKey.p8)" APNS_SANDBOX=true
supabase functions deploy

Then put the project URL and anon key into Config/Secrets.xcconfig. Thirteen Edge Functions deploy from supabase/functions/: otp-start, otp-check, whoop-callback, whoop-token, fitbit-token, fitbit-sync, plaid-link-token, plaid-exchange, plaid-sync, plaid-disconnect, lifo-agent, lifo-nudge, and the shared modules under _shared/. Two of them declare verify_jwt = false in config.toml: whoop-callback, because a browser following Whoop's 302 carries no Authorization header and cannot be made to, and whoop-token, which validates the bearer itself with resolveUser before touching account data. Stating it in config rather than passing --no-verify-jwt means a deploy from anywhere gets it right.

Two server-side steps cannot live in a migration. The hourly nudge schedule needs the project's own function URL and the service role key, so supabase/functions/lifo-nudge/schedule.sql is run once from the SQL editor after storing both in Vault. And the auth email templates must be pushed, because Supabase's stock templates send a magic link and the app's sign-in is a six-digit code that has to be typable.

3 · Provider developer accounts

Request every scope listed in WhoopCollection including offlineClient id in the xcconfig; secret in function env

4 · The workout catalog

deno run --allow-net --allow-read --allow-write scripts/catalog/verify.ts \
  --out supabase/migrations/<stamp>_workout_videos_seed.sql
supabase db push

Curation is an edit to scripts/catalog/catalog.json plus a verify run. The script checks every id against YouTube's keyless oEmbed endpoint for title, channel and plausible duration, refuses an empty catalog, and writes a seed whose last statement deletes every row not in the verified list, so a seed run is a full sync. The first seed is a migration Supabase has already recorded and will never re-run, which is why later passes write a new timestamped file with --out. The catalog ships at 122 verified videos.

5 · Device

HealthKit background delivery, the Whoop and Fitbit OAuth round trips, the Plaid universal link, a real HKWorkoutSession, the watch hand-off and push delivery cannot be verified in the simulator. All need a physical device with a signing team, and the watch checks need a paired watch. The list of what is still pending on hardware is in Appendix A.

23.2Secrets

There is no runtime .env on iOS. The app is a signed bundle; anything shipped inside it is extractable. The governing rule is therefore: what must never leak lives server-side.

TierLocationContentsIn git?
1 · Build configConfig/Secrets.xcconfigSupabase URL and anon key, Whoop client id and redirect, Plaid redirect, Fitbit client id and redirect, ElevenLabs keyGitignored. Template committed as Secrets.example.xcconfig
2 · RuntimeKeychain, per account slotSupabase session (access and refresh token), Whoop tokensNever
2b · RuntimeUserDefaults, per account suitePlaid sync cursors, connection state, tour and migration markers, the APNs tokenNever; dies with the app container on purpose
3 · ServerEdge Function environmentSUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY, OPENAI_API_KEY, WHOOP_CLIENT_SECRET, FITBIT_CLIENT_SECRET, PLAID_SECRET, Twilio credentials, OTP_PEPPER, APNS_KEYNever. Never on the device either
3b · DatabaseTables with no client policiesplaid_items.access_token, fitbit_connections tokens, whoop_connections tokens, lifo_usage, otp_eventsReadable only by the service role from inside a function

Nothing in tier 1 is truly secret except the ElevenLabs key. The anon key is designed to ship in clients and is safe precisely because RLS gates every row; the OAuth client ids are public by design. The xcconfig has one trap: // starts a comment, so every URL in it breaks the scheme separator with $() or the value truncates to lifeos:.

service_role is the one that mattersIt bypasses RLS entirely. It belongs only in an Edge Function environment and in Vault for the cron schedule: never in an xcconfig, never in the app target, never in git. Every other secret in this system is recoverable by rotation; this one grants total read and write access to everything, including three tables of plaintext bank and wearable credentials that are an accepted single-user trade and must be encrypted before a second person's data lands in them.

23.3Shipping to TestFlight

Everything the repo can settle is settled: display name, bundle id, team, iOS 26 floor, export compliance declared exempt. The parts that need an Apple ID are in docs/handbook/testflight-release.md; the two that bite are here.

Bump the build number first, and commit it. App Store Connect rejects a (version, build) pair it has already seen, and it rejects it after the upload finishes. CURRENT_PROJECT_VERSION is 17 today, in both Debug and Release; raise it for every upload, even a re-upload, and a rejected upload still burns the number. Through build 15 the number in git never moved off 1 because each archive was made from an uncommitted edit, so nothing in the repository could answer what was uploaded last. Committing it is what made the guess go away.

Then: destination Any iOS Device, Product → Archive, Distribute App → TestFlight, accept automatic signing (the Apple Distribution identity, not the Apple Development one a local archive uses). Internal testers get the build with no review. Two warnings are not failures: the missing dSYM for LinkKit.framework is Plaid shipping no debug symbols in any slice, and must not be silenced by stripping the app's own symbols; and the first Live Activity request on a fresh install raises the system's own consent alert.

The app icon is rendered from docs/brand/lifeos-icon.svg with headless Chrome at 1024 pixels. The original artwork clipped to a squircle and left the corners transparent; iOS applies its own mask and rejects an icon with an alpha channel at validation, so the shipping SVG lets the gradient run to the edges. Check hasAlpha reads no with sips before committing.

23.4Testing strategy

Logic that can be tested without a simulator lives in the package and is developed test-first. Feature view models are exercised through the native checks harness against the real store, because the Xcode project still has no test target. SwiftUI view bodies are verified by design-preview captures and a build, because asserting on view structure is ceremony that breaks on every layout change without catching real defects.

The counts below are from runs on 15 September 2026, on this machine, against the tip of main:

$ cd scripts/catalog && deno test --allow-all 2>&1 | tail -2

The one test that matters mostFor every screen, an empty store must produce a snapshot whose readings are all nil. It is a four-line test per feature and it is the regression guard against the single worst bug this app can have: a confident zero where there is no data.

Two habits keep the suite useful. Assertions are written so they cannot pass for the wrong reason: the Plaid cursor tests were rewritten so the "cursor did not move" assertion fails on an empty store, and the money tests dropped a stale comment that described a case they did not cover. And when a check fails during a slice, the rule is fix the cause, never the check: the strength-session check that regressed "Repeated save creates one workout" was fixed by deleting the row it left in the shared context, not by relaxing the assertion.

23.5The design preview and native checks harness

Since 14 September 2026 the app has a DEBUG-only launch argument, --design-preview, that mounts a fixture instead of the signed-in shell. It exists because the recorder, the sensors and the Live Activity cannot be reached by swift test, and because every design QA capture needs the same screen in the same state on every run, with no account loaded.

ArgumentEffect
--page=galleryThe default: a gallery of surfaces
--page=activityBegin Activity over HealthActivityFixture, a fixed WHOOP recovery of 82 percent and a live reading of 152 bpm
--page=player --video=<id>The video player on one catalog id, used for the embed spot-check
--page=checksRuns ActivityRecorderChecks and prints one PASS or FAIL line per check to the console
--page=inbox, --page=settingsThe notification inbox and the settings screen
--live, --strength, --dark, --live-activity, --hud-collapsed, --hud-expandedDrive the in-session fixture: a running session, a strength activity with reps, dark mode, a real Live Activity request, the rings folded to a bar

The checks are the recorder's test suite. Each is a named closure that builds a recorder over an in-memory store with injected answers for Health authorization, the watch bridge and the age, drives it, and asserts. They cover the paths a unit test cannot: a timer starting without Health access, paused readings accruing nothing, a draft restoring after relaunch, a second account being unable to see the first's draft, a watch that never answers, a packet with an unknown version. The rule that applies to them is the same as for tests: fix the cause, never the check.

23.6Driving the simulator from the terminal

idb is not installed and simctl cannot tap, so UI automation goes through clicks at absolute screen coordinates with cliclick, and only while the Simulator is frontmost. The recipe that works, run before every click:

osascript -e 'tell application "System Events" to set frontmost of process "Simulator" to true'
sleep 1
cliclick -w 150 c:X,Y

Coordinates come from the Simulator's own geometry: the device screen is drawn into the first AXGroup of the window, so read its position and size through System Events and scale a pixel measured on the full-resolution screenshot (1206 by 2622 for an iPhone 17) into it. Re-read the group after every boot or window move, because the origin changes. Screenshot after every tap rather than firing three and checking at the end, since a tap during a transition is swallowed. The simulator keychain survives simctl uninstall, so a reinstall skips onboarding; xcrun simctl keychain <sim> reset clears it while the device is booted. Never tap within a hundred pixels of a Plaid entry point without a screenshot confirming what is under the point: on 1 September 2026 a mapped tap landed seventy pixels high, opened Plaid Link and sent a real login code. Build destinations must be iOS 26 runtimes; check xcodebuild -showdestinations, not simctl list devices.

23.7Working in parallel

Five or six sessions routinely run against the one checkout at /Users/shivvyas/LIfeOS, switching branches and pushing under each other, so HEAD in the shared checkout can move mid-task. The conventions that make this survivable:

  • Never commit to main. A branch per logical change: feat/, fix/, docs/, chore/. Branches are reviewed and merged by hand; unrelated changes mixed into one commit or dumped on main make that impossible.
  • Conventional commits. type(scope): imperative summary with a short body explaining what and why, matching the history. No em dashes anywhere in a message, and no attribution trailers.
  • A private worktree for any multi-commit task. git worktree add .claude/worktrees/<name>, then copy the untracked Config/Secrets.xcconfig in, because the app will not sign in without it. Never under a temporary directory that a tool may clear mid-task. Re-read origin/main immediately before every push.
  • Each slice leaves a paper trail. A spec under docs/superpowers/specs/, a plan under docs/superpowers/plans/, and a QA report under docs/design/<slice>/report.md with the captures beside it. The report records every deviation from the plan and every check still pending on hardware.

23.8Guards that run without a test

scripts/check-typography.sh greps the app and package sources for any font declared outside LifeOSType: a literal point size, a UIKit systemFont(ofSize:), a rounded or serif design, or one of Apple's semantic text styles. The app once carried 376 hand-written font calls across 28 sizes because nothing stopped a screen inventing its own. Adding a step is a deliberate edit to Typography.swift, not something that happens by accident on a Tuesday. It exits non-zero on any hit.

The schema test in 21.13 is the other guard worth knowing by name. When you add a field to an existing model, add its name to the list there; the test reads the schema itself rather than the source, so it catches a default removed by a refactor as well as one never written.

23.9Study notes

Read in this order

  1. Config/Secrets.example.xcconfig, every key annotated with where its real secret lives.
  2. supabase/config.toml, the auth and function blocks.
  3. docs/handbook/testflight-release.md.
  4. LIfeOS/App/LIfeOSApp.swift and App/Surfaces/SurfaceDesignPreview.swift, for how --design-preview takes over the scene.
  5. LIfeOS/Features/Activity/ViewModel/ActivityRecorderChecks.swift.
  6. scripts/check-typography.sh and scripts/catalog/verify.ts.
  7. LifeOSKit/Package.swift, for the eight targets and their dependency edges.

Check yourself

  • Why does a clean checkout build without secrets? xcconfig substitution of a missing variable is an empty string, not an error.
  • Why does whoop-callback skip JWT verification? A browser following Whoop's redirect carries no bearer; the function holds no secret and only redirects into an app that checks PKCE and state itself.
  • What must happen before every TestFlight upload? Raise CURRENT_PROJECT_VERSION in both configurations and commit it.
  • Where do the recorder's tests run? On a simulator, through --design-preview --page=checks, because they need HealthKit, Bluetooth and ActivityKit.
  • Why a worktree under .claude/worktrees and not a temporary directory? A temporary directory can be cleared mid-task; the worktrees directory persists and is where every other session puts its own.

Chapter twenty-four

24Cost and the allowance

Almanac ships free, so every user costs money and none of them pay it. That single fact caps the architecture. This chapter says where the money goes, which lines are metered by a constraint in the database rather than by good intentions, and what the app costs to run today.

24.1The ceiling

Total running cost must stay under roughly two dollars per user per calendar month, covering cloud inference, speech, bank data, the database, and notifications. There is no revenue per user, so this comes out of pocket and unit economics decide what can be built. The number was fixed on 25 August 2026 and nothing since has moved it.

The requirement is that spending cannot exceed the allowance, not that it usually does not. Those are different engineering problems, and only the first survives concurrency and a looping client. So the lines that scale with use (cloud tokens) are capped in Postgres, the lines that scale with connections (Plaid) are bounded by a count the person controls, and the lines that scale with nothing (Supabase, APNs, Vercel, YouTube) are on free tiers whose limits are named below.

The allowance is internal Users are never shown a balance, a meter, a percentage, or a dollar figure. It exists to bound what the app costs to run, not to be a feature. The only moment it becomes visible is when it runs out, and then it is one sentence: exhausted comes back as a 429 from lifo-agent, and Chapter 14 shows how the coach screen turns that into words.

24.2Where the money goes

Every line below is either metered, bounded, or free. Nothing in the app calls a paid service without one of the three applying.

LineProviderScales withHow it is boundedWhat leaves the device
Coach chat, answers, sector notesOpenAI gpt-5-mini through lifo-agentTurns per user150,000 tokens per user per day, kind chatThe off-device render of ContextBundle: derived numbers, never raw series
Morning nudgeOpenAI gpt-5-mini through lifo-nudgeOne send per user per day4,000 tokens per user per day, kind nudge; a fallback sentence when spentThe trigger's few figures; about 300 tokens in, 60 out
Speech in (Scribe) and out (Flash v2.5)ElevenLabs, called from the appSpoken turns, characters spokenVoice off by default; replies capped at 1,200 characters; key rotation is the only kill switch todayThe recorded WAV of a question; the text of a reply
Bank syncPlaid, four Edge FunctionsConnected Items per user per monthOne Item per bank; a failed exchange removes the Item so nothing bills for a row that was never storedNothing; transactions come back to the phone and stay there
Sign-in codesResend (email), Twilio Verify (SMS)Sign-insEmail is the default and free; SMS only for US and India numbers, 45 s guard, pumping-prefix limitsAn address or number, hashed with a pepper in otp_events
Database, auth, functions, storageSupabaseRows, function invocations, avatar bytesFree tier; see 24.4 for the limits that would push it overNotes, profile, avatar, friends, messages, shared stats, tokens
